- Published
A bipartisan group of US senators has signed a letter demanding an urgent investigation into reported disruptions to SpaceX's Starlink internet network in Ukraine.
Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and protect its own skies, but on Tuesday night Ukraine said it unexpectedly restricted how fast drones could fly while maintaining internet connection.
In the letter, sent on Thursday to the US Department of Defense inspector general, the senators say they have "grave concern" about reports of speed restrictions between 12 and 14 October.
The White House and Pentagon have not responded to the suggestion the US might have had a role in the alleged slowdown.
The letter, led by Jeanne Shaheen - a Democrat on the Senate's Foreign Relations Committee - calls for the inspector general to find out whether the restrictions were caused by the US defence department or its contractors.
It says "restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine's ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure".
Starlink, which is owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, restricted speed limits on Tuesday night to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.
The senators also say they are "deeply concerned" by reports of disruptions or "glitches" affecting intelligence-sharing and threat-warning capabilities relied upon by personnel operating in Ukraine.
"We are particularly alarmed by incidents in which U.S. diplomatic, military, and security personnel were unable to reach designated bunkers during Russian air raids," the statement says.
"Given the potentially deadly consequences, these incidents require immediate investigation," the senators add.
The letter's signatories include Republican Senators Thom Tillis, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and John Cornyn, alongside Senators Richard Durbin, Jack Reed, Richard Blumenthal and Christopher Coons from the Democrats.
SpaceX owner Elon Musk has suggested the US government may be behind restrictions.
On Wednesday Musk wrote on X that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]".
Starlink is a civilian service that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas. Starshield, which relies on the Starlink network, is designed for government and military use. Both are owned by Musk's SpaceX.
Ukraine's President Zelensky has accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing to pressure Kyiv into ending attacks against Russian energy sites.
On Thursday, Zelensky said Ukraine's attacks would continue after Russia had continued striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure during an "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday.
Zelensky said he had restricted attacks for three days and would agree to the "energy ceasefire" if Moscow also abided by it. However, he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced.
The Kremlin never said it had agreed to the deal and Russia said Kyiv had also tried to hit refineries on Wednesday - which Ukraine denied.
Zelensky has also criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace, struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort.
That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which has sent fuel costs skyrocketing.

- Published
A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window at a hotel in Cyprus has been fined â¬3,000 (Â£2,500) for causing his death.
Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him, Paphos District Court previously heard.
The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas.
Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced on Friday morning.
He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter."
The judge described the incident as a "fatal and tragic momentary error", while Foster's lawyer Alexandros Alexandrou argued the case should have "never gone to court".
"Within this three months, there was a lost opportunity for this man to grieve as he wanted to, to be with his family," Alexandrou said.
Foster, an auditor, arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident with his wife, two children and in-laws.
They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening.
At about 18:00, Foster, his father-in-law and son walked towards an elevator and was playing with his son, Alexandrou said.
The court was told as they approached the lift, the boy noticed a waterpark outside.
It was said Foster pushed the lift button, placed the child on the windowsill and the "inconceivable" unfolded before he could react.
"The window did not appear to carry markings that would necessarily have alerted the defendant to the fact that one section was open," said District Judge Froso Christodoulidou.
She added there was no evidence to suggest Foster had sufficient time to examine the condition of the window before the fall.
Christodoulidou added no sentence could outweigh the "personal consequences of the loss of his child".
Police were called to reports of a child falling "under unknown circumstances" at about 18:40.
The boy was taken to Paphos General Hospital and later pronounced dead.
In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy "fell before he had a chance to grab him".
While Foster had alcohol in his system, it did not form a significant part of the case against him - and his lawyer said there was no testimony he was drunk.
Alexandrou said Foster was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident and had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened.
The court heard the window was 2.85m (9.3ft) wide and 1.2m (3.9ft) high.
In a statement outside court, Alexandrou described his client as an "incredible father".
"[He is] an exemplary family man with a beautiful family behind him, that support him, that embraces him, that has always been by his side."
Speaking via a translator, Alexandrou said Foster was only now confronting what had happened because the court proceedings were very stressful for him.
He added: "Now that the entire proceeding has finished, now this eruption of emotions from the loss of his child will probably be immediate."

The Scoop
A merger between two Wall Street boutique firm collapsed after senior bankers balked at their retention bonuses.
The deal between advisory firm Perella Weinberg Partners and investment bank Piper Sandler envisioned paying Perellaâs highest producers $2.5 million in shares of the combined company to stay on for as long as three years, according to people familiar with the matter. The rest of its partners were split into tiers and offered bonuses of between $500,000 and $1.5 million.
Perella CEO Andrew Bednar called some partners individually to describe their retention packages and gauge their reaction, the people said. They were almost uniformly negative, with the offers deemed âoffensively low,â in the words of one banker, compared to the millions that top dealmakers at the firm make per year. That opposition led to the talks ultimately falling apart, some of the people said. The Financial Times earlier reported that the deal had collapsed. A spokesperson for Perella did not respond to requests for comment.
Perella Weinberg went public in 2020 and had seen its shares lose half their value since early last year. Bednar had sought a deal with at least one other bank earlier this year, although talks only progressed with Piper, some of the people said.
Rohanâs view
Expect to see a wave of departures from Perella in the coming weeks and months. Recruiters at rival banks are already fielding calls and making their own, Iâm told. Bankers donât want to work at troubled businesses, and seeking a deal signaled just that. Perella, the junior partner in these talks, had been seeking some kind of deal for months before alighting on Piper.
Bankers, especially rainmakers, have healthy egos. Itâs difficult enough to lock them up, but itâs a critical step in talent-driven mergers like this. Failing to do so highlights exactly the risk that companies take when they try to strike deals.

Israeli settlers attack Palestinians in West Bank during olive harvest
The BBC has witnessed Israeli settlers attack Palestinians and set fire to olive trees in the occupied West Bank.
About a dozen settlers dressed in black charged down a hill near an outpost â illegal under international law - to a field where Palestinians and activists were harvesting olives. They torched about a dozen trees and hurled stones from slingshots.
Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was at the scene, was taken to hospital where she told reporters she "got jumped" and described being kicked on the ground.
The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year. It says this year levels of settler violence have reached an all-time high.
The BBC's Middle East Correspondent Lucy Williamson reports.

- Published
The western Canadian province of Alberta will ask its citizens on Monday whether they want to remain part of Canada or kick-start the process of holding a binding referendum on separation.
The vote will mark a major test of the country's unity, the first in decades.
Alberta's leader, Premier Danielle Smith, announced in May that the question on independence would be put to voters, though she herself supports a unified Canada.
There has been a growing separatist sentiment in the oil-rich province in recent years, and the vote comes after 300,000 people signed a petition asking that a referendum be held on the matter.
Here's why some Albertans are calling for independence and what comes next.
What will the referendum question ask?
The question being put to voters won't be a simple "stay" or "leave".
Instead, Albertans will be asked: "Should Alberta remain a province of Canada or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?"
The premier's office clarified to the BBC that voters will have a choice of checking two boxes - option A being to remain in Canada and option B being to start the legal process to hold a binding separation referendum.
There are 10 questions. What about the others?
There are nine other questions that have been put to voters, though they have been overshadowed by the one on independence.
They deal with two main topics: immigration and Constitutional matters.
For the most part, all of them seek to ask Albertans about options to gain more autonomy from Ottawa.
On immigration, voters will be asked whether they want the province to have increased control over immigration, to bring it to "more sustainable levels" and introducing a law requiring people to provide proof of citizenship to vote in an Alberta provincial election.
The rest focus on access to social services like healthcare for non-permanent residents.
The Constitutional questions include one seeking to allow provinces to push for the power to elect provincial judges and for an elected Senate. Senators in Canada are currently appointed by the governor general on the advice of the prime minister.
Why is this happening?
The referendum question is a result of a push by a group of Albertans who have been advocating for the province to be independent from Canada.
Over the past year, they held townhalls across the province to gauge interest from the public. They then launched a citizen-led petition to separate earlier this year, which gathered more than 300,000 signatures.
But the petition was blocked by an Alberta court early this year.
A judge ruled that Alberta, which authorised the gathering of signatures for a proposed independence referendum under a citizen petition law, failed to consult indigenous First Nations whose land would be affected should the province become an independent state.
Meanwhile, another group led by a former deputy premier of Alberta, Thomas Lukaszuk, collected signatures for an anti-separation petition called Forever Canadian. That was signed by more than 400,000 Albertans.
The province's population is slightly more than five million.
Smith said in May that she was "deeply troubled" by the court decision, and will not let "a single judge silence the voices of hundreds of thousands of Albertans".
Her government has appealed against the decision, she said. But in the meantime, "kicking the can down the road only prolongs a very emotional and important debate".
She has also faced pressure from separatist Albertans, some within her own political party, to hold a referendum on independence regardless of the legal decision.
Who are the separatists, and what do they want?
The separatist movement is led by Mitch Sylvestre, a gun shop owner from the town of Bonnyville, and Jeffrey Rath, a lawyer based in Calgary. It has been supported by other figures along the way.
Both Sylvestre and Rath are members of a group called the Alberta Prosperity Project, which argues that the province's economic growth has been hindered by years of Liberal party rule in Ottawa.
In particular, many in the movement are frustrated with environmental policies that they believe have stood in the way of building pipelines and unlocking resources from the oil-rich province, which traditionally leans conservative.
They also believe that Alberta contributes far more to the country than it receives, and that Ottawa has a disproportionate say in its internal matters.
The sentiment is rooted in "western alienation" - a term that has been used for decades to describe the sense by some in Canada's western provinces that they are often overlooked and underrepresented by federal politicians in Canada's capital.
But the movement is not uniform in its demands.
At a separatist townhall last year, some told the BBC that they wanted to use the threat of independence as a bargaining chip with Ottawa, while others said they would like to follow through with a provincial divorce.
A few said they would be open to Alberta joining the US.
Rath has told the BBC that he believes Alberta has more in common culturally with parts of the US than the rest of Canada.
He has also travelled to Washington several times on what he has described as a "fact-finding" mission, where he and other separatists met Trump administration officials to see if the US government would support an independent Alberta with a line of credit.
Rath has not publicly named which Trump officials the group has met.
When will we know the results?
Alberta Elections have their work cut out for them.
All the ballots - a separate colour-coded one for each question - will be counted by hand.
They have 48 hours to complete the count, which starts at 20:00 local time on Monday (03:00 BST Tuesday) and can be delayed if there are voters still in line.

The News
Concerns over the health of former South African President Jacob Zuma have raised questions about the future of uMkhonto weSizwe (MK), the populist party built around him that has redrawn the countryâs political landscape.
The 84-year-old was taken to hospital two weeks ago. Since then, MK officials and the Zuma Foundation have circulated conflicting accounts about his condition. The party initially described Zuma as healthy and undergoing routine checks before returning home. That claim was later contradicted by the foundation, which said he remained in hospital and declined to provide regular updates.
In a sign of the impact on the party, MK canceled its flagship Siyathatha rally less than three weeks before South Africaâs municipal elections. The uncertainty has become a political issue because of Zumaâs central role in the party he publicly launched nearly three years ago, after switching from the African National Congress (ANC) ahead of a general election.
MK emerged from the 2024 poll as one of the biggest forces in South African politics, winning nearly 15% of the vote on promises to scrap the constitution, expropriate land without compensation and nationalize banks, insurers and strategic mines. Its performance accelerated the slide of the ANC, once led by Nelson Mandela, which lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since the end of apartheid and was forced to form a coalition government.
Still, the MKâs rise has been punctuated by leadership turmoil, internal purges, and recurring disputes over candidate selection. Zumaâs absence from public campaigning has heightened questions about whether the movement can maintain its momentum without him.
Natasha Marrian, a political analyst at the Bureau for Economic Research, a South African think tank, said the MK party, launched as a breakaway outfit for Zuma supporters who opposed the ANC leadership of President Cyril Ramaphosa, was a Zuma project from the outset. âHe is the partyâs central drawcard,â she said. âThereâs no clear center holding it together in his absence.â
Know More
Zumaâs son, Duduzane, serves as the partyâs first deputy president and is widely regarded as a potential successor, but analysts question whether he can replicate the appeal of his father, who led South Africa from 2009 to 2018 before being ousted amid corruption allegations and a wider state capture scandal.
âDuduzane is a completely unknown political figure,â said AndrÃ© Duvenhage, a political analyst at South Africaâs North-West University. âHe comes from a business background.â
The ANC may benefit from Zumaâs absence, said Musa Xulu, an independent political analyst, adding that if he remains largely absent from the campaign trail, some ANC voters who followed him could drift back. âThe ANC is becoming the biggest beneficiary of Zumaâs current disappearance from public politics. The MK party is Jacob Zuma and Jacob Zuma is the MK,â Xulu said.
Notable
- The ANC secured a legal victory ahead of the 4 November 2026 local government elections when the Constitutional Court ruled in its favour, ordering the electoral commission to reinstate 181 disqualified candidates onto the ballot papers.

0549a0e5c89e.text:
Fast-flying Shahed drones spur new class of interceptors
Drone tech company Powerus eyes rocket or jet-powered interceptors as the next product target.
WASHINGTON—A surge in Russia’s use of jet-powered Shahed drones in Ukraine has spurred the need for super fast interceptors to defeat them. And it’s a problem U.S.-based dronemaker Powerus hopes to solve.
“We constantly need to move ahead of the threat. The next threat that we see to get in front of is the jet-powered Shahed drones,” Brett Velicovich, cofounder and president of the dronemaker Powerus, told Defense One. “Jet-powered Shaheds are very difficult to defeat because of how fast they are, and so to defeat those, we need jet-powered interceptors. So that is one of the things that we're looking at…to be able to fly an interceptor at 600 kilometers per hour, 700 kilometers per hour. That's going to require a lot more automation. It's going to require a lot more R&D.”
Newer versions of Shahed drones propelled by jet engines have increasingly been appearing on the Russian-Ukrainian battlefield in recent months, pushing Ukraine to fortify its air defenses. Those fast flying Shaheds require interceptors that can match those speeds—around 370 mph, or 600 kilometers per hour. Other versions of the Shahed fly just over 100 mph. There’s also concern that other security risks could crop up as other nations adopt the newer Shaheds.
Powerus is just about a year old and has former Pentagon and first Trump administration officials on its board.
Velicovich doesn’t have a target date for developing its rocket or jet-powered interceptor, but the goal is to move quickly.
“I spend a lot of time in Ukraine. There's a good chance that by the end of this year, the majority of Russian drones that are sent into downtown Kyiv will be jet-powered,” he said, “so we really need to move at that timeline.”
But churning out rocket- or jet-propelled interceptors at the same rate as the upgraded Shahed drones can be costly and difficult.
“They can build these things for $20,000-$30,000, and they can turn them out in massive, massive quantities. And so, to do that in an interceptor is very difficult,” Velicovich said. “But the technology is getting cheaper and cheaper, so we'll find a solution for that I think pretty soon. The entire industry is racing to figure that out.”
Powerus, which recently went public, has been busy in recent months.
The Rock Hill, S.C.-based company unveiled its fully autonomous interceptor, Guardian 3, during the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference here. The anti-drone tech is the latest addition to a family of interceptors, including the semiautonomous Guardian 2 and remotely piloted Guardian 1.
“Guardian 3 takes that final terminal phase of a manual operator out of the loop, and it is fully automated, similar to how you might fire a Patriot missile. The difference between us and the Patriot missiles is that…you can build these Guardian 3 systems in the thousands very easily,” Velicovich said.
The company aims to produce 5,000 interceptors per month by November, with an ultimate goal of being able to deliver 10 times that.
“We want to get to that point where it's just massive, massive scale because these things are a lot like artillery rounds, and we need to build them like artillery rounds. So we need more companies out there that have the industrial capacity…to turn these things out,” he said.
Also at the conference, Powerus signed a deal with Parsons on the showroom floor to pair its radar systems with Guardian interceptors to detect oncoming drone threats.
Earlier this year, the Air Force tapped Powerus in an $82 million deal for counterdrone systems, which includes the Guardian family of interceptors. The company has also branched out to international buyers, striking an unspecified deal with the Pakistan army for unmanned aerial systems.

35d604561890.text:
- Published
US President Donald Trump has renewed his sharp criticism of Volodymyr Zelensky, saying the Ukrainian leader is "more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin".
Trump, who recently made a controversial deal with Moscow to import its diesel to the American market, called Ukraine's fresh wave of strikes on Russian oil refineries a "disgrace".
Zelensky had paused the attacks for three days at Trump's request for a ceasefire on energy targets, but said on Thursday they would resume because Moscow had never stopped.
Tensions between Washington and Kyiv have escalated recently over the US-Russia diesel deal and restrictions on Ukraine's satellite communications on the battlefield.
Zelensky has not commented on Trump's latest criticism, however thanked "real leaders" for their support as he arrived at an EU summit in Brussels on Friday.
He was flanked by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President AntÃ³nio Costa.
"Of course we supported President Trump's energy ceasefire but we've seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute," Von der Leyen told reporters, adding that sanctions on Russia "have to increase".
Moscow said it had never agreed to the energy ceasefire that Trump suddenly announced last week.
Costa did not mention the US, but said that "this is no time to withdraw support" to the country and "no time to relieve Russian sanctions", as the US has done in agreeing to the deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes of its diesel.
The summit's agenda focuses on funding for Ukraine and helping it get through another cold winter - the fifth since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
"Russia is trying everything to destroy the energy and water infrastructure," Von der Leyen told Zelensky before the summit began, "but we stand by your side, we support you as we did in the other winters."
Zelensky said his country wants the war to end "as quick as possible", but added that Russia is not showing signs that it wants the same thing.
"That's why we have to prepare for the winter. A winter package is not only energy, it's also defence and funding," he said.
Deadly attacks on Ukraine continued overnight, with several people killed in a Russian drone strike in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, while some 270,000 households were without power after strikes in the western Volyn region, the local governors said.
Trump's comments about Zelensky, during an interview with US outlet Newsmax on Thursday evening, reflect the deteriorating relationship between the US and Ukraine.
The US president said he is "not a big fan of Zelensky" and that he is "not a good guy for us to deal with.
"He doesn't want to settle. He says he wants to settle, but he doesn't," Trump said.
"As you know, Putin hates Zelensky, and Zelensky hates Putin," he added. "And when you have that kind of hatred, it's very hard to get something settled."
When asked about Ukraine's renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries, Trump said it was "a disgrace".
"All he's doing is making the world oil price higher... There are a lot of targets that you can hit."
Trump is frustrated at Ukraine's continued targeting of Russian oil refineries because it affects Moscow's ability to export its diesel to America, as per the deal the US recently made with Russia, in an effort to bring down fuel prices.
Since the war with Iran started in February, US fuel and especially diesel prices have skyrocketed, souring Trump standing with the American public - something he wants to fix before next month's mid-term elections.
The diesel deal infuriated Zelensky, who called it a gift to Putin and an "investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged."
His anger was further heightened earlier this week, when restrictions were placed on the US-owned Starlink internet network, which is critical for Kyiv's military abilities to defend itself.
On Tuesday night, when the communications network was limited, there were several deadly Russian strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying there was no prior warning of the incoming attack.
The Trump administration had previously warned that it could withhold intelligence sharing - which is crucial for Ukraine's defences - if Kyiv does not stop hitting Russia's oil refineries.
Zelensky has been holding back-to-back talks with EU leaders while in Brussels. On Thursday he met Nato chief Marke Rutte, as well as the leaders of Poland, France, Denmark and Belgium.
A day earlier, he met UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at No 10 in London.
At the summit on Friday, Zelensky also held talks with the chiefs of the European Council and European Commission, and was set to meet the prime ministers of Hungary, Finland, and Sweden.
Ukraine also continued its strikes against Russia overnight. The airspace above Moscow was closed for several house, causing flight delays, as 644 drones were intercepted above 26 Russian regions, the defence ministry said.
Ninety-four Ukrainian drones were shot down as they approached Moscow, the mayor said.
In the Vladimir region, east of Moscow, the governor said that Ukrainian drones were intercepted to prevent an attack on heating infrastructure in the area.
And the governor of the southern Rostov region said that Ukrainian drones hit industrial and warehouse facilities, causing a fire and injuring one person.

c8294e35d4ca.text:
The Scene
From the deck of one of the large tugboats used to guide giant crude tankers into Fujairahâs port, the UAEâs race toward its âZero Hormuzâ strategy is visible in every direction.
A carrier capable of moving two million barrels of oil was loading at the portâs lone jetty able to handle such vessels. Smaller ships occupied other berths, and one tanker was loading at an offshore mooring, with a UAE naval corvette standing guard nearby. On the horizon, in the haze, several more tankers lay anchored, engaged in ship-to-ship transfers, taking on oil shuttled through the Strait of Hormuz under US protection for delivery to customers around the world.
Fujairah â one of the UAEâs poorer emirates better known for its low-cost resorts and mountain escapes â is at the center of a regional push to reduce Iranâs leverage over Gulf trade through the Strait of Hormuz. Geography has become its biggest asset, and itâs not alone. Saudi Arabia is expanding its pipeline network, and Kuwait is in talks with Riyadh and the UAE to move crude through their respective links. Oman is also a likely beneficiary of the Hormuz disruption, with separate pipeline plans for its ports to safely ferry fossil fuels trapped in the Gulf.
For Fujairah, this race to bypass the strait could lead to a new liquefied natural gas plant, a refinery, and âa much bigger port,â Fereidun Fesharaki, chairman emeritus of energy consultancy FGE NexantEC, told Semafor. âThis wretched war has created for Fujairah a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.â
Know More
Fujairah had been preparing for this opportunity long before the US-Iran war erupted on Feb. 28. Abu Dhabi opened a pipeline to the port in 2012 with a daily capacity of 1.8 million barrels of crude, giving itself an outlet beyond Hormuz, just in case. Photos of the port and coastline in the late 1990s show minimal oil storage and loading infrastructure. Today, tank farms line both sides of the coastal highway near the port, and a network of pipes moves products among terminals and to ships. A rail link from Abu Dhabi moves goods and recently began carrying passengers.
Glancing at a map of the UAE makes shifting assets east to the Gulf of Oman seem a relatively simple feat for a wealthy country dependent on exporting its resources. But the topography is a challenge: Craggy mountains press against the coastline, making land reclamation the only way to expand.
And while the opportunity is clear and few doubt the UAE governmentâs ability to execute, the territory is still subject to the same risks affecting the region.
Being outside Hormuz provides some protection for ships, but the vessels, tank farms, and port infrastructure remain vulnerable. Iran has attacked them all. War insurance has always been an issue for operators in Fujairah, and insurers have indicated they would need to see six months of stable peace before lowering premiums, according to two people familiar with the matter who have negotiated with insurance companies.
Thus far, Fujairahâs port has focused on the most valuable trade, leaving the import and re-export of building materials, consumer goods, and machinery to the much larger facilities in Dubai and Abu Dhabi.
That is changing. Cargo trucks now line the highway for some 10 miles, waiting for a chance to enter the ports. Ship-to-ship transfers are rising rapidly, from just a handful before the war to 80 in August and 120 in September, according to a person familiar with port operations. They mostly involve crude, but also aluminum, bauxite, and steel.
At a dinner during the Energy Markets Forum, organized by Dubai-based consultancy Gulf Intelligence, the word âresilienceâ was overused, but in this setting, it was appropriate: These are the people who have helped move oil consistently from one of the worldâs most volatile regions for almost a century.
The businessâs boom-bust cycle also came up. 8b7c81b75ae8.text: Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh said Friday that the economy has largely performed as expected since September's rate hike, hinting that little has changed in the central bank's outlook. Why it matters: The Fed is weighing another interest rate increase later this month as inflation heats up and the economy remains strong. What they're saying: "Over the month or so that's transpired since then, the world has broadly conformed to our expectations," Warsh said at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, referring to the Fed's September meeting. Warsh, interviewed by IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva, offered no explicit signal about October: "I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year." His remarks come just before the Fed's standard pre-meeting blackout period ahead of the Oct. 27-28 policy meeting. "It's hard to be in a discussion with central bankers and not compare notes and hear the same thing about the surge in prices," he said, alluding to conversations with international counterparts in Bangkok. State of play: The Fed raised rates last month for the first time since 2023 to contain inflation fueled by the Iran war. Minutes showed most officials expected another hike this year, though the timing remained unclear. Vice chair Philip Jefferson, New York Fed president John Williams and governor Christopher Waller have signaled that the Fed could hold off in October, with Waller noting that rate hikes need not come at consecutive meetings. Friction point: Fresh data this week showed inflation accelerated in September, with signs of price pressures extending beyond energy into services. Odds of an October hike jumped to 50% from 22% after Wednesday's hotter-than-expected inflation report, before retreating to 28% Thursday afternoon, per CME FedWatch. Between the lines: Warsh acknowledged that AI is boosting spending before its longer-term productivity benefits materialize, while investment beyond AI is also strengthening the economy. Warsh said AI was contributing to a "massive investment surge" in the U.S., calling the investment boom "probably the most important thing that's happening in the global economy on the upside." Warsh said AI could ultimately make economies more productive and generate greater wealth. But he said the AI transition was "likely to be a very bumpy one." What to watch: Warsh announced that the Fed will hold the first field hearing of its productivity and jobs task force on Nov. 16 in the Bay Area, bringing together outside experts to examine how AI and other technologies are reshaping the economy. The task force is one of five Warsh launched shortly after becoming Fed chairman to rethink how the central bank approaches monetary policy.

Stargazers and astronomers are preparing to enjoy a festival that celebrates the beauty of the night sky.
The annual Exmoor Dark Skies Festival is being held from 16 October to 1 November and this year is its 10th anniversary.
Taking in villages and towns surrounding Exmoor National Park, the event offers walks, talks and shows - putting the dark, clear, night sky into full focus.
But what is the event all about - and what is behind its success over the past decade?
More from Somerset
What is the festival about?
The event celebrates the national park's status as a Dark Sky Reserve.
Granted by the International Astronomical Union in 2011, the status aims to safeguard the right of any citizen to enjoy the night sky by helping to limit light pollution.
Festival organiser Julie Colman said: "We bring together lots and lots of events across the two-week period, celebrating the skies, the wildlife, the wellbeing elements of it."
There are about 80 events taking place across the park, from moonlit swimming and astronomy sessions, to bioluminescence walks and planetarium shows.
Why is Exmoor a good spot to stargaze?
Colman said there is "very little light pollution on Exmoor", adding it "enables the dark to be really dark with none of the pollution impacting".
"In the core of the reserve, there's an area where there is no light at all in a huge area - and that just makes the sky so much clearer and you're able to see some incredible constellations.
"You can see the Milky Way - it really is fantastic."
Photographs taken during previous dark skies events show incredibly clear views of the stars against a clear, dark backdrop.
Has it been good for tourism?
The National Park said it designed the event in 2017 to, in part, help local businesses towards the end of the traditional tourism season.
In Dunster, on the edge of Exmoor, the Yarn Market Hotel manager Antony Brunt said in recent years, "it has become much more widely known - and now we literally have people ringing us up to book".
The hotel hosts special trips during the festival, led by a local astronomer, and runs visits to various sites and events across the park.
Brunt said the festival brings in people from all over the UK, adding: "It's getting to a quieter time of year and these people, they really enjoy coming down.
"We have a group that come each year, in fact, twice a year. For people to come regularly twice a year to the same hotel, they must be enjoying the stargazing part of the weekend."
The growing popularity of the festival meant that many events sold out before the opening day.

81005b278cd6.text: Geothermal — power drawn from the Earth's natural heat — is pulling off something remarkable in today's hyper-polarized America: Winning fans across the political spectrum. Why it matters: The bipartisan appeal, combined with surging electricity demand from AI , is helping fuel investment in a niche energy source yet to prove it can compete at scale. Driving the news: Geothermal received unusually extensive attention in a bipartisan Senate bill introduced late last month to expedite infrastructure permitting . The House this summer passed a package containing several of the same geothermal provisions, including measures sponsored by lawmakers as ideologically distant as Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Mike Kennedy (R-Utah) . The rising cachet of geothermal is the product of three trends converging: Technologies adapted from the oil and gas industry, including fracking, are making it possible to tap heat in more places than just far-flung hot springs and volcanoes. Tech companies, on the hunt for reliable electricity, are willing to pay a premium for next-generation geothermal to power data centers. Investment is surging as companies race to scale a renewable energy source that can generate power around the clock. Catch up quick: The geothermal-specific provisions in the Senate bill go further than the broader permitting reforms offered to other renewable energy sources, including wind and solar. The bill would make it easier for geothermal developers to explore and lease federal land, speed up drilling permits and exempt certain activities from environmental reviews. Geothermal retained federal clean-energy tax credits in Republicans' sweeping tax law last year, even as wind and solar faced an accelerated phaseout. State of play: Fervo Energy, an advanced geothermal company that went public earlier this year, is at the leading edge of this convergence. It was founded nearly a decade ago by Tim Latimer, a former drilling engineer in the oil and gas industry. "I don't think any of us saw in 2017 that a few years later we would be in the biggest demand power boom for electricity that we had ever experienced," said Latimer during a recent on-stage interview with Axios in an event aptly titled "The energy source nobody argues about." The AI boom has "accelerated our business tremendously." Chart: Amy Harder/Axios; Note: Other includes project finance and debt. Fervo's IPO proceeds reflect capital raised at the time of its listing, not its current market value; Data: Currence The intrigue: Geothermal's appeal crosses traditional political divisions precisely because it doesn't fit neatly into Washington's usual energy-policy boxes. Its renewable characteristics appeal to Democrats. Its reliance on drilling expertise and overlap with the oil and gas industry appeals to Republicans. Its ability to provide stable, carbon-free electricity makes it attractive to utilities and tech companies. By the numbers: The average winning bid for federal geothermal leases has surged, reflecting growing commercial interest. The average winning bid in 2023 was $10 an acre, and so far this year, the average is $182, according to Guy Cohen, a geothermal analyst at the market intelligence firm Currence. A record $1,207-an-acre bid was placed for a single parcel in Utah this summer . Reality check: Geothermal's political popularity and investment boom are running ahead of its commercial reality. The technology remains expensive, and questions persist about whether it can reliably generate electricity over decades. Geothermal currently generates less than 1% of U.S. electricity, and those eye-popping leases are for the right to explore for geothermal, not for active geothermal wells. Fervo's stock has fallen nearly 70% from its first-day closing price following its IPO earlier this year, amid what Axios Pro calls a broader slowdown among energy startups. Tom Erb, Fervo's government affairs and policy manager, says the construction costs at its flagship project in Utah are about half those of new nuclear plants. He acknowledged that underground heat can diminish over time, requiring additional drilling, but said those costs are factored into company projections. What they're saying: Jigar Shah, a former Energy Department official under President Biden, says geothermal's current momentum still depends on state policies encouraging clean electricity and tech companies willing to pay a premium. "I don't think this moment would work without above market mandates from states or the data centers," Shah said. Friction point: Geothermal has also encountered local opposition, particularly over water. Traditional geothermal projects can disrupt hot springs and wetlands critical to wildlife, said Patrick Donnelly of the Center for Biological Diversity. Newer technologies like Fervo's avoid some of those risks, he said, but questions remain about their water consumption. What we're watching: Geothermal has found something rare in Washington: Political consensus. The test now is whether that consensus survives the industry's growth.

d9912477397a.text: Wall Street appears to be hitting its limit on AI, and financiers are starting to say the quiet part out loud: All of this AI spending doesn't look like it can pay off, at least not for everyone. Why it matters: The gap between what it costs to build AI infrastructure and what companies are actually paying to use it is widening. Wall Street's anxiety is surging as the debt piling up to fund data centers and chips looks increasingly disconnected from economic reality. Driving the news: A massive gap is opening up between AI infrastructure spending and expected returns. While AI providers are projected to spend $7 trillion on infrastructure through 2030, research from Gartner forecasts they will generate no more than $3.6 trillion in related revenue over that same period. More than $4 trillion in AI infrastructure spending could be at risk of write-downs by the end of 2032 if companies maintain their current investment pace. Gartner also predicts that more than 80% of specialized AI cloud providers, known as neoclouds, will cease operating independently by 2030. Case in point: CoreWeave, one of the largest neoclouds with among the closest ties to Nvidia — the AI boom's financial and spiritual foundation — has faced a multi-day selloff of its stock and debt. Yields pushed above 15% and its stock tumbled 15.5% before rebounding after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang spoke up on the company's behalf. Follow the money: Sources on Wall Street used to tell Axios that as long as the AI buildout was paid for in cash, there was nothing to worry about. But today, a third of the capex being spent on AI is coming from debt, and capital markets are showing signs of severe fatigue. It's getting harder to secure financing. Global AI-related debt issuance plunged to $23 billion in September 2026, down sharply from $113 billion in June, per the Financial Times . Banks are actively pulling back to avoid concentration risk, with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon confirming his bank is tightening up on credit. Infrastructure projects and providers are struggling: approximately $18 billion in bank loans for an Oracle data center campus recently slid into stressed territory, while Nvidia-backed AI cloud provider Firmus shelved an IPO that sought a valuation north of $30 billion. Zoom in: The constant spending relies on the belief that compute demand will never falter — a belief that has structural cracks. Reflection AI co-founder Ioannis Antonoglou told Semafor that businesses may need "a decade or two decades" to fundamentally redesign their operations around AI. That's 10 to 20 years of companies slowly adopting the technology that's being built (expensively) today. Between the lines: This creates a mismatch: Data centers and chips require enormous investment today, but the returns that could justify that spend will take years to materialize. Put bluntly, there is a massive gap between AI spending and AI revenue, one that won't close for many, many years. At the same time, companies that are adopting AI quickly are getting smarter about using tools more efficiently, turning to open-weight models that are less compute-intensive to cut costs. Reality check: Look at Anthropic's latest financials for a counterpoint to the bears. The company is raking in cash, turning free cash flow positive in the third quarter and growing revenue nearly 50% compared to the April-to-June period. But even Anthropic's staggering growth has slowed, albeit expectedly because trees can't grow to the sky. The bottom line: The debt-fueled AI buildout is not an isolated problem for tech investors alone to worry about. The stock market and economy have become increasingly tied up with the AI boom. If the AI bet doesn't work, markets and the economy could falter as well.

37a079dab129.text: MAGA activists are pushing for President Trump to resort to extraordinary measures — including martial law — if they believe the midterm elections are "rigged." Why it matters: Some of the proposals go far beyond Trump's legal authority — and there's no evidence that the elections will be rigged. But people in this orbit have close access to the president. Prominent MAGA election activist Tina Peters met with Trump this month. Convicted in 2024 of crimes tied to a breach of election equipment, Peters was released this year after Colorado Gov. Jared Polis (D) commuted her sentence. Peters and her attorney, Peter Ticktin, also visited Trump at the White House in late June . Peters did not respond to attempts to contact her for comment. Zoom in: On a September 30 video call for MAGA election activists streamed on Rumble, speakers warned of widespread election security breaches they believe will occur in November — and urgently pushed for remedies. Ticktin, Trump's childhood friend, said on the call "there would have to be martial law in the event... [of] another rigged election." "They'll probably need to be commandeering of ballots and election equipment to make sure that we can get to the bottom of it before anything further occurs," he later told Axios. Gregory Stenstrom, who testified about alleged voting irregularities in Pennsylvania in 2020, said he most wanted the election paused over security concerns. Alternatively, he proposed Trump invoke the National Emergencies Act to force states to change how they run elections. Stenstrom could not be reached for comment. Peters was also on the call. She's been promoting her own plan online since August, which calls for switching to hand-marked paper ballots and a manual recount of all votes where feasible. "Her plan is secure the paper ballots and recount by hand," Ticktin said. In an interview with Colorado Public Radio, he further explained this "would eliminate whatever effect the machines have." State of play: The streamed call is a regular feature in this activist community, drawing voices from across the country. Steve Stern, the host, directs his viewers to sign up through the Republican Party to become poll workers and observers for November. Stern declined an interview request. Reality check: "Emergency powers are not just a blank check for the president to go do whatever they want. The president still has to act within the Constitution and within statutes set by Congress," said Derek Tisler, counsel for the Brennan Center's elections and government program. He said those legal limits include : Election timing: Congress sets the date of federal elections. Trump cannot unilaterally delay the midterms. Counting and voting systems: States choose their voting systems and determine how votes are counted, subject to federal law. Trump cannot mandate a nationwide hand recount or order machines replaced. Emergency and martial law authority: Emergency powers do not allow Trump to override state election laws or constitutional restrictions. Martial law would not give Trump authority to seize control of election materials or override federal and state election laws. The big picture: Skepticism about the 2020 election extends into Trump's administration, including officials now involved in election integrity. Heather Honey, most known for denying the results of the 2020 election in Pennsylvania and Arizona, is now the Homeland Security Department's deputy assistant secretary for election integrity and senior advisor to the ICE Director. White House adviser Peter Navarro continues to promote his own report of mass election fraud and irregularities around the 2020 election. Between the lines: "This election did not sneak up on the administration. They've been in office for 21 months. We're 20 days away from this election, and they haven't done any of this stuff," said David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told Axios in a statement: "Americans deserves elections that are safe, secure, and transparent to ensure full confidence in the results. President Trump believes every legal vote must count, every election must be protected, and Americans must have complete confidence in the integrity of our elections."

After Booting 760K People From ACA Plans, Trump Administration Has Added Some Back
Late last month, the Trump administration announced that it had cut 760,000 people from the Affordable Care Act rolls, claiming fraud and improper enrollments and touting billions in potential taxpayer savings.
Not all of those kicked off were fraudulently enrolled, KFF Health News has learned. Insurance industry sources said the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has reinstated a small number of people whose coverage should not have been canceled. More could follow in the coming weeks if enrollees discover they are uninsured when they go to use their coverage.
Still, the sweep was long overdue, say supporters such as Brian Blase, whose Paragon Health Institute has supplied many of the sometimes controversial findings cited by those who allege widespread enrollment fraud in the ACA. But other policy experts question how many legitimate consumers were caught in the dragnet, perhaps because they failed to open a letter from their insurer or answer a phone call.
Questions continue to swirl, even as a second phase of the anti-fraud effort is underway. An additional 419,000 sign-ups are being scrutinized. Insurers must let CMS know how many of those enrollees don’t respond to outreach efforts by “around mid-to-late November, after the midterm elections,” said David Merritt, senior vice president of external affairs at the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association.
He confirmed that some BCBS members are among those who have been reinstated. He also said that CMS has an expedited review process for those who discover they have been improperly disenrolled.
Overall, however, the administration is providing few details about the cancellations, such as how robust the outreach was to those it targeted, how long it takes for people to get reinstated after discovering their coverage was wrongly canceled, and how many such cancellations have been reversed.
“It may be true that some of those enrollments were not authorized, but it can be equally true that people got lost in the shuffle and have a valid enrollment. Without more information, it’s almost impossible to tell,” said Katie Keith, a director of the Center for Health Policy and the Law at Georgetown Law. “That they are not being very transparent is telling too,” she said of the administration.
The enrollment cut comes as part of a larger Republican strategy to focus on fraud in government programs, including Medicaid and hospice care, which polls show resonates with GOP voters.
At an Oct. 14 press conference, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz touted the removal this year of subsidies for about 189,000 ACA enrollees with duplicate Medicare, Medicaid, or Children’s Health Insurance Program coverage, citing not fraud but a failure to look for concurrent enrollments or continued coverage for dead people. They credited an effort begun last year by the Trump administration to restore more frequent data matching checks than were done under the prior administration.
Unauthorized sign-ups by rogue insurance agents seeking commissions and other potential impropriety in the ACA marketplace — applicants’ providing incorrect income estimates, for example — has been a concern for several years, with much debate over the magnitude of the problem.
Even so, how the recent move to cancel the 760,000 enrollments will play out politically is uncertain. Healthcare costs are tied with gas prices as a top concern for voters. It is likely that many removed from the ACA are in red states, such as Texas, Florida, Louisiana, and Mississippi. Those areas saw rapid growth in ACA enrollment from 2020 to 2025, driven in part by now-expired enhanced subsidies put in place during Joe Biden’s presidency. Additionally, the cancellations target only enrollees in states that use healthcare.gov, the federal ACA marketplace. The 21 states fully running their own marketplaces generally have more robust fraud prevention programs, such as multifactor authentication, and have reported few or none of the kinds of unauthorized sign-ups plaguing the federal marketplace.
“To the extent there is a reaction depends on whether the government got it wrong, whether people try to get care and then find out their coverage is no longer active,” said Adrianna McIntyre, assistant professor of health policy and politics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.
How It Played Out
According to information the agency provided to KFF Health News, CMS in June selected for further review nearly 1.2 million enrollments that had all of what it deemed four warning signs for fraud:
- The application included no Social Security number or immigration document number.
- A broker was involved in the sign-up process.
- The plan had no monthly premium payment.
- The enrollee had had no contact with their insurer and no claims filed.
Then, as first reported by KFF Health News, CMS sent lists of those ACA accounts to specific insurers, instructing the carriers to review them and use at least two methods of contact — such as a phone call and a letter — to try to reach the enrollees. Policyholders were given 30 days to respond to the insurers’ outreach and provide the missing information. CMS disenrolled those who didn’t respond.
Johnny Wallin, chief operating officer of Texas-based Marketplace Insurance Exchange, which helps clients in about 35 states enroll in coverage, said insurers reached out to his organization for help contacting people on the CMS lists, prompting “an all-hands-on-deck” effort by agents to reach clients, some of whom were vacationing overseas.
“Getting them to answer the phone isn’t easy,” he noted, although he suspects his agents had a better chance of getting a reply than an insurer because their clients are familiar with their phone numbers. Still, they could not reach about 60 of them.

The nation’s uninsured rate hit a historic low when Xavier Becerra was health secretary. Now he wants to be California’s next governor as states stare down the biggest rise in the uninsured rate in a generation.
Next Governor To Face Thorny Choices After California’s Rapid Medicaid Expansion
In March 2025, when California ran out of Medicaid funds to pay doctors and hospitals, the state borrowed $3.4 billion to keep the program afloat. It was, as a spokesperson for Gov. Gavin Newsom insisted, nothing new. Indeed, a handful of times over the years, the state had taken out internal, short-term loans to sustain its healthcare program for the poor and disabled.
The unprecedented move came a few months later, when Newsom and Democratic state lawmakers agreed to pay down the loan — which grew to $4.4 billion — over 10 years instead of later in the year. California’s healthcare safety net, it seemed, was buckling.
Rising healthcare costs systemwide were partly to blame. But so were several state-led expansions that made California’s Medicaid program, known as Medi-Cal, one of the nation’s most generous.
Now, with congressional Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act expected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion over 10 years, California and dozens of other states must contemplate the limits of their generosity. The problem is particularly acute in the nation’s most populous state, which spends more on Medicaid than New York and Texas combined.
“We know we can’t afford to serve everybody we want to serve in the model that we have today,” said Mark Ghaly, the former top Newsom health official who now co-chairs the Future of Medi-Cal Commission, a 29-person panel with the goal of modernizing and sustaining California’s Medicaid program for those who need it. “What can we do differently? What can we do smarter?”
The 2025 law that Newsom, a Democrat, has dubbed President Donald Trump’s “Big Ugly Bill” is expected to leave millions more Americans without health insurance, mostly because of new work requirements. It also curbs the use of healthcare provider taxes and other strategies states have deployed to maximize federal funds. Some state lawmakers and consumer advocates have argued the federal cuts, along with rising costs, present an opportunity for the next governor to overhaul a program plagued by long appointment wait times, low reimbursement rates for healthcare providers, and volatile financing.
“If we continue to just give millions and millions into the same system and expect something different — I’m sick and tired of that,” said Caroline Menjivar, a Democratic state senator representing a Los Angeles-area district where roughly half of constituents rely on Medi-Cal.
Democratic lawmakers, who have often clashed with Newsom on Medi-Cal rollbacks, succeeded in getting him to delay a number of painful cuts until 2027 in hopes that a new governor might reverse them.
So far, neither of the candidates running in the November election to replace Newsom have offered substantive proposals for weathering the upheaval health policy experts say is on the horizon for a program that covers 1 in 3 Californians — roughly 13.6 million people.
Republican Steve Hilton, a former Fox News commentator, wants to pare back Medi-Cal eligibility and has promised to end coverage for immigrants without legal status, citing that benefit as an example of “wildly unsustainable” state spending. Democrat Xavier Becerra, who has spent decades trying to expand government-funded healthcare, has promised to protect Californians from the massive federal cuts.
Expanding Coverage
President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the law that established Medicaid and Medicare in 1965 to cover certain low-income groups, such as families with children, older people, and those with disabilities. Over the past six decades, states have substantially widened that pool, most notably under the Affordable Care Act’s Medicaid expansion to childless adults.
Starting in 2024, California offered healthcare coverage to all low-income residents, regardless of age or immigration status, although lawmakers scaled that back this year. At the same time, the state opted to cover a slew of non-mandated benefits such as physical therapy, hospice care, and housing assistance.
“California has always struggled with wanting to have as broad a program as possible but then having to figure out a way to pay,” said Jennifer Kent, who oversaw Medi-Cal under Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat. “There is no population that we have met that we don’t want to offer coverage to, and we’ve never met a benefit that we don’t like.”
Since 2010, California’s Medi-Cal enrollment has nearly doubled while spending has ballooned from $50 billion a year to $222 billion. It now makes up more than 40% of overall state spending, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Conservatives argue the program is bloated and rife with fraud. They say the federal changes will force states to refocus resources on the neediest.
“The role of the safety net programs was just that — to be a safety net,” Hilton said in an interview. “I don’t think it’s a particularly positive boast to say 40% of Californians should be on a program that was designed for people living in poverty.”
Becerra declined an interview request.
Nelly, a 59-year-old from Los Angeles County, was one of millions who have benefited from the state’s Medi-Cal expansion, but she was initially reluctant to sign up.
For years after she left her corporate job to care for her ailing mother, Nelly said, she didn’t consider applying. She remained uninsured until three years ago, when she woke up and couldn’t see out of her left eye.

On a misty and breezy morning last fall, Marc Hamric, a North Carolina Division of Marine Fisheries veteran, and two other technicians were conducting field work in Turnagain Bay, a remote area near Cedar Island.
They had brought their boat ashore, but because the water was so rough, it came loose and floated away.
One DMF technician swam after it and had trouble hoisting himself aboard. Hamric swam to rescue him. Meanwhile, the technician managed to get on the boat and steer back to shore, but didn’t know Hamric had followed him into the bay.
As the two technicians searched the water for Hamric, one was on speaker phone with the team’s supervisors, sobbing as he explained what happened. The technicians eventually found Hamric in the water. They tried to resuscitate him. Shortly after an ambulance arrived, medics pronounced him dead.
Chloe Dorin, then a biologist with DMF and one of the supervisors, was on the call. “I heard the whole thing,” Dorin said in an interview. “It has been a little over a year now, and I still think about him every day.”
The Carteret County sheriff ruled Hamric’s death an accident. Yet current and former employees say DMF routinely requires technicians to work while sleep-deprived and in dangerous conditions: in rain, wind and fog as dense as fresh concrete.
Interviews and government documents depict DMF as a floundering bureaucracy that jeopardizes the safety of its technicians who work on the water. The division has also failed its state-mandated duty to protect aquatic life and coastal habitats, in part because of incomplete and incorrect scientific data, according to court records, state reports and employees.
Some current and former employees who shared their experiences asked not to be named for fear of retaliation. Inside Climate News also relied on internal emails, legislative and federal documents, a confidential whistleblower report filed with the state auditor’s office and a recent superior court ruling against the division.
DMF, which is housed under the N.C. Department of Environmental Quality, is responsible for the stewardship of the state’s fish, clams, oysters and crabs in all coastal waters up to three miles offshore.
It must comply with federal requirements, legislative mandates and rules passed by the state Marine Fisheries Commission, itself mired in internecine politics between commercial fishermen whose livelihoods depend on their catches and recreational anglers who fish out of tradition or need.
DMF did not answer questions from Inside Climate News about the allegations but provided a statement:
“The Division of Marine Fisheries is aware of claims made by former employees who recently left the agency. An initial review by the Division has found these claims to be unsubstantiated, misinformed or lacking proper context. The Division takes its role to provide science-based guidance to the Marine Fisheries Commission very seriously.
“There are policies in place to maintain a safe working environment for employees and ensure that fisheries data is reliable. DMF is always looking for ways to improve and is evaluating the feedback from these former employees to determine if there are additional steps we can take to improve safety and transparency.”
After two years, Dorin said the workplace culture at DMF eventually became too much to bear. Not only was she concerned about worker safety, but she came to doubt some of the science that underpinned DMF decisions. She said she had uncovered several years’ worth of incorrect data regarding hard clams and poor scientific sampling protocols for bay scallops. She saw technicians break down under pressure.
“There are extraordinarily capable, hardworking people at DMF. In many ways, they are exactly why I feel compelled to write this,” she said in her Sept. 10 resignation letter to DEQ leadership, several state lawmakers and Gov. Josh Stein.
“I have watched good people be ground down by a dysfunctional system,” Dorin wrote. “I believe serious consideration should be given to dissolving the division in its current form and rebuilding it from the ground up.”
Stein’s office did not respond to a request for comment on Dorin’s letter.
In 1997, the state legislature passed the Fisheries Reform Act to address overfishing and plummeting fish stocks. Yet over the past 29 years, DMF has failed to manage fisheries and protect aquatic life and coastal habitats, according to court documents.
Of the 13 species under DMF’s care, seven have collapsed, two are depressed and the status of three others are unknown, court documents show. Only one, red drum, is recovering. None shows signs of long-term viability.
DMF’s challenges—not only politics but also coastal development, degraded water quality and climate change—are legitimate, former and current employees say, but they don’t explain all of its missteps.
“We’re so impressed with short-term economic gain that we don’t take the long-term viability of the resource”—the fish and their habitats—“into consideration,” said Louis Daniel, a marine scientist and a DMF employee for 21 years, including nine as its director. He left the division in 2016, after he was demoted by then-DEQ Secretary Donald van der Vaart, an appointee of Republican Gov. Pat McCrory.
“What’s in the best interest of the resource is in the best interest of everybody, and that’s where we have failed miserably as a state,” Daniel said.
Hamric had been with DMF for 28 years. He was beloved by his colleagues, employees said, and he won a DEQ Distinguished Employee Award in 2024. In her resignation letter, Dorin addressed his death. “There have understandably been many discussions about safety since then,” she wrote. “But there is a question I believe has received far too little attention: Why were staff operating on the water under poor conditions in the ﬁrst place?”

Prediction market Kalshi is in no rush for the Supreme Court to wade into its battle with states.
The company agrees with skeptics like the NFL that justices must eventually opine on whether states and tribes should regulate its sports event contracts as sports bets, a Supreme Court litigator working with Kalshi told Semafor. But it also believes that pending rehearing petitions and forthcoming Commodity Futures Trading Commission rules are currently muddying the waters, the litigator said.
Kalshi, represented by the attorney who convinced justices to strike down Trumpâs tariffs, recently requested a month-long extension from the court. That extension, coupled with Kalshiâs rehearing petitions, has led the gaming industry to believe the company lacks confidence in its case.
âItâs fitting that as Halloween approaches, Kalshi seems spooked by the idea of the Supreme Court taking up the case next year,â American Gaming Association spokesperson Rob Lockwood told Semafor. âBecause they donât want to risk losing sports gambling â which is roughly 85% of their total volume!â
The litigator disputed that characterization, calling the extension request a common move that was necessary for Kalshi to respond to the amicus briefs due the same day. Nevada, they noted, recently requested a similar extension in a related case.
Know More
The Supreme Court has until January to decide which cases it wants to hear in its current term, which began earlier this month. A clash between federal appeals courts has made the prediction markets litigation a likely pick: The Third Circuit has sided with Kalshi, while the Sixth and Ninth Circuits have sided with the states.
Kalshi has filed rehearing petitions asking the Sixth and Ninth Circuits to review their latest rulings, citing the forthcoming CFTC rules. Nevada has already pushed back on the Ninth Circuit request, arguing that the pending regulation âwould not change the outcome here.â
CFTC Chair Mike Selig, whoâs defended prediction markets in courts across the country, told Semafor earlier this year that he would âwelcomeâ a Supreme Court ruling. That âwould really settle the matter,â he said.

This story is part of an investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project. Read the other stories here.
In August 2022, dozens of protesters spilled into the streets of Kayar, a fishing town on Senegal’s Atlantic coast, demanding the closure of a nearby fishmeal plant, Touba Protein Marine.
Marching from the fishing wharf to the factory, they carried signs reading “Kayar is sick” and chanted, “Time to respect our Kayar.” The factory, they said, had been built less than a third of a mile from residential homes, triggering local health problems.
That same year in Vietnam, hundreds of residents on the country’s northeastern coast surrounded another plant and, for days, blasted loudspeakers at it in protest.
In India, in 2024, the odor from fishmeal factories spurred protests that lasted more than 100 days, ending in a boycott of local elections and in villagers convening parallel meetings to pass resolutions against the plants.
These uprisings were not set off by the kind of industrial disaster that usually commands global attention. What brought people onto the streets was the foul smell of fishmeal: the protein-rich powder manufactured in poorer coastal communities by unloading, cooking, pressing, drying and grinding up fish.
Today, two-thirds of global aquaculture—a $313 billion industry and the fastest-growing food sector in the world—grows species that are fed fishmeal and fish oil.
“We don’t invite family or friends here because we are embarrassed that we live in a place that smells like it’s rotting,” a man in Songkla, Thailand explained. Those living near plants describe nausea, headaches, eye irritation, dizziness, coughing fits and loss of appetite. They recount laundry brought in early, doors kept shut in coastal heat, sleep interrupted at night and a low-grade sense of agitation that comes from never being able to trust the next gust of wind.
A global investigation of this product’s hidden costs by The Outlaw Ocean Project revealed that the industry’s rancid odor was among the least tracked, most personally intimate and widely suffered impacts of aquaculture.
The investigation documented complaints about stench made relating to at least 60 plants in 15 countries. And we found that globally, more than 9.5 million people live within a mile of fishmeal plants—including nearly 1.7 million under the age of 15.
Farmed seafood sold at Walmart, Kroger and Costco was fed fishmeal tied to stench complaints at plants in India, Vietnam and Peru, according to Bait to Plate, an online tool created by the Outlaw Ocean to track the aquaculture industry.
For some communities, the stink corroded the local economy by undercutting tourism and scaring away restaurant patrons and beach visitors. In Mar del Plata, Argentina, the smell from fishmeal plants was so bad that tourists visiting a local hotel sometimes had to step into the courtyard to vomit, while in Huaquillas, Ecuador, residents told a daily newspaper that the smell was “unbearable” and “impossible to be around.”

Donate Now
The foul smell was more than just a nuisance, it was also an indicator of the release of noxious chemicals like ammonia, hydrogen sulfide, cyanide and methane, which have been known to cause serious health problems, including pulmonary edema. The worst part of the odor comes from trimethylamine, or TMA, a colorless “fishy” gas identified as “strongly toxic and carcinogenic,” by the Society of Chemical Industry.
Yet emitting bad smells is typically seen as more of an inconvenience than an actual environmental or health hazard, even if it results in sickness.
“The technology for detecting and characterizing complex odors has not developed to the level of a reliable surveillance method, which has hindered regulatory frameworks,” stated a group of environmental engineers at Florida Atlantic University.
While many studies focus on the health and environmental impact of specific chemicals emitted by sewage plants, livestock operations, composting facilities, landfills, paper mills or petrochemical industries, little research has concentrated on the impact of smell, according to a study in the journal Environmental Health.
Fishmeal stench is not an unsolvable problem. When factory owners have tried to reduce it, they have usually succeeded. In 2008 in the U.S., in 2021 in South Africa and in 2022 in Yemen, plant owners installed various types of devices, some of them called scrubbers, that researchers later concluded had drastically reduced the foulest-smelling chemicals. Scrubbers, however, are not more common partly because they can cost upwards of a million dollars.
Costs notwithstanding, there are deeper reasons that stench stays far away from consumers. In wealthier nations, plant neighbors more often successfully pressure their governments to require odor controls.
In North Carolina, for example, multiple juries found in favor of plaintiffs suing the largest pork producer in the world. One appeals court judge wrote that the medical risks and stench of spraying untreated hog waste high into the air “violated homeowners’ rights to the healthful enjoyment of their property.”
But in poorer nations, where the vast majority of fishmeal plants are located, people living in the industrial areas where these plants are built usually lack political clout. Their governments are also more desperate for revenue and more reluctant to put up regulatory burdens that may scare away foreign investment. As a result, there is little incentive or pressure for foreign fishmeal producers to fix a problem that does not directly impact their bottom line.
