The Signal Interview
Nobuhiro âNobuâ Toriiâs appointment as CEO of Suntory last September returned the leadership of the group behind Yamazaki whisky to its founding family, 126 years after his great-grandfather, Shinjiro Torii, set up shop as a wine importer in Osaka. But the younger Toriiâs succession was an abrupt and unplanned one.
Takeshi âTakâ Niinami, Suntoryâs first non-family CEO, quit after police searched his home for suspected illegal supplements. They found none, and the high-profile executive denied having broken the law. But the board decided that Niinamiâs resignation was necessary, and elevated Torii from his role as president, which heâd assumed just a few months earlier.
It was a rare upset in a family business that prizes stability, and Toriiâs message in his first interview with a Western news outlet since becoming CEO is that he brings a steady hand and a long-term focus. But he also displays an ambition to turn an increasingly tough market for the alcoholic drinks with which Suntory is synonymous to its advantage.
Niinami was a dynamic, âhands-onâ leader, integrating deals like the 2014 acquisition of Jim Beam bourbon while family chairman Nobutada Saji âkept our corporate culture,â Torii says. Toriiâs own role combines those two imperatives, he implies: âI donât have any aggressive strategy, but I really want to keep our corporate culture,â he says. â[The] culture is very important for the further growth of the company.â
The onetime bankerâs challenge is that he took the reins as the groupâs growth had faltered, with operating income falling last year on almost flat revenues of about $22 billion. Most notably, spirits consumption in Suntoryâs largest markets has been in decline after peaking during the pandemic. Companies across the industry have been idling facilities, with Suntory pausing production at one of Jim Beamâs three Kentucky distilleries to upgrade the site while demand is low.
Toriiâs task is to find growth in new countries and categories while showing that he can find opportunities again in the core liquor business. The group has predicted a rebound in its profits this year, and its new CEO is projecting optimism.
His familyâs willingness to think across generations will be central to Suntoryâs ability to achieve its goal of becoming the world leader in whiskies and ready-to-drink spirits, he suggests. âIt takes at least five to 10 years to have a good whisky, so the strategy must be long-term-oriented.â
A private company looks for long-term opportunity
Suntoryâs history informs Toriiâs reticence about making sudden strategic turns. The spirits industry is not a fast-moving consumer goods business but a slow-moving one, he says, recalling how the company misread demand for one of its brands more than 40 years ago. âWe believed Suntory Old Whisky would continue to sell more, more, more, more, more, and that was a mistake,â he says. âOnce we change the strategy in the whisky business, it will take many, many years to recover.â
Toriiâs group has a Tokyo-listed subsidiary, Suntory Beverage & Food, but the holding company itself is private, he notes, allowing it to take a longer-term view of the market. âWe donât have any stock price. So now itâs a good chance for us to strengthen our brands,â he says. Shares in publicly listed spirits companies such as Diageo and Pernod Ricard have been falling for several years, he notes, so âthey have to control their stock price by cutting some costs.â
âWe are still investing in our brands while our competitors seem not to invest a lot,â he says, describing his rivalsâ market behavior as âdefensive.â
Toriiâs belief in private companiesâ superior ability to invest through cyclical downturns echoes that of Sazerac, the US drinks company whose unsolicited bid for Brown-Forman was rejected by the Jack Danielâs maker this year. But he suggests that Suntory is unlikely to be so ambitious about acquisitions.
More than a decade on from the balance sheet-stretching Jim Beam purchase, Suntoryâs financial capacity is ârelatively strong,â Torii says, but he notes that interest rates have increased, which would make any purchase more expensive to finance.
âOur first priority now is [to] invest in our brands,â he stresses.
Asked whether he expects further consolidation in the liquor industry, Torii replies with a joke. âWell, itâs already consolidated, and if some spirits company [should have] an interest to acquire us, I would consider [it],â he laughs. But he quickly confirms that the familyâs controlling stake would let it block any unwanted transaction.
How demographics and diversification shape Suntoryâs strategy
Investors have grown concerned that young consumers are more abstemious than their parents were at the same age. In a speech in New York earlier this month, Torii said people were becoming âmore intentional in their alcohol consumptionâ but also more focused on the quality of the drinks they chose, which he believes will favor his products. âAt Suntory, quality is not a department; quality is a philosophy,â he told his audience.
âThe biggest difference between my generation and the younger generation is probably this one,â he says, gesturing to an iPhone. His point is not just that more people are socializing virtually rather than in bars and restaurants; it is that the high cost of their electronic devices has made them more selective about other spending.
âWe have to educate younger generations to understand the attractiveness of whiskies or other spirits,â Torii says. Still, he sees little evidence that recent inflation gains are making them sharply more cost-conscious about their drinking.
Instead, he thinks that consumers may be acclimatizing to higher prices. Twice in the past six years, Japanese customers raced to stock up on Suntoryâs products before the government raised liquor taxes, he says. The third such increase went into effect this month, but this time there was no such rush.

The Signal Insight
When Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni moved to trademark her voice last week, she highlighted growing fears about AI deepfakes sounding ever more convincingly like the people they impersonate, from politicians to CEOs. But she also shone a spotlight on the fast-developing business of helping prominent individuals secure rights to their voice likenesses â and on the companies that say âvoice AIâ will soon become how many people handle customer service and corporate sales calls or interact with devices from cars to robots.
ElevenLabs established itself as one of the most highly valued of those startups this month with a $300 million employee tender, at a $22 billion price tag.
The London-based company has worked with celebrities from Matthew McConaughey to Sir Michael Caine to trademark their voices, and created a custom voice for Yahoo based on its co-founder, Jerry Yang. It says it has developed comprehensive safeguards to detect and prevent unauthorized voice cloning or other abuses.
Most of ElevenLabsâ revenues come from corporate customers like Deutsche Telekom and Revolut, and co-founder Mateusz âMatiâ Staniszewski says businesses should prepare for a world in which customers increasingly expect to speak to AI agents rather than type with chatbots.
âVoice will be one of the key interfaces in the future; for a lot of use cases, the primary interface,â he predicts. âVoice is easier, it conveys a lot more information than text would, and it allows the technology to be present but not overwhelming.â
This conversation has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson: Give us an example of the benefits you see in voice AI.
Mati Staniszewski: We have an AI interviewer for [sales and development representative job candidates]. Usually you go to the website and fill in a form. We added [the option] to speak with an agent, and a lot of people started engaging through conversation, and two things happened. One, the ease of making it quicker for you to speak than to type resulted in us having a lot more people [applying]. Two, people started leaving a lot more information than they usually would. Weâve had more than 3,000 leads come through this so far, and more than 500 were qualified, so they were good leads.
What should CEOs do to make sure their human employees are getting the most out of their AI agents?
If you donât get this right, the other parts wonât matter. Ultimately, for an agent to work, it needs the right knowledge. It needs the right set of steps and workflow. It needs to understand what itâs doing. Like a human, it needs a lot of coaching in the early phases to make sure it works. And it needs the right guardrails and safeguards, so it doesnât go off-script.
You donât want competition between [humans and agents.] You want to find a way to bring people to manage the agents and be rewarded fairly for doing that well. And itâs not a one-and-done process. You keep improving, you keep iterating, and sometimes [you] need to jump in. You want to make sure that there is a loop: agent to human to agent. The key thing across all those efforts is that the AI agent needs to know when to bring in a human agent.
Are you looking to go public anytime soon?
We would love to go public one day. We would like to be ready â ready, but not necessarily go public â in the next 18-24 months. And then decide based on the wider side of triggers.
Whatâs the advantage, do you think, of going public when thereâs been plenty of capital to power your growth so far?
We would love for [our users] to have the ability to be part of the journey, and the later you do it, the lower ability they will have. We see a lot of people building with ElevenLabs, and weâd love for them to have an ability to be part of that. There are other [advantages], but we are building a company to stand the test of time, and the companies we work with are looking for partners that are planning to be here in 50 years, in 100 years, and we want to be that company.
Sir Michael Caineâs voice is a big part of his identity as an actor. Why did he decide to work with you rather than against you?
We created, effectively, a marketplace where people can [record] their voice, we authenticate it, they can share it, and they earn compensation as a result. So weâre trying to bring the industry on board, and [people like Michael Caine] want to be part of that future too, assuming you find a way to respect their work and give them the ability to earn compensation [from it].
CEO impersonation scams seem to be very prevalent. Have you ever had that problem with your technology?
With our technology, you always have transparency into how [an AI voice] was generated. You can take action. So, if somebody [was scammed], we could assist. Iâm not familiar with any CEO that was impersonated, but we have guardrails. So if you try to ask about money, that gets either blocked or detected and flagged for human review, so we can proactively take action. And then, if you want to clone a voice to a high [quality], you need to go through an additional authentication mechanism. So you cannot just clone a voice that easily.
Notable
- Staniszewski sees his companyâs European roots â it was born in Poland and is based in London â as âa huge advantage.â London has plentiful talent which wants to âbuild something ambitious on a global scale,â he says. And because ElevenLabs focused from the start on the polyglot European marketplace, creating a model that could work equally well in many different languages âwas never an afterthought.â

Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi has told Israel to stop its "forced establishment" of settlements in the West Bank and reverse its actions, his office said.
The "Palestinian question" is "the greatest historical injustice of this century", Wang told Israeli President Isaac Herzog in a face-to-face meeting on the sidelines of a conference in Azerbaijan on Thursday.
Beijing has been a longstanding supporter of the Palestinian cause and has maintained that a "two-state solution" is the "correct direction".
It has also been positioning itself as a mediator for conflicts in the Middle East.
In 2023 Beijing brokered a deal to restore diplomatic ties between Iran and Saudi Arabia after years of hostility. Earlier this year, it was part of efforts, along with Pakistan, to propose a ceasefire in the US-Israel war against Iran.
Beijing's efforts to tackle the war in Gaza have focused on Palestinian unity.
In 2024 Beijing got rival Palestinian factions to agree to form an interim "national reconciliation government" for the occupied West Bank and Gaza after the war with Israel, although it was never implemented.
Now, Wang says the "immediate priority" is to fully open access to Gaza and stop the continued spread of a "humanitarian catastrophe".
China is willing to work with the international community to get the parties to return to dialogue and "seek a political solution to the conflict", Wang said.
In a post on X, Herzog said he was "pleased" to meet Wang and their talk "focused on the relations between our countries and the situation in the Middle East".
"I emphasised Israel's desire for peace in the region, alongside the strategic threats to our security, first and foremost from Iran and its terror proxies," he wrote.
China maintains close ties with Iran and is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which had previously come under US sanctions because of Tehran's nuclear programme.
One year into the ceasefire, people in Gaza continue to live under the regular threat of Israeli strikes, displacement and food security challenges.
Although large-scale bombardment has stopped, Israel has continued strikes in Gaza almost every day. More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli strikes there in the year since the ceasefire started in October 2025.
The US-brokered ceasefire was the first phase of a deal to end the war in Gaza, which had been triggered by a deadly Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.
But progress into the deal's next phase has been stalled, with both Israel and Hamas accusing each other of violating the terms of their agreement.

Cheq, a cybersecurity company that verifies AI shopping agents, says it recorded a 100x surge in agentic traffic over a 45-day period following the release of consumer AI agents like Instinct and Metaâs Muse. While agents still make up a small fraction of online shoppers, theyâre growing quickly, especially among a constant drumbeat of consumer agent releases, Cheq CEO Guy Tytunovich said.
But not everyone is on board: Amazon and eBay have blocked agents to reinforce control over their ads businesses and checkout experiences.

Reedâs view
Fear is rising that the AI bubble is about to burst under the weight of mounting debt, as my colleague Liz Hoffman detailed yesterday, including this great quote from an unnamed data-center financier: âWeâre not an ATM for your dystopian future.â
Perhaps lenders have grown tired of funding the data center buildout, but money is not going to be the thing that finally causes the AI train to go off the rails. Everything is bottlenecked. Itâs not just chips, memory, and EUV machines. Itâs refrigeration units that cool the GPUs and the raw materials needed to make components, like glass.
If it werenât for this bottlenecked supply chain, itâs likely AI revenues and user numbers would be growing much faster. Every time companies reach a new level of token efficiency, some new use case for AI is born that burns through ever more compute, proving Jevons Paradox. My favorite example of late: Decompiling video games to create mashups, something that used to take people years to do manually can now be done by AI in a weekend. It may be the thing that finally turns Gen-Zers into fans of AI.
The total addressable market of AI is roughly 100% of the earthâs population, and demand for it will continue to soar. The enterprise market has only dipped its toes into AI, and the consumer hasnât even begun to dive in. Anthropic told investors this week that itâs making 85% gross margins. Even if that number is a gross exaggeration, this is a cash cow business. Theyâll service their debt obligations, in other words.
I agree with the lender who lamented being an ATM for the AI industry, but probably for a different reason. Why would you want to lend money for measly interest payments when you could invest and get a massive return? Thereâs a reason hyperscalers and neoclouds reached for debt: Itâs relatively cheap.

49483d514981.text: By — Elaine Kurtenbach, Associated Press Elaine Kurtenbach, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/fed-chair-warsh-says-price-stability-is-key-but-shies-away-from-signals-about-rates Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Fed chair Warsh says price stability is key but shies away from signals about rates Economy Oct 16, 2026 1:21 PM EDT BANGKOK (AP) — Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said Friday he won't prejudge what the U.S. central bank will do about interest rates at its upcoming meetings in October and December. The Fed increased its key interest rate by a quarter-point to about 3.9% in September, its first increase in three years, and stubbornly elevated U.S. inflation will likely lead it to hike that rate again in coming months to slow spending and help cool price pressures. WATCH: Warsh says 'inflation is too high' after Fed raises interest rate 1st time in 3 years But Warsh offered no fresh signals during a "fireside chat" with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva at a meeting of financial leaders in Bangkok. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "At the Federal Reserve, we made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago," Warsh said. "I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year." READ MORE: How much longer will consumers be willing to muscle through higher prices? The Fed's September rate hike defied U.S. President Donald Trump's repeated calls for the Fed to cut rates. The president criticized the Fed's rate-setting committee, though he still expressed support for Warsh, whom he appointed earlier this year. The global surge in prices is a key concern of central bankers and financial leaders meeting in Bangkok. According to minutes released from the most recent meeting, most Fed officials expect that another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year. That would raise borrowing costs for mortgages, car loans, and credit cards over time. WATCH: Economist breaks down new inflation report and what's driving prices higher Warsh said the surge in investment driven by the craze for artificial intelligence is one of the factors behind higher inflation and the Fed's task force on issues related to AI will meet Nov. 16. "I'd say the advent of this new technology is probably the most consequential change to the U.S. and the global economy in my lifetime to this point," he said. Unlike military conflict and other shocks that are driving prices higher, Warsh said he believes AI will bring "huge benefit" to the world economy in time. For Fed economists who struggle to foresee the future using data that lags behind today's realities, AI could prove a vital tool, he said. READ MORE: Wholesale inflation hits levels not seen since 2022 "We torture data with old fashioned models to try to find out what's underlying inflation trends. Not so long from now, it won't be torture. We will have access at the fingertips of central banks to all the information in the world, and we'll be able to use new analytical tools to distill that data," he said. AP Economics Writer Christopher Rugaber in Washington and AP journalist Haruka Nuga in Bangkok contributed to this story. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. The Scoop
Investors are pouring cash into a hot new sector of the AI economy: model routing â a practice allowing developers and companies to easily switch between different AI models.
Startup TrustedRouter, which launched publicly six weeks ago, is among a growing crop of model-routing firms looking to cut AI costs and reduce businessesâ dependence on any single model maker. The company this week closed a $6 million seed round, led by Sierra Ventures, it told Semafor.
The biggest player in the routing space is OpenRouter, which started with a $12.5 million seed round in February 2025 and has since agreed to sell to payments provider Stripe in a $7.5 billion deal.
TrustedRouter, CEO Joseph Perla said, aims to differentiate itself by offering end-to-end encryption and verifiable confidential computing for some open-weight models, meaning neither TrustedRouter nor the data center running the model can read a customerâs prompts or outputs, unlike with closed models from OpenAI and Anthropic, which donât currently offer the same guarantees.
OpenRouter also doesnât offer those protections, according to Perla: âSecurity is just a pure baseline. It just has to be secure.â
Know More
Perla, a former Facebook engineer and early Lyft hire who has founded and sold several startups, hopes to win over businesses that are seeing their AI spending balloon, but also putting a premium on keeping their data private.
âIf we all encrypt our AI chats,â Perla said, âwe can slow downâ the cycle in which frontier labs absorb user data to train future models.
He said Chinese AI models, including those from DeepSeek, Zhipu, and Moonshot, are among the most popular on his platform, but he wants to also see a more vibrant American open-source ecosystem. Thereâs been a flurry of Western open-weight releases in recent weeks, including from Reflection AI and Mistral; on Thursday, Meta released what it called âthe most capable US open-weight model to date.â
Eventually, Perla said he wants to launch the âNew York Token Exchange,â a marketplace for AI models in which thousands of models from thousands of hosting providers â any data center willing to run an open model â would compete to serve each request, turning AI tokens into a commodity that could be traded with futures, hedges, and price indices, like oil or electricity. He hopes to stage âmodel IPOsâ for new open-weight releases.
J.D.âs view
Thereâs clear demand from developers for routing services, and TrustedRouter could fill a void for the most privacy-obsessed among them. Whether it goes from niche to mass market could depend on how competitive open-weight models get. If they keep lagging behind their closed competitors at OpenAI and Anthropic, some enterprises and developers will put up with the higher cost and lack of encryption to get a better output for their most advanced tasks.
A project I oversaw last week, in which we analyzed thousands of cable news segments about data centers using AI, cost about $140, because we used advanced closed models. Running that through TrustedRouter on encrypted, confidential infrastructure with less advanced Chinese models would have cost under $20, though the output likely wouldnât have been as good. These kinds of tradeoffs will keep confronting tech leaders as long as that disparity persists.

Republican strategist Alex Conant said Democrats are banking on Trump motivating their base to vote, an approach they've routinely used over the last decade. The lack of a shared lexicon is undermining responsible AI-military integration
We need a common way to talk about military AI—across services, agencies, and indeed, the world.
Today’s headlines are full of killer robots and doomsayers, but the most urgent risk in military AI is more mundane: the people shaping it share neither a common lexicon nor common data.
The problem is not a lack of discussion. The authors have taken part in many global deliberations, both as conveners and as private-sector representatives, and we can report: If the world is to forge responsible governance of AI in the military domain, it will need shared definitions and a way to fuse relevant developments and decisions into something approximating “ground truth.”
The players in AI-military integration come from every realm: governments, militaries, the private sector, academia, the legal system, civil society, human rights, technology, journalism, and more. In multilateral negotiations and colloquial parlance, they speak varied languages—literally and topically. They are guided by varied incentives: some are eagerly pursuing AI-military integration, while others are trying to regulate it. A word like “autonomy” means something different to a general, an engineer, a lawyer, and a human rights advocate, not to mention the nuances born of the 200 or so countries they call home.
The staggering breadth of these players, combined with the wide range of AI applications, means that data about their actions is scattered. It can be found in government contract announcements, legislation, news coverage, court documents, patent applications, and beyond, in nearly every global language. This has made it impossible to track and compare developments within and across countries.
Without common language and common data, humanitarian organizations often talk past supply-chain experts. Tech executives fail to communicate effectively with academic researchers. Efforts to develop responsible AI-military integration cannot move ahead.
This is not a new concern. In 2024, the Responsible AI in the Military Domain Summit, or REAIM—the preeminent forum for global discussions of the topic—urged stakeholders to begin “fostering a common understanding of…capabilities and limitations [of AI-military integration], and a shared understanding of the possible applications…and their potential impacts, including both benefits and risks.” The same year, the United Nations Institute for Disarmament Research Roundtable for AI, Security, and Ethics identified six priority areas for governance, including: “Building a shared and solid knowledge base on AI in the military domain, developed through cross-regional, inter-disciplinary and multi-stakeholder input.” And last year’s report by the Global Commission REAIM urged states to “maintain international repositories of best practices, including AI concepts and definitions, AI capabilities in specific contexts of application…and military AI policies” to support national and international regulatory efforts.
One effort to bridge the data gap is the AI-Military Integration Database, operated by AIMID, a private company whose CEO is one of the authors. The database does a daily scan for news and information about AI-military integration in more than 20 languages—news reports, company announcements, academic articles, legislation, contracts, think tank reports, and more. The result is an ever-growing knowledge graph: a structured, footnoted map of actors, technologies, events and the relationships between them. This makes it possible to see which countries are doing what, with what technologies, from what companies, and for what use cases. In short, AIMID aims to deliver a single, verifiable picture of global AI-military integration, a data-driven “ground truth.”
Among other benefits, the database aims to help allies and partners pool knowledge about testing, evaluation, verification, and validation—supporting innovation and interoperability while avoiding the costly duplication of technical efforts. It might also help reduce tension between global rivals by providing empirical reference points, reducing dangerous interstate misperceptions, and ensuring that states’ security policies are anchored in evidence rather than ambiguity. For anyone concerned with responsible AI-military development—governments, businesses, NGOs, academics, or average citizens—AIMID serves as a unique resource,
But more than merely recognizing that data fragmentation is hindering responsible military-AI progress, defense leaders around the world should next fund and adopt the tools necessary to fully understand the data and intelligence-gathering side of this new ecosystem. Indeed, while organizations like AIMID cannot fully solve the fundamental problem of data fragmentation, they represent some of the best resources available.
This commentary is published in coordination with the 2026 Global Security Forum, of which Defense One is a media partner.
Dr. Jason Warner is the CEO of the AI-Military Integration Database (AIMID). He holds a Ph.D. from Harvard University.
Sofia Romansky is a Strategic Analyst at The Hague Centre for Strategic Studies (HCSS) and Subject Matter Expert for the NATO Defence Education Enhancement Program (DEEP). She previously served as the Project Coordinator of the Global Commission on Responsible Artificial Intelligence in the Military Domain (GC REAIM).

A Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker.
Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back.
This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months.
The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control.
While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September â and suffered few casualties in return.
The Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front".
Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day.
He is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed.
This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower.
Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield.
Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability.
Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine.
Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy.
Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground.
The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion.
An infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times."
He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target.
Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous".
"The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive."
Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation.
In Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation.
"As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed."
"I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy".
That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present.
"The real value of this is securing advantageous positions, favourable lines, and a bridgehead that grants us a superior position," Andriy Hitt, Revenge Bridge chief of staff, explained.
"This allows us to create the necessary conditions for subsequent successful operations, seize the initiative in battle, and plan future successful manoeuvresâ¦ each of these actions is a building block towards victory."
All this could be threatened by the limitations on US technology, and American intelligence. Relations between Kyiv and Washington are at an all-time low.

803ac97aef4c.text: It was an economy bursting at the seams: robust growth powered by a tech boom, low unemployment, elevated inflation and Fed rate hikes to try to cool things down. The big picture: That was the situation in the year 2000, and it reminds us a great deal of the conditions in 2026. The worrying part, however, is this: Then, as now, there were early warning signs that the technological boom powering the good times may not last forever. And indeed, the cracks that appeared in the tech sector in 2000 would spill over into a broader bear market and mild recession in 2001. We're not predicting that this time. History only rhymes; it doesn't repeat. But it is a historical episode worth weighing when thinking about the range of possibilities for how things may go in 2027 and beyond — particularly this week, as the debt markets funding the AI build-out have wobbled. Flashback: While 2001 was a nasty year for the U.S. economy — a full-fledged tech bust exacerbated by the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks — the year before was pretty great by nearly every measure. The unemployment rate reached a multi-decade low of 3.8% in April 2000 and closed the year at a mere 3.9%. GDP rose 4.1% for the full year, powered by stunning rates of productivity growth. It coincided, however, with high inflation, driven particularly by surging energy costs. The Consumer Price Index was up 3.4% over the course of the year. Zoom in: Against that backdrop, the Alan Greenspan-led Fed felt compelled to try to cool things down, lest that inflation become more entrenched. The central bank increased rates three times that year, including a super-sized half-point in May. But here's where the parallels to today get even more interesting: Greenspan's justification for rate hikes could be lifted from today's Fedspeak about the AI boom — or would be if today's central bankers shared his penchant for circumlocution. What they're saying: The "profoundly beneficial forces driving the American economy to competitive excellence are also engendering a set of imbalances that, unless contained, threaten our continuing prosperity," Greenspan told Congress in February 2000. "The problem is that the pickup in productivity tends to create even greater increases in aggregate demand than in potential aggregate supply," he said. "This occurs principally because a rise in structural productivity growth has its counterpart in higher expectations for long-term corporate earnings." "This, in turn, not only spurs business investment but also increases stock prices and the market value of assets held by households, creating additional purchasing power for which no additional goods or services have yet been produced." Between the lines: He was talking about the productivity boom driven by the internet and related IT innovations of that era, but it is very much applicable to the AI boom today. Yes, AI-fueled productivity could create a boost to the economy's supply potential in the future, with corresponding noninflationary growth and higher incomes. But that's in the future. Right now, that potential is causing surging asset prices and rising demand for inputs to the build-out, pushing inflation higher. Reality check: The stock market peaked in March 2000. By 2001, an all-out tech rout was underway, as much of the investment in fiber-optic cable and other internet infrastructure was ahead of its time. That reversed the playing field for the Fed, as the wealth effects and an investment boom that appeared to be overheating the economy in 2000 instead dragged it down. The Fed enacted a surprise half-point rate cut on Jan. 3, 2001, and would ultimately cut rates 11 times (!) in 2001. Yes, but: Interestingly, while the tech bust hammered Americans' wealth, employment prospects and capital spending, the turn-of-the-century productivity gains continued throughout that recession and the ensuing jobless recovery. The bottom line: Even if the AI boom drives the kinds of long-term productivity surges its proponents anticipate, there is a risk of a bumpy path ahead — and policymakers would do well to study the parallels from 26 years ago.

Triceratops’ massive skulls were built for horn-to-horn grappling. The rhino-like Centrosaurus could withstand stabbing its nose horn up and down. And the parrot-faced Psittacosaurus would have been wise to avoid a fight: Its head was ill-suited to handle blows.
New simulations using 3-D models of the heads of five different horned dinosaurs reveal what forces the skulls could withstand in battle. The results provide insight into how these dinosaurs evolved to use their face-based armory in combat, researchers report September 24 in PeerJ.
Ceratopsians — horned dinosaurs like Triceratops — have been hypothesized to use their imposing headgear as armaments for battling with other members of the species.
Fossilized facial injuries consistent with head-to-head violence have provided physical clues. “We know from many fossils that ceratopsian skulls tended to get banged up a little bit … in very particular spots on the frill or on the cheek,” says Andrew Farke, a paleontologist at Raymond M. Alf Museum of Paleontology in Claremont, California. But little else was known about how ceratopsians actually used their horns in battle.
Studying the biomechanics of the animals’ weaponized skulls could provide information on what movements and forces the dinosaurs evolved to tolerate. Such biomechanics research had previously been done on the bite stresses of theropod dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus and on the forces felt by the club tails of armored dinosaurs, says vertebrate paleontologist Eric Austin Ames Jr.
Ames and his colleagues at the University of Bristol in England developed digital 3-D models of six skulls across five ceratopsian species spread across the group’s evolutionary tree. They simulated the combat stress experienced across the skull, varying the direction of attack and how the weaponry was used. Higher stresses in the skull meant a greater risk of mechanical failure, Ames says. The dinosaurs are more likely to have evolved to fight in a way that was well-tolerated by the skull’s mechanics.
The team found that early members of the group from about 125 million years ago — like the hornless, husky-sized Psittacosaurus — didn’t have skulls well-suited for combat of any type. The pig-sized Protoceratops had a skull that tolerated ramming fairly well. Larger, later-diverging species like Centrosaurus and the three-horned Triceratops and Spiclypeus appeared adapted to a wider range of combat styles.
Centrosaurus may have been a specialized stabber, lunging its head to jab at opponents. “When we tested [the skull] with vertical forces, it actually handled the stresses really well,” Ames says. “But when we tried side-to-side, it did not perform very well.”In contrast, Triceratops and Spiclypeus had skulls that tolerate the forces generated by interlocking horns and wrestling.
Ames thinks ceratopsians’ horns and frills probably first evolved for social and sexual display, but were soon used for full contact purposes. “Throughout their evolutionary history, their [horns’ traits] started to really explode in diversity and that coincided with different intraspecific combat styles,” he says. “This is something we see in modern herbivores.”
Much like with the antlers and horns of modern deer, buffalo or antelope, these weapons could have easily been turned on predators as well. “These adaptations are kind of like a Swiss Army knife,” Ames says. “They can be used for multiple things.”
The team created its 3-D models from surface scans of fossilized skulls. More detailed models that better simulate the complicated internal structure of these dinosaurs’ immense, bizarre skulls could provide even more insight to this prehistoric fight club, Farke says.

A pastor and his wife have been arrested in South Africa after 200 people, some in chains, were found held at a suspected illegal rehabilitation centre in the north-eastern part of the country.
The facility, operated from a church in Mpumalanga province, was discovered during an operation by officials in the area on Thursday.
Authorities said they uncovered "gross inhumane conditions" when they raided the facility, with some patients found with "sores all over their bodies" and "others chained to each other".
Police have since charged the couple, who were running the facility, with kidnapping but could add more charges. They have not yet commented.
Illegal rehabilitation centres have mushroomed in South Africa in recent years as drug use spirals in the country.
Last year, the department of social development said it had uncovered over 100 unlawful facilities operating across the country, mostly in Gauteng province, home to the country's largest city, Johannesburg.
A girl of 16 and a boy of 11 were found being kept in the same room as adults in the Mpumalanga centre.
The couple running it told officials they were housing 60 people, but upon inspection, more than three times that number were found, including more than 30 women.
The group, mostly believed to be drug addicts, were found in crowded rooms and without access to functioning bathrooms or running water.
"Some [of them had] been at the alleged illegal centre for a while," the department said.
Gift Skhosana, one of those held at the facility, told local broadcaster Newzroom Afrika it was "common practice" for patients to be chained.
"They chain us as punishment [and] when you gain entry," he said.
Despite this, Skhosana, who was a drug user, said the facility helped him get clean and overcome his addiction.
Another person, who was not named, said his experience with the facility left him needing help mentally.
The couple charged a monthly fee of 3,000 rand ($182; Â£137) to house the patients, of which almost a half would go to the church.
Fourteen of those found at the centre have since been taken to hospital for further medical treatment, police said.
Officials said 132 have been reunited with their families.
The couple is expected to appear in a local court on Monday.

0c1a14d530b7.text: By — Bill Barrow, Associated Press Bill Barrow, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-will-rally-georgia-republicans-despite-party-divisions-in-battleground-state Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump will rally Georgia Republicans despite party divisions in battleground state Politics Oct 16, 2026 10:57 AM EDT ATLANTA (AP) — Donald Trump's midterm campaign blitz arrives in Georgia on Friday for a rally with top Republican candidates in a state that has long been the epicenter of the president's false claims about election fraud. In Dalton, the population center of conservative northwest Georgia, Trump will appear with Senate candidate Mike Collins and gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson as part of the White House effort to boost Republican enthusiasm in an election that could reshape the final years of Trump's second presidency. WATCH: Inside Georgia's Senate race and Collins's uphill battle against Ossoff "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party," said White House spokesperson Davis Ingle. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Yet unlike some of Trump's recent trips to solidly Republican states — Alabama, Montana, Tennessee — Georgia is a critical battleground. That means Jackson, a billionaire businessman, and Collins, a two-term congressman, need more than Trump stalwarts to defeat their respective Democratic opponents, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms and Sen. Jon Ossoff. "I'm surprised Georgia Republicans want the president here," Ossoff said. "The president coming to town reminds Georgians that Donald Trump and Mike Collins" have pushed policies that have "driven the cost of groceries, fuel and healthcare to their all-time highs." READ MORE: Talarico compares his campaign to David and Goliath after GOP invests over $158M against him Collins spokesperson Meyer Siegfried said the congressman welcomes the president's attention. But he also stressed that Collins is a "bipartisan workhorse who will work with anybody," while adding that "Ossoff hates Trump more than he loves our state." Bottoms also seemed thrilled with Trump's visit. "When Donald Trump says he wants people to imagine that he is on the ballot, I am asking the people of Georgia to do just that," she said, pointing to Jackson's promise to be Trump's "favorite governor." WATCH: Georgia's Ossoff and Collins face off in Senate debate The risks have been evident even in the heavily Republican corner of Georgia where the president will visit. Voters there sent erstwhile Trump ally Marjorie Taylor Greene to Congress before she broke with the president and resigned. Trump won the district by about 37 points in 2024 and Greene won by 29. In the April special election to replace Greene, Republican Rep. Clay Fuller won by 12 points. Republican candidates have run separately The Dalton event will be the first time this fall that Jackson and Collins have appeared at the same venue. That contrasts with Ossoff and Bottoms holding joint rallies across Georgia, with the next scheduled for Saturday in Cobb County outside Atlanta. Collins has been dogged by anemic fundraising and controversies that leave even Republicans questioning his viability against Ossoff. Jackson has focused on sharing the stage with other statewide Republican nominees and party leaders, and none mention Collins. "That was not a neglect," Trump's former agriculture secretary and onetime Georgia Gov. Sonny Perdue said after one rally. "I think it was really respecting a Rick Jackson event and focusing on his election as governor." Asked about the joint rally, a Jackson spokesman said only, "Rick will be in Dalton and looks forward to reminding Georgia voters that bad mayors do not make good governors." Trump was last in Dalton on Jan. 4, 2021, the day before Ossoff and Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock won concurrent Senate runoffs. He had already lost the presidential campaign to Joe Biden but was unwilling to accept it. "There is no way we lost Georgia. There's no way," Trump said that day. "That was a rigged election but we're still fighting it." Election denial lingers in Georgia Collins was elected to Congress in 2022, and he's echoed Trump's lies about 2020. He declined to recant those views this week when Ossoff pressed him during a debate. "There was a lot of doubt in that election. Yes, Joe Biden was the president," Collins said, without saying Biden was duly elected. Trump endorsed Collins days before his June runoff victory over former football coach Derek Dooley. When announcing his decision, Trump complained that Dooley had conceded that Biden was elected legitimately. Gov. Brian Kemp did not endorse Collins until September, and he warned voters during the primary that the congressman could not win in November. Trump did not endorse Jackson until after he'd won a Republican primary runoff over the president's original pick, Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, who had been part of Trump's effort to overturn Biden's victory. The president cited Jones' loyalty in his endorsement. Jackson doesn't regularly mention Trump like he did during the primary campaign, when the first-time candidate compared his business background to Trump. He's more likely in recent weeks to compare himself to Kemp. But the governor won't be with his fellow Republicans on Friday, according to his top political adviser. "He has a family obligation that day," said Cody Hall. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 25c4dff1172f.text: By — Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/talarico-compares-his-campaign-to-david-and-goliath-after-gop-invests-over-158m-against-him Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Talarico compares his campaign to David and Goliath after GOP invests over $158M against him Politics Oct 16, 2026 10:44 AM EDT At a packed rally in Texas on Thursday, James Talarico compared his U.S. Senate campaign to David — who fought Goliath — as the Democrat faces more than $158 million in outside spending by Republican leadership and the world's richest man, Elon Musk. Talarico told rallygoers under bright lights that David may not have had Goliath's strength, but he had a slingshot. READ MORE: Frustrated with Trump, voters overwhelmingly want change, AP-NORC poll finds "You are my slingshot," he continued, without mentioning Musk or the other spending against him. "We are going up against our own Goliaths." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The description falls in line with Talarico's past rhetoric painting politics not as right versus left, but the ultrawealthy versus everyone else, as he tries to become the first Democrat to win statewide in over 30 years. Talarico's own campaign has raised record amounts of money in one of the nation's more expensive and competitive Senate races. The national conversation around Talarico's campaign has evolved over the past months. Initially, the state lawmaker was considered just the latest of several Democratic candidates over the past years who gave the party a hope of flipping Texas, only for that hope to deflate come Election Day. WATCH: An accounting of Trump's promised payouts and questions they raise Now, Talarico is seen as a real contender to win the seat against Republican candidate Ken Paxton. Talarico's success so far can partly be chalked up to voters' apprehensions toward Paxton, who faced questions in his past over corruption, including being impeached by his own party in the Texas legislature. He was later acquitted. Texas will help decide control of the U.S. Senate While outside spending in support of Paxton has flooded the Texas airwaves with ads, Talarico's campaign itself has outpaced Paxton's in fundraising from donors eager for Texas to forgo its solidly Republican title. The prospect of a flagship GOP state turning blue doesn't just fill Democrats with glee and Republicans with alarm. Whoever wins will help determine which party controls the Senate in President Donald Trump's final two years in office, making it either smooth sailing for Trump or a bog of investigations and opposition. WATCH: Inside Georgia's Senate race and Collins's uphill battle against Ossoff Talarico, a seminarian and state representative, has also tread a very careful path — as nonpartisan as he can — from the major metros that already tilt Democratic, along the border towns that flipped from blue to red last election, and to the rural Republican high plains and desert. The candidate has distanced himself from former President Joe Biden's administration and his own party, and while progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders is coming to Texas this month, he won't be sharing a stage with Talarico. Talarico's talk of affordability resonated at rally Talarico's strategy is to take direct aim at what voters say they are most concerned about: the costs that have inexorably grown for years. That unaffordability, Talarico argued at the nighttime rally in Texas that was packed with younger voters, is because billionaires and corrupt politicians have rigged the system. It resonated. "They think that they can buy us, and that they can essentially be the kings of the country," said Kaitlyn Johnson, a 29-year-old bartender who attended the rally. WATCH: Democratic and GOP strategists on how Trump's unpopularity is shaping the midterms Johnson felt that Talarico put words to that feeling she'd held for a while, and the high costs keep nagging at her, too. "I make decent money," she said, "but there's no way in hell that I'm going to be able to buy a house anytime soon." Paxton has backing from Musk, Trump Trump and Republicans are well aware of Talarico's ability to connect with voters, and of Paxton's struggles to find purchase in what would otherwise be a relatively easy race for a Republican. The president has made several trips to Texas to rally for Paxton. Paxton has received significant financial support from Musk, who last year headed Trump's Department of Government Efficiency. Musk contributed $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, federal campaign spending filings showed Thursday. The Senate Leadership Fund gave $158 million to Texas PAC, the largest contributor to Paxton's campaign. Musk also provided $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group that supports Paxton. The rally Thursday in the small city of San Marcos south of Austin follows nine days earlier this month when Talarico was out of the public eye due to the flu. His absence sparked a swirl of conspiracies online, including the false claim that he was at a mental health treatment center in Ohio. Shared by conservative social media influencers, the claim quickly fell apart at closer inspection. Associated Press reporters Thomas Beaumont and Joey Cappelletti contributed. Pope Leo XIV has been pictured celebrating Mass from hospital, in the first images of him released by the Vatican since he underwent lung surgery.
The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.
The images shared on Friday showed the Chicago-born Pope wearing a green robe while standing behind a makeshift altar on the tenth floor of the hospital.
Pope Leo "celebrated with the medical and nursing staff" and thanked workers for their service, the Vatican press office said.
On Friday, the Pope's doctors said tests had shown "a steady improvement in his general condition" since his procedure.
His doctors said that a chest X-ray indicated "good recovery of the operated lung".
The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.
"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before he spent a "peaceful night" at the hospital.
Pope Leo first announced that he would be having the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.
The Vatican has stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure.

754c09d9a8c4.text: By — Stephen McGrath, Associated Press Stephen McGrath, Associated Press By — Veselin Toshkov, Associated Press Veselin Toshkov, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/drone-strikes-in-the-black-sea-raise-fears-of-russian-escalation-to-test-natos-response Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Drone strikes in the Black Sea raise fears of Russian escalation to test NATO's response World Oct 16, 2026 10:35 AM EDT SOFIA, Bulgaria (AP) — A string of drone attacks on at least seven cargo vessels in the Black Sea this month, off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, has some members of the alliance wondering if Russian President Vladimir Putin is seeking escalation to test their support for Ukraine in its war against Moscow's full-scale invasion. The attacks in the two countries' exclusive economic zones threaten a global shipping route and have left two people dead, with at least 25 still missing. They also run the risk of drawing other countries directly into the war for Ukraine. READ MORE: Drone strike on ship in Romanian waters raises fear that war in Ukraine is spreading Throughout the war, Russia has repeatedly bombarded Ukraine's Black Sea and Danube river ports, leaving Kyiv increasingly reliant on alternative routes to get its grain exports to markets in Africa and the Middle East. Russian drones have repeatedly violated Romanian airspace near some of Ukraine's Danube ports. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. In the latest incidents, fires broke out on two ships struck by drones Wednesday and Thursday, one in Romania's territorial waters. Romanian President Nicusor Dan said Thursday in Brussels that "two drones" had hit the vessels but did not say whose drones they were. "There will be a reaction from the Romanian state," he warned. READ MORE: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries as relations with Trump sour Increasingly, the suspicion falls on Russia. "There is no logic in Ukraine attacking its own ships and crews, given that the outcome of all these attacks favors Russia — and indeed, the logic points in that direction," Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told his country's Parliament. "The problem is that we cannot prove it." Multiple vessels struck by drones in October The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader, a chemical tanker traveling from Tunisia to Romania, was struck by a drone Thursday and caught fire. Five crew members were rescued but another seven are missing. On Wednesday, a drone strike and fire were reported on the Comoros-flagged Yara J, a chemical and oil tanker traveling from Turkey to Romania. Romania's acting Defense Minister Radu Miruta said an investigation was underway. WATCH: Ukraine resumes strikes on energy targets, saying Russia never stopped its attacks On Tuesday, two ships were struck by drones off Bulgaria's coast. Rescuers evacuated all 15 crew members from the Ukraine-operated Chelsea 3, sailing under a Maltese flag, but 11 crew from the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity are still missing. The crew of the Chelsea 3 reported the ship's deck and hull were hit by three aerial drones. Earlier this month, sea and aerial drones attacked two other commercial vessels in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. A Togo-flagged ship sank with no sign of the 12 sailors reported on board, while a Bulgarian ferry evacuated 18 crew members from a Palau-flagged vessel that was damaged. A day earlier, a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying corn caught fire following a drone attack and later sank off the coast of Romania. Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as "a horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel" in neutral waters. Russia's ambassador in Sofia, Bulgaria, said she didn't have any information from the Russian defense ministry. NATO's defense clause under scrutiny NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said on X on Thursday that he met Radev and Dan to discuss security in the Black Sea and "the latest attacks on commercial shipping." "NATO has strengthened our posture along the eastern flank including with increasing counter-drone capabilities," he said. "NATO will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defense posture as needed." WATCH: Ukraine less reliant on U.S. as Trump-Zelenskyy rift deepens, former ambassador says Article 5 of the NATO charter has a mutual defense guarantee — an attack on one is an attack on all — but Romanian defense analyst Radu Tudor said it was uncertain as to whether it covers many of the Black Sea drone strikes because they occurred in the alliance members' exclusive economic zones. "It's a matter of discussion whether the exclusive economic zone is included in the Article 5-type reaction or not," he said. "And it seems that until now, it isn't — which raised a lot of questions." NATO has been too slow to respond in the Black Sea, he argued. "Tens of incidents are happening and Russia is getting closer to NATO borders. … Words are not enough," Tudor said. A growing threat The Black Sea drone incidents in October are just the latest in a long string of drone airspace incursions to rock Romania and other NATO members since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. While most have come from Russia, Ukrainian drones have also crossed borders. In August, Romania deployed two F-16 fighter jets to destroy a naval drone that was reportedly carrying explosives and was spotted near a major Black Sea gas project, a decision that Acting Defense Minister Miruta said was made to "protect the lives of the several hundred people" working on the gas platform. Protesters and anti-riot police have clashed in Albania's main cities in scenes not witnessed for decades.
Government buildings have been attacked and some private businesses, too.
So what is happening?
How big and unusual are these protests?
Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale.
And the clashes have spread beyond Tirana - to include the main cities of DurrÃ«s, ShkodÃ«r, LezhÃ« and Vlora in the west, GjirokastÃ«r in the south and KorÃ§Ã« in the east.
The new demonstrations were announced as a student movement, ostensibly demanding action by the government to help with the high cost of education fees and books - and the higher cost of living.
Secondary schools joined in, swelling the numbers.
Before too long, masked protesters threw stones at police, and they responded with water cannon, tear gas and batons.
Many were incensed by scenes of a young man being carried away, his broken leg dangling with him in agony.
Apologies were expressed but failed to calm the situation.
A floor of the education ministry was set on fire, with other government institutions ablaze, too.
Every evening, throughout the summer for some 135 days in a row, Albanians in central Tirana would hold pictures of a pink flamingo, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama - now in his fourth term - to resign.
The protests began over a mega-tourism project on the Adriatic coast linked to US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Demonstrators said the bird would become extinct on an island near the coastal city of Vlora, if the plans for a luxury development went ahead.
The public anger comes as allegations of corruption among ministers and other senior officials grow louder.
One deputy prime minister has fled the country, another has been ordered to step down as investigations continue.
So has the Flamingo movement radicalised?
The flamingo protesters say they have no links to any political party - one of their slogans being "Rama in jail, Berisha in jail". While Rama is prime minister, Sali Berisha is Albania's main opposition leader - as well as a former prime minister and president.
They were attended by young and old, parents with children and sometimes their grandparents. Some of the participants took pride in cleaning up after every night.
But after months and an unusually hot summer, their numbers dwindled - with no sign that the government was meeting their demands.
The current movement appears far more violent. Dozens of police have been hurt, and the eyes of Europe are now watching what happens next in a country viewed as one of the top candidates for EU membership.
Several young protesters told the BBC that what was going on now was a new phase born of the previous movement.
Five months of peaceful protest had been "met with humiliation, ridicule, mockery," complained one young woman called Livia. "That was a clear message from the government that our voice will not be allowed to be heard."
Another called Brunela told the BBC's What in the World programme she was worried about what might happen next: "I am very terrified because the media and the government is reacting, especially now. It was not just my voice, it is the voice of Albanian youth."
An overlap between the two sets of protests may well have occurred, even though flamingo leaders have not publicly stated so and no representative of the student movement has come forward.
After all, their main concerns relate to corruption, which the prime minister says must be investigated by the justice system.
How is the government handling the unrest?
Rama has been touring some of the damaged buildings and blaming Sali Berisha for instigating chaos.
"All of this is the work of the very same hand - the hand that has gripped the Albanian opposition by the throat, the hand that has burned and destroyed Albania more than once, and is now prepared to burn and destroy it again to prevent any progress. It is a blind struggle, fuelled by the most irrational hatred," he said on Friday.
The prime minister has ruled out resigning, promising to "listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward".
Berisha's Democratic Party has often tried to get people out to oust Rama.
But the number of his loyal supporters, who have also protested for months and at times clashed with police, has been low in comparison to the current attendance.
So there is some scepticism about Berisha's ability to mastermind the trouble, though he may well seek to capitalise on it.
On the other hand, the Albanian media have suggested that secret services of foreign countries may be involved.
Unfounded allegations have been made against Serbia, with commentators suggesting Belgrade is envious of Albania being often cited as potentially next in line to join the EU.
Indeed, without mentioning names, Prime Minister Rama echoed the allegation on Friday.
"These are foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace... they do not want Albania to be part of the united European family," he said, adding: "Do you think it is a coincidence that every time Albania receives another green light... or draws closer to that great ambition - that historic objective - flames suddenly erupt? It is no coincidence at all! None of what is happening now is a coincidence."
Is Albania safe to visit?
Although the street violence has taken place in many cities, it remains contained for the time being.
The UK government has urged visitors to check media, external for latest information, stay away from "demonstrations, large-scale gatherings or political rallies" and follow advice of local authorities.
Albania is a popular tourist destination, and the government in Tirana has warned that violence tarnishes the country's image, affecting both tourism and its European path.

Dozens of masked settlers have attacked Palestinians and set fire to cars and olive trees during the annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank.
A BBC team witnessed one of several attacks in farmland near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A local official said the attacks had injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian American citizens. A foreign journalist was also among those hurt.
Driving into the area early in the morning, we came across the first signs of the violence: a stream of cars carrying wounded Palestinian olive farmers racing out along the narrow stony track, piled high with olive picking equipment, as smoke rose from several fires nearby.
The bloodied face of Majdi Fheed peered out from the backseat of one car.
"We were getting our olive trees and almost 15 Jewish guys â¦ started attacking us with guns, with rocks, with special weapons. They hit me on my head [and] my neck â look, I am bleeding!"
Yaser AlKam, a council member from the neighbouring village of Turmus Aya told me Majdi - an American citizen - was attacked by settlers with nail-studded sticks, and needed treatment for deep wounds on his head. His elderly mother was also injured.
Another man ferrying the injured to hospital told us that settlers had attacked them with sticks while they harvested their olives, and had burned three cars â including one of his own.
"As soon as we got to the land and put our things on the ground, they started to come, so we ran away" said a woman next to him.
Asked about the violence, a US State Department spokesperson said they were aware of the reports.
"Weâ¯condemn criminalâ¯violenceâ¯by any partyâ¯in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions,â¯of those responsible," the spokesperson said.
Watching the vehicles stream past her, 73-year-old Imm Khaldoun told me emphatically that, no matter what happened, she would always return to her land. "This is my land. It's my right [to be here]" she told me.
The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year.
Olive picking in the West Bank is now a test of speed, with trees rapidly stripped of fruit as soon as the sun rises, before violent Israeli settlers attack.
In another olive orchard nearby, we watched as dozens of farmers used power-tools to strip the trees as fast as they could â one eye on the ridge above us, where a group of settlers at a new illegal outpost had already gathered, and were watching the olive harvest below.
Standing on ladders, the Palestinian farmers worked quickly, sending streams of olives onto the plastic sheets laid out under the trees. Three villages had come together to harvest these olives, the landowner Amin Khalil, told me, as a form of protection against attack. He said his land was now surrounded by seven Jewish settlements and outposts.
All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts â small encampments on hilltops â are illegal under Israeli law as well, but many still receive state support.
"This is a hotspot â there are seven settlements around here," Amin Khalil told me. "This year, all the people came together because when there are just a few people working alone at the edge of the village, the settlers attack. So all the families are working together today."
But the tactic doesn't work today. As we watch, dozens of settlers, all dressed in black, begin moving down the hill towards us, setting fire to several groups of olive trees.
There are shouts of panic from the Palestinian farmers, yelling for children to get out of the field. Some begin swiftly wrapping up the olives to leave.
But with large numbers of people on both sides, the confrontation stalls into an uneasy stalemate. We see settlers with slingshots hurl stones towards us, and young Palestinian men running to throw stones in return.
As Israeli forces arrive, the standoff explodes into action. Settlers begin running down towards us as the farmers swiftly retreat. Some Palestinians set off fireworks to try and push the settlers back.
American journalist Heidi Levine of the Washington Post was injured in the attack. She described how dozens of settlers ambushed her as she was reporting at the scene.
"I got jumped," she said. "I was on the ground and they were kicking me and I was trying to hold onto my camera and my bag. I had my helmet and flak jacket on which protected me. They made me stand up and they kicked me again, and this went on for at least 10 minutes."
In a statement, Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray said Levine had been clearly identifiable as a journalist.
"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," he said.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said personnel had been despatched to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation". It said a female journalist had been injured during the confrontation. And that "all circumstances" surrounding the incident would be examined.
As the farmers retreated, the sound of live ammunition cracked across the fields. It was unclear if settlers or Israeli forces were firing.
Minutes later, Israeli forces began firing tear gas into the Palestinian fields to end the confrontation â a well-worn Israeli pattern of managing these conflicts.
The UN says settler attacks on the olive harvest this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others across the West Bank.
Illegal Jewish outposts have mushroomed here over the past few years, clustering in closer around Palestinian olive groves.
What we witnessed was part of a pattern being repeated day after day, as settler outposts here increase.
The yearly olive harvest has become a litmus test of how the policies of Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government are affecting Palestinians here, by presiding over growing violence by extremist settlers

Alexisâs view
The Iran war is shaping up to be the catalyst of a seismic shift in Africaâs energy sector. And, in the case of the continentâs richest man Aliko Dangote, the conflict has proven the old adage that luck is what happens when preparation meets opportunity.
Dangoteâs mega-refinery on the outskirts of Lagos State has revealed the scale of a West African market underserved by locally refined fuel, while upending conventional thinking by showing African refineries can supply markets in Europe and Asia. At the same time, disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has exposed the vulnerability of nations that are heavily dependent on fuel imports: South Africa and Kenya have hiked prices, which runs the risk of driving inflation. Meanwhile, President Bola Tinubuâs removal of Nigeriaâs subsidy three years ago has allowed prices to skyrocket, turning the cost of fuel into a key campaign issue ahead of Januaryâs election.
Policymakers have been quick to react to the altered energy dynamics. South Africa announced plans to increase its strategic oil reserves for the first time since the end of apartheid to mitigate supply shocks, Angola wants to implement faster exploration concessions while urging southern African governments to help finance a new refinery, and plans to build refineries in Uganda and Tanzania have gathered pace.
Fola Fagbule, who heads the Kenya regional office of multilateral lender Africa Finance Corporation, which helped to finance Dangoteâs Lagos refinery, called the impact of the Nigerian billionaireâs project a âBig Bangâ moment. He told me various projects are being developed across the continent âas a result of the new realities in the energy market.â
The shift has potential pitfalls. Daniel Evans, global head of fuels and refining research at S&P Global Energy, acknowledged the increased appetite for downstream investment across Africa, but warned difficulties remain around projects that require high levels of capital expenditure.
But a new generation of refineries has the potential to transform economies, not only protecting countries from future energy shocks but providing the baseload power needed to ramp up manufacturing. As Fagbule put it, the legacy of this paradigm shift could be how it triggered âmassive, large-scale industrialization in Africa that nobody expected.â
