42a8120d018d.text: By — Haven Daley, Associated Press Haven Daley, Associated Press By — Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/man-who-stopped-the-oregon-elementary-school-shooter-has-2-daughters-at-the-school-his-mom-says Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Man who stopped the Oregon elementary school shooter has 2 daughters at the school, his mom says Nation Oct 16, 2026 3:01 PM EDT BEND, Ore. (AP) — The man who stopped a deadly elementary school attack in Oregon by shooting the teenage gunman inside the building is the father of two girls at the school, his mother said Friday. In a statement read to reporters Friday, Kenda Freeman said her son, Kaylub Giamanco, intervened in Thursday's attack at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend and shot the teenage shooter. Three students and a teacher were killed in the attack, and a fourth student and another teacher were critically injured. READ MORE: Teen shooter kills 4 at Oregon elementary school before being shot by a witness "He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support," Freeman said, noting that her son is a lifelong resident of Bend, a mountain-ringed city of about 100,000 in central Oregon that has grown quickly in recent decades. Police have not yet identified who shot the gunman, only saying that the suspect was found dead inside the school minutes after the shooting was first reported. They also haven't named the gunman. At a news conference hours after Thursday's attack, Gov. Tina Kotek — without naming him — praised Giamanco for following the gunman into the school, saying he helped end the rampage and likely saved lives as police began arriving on the scene. "To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life: Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," said Kotek. Memorials with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals popped up around the school, which sits in a densely packed neighborhood filled with newly built homes. Brooke Olsen, whose daughter is a kindergartner at Silver Rail, said she was amazed that a member of the public pursued the shooter. "I think it's miraculous that someone was there before law enforcement even arrived to stop further tragedy from happening," Olsen said Friday, weeping at times. "I'm feeling very grateful." The shooter used a gun bought by his mom A makeshift memorial at a sign marking the Silver Rail Elementary School near a cordoned-off area, following a shooting, in Bend, Oregon, on Oct. 16, 2026. Photo by David Ryder/Reuters The 16-year-old suspect, identified only as a Bend resident, was found dead inside the school minutes after the first calls for help, Police Chief Mike Krantz said. Police said he got into the school by shooting through locked doors. The children who were killed were ages 5, 8 and 11, Krantz said. Authorities didn't give details about the teacher who was killed. Another 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded in the attack and were taken to a hospital in critical condition, he said. The attacker used a pump-action shotgun that was purchased by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation. Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if provided by a parent or by someone else with the parent's consent. Police said they didn't know if the shooter knew anyone at the school or if he had attended it. Police respond within minutes The first 911 call came early in the afternoon from someone outside the school who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, the police chief said. More 911 calls came from inside the school, and officers arrived within minutes, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said. The attacker was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, she said. READ MORE: 3 students and a teacher killed in Oregon elementary school shooting, police say The school has students in kindergarten through fifth grade, with about 450 enrolled last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education. Children were taken by bus to a nearby church serving as a reunification center for families. Parents hugged, kissed and held their kids' hands as they walked to their cars, with some bringing along favorite stuffed animals or other comfort items from home. A community grieves Shaken residents held a vigil Thursday night, where children drew hearts in chalk on the sidewalk and held candles side-by-side with adults. Classes and all other activities were canceled Friday for the area's 32 schools. Bend, the biggest city in central Oregon, is about 125 miles (200 kilometers) southeast of Portland. It has ballooned in population over the past three decades and is a tourism and outdoor recreation hub. The shooting was the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year, according to a database maintained by The Associated Press and USA Today in partnership with Northeastern University. Just four years ago in Bend, a grocery store employee who had served in the U.S. Army attacked a gunman who was spraying shots inside the supermarket. Both the employee, whom police hailed as a hero, and a customer were killed, and the gunman died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Durkin and Tucker reported from Washington. Associated Press reporters Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City, Gene Johnson in Seattle, Ed White in Detroit and John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed. 7cc2f2cb2a26.text: President Trump said Friday that his administration did not disrupt an Elon Musk -owned satellite system used by Ukraine to wage war against Russia. Why it matters: The restrictions imposed earlier this week on the system hampered the Ukrainian military's ability to intercept Russian attack drones for 24 hours. It raised concerns that the Trump administration and possibly Musk were retaliating against Ukraine for its attacks on Russian oil refineries and President Volodymyr Zelensky's criticism of Trump's diesel deal with Russia. What he is saying: "I just checked this morning — it wasn't us," Trump told reporters. "I don't know if it was anybody, because it wasn't me and I don't think it was Elon." He was responding to a question about a Reuters report that the order to slow the satellite system came from the White House. Trump said that from what he was briefed the system is currently fully working with no restrictions. do we need this? no one is saying otherwise The other side: Ukrainian officials remain highly skeptical of Trump's claims and believe someone in the U.S. government participated in throttling the systems. "Our guys who speak to SpaceX say the White House was involved in the decision," a Ukrainian official said. Catch up quick: The Ukrainian military uses SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system to control and operate its reconnaissance and intercept drones. When Starlink doesn't operate at full capacity, Ukraine's ability to gather intelligence, use interceptor drones and conduct long-range strikes against Russia is impeded. Ukraine relies on two satellite systems: One is SpaceX's Starlink, which it uses for communications, ground forces, logistics and defensive drones — ones that shoot down incoming drones. The other is Starshield, which is controlled by the U.S. government and used for offensive military purposes. Both systems were restricted, according to Ukraine. In a post on X on Wednesday, Musk hinted the U.S. government was involved in disrupting Starshield. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote. The big picture: The limitations came days after a new crisis erupted between the U.S. and Ukraine over Trump's agreement to lift sanctions on Russian oil sales. Zelensky criticized the move, then Trump called for Ukraine to elect a new president.

Sea World Orlando in Florida and La Ronde theme park in Montreal, Canada, confirmed on Thursday they had temporarily closed rides, bringing the total number of roller coasters halted to 11. READ MORE: Roller coaster rider's death puts spotlight on safety of ever more thrilling rides Police and a state regulatory agency are investigating what caused Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old school employee from Atlanta, to fall from the Goliath coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday. Witnesses described seeing him ejected from the coaster; some people who rode the Goliath before him that day said they had concerns about its restraints. Nine of the roller coasters taken out of service have the same manufacturer and a similar restraint system as the Goliath at Six Flags. Mom says her son's restraint didn't work properly Erica Billups said her son and daughter rode Goliath about an hour before Kariem's death and encountered a problem with the restraint on one seat. Her son initially sat in that seat and tried to lock it, but then moved when it repeatedly became unlocked. The roller coaster embarked with the seat empty and the harness up, she said in a post on X. She confirmed the post in a text message to The Associated Press on Thursday. She said staff did not tell her kids there was a problem. Summer Bates, who was at the Georgia park with her husband and three children and saw Kariem fall, told the AP previously that her older two children kept trying to push their restraints down tighter while on the ride. She understood why they were doing that later when she was on the coaster, she said, because the restraints didn't feel secure. Six Flags did not immediately respond to an email for comment on any issues with restraints. At least one of the other closures is for safety La Ronde in Montreal said one of its coasters — also named Goliath — is offline "while we conduct a thorough safety review in collaboration with the ride's manufacturer." Sea World Orlando said that it closed its Mako roller coaster with no set date to reopen. Neither La Ronde nor Sea World Orlando said why those specific rides were closed. Both were manufactured by the Swiss company Bolliger & Mabillard, which also built the Goliath ride in Georgia and eight of the other coasters that Six Flags closed. Bolliger & Mabillard declined Thursday to answer questions about the shutdowns. In an updated list of ride closures provided Thursday, Six Flags no longer included the Goliath coaster at its Six Flags Magic Mountain park in California. The coaster has a different manufacturer and restraint system from the others. Six Flags had listed it as closed earlier in the week. Online photos and videos of most of the closed coasters show each equipped with so-called "clamshell" restraints, mounted in front of each seat on a vertical bar that sits between the rider's knees. The bar locks the padded restraint into place over the rider's lap and upper legs. READ MORE: Man killed on a Six Flags roller coaster was thrown from the ride and hit other patrons, police say It's unclear from the images whether any of those coasters also have seat belts or other secondary restraints. Goliath in Georgia has no such backup restraints. Dennis Speigel, a theme park consultant and past president of the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions, a trade group, said the similar restraint systems are almost certainly why most of the coasters were closed. Speigel said they're likely to remain shut down until investigators have determined what went wrong on the Georgia coaster, but he said that "obviously it was something with the restraint." Roller coaster manufacturers decide what type of restraints to use after considering speed, force and the track's transitions, said Brian D. Avery, a University of Florida professor and amusement ride safety expert. He advocates the use of a backup restraint for riders, but there is a long-running debate in the industry over whether that would increase wait times, Avery said. Bolliger & Mabillard says it is investigating The company said in an email it would have no further comment until it had a "better understanding of what transpired" on Monday. Kariem was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride. Goliath, one of Six Flags Over Georgia's headline attractions, towers above the park's entrance. It opened in 2006 and features a series of hills and turns. It doesn't take riders upside down, but its first hill rises to 200 feet (61 meters) and it has a top speed of 70 miles per hour (112 kilometers). Nick Mendenhall, who had just ridden Goliath with his son and was watching the coaster cars passing overhead, said it looked like Kariem was hovering because the car was moving underneath him. He fell headfirst back into the coaster, Mendenhall said, and then was ejected from the ride on its final turn. Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder
Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.
Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.
Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.
"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.
"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."
Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.
It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.
The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.
It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.
Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws â which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services â will help Australians become happier and healthier.
But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.
The choice
Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.
Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.
It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.
He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order.
"You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC.
"I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."
The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.
Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."
Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.
Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see â and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.
Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.
But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.
Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction, external; that algorithms â often unsolicited â serve up content which harms users' mental health, external, and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline.
Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line.
"The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.
While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change.
"Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.
Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s â a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.
More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.
The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off.
"This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said.
"If people want to doom scrollâ¦ that's fine, that's up to them."

a710d13eda99.text: By — Rob Gillies, Associated Press Rob Gillies, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/prime-minister-mark-carney-says-u-s-is-trying-to-break-canada-as-alberta-votes-on-separation-path Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Prime Minister Mark Carney says U.S. is trying to break Canada as Alberta votes on separation path World Oct 16, 2026 2:07 PM EDT CALGARY, Alberta (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned Thursday that the United States is trying to break Canada so it can "own us" as he urged oil-rich Alberta not to begin a process toward separation in Monday's referendum. The vote is not a direct referendum on independence. Alberta, which has the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation. "This referendum comes at the worst possible time," Carney told a large pro-Canada rally in Calgary. "The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us." READ MORE: Carney and Macron deepen ties as Canada turns toward Europe and away from U.S. dependence He did not directly mention the U.S. or its President Donald Trump in that passage, but has done so in similar past speeches. Carney's warning came as U.S. President Donald Trump wages a trade war with Canada and after his repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state. Carney has argued that Canada needs to become more economically resilient and less dependent on the United States. Carney urged Albertans not to use the vote simply to send Ottawa a message, saying a decisive result could settle the separation question. "Don't be fooled by the idea you can 'send a message' with your vote," Carney said. "This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division and great uncertainty." Carney makes the case for Canada Carney, who grew up in Alberta, spent Thursday campaigning in Calgary before addressing the Forever Canadian rally at the BMO Centre. His office estimated about 5,000 people attended, with some waiting more than two hours to get through security. Organizers were also holding a second rally with Carney in Edmonton on Friday. Earlier Thursday, he pointed to the many Albertans who were born or educated elsewhere in Canada and to firefighters who come from across the country to help Alberta during wildfires as examples of the ties binding the province to the rest of Canada. Attendees react during the Forever Canadian rally at the BMO Centre, ahead of a non-binding referendum on Alberta sovereignty, in Calgary, Alberta, Canada, on Oct. 15, 2026. Photo by Todd Korol/Reuters At the rally, Carney also acknowledged the grievances that have fueled alienation in Alberta. "The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real," he said. Carney said that while growing up, Ottawa made Albertans feel "like our resources weren't our own" and that more recently the province was made to feel its energy contributions were "against the tides of history." A Liberal prime minister finds unlikely support The setting is striking for a Liberal prime minister. Alberta has spent decades feuding with Liberal governments in Ottawa, particularly over energy and federal power. But Carney has broken with some of the policies associated with his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, fast-tracked a proposed new oil pipeline to the Pacific and called Canada an energy superpower. READ MORE: Carney says Canada can emerge from Trump's trade war with a stronger and independent economy Carney pointed to the Pacific Link pipeline as evidence of a changed relationship, saying it would create more than 140,000 jobs and generate revenue for social programs. His biggest cheer came when he said the pipeline would reduce Canada's dependence on the United States. "Careful, they might think that's election interference. A little touchy," Carney joked, drawing laughter. He was referring to U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra's warning to Canadian politicians not to interfere in the U.S. midterm elections. Tanya Clemens, co-chair of the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide, acknowledged Carney presents a challenge. "He's formidable for sure," Clemens told The Associated Press. Clemens argued, however, that Carney's agreements with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith amount to "pinky promises" that do not resolve long-standing grievances with Ottawa. Keith Wilson, another leader of Let Alberta Decide, rejected Carney's argument that global instability made this the wrong time for the vote. "The worst timing for this, why? I don't understand what's the logic," Wilson said. "Then it's the best time for him to get back to Ottawa." Wilson said Carney should ask Parliament to repeal federal measures that separatists say have hurt Alberta, including authority he says could be used to tax oil exports in retaliation against the United States. He predicted Carney would eventually impose such a tax despite Carney saying he sees no value in using Canadian energy exports as leverage against the U.S. "It's one cabinet meeting away," Wilson said. "He's gonna do it. He has to do it." READ MORE: Carney pitches Canada to global investors amid trade war with Trump Smith, who called the vote but supports remaining in Canada, cast her ballot Wednesday and said she voted for Alberta to remain in Canada. She has said support for separation remains too high for her liking. "Canada can still work," Smith said after voting. "We just need to make some changes." Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University, called Carney's popularity in Alberta "highly unusual" for a Liberal prime minister. Price, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-casts-doubt-on-press-secretary-katie-zacharias-future Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter White House press secretary Katie Zacharia leaving the job after Trump casts doubt Politics Updated on Oct 16, 2026 4:09 PM EDT — Published on Oct 16, 2026 1:49 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Katie Zacharia is departing as White House press secretary, a person familiar with the matter said Friday, after a short and rocky tenure that was defined by questions about her professional background and lack of polish in fielding questions from journalists. The person, granted anonymity to discuss a personnel decision not yet made public, said Zacharia would be transitioning out of the role. The shift comes after President Donald Trump cast significant doubt on her future earlier Friday, telling reporters that he would have a discussion with her following his weekend travel — and that if he were her, he would reconsider the job. READ MORE: Katie Zacharia's debut shows the pitfalls and possibilities of White House press secretary's role Zacharia had come under immediate scrutiny when she appeared uncomfortable during her inaugural briefing on Tuesday, delivering halting remarks touting the president and his accomplishments. Her 14-minute briefing was followed by criticism that the conservative commentator had long called herself a lawyer when she had not passed a bar exam nor was otherwise credentialed to practice. Zacharia was a surprise choice when Trump announced her appointment on Oct. 9, as the successor to Karoline Leavitt, the youngest-ever White House press secretary who had been part of Trump's inner circle for years. The chaos surrounding her appointment was reminiscent of some of Trump's short-lived staff picks from his first term. Trump said he told Zacharia that she might want to change her mind about the job, and said he thought she had been treated unfairly by the press. "I told her, 'I think you're better off being happy,'" Trump told reporters on the White House lawn as he left for a rally in Georgia. "I said, 'Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider.' I said, 'You think about it, but I would reconsider.'" Messages to Zacharia seeking comment were not returned on Friday, and the White House offered no immediate comment. In his own comments, Trump said he told his press secretary, "'Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this,'" and that he wanted "her to have a good life" and not be subjected to criticism, which he likened to being "brutalized by the media." The president said he'd make a final determination later, perhaps after his campaign travel on Friday and this weekend, adding, "When I get back, we're gonna talk." He was asked who might replace Zacharia, and said that there were a lot of people who wanted the job. Zacharia's first official day on the job was Monday Zacharia's short tenure has been defined by criticism for a lack of polish in fielding questions from journalists and questions about her professional background. In her briefing on Tuesday, she took questions from just three reporters, all from conservative-leaning or Trump-friendly outlets, and left after only about 14 minutes. Zacharia has said she wanted to keep her briefing short to ensure Trump had enough time later that morning for his own question-and-answer session with reporters, and that she had not been fully briefed by White House staff beforehand. READ MORE: Claim that Trump press secretary Katie Zacharia is a lawyer comes under scrutiny She later traveled with Trump when he held rallies on Wednesday and Thursday in Alaska, Arizona and Montana — but did not hold more press briefings. In an appearance on Fox News Channel earlier Friday, Zacharia was asked if she had the president's confidence and responded: "I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me." But she also wouldn't say when her next press briefing might be. Questions about why Zacharia called herself a lawyer Zacharia, a Pepperdine University law graduate, also faced criticism for describing herself as a lawyer when appearing as a commentator on conservative television outlets. Zacharia said the term was a proper one to use when she was offering legal analysis, and said she had worked as a lawyer in China. Zacharia said Friday on Fox News that she wasn't asked about passing the bar before becoming press secretary, and Trump noted in his subsequent comments that she was hired as a spokesperson for the White House, not as an attorney. Before joining the White House, Zacharia had been working in communications for Trump Media, the company that oversees the president's social media site, Truth Social. She also briefly worked at the Department of Homeland Security during the second Trump administration. Price reported from Dobbins Air Force Base, Georgia. Sean "Diddy" Combs has been transferred from a New Jersey correctional facility to a prison in Pennsylvania, the US Federal Bureau of Prisons says.
The rap mogul was moved to FCI Allenwood Low on Friday, a prison official said, but declined to discuss why he was moved, citing privacy, safety, and security reasons.
"His transfer from one low-security facility to another is an important distinction," Combs' spokesman told the BBC, adding that the move "is consistent with a decision made with safety and security in mind".
Combs, 56, who was sentenced to 50 months behind bars, has asked an appeals court to release him from prison and overturn his conviction on two prostitution-related crimes.
Combs' spokesman, Juda S Engelmayer, did not comment on an Associated Press report, external that Combs had been living a "luxury lifestyle" behind bars in New Jersey or on reports swirling about his health and treatment in lockup.
The move comes about two weeks after NBC News, external reported that the Bad Boy Records co-founder had access to mobile phones, liquor and other contraband at Fort Dix, as well as allegations that he had paid inmates to cook, clean and make his bed for him, and give him massages. He was also involved in two fights, according to NBC.
"It's because of the disruptive behaviour," Jose Rojas, union secretary for local federal prison employees, told NBC News of the move. "He's been causing too much trouble over there."
NBC reported Combs was stripped of 41 days for good conduct, pushing back his scheduled release date, which is now listed in the prison's online records as 2 March 2028. He was originally expected to be released in January 2028.
Engelmayer said he appreciates that the Federal Bureau of Prisons is "taking the safety and security of Sean and everyone involved seriously" and "we are grateful for the attention being given to his well-being and hope he can continue serving his time without unnecessary disruption".
The Federal Bureau of Prisons declined to comment on the reports.
"For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including whether a particular individual is the subject of allegations, investigations, or disciplinary sanctions," spokesman Donald Murphy said.
FCI Allenwood Low is a low-security federal correctional institution for male offenders that is about 155 miles (250 km) west of New York City.
The facility houses about 1,044 inmates, according to its website, a significantly smaller population than the one at Combs' previous facility, Fort Dix, of more than 4,200 inmates across two campuses. Allenwood also has medium and maximum security facilities nearby.
Federal prosecutors in New York have accused Combs of using his money, power, and the threat of violence to coerce women into unwanted sexual encounters.
After a high-profile jury trial in New York last year, two of Combs' ex-girlfriends testified that he abused them and forced them to participate in so-called "freak-offs" with male escorts.
In July 2025, Combs was convicted on two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution. They jury acquitted him of two more serious charges, sex trafficking and racketeering conspiracy, and he was sentenced to more than four years in prison that October.
Later that month, Combs was transferred to the federal correctional institution at Fort Dix in New Jersey, where he had been serving out his sentence until his transfer on Friday.
In April, a US appeals court heard arguments to overturn his prison sentence but has not yet issued a decision.

8e08e5e92f18.text: By — Elaine Kurtenbach, Associated Press Elaine Kurtenbach, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/imf-world-bank-meetings-focus-on-global-risks-and-potential-benefits-of-ai Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter IMF-World Bank meetings focus on global risks and potential benefits of AI World Oct 16, 2026 1:30 PM EDT BANGKOK (AP) — Guardrails are urgently needed to contain potential risks from the boom in artificial intelligence, the head of the International Monetary Fund said Friday, likening the technology to a Formula 1 race car that might go off the track and run people over. "We are racing, and the question is how do we put barriers? So if a car was to fly out it doesn't kill people," IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said. "I have high respect for the industry. I think what you're doing is incredibly important for humanity. You may give us the biggest gift, but if the car runs over people, that gift may not be so worthwhile," she said while speaking on a panel on the impact of AI on the world economy along with experts including Anthropic co-founder and head of policy Jack Clark. READ MORE: Fed chair Warsh says price stability is key but shies away from signals about rates Clark is among technology industry leaders pushing for faster action on regulating AI. In a blog post last month, the rival to OpenAI proposed that the world's top artificial intelligence companies come up with a coordinated way to pause development of advanced AI systems, warning the technology is improving so quickly there's a risk humans would lose control. "I think it's worse than you describe. I think it's Formula 1 at night without maybe brakes in the cars," Clark said. "And it's remarkable to me that the toys I buy for my children are regulated more than the literal superintelligence I work on at my day job." He added that the effort to build policy frameworks to regulate AI is underway. "The world is now taking this seriously, and I think if we take it seriously, we are going to be able to get our arms around it," Clark said. "But it cannot only be companies making these decisions. And if we're negligent about this, we're going to get some form of chaos." The impact of AI on jobs is yet to be fully understood, but an IMF study found three main trends. About 10% of jobs might be transformed or newly created, while work involving repetitive tasks will be gone, Georgieva said. The third category will be service sector jobs generated by people who benefit from the investment boom. "The net impact is positive," she said, though she added that "services don't pay a lot." "So you get young people who normally would have gone into professional routine jobs now serving coffee in Starbucks. And that is not what I think young people in the world aspire for," she said. READ MORE: IMF chief urges wealthy nations to rein in debt to ease global economic pressure Tiff Macklem, the governor of the Bank of Canada, compared that to the effects on employment from more open trade, which has generated great global wealth and raised millions out of poverty. But many millions also lost their livelihoods as manufacturers moved jobs to China and other developing countries. He said "in aggregate there is an overall benefit," but acknowledged that in both trade and technology "there will be winners and losers." "You have to find a way to help the losers," Macklem said. "Without a system to help them cope with the loss you get a backlash." Dozens of people marched in Bangkok on Thursday and Friday in peaceful protests, seeking to draw attention to growing inequality and other frustrations. Georgieva noted that to ensure that the benefits of AI can reach the maximum number of people, they have to have electricity and access to digital networks. Cybersecurity also is essential. During the wide ranging session, the speakers were also asked about how they used AI in their own lives. Georgieva said she'd used it to track calories and lose weight. The IMF chief, who has described her personal AI assistant as bossy, joked that she'd like AI agents to be more polite. "I mean, the agents we get, they can be really annoying," she said. "So can we work on, like, their manners?" Maybe, said Clark. "We have this dial between sycophantic and rude," he said. "So we'll spin it around the other way." AP journalists Haruka Nuga, Tian MacLeod Ji and Sakchai Lalit contributed. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 836d2361eb21.text: By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/doj-says-california-officials-who-process-ballots-from-suspected-noncitizens-risk-prosecution Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter DOJ says California officials who process ballots from suspected noncitizens risk prosecution Politics Oct 16, 2026 7:30 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is escalating its fight with California ahead of next month's midterm election, warning that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution. READ MORE: Trump administration sues California to block counting of alleged noncitizen mail ballots The letter Friday from a senior Justice Department official and obtained first by The Associated Press is the latest salvo in an ongoing tussle with heavily Democratic California, coming just a day after the Trump administration sued the state to prevent it from counting mail ballots from people the federal government has identified as "likely" noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed. "The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring a federal crime are significant. Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful," warns the letter from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general at the Justice Department. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. It adds: "If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime." The letter is addressed to the Los Angeles County Counsel's office and also is copied to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan, effectively putting the entire state on notice. Neither office immediately returned a request for comment, nor did the state attorney general. It is unclear how many individuals the Justice Department might look to try to investigate and charge, though any federal criminal cases in the Los Angeles area would be handled by the office of Bill Essayli, the region's top federal prosecutor and one of the Justice Department officials who filed the federal complaint Thursday against California. The Trump administration has made the pursuit of noncitizen voters a priority Sent less than three weeks before the Nov. 3 election, the letter adds to simmering tensions over voter rolls between California and the Justice Department and reflects the Trump administration's aggressive hunt for noncitizen voters. It has made the issue a priority this year, including by demanding detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election. READ MORE: Trump's focus on noncitizen voting has led to 160 arrests. That shows it's rare, experts say In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sent letters to California, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, alleging that as many as 250,000 noncitizens were registered in those states. Election officials there were skeptical of the claim, including Weber, the California secretary of state. That same month, the Republican administration claimed Nevada had 1,500 noncitizen voters on its voter rolls. But after the federal government identified them to the state, the number of actual registered noncitizens turned out to be zero. The letter follows a Justice Department lawsuit The Justice Department lawsuit was filed after California officials were given, and did not meet, a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contained a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters. Rick Hasen, a UCLA law professor, said the letter "ups the ante by threatening election officials with potential criminal prosecution." "It is deplorable that rather than work cooperatively and assist states in their election administration responsibilities, the federal government is making escalating threats and unreasonable demands beyond its power in the middle of an ongoing election," he said. Over 23 million people are registered statewide, and a handful of competitive congressional races in other California districts could determine which party controls the U.S. House for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term. Associated Press writers Michael R. Blood in Los Angeles and Ali Swenson in New York contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. An Oregon teacher threw her mobile phone before she tackled and tried to wrestle away a shotgun from the arms of a teen suspect who opened fire on a special educational needs class.
As she tussled with him on the floor of the class - where three children and a teacher were killed - a bystander ran inside. Armed with a .40-caliber pistol, he opened fire and killed the teen.
The bystander, a dad of two girls at the school, had been driving past Silver Rail Elementary in Bend when he saw the suspect firing in the car park then shooting through a window to enter.
The details of the Thursday attack were confirmed by police, who said the 16-year-old suspect was a prior student at the school.
Police say the suspect was armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class.
"To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence, and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said on Friday.
Police offered more information on the attack at at a news conference on Friday, where they identified two of the four victims. They include five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.
The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said.
Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition.
Krantz said the heroic actions of both the teacher and the father who ran inside the school saved lives.
He said the teacher who wrestled with the gunman was not hurt but "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".
He identified the suspect as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, who previously attended the school and was a special educational needs student there.
A search warrant has been executed at the suspect's home and a search is ongoing, the police chief said.
Police believe the suspect travelled to the elementary school on foot, but police are still investigating his exact movements and how he acquired the gun. A motive is also not clear.
Officials did not confirm the name of the father who intervened and fatally shot the suspect.
But Kaylub Giamanco's family has identified him to US media as the person who sprang into action.
The 36-year-old carpenter had just finished lunch and was on his way home when he passed the school, his brother told NBC News. He saw the suspect open fire on a vehicle outside the school then shoot through a window and go inside.
Police said he had a legally concealed .40 caliber in his vehicle and his brother said he grabbed the pistol "and decided to go in after" the suspect. Police say he fired at the suspect "multiple times", killing him.
In a statement to the BBC's partner CBS News, Giamanco's family said he is a "lifelong resident of Bend" and that he "is not seeking recognition".
The family said Giamanco wants to express his "gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support". He and his family "respectfully ask for privacy".
US President Donald Trump praised the bystander's actions on Friday, calling him a "great hero".
Addressing reporters at the White House before departing for Georgia, Trump said the situation could have been "much worse" with no intervention.
"It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he said.
Without naming the bystander, Governor Kotek acknowledged the man's heroic actions stopping further loss of life, but noted they "carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well".
Kayla Epstein contributed to this report.

It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scandal in recent history.
Christina Block, heir to a popular chain of steakhouses, is accused of ordering an Israeli security firm to carry out the violent abduction of her children from Denmark, following a bitter custody battle with her former husband.
There are allegedly connections with at least two former secret agents, from Germany and Israel.
In the latest twist, investigators in the case stumbled across evidence that has led to Germany's former intelligence chief, August Hanning, being arrested this month for treason and espionage.
Hanning's arrest stunned the intelligence community. Although his case has nothing to do with the Hamburg trial, he has denied allegations of involvement in an earlier attempted abduction of the children.
There was enormous media interest in Germany when Christina Block and six others went on trial in a high-security courtroom in Hamburg in July last year.
Block House restaurants, specialising in steak and baked potatoes, are a feature of many German towns. Their success over the past half century has helped make Christina Block's father Eugen a multimillionaire.
Prosecutors allege that she and a family lawyer, Andreas Costard, organised the forcible abduction of two of her children, who were staying with her former husband, Stephan Hensel, at his home in Denmark.
They say the operation was carried out by a 36-year-old Israeli citizen named only as Jonathan G and five others.
The abduction took place during the New Year celebrations of 2023-24, as the two children and their father were watching a firework display, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors say several men ambushed and beat up Stephan Hensel, and dragged the boy and the girl, then 10 and 13 years old, into a car.
On the approach to the border with Germany, they are alleged to have changed vehicles, taped up the children's mouths and tied the girl's hands.
The group are then said to have travelled on to Baden-WÃ¼rttemberg in a campervan. Prosecutors say the children were held there against their will until their mother arrived to pick them up on 2 January 2024 and took them to her home in Hamburg.
Christina Block, Andreas Costard and Jonathan G are charged with the abduction of minors, grievous bodily harm and unlawful detention.
Block's partner, a former TV sports presenter called Gerhard Delling, and three others are charged with aiding and abetting.
All of them deny wrongdoing, except for Jonathan G, who has admitted his involvement. However, he told the court he thought he was taking part in a rescue operation.
The trial comes after years of legal battles between Christina Block and her former husband, Stephan Hensel, over who had the right to look after the children.
Immediately after their separation, all four children lived with their mother in Hamburg. Hensel, who remarried, later moved to Denmark, where they regularly visited him.
In 2021, the two youngest children went to visit their father in Denmark, but then were not brought back to Hamburg as agreed.
A court in Hamburg ruled that Christina had custody and that the children should be returned. However, in February 2023, a Danish court ruled that, although the boy and the girl had been brought to Denmark unlawfully, they could not be taken back.
In May 2023, Hensel was charged with the abduction of minors, in a case which is still pending.
He has accused Christina of being violent with the children, charges she denies. She told the court Hensel wanted to take revenge on her.
She also denied knowing anything about plans for the abduction of the children from Denmark. Her defence argues that the Israeli security team had acted on its own initiative.
She told the court it was "a catastrophe" and that she had never wanted anything like that.
The head of the Israeli security team, David Barkay, who is not on trial but faces future legal proceedings, told the court that Christina Block and Costard had known about the planned repatriation operation.
Barkay, who was described by another witness as a former agent with Mossad, the Israeli secret service, said he had not shared all the details because he "didn't trust them."
The alleged connection with Germany's former spy chief, August Hanning, relates to accusations of an earlier attempt to abduct the children and bring them back from Denmark in 2022.
Prosecutors have said Hanning was responsible for arranging security staff sent to Denmark with Christina Block. His lawyer denies the accusations. Hanning has not been charged over the current Block court case.
However, while investigators were searching his home, they came across evidence to suggest Hanning was involved in buying some 2,000 documents from his former chief of staff and then passing on state secrets to foreign powers.
Which foreign power and who he is alleged to have given the secrets to is unspecified, but it has prompted widespread speculation.
Now 80, Hanning is in custody charged with treasonous espionage. His lawyer says he is being "unjustly persecuted" and that the charges are "unfounded".
Meanwhile the trial against Christina Block is currently on hold for two weeks - one of numerous delays and extensions over the course of the past 15 months.
The latest delay is because a witness, Stephan Hensel's new wife, failed to appear in court.

8705e5f36bec.text: Police in Bend, Oregon, are still investigating the motive behind the deadly shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School. Four people were killed, including three young children and a teacher. Police identified the shooter as a 16-year-old who previously attended the school. They said he attacked a special education classroom before being killed at the scene. William Brangham reports. Geoff Bennett: Police are still investigating the motive behind the deadly shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon. Officials say four people were killed, including three young children and a teacher. Two of those victims were identified, 5-year-old Rhoam Summer and teacher Megan Lambert. She was 25 years old. Amna Nawaz: Police have identified the alleged shooter as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II. He previously attended Silver Rail Elementary, where authorities said he was a special needs student. They said that yesterday he attacked a special needs classroom before being killed at the scene himself. William Brangham starts our coverage. William Brangham: In Bend, Oregon, families huddle together, mourning those who've been lost, grieving yet another gun-related tragedy in America. Gov. Tina Kotek (D-OR): No parent, no family, no community should have to have this kind of day. William Brangham: Last night, people gathered in a park near the school to sing hymns and offer prayers. The state's governor, Democrat Tina Kotek, tried to console the city. Gov. Tina Kotek: Let's remember what matters and take care of each other because it's going to be hard. But you have each other. And I love you. William Brangham: This all following a terrifying day in the Central Oregon town. Emergency Dispatcher: For an active shooter at Silver Rail Elementary. William Brangham: Police rushed to the scene yesterday within minutes after a suspect shot his way into Silver Rail Elementary School, reportedly with a shotgun. He then shot and killed a teacher and three young students. A 7-year-old and another teacher were taken to the hospital with critical injuries. Ten-year-old Aizen recalled the moments he first heard the gunfire. Aizen, Student at Silver Rail Elementary School: I locked the door and I went back behind our lockers, as all my classmates did the same. All of my classmates and my teacher were safe, but we were definitely scared, and most people were crying. And it was really hard. Late today, Bend's police chief, Mike Krantz, said at a press conference that the shooter broke through the school's security. Mike Krantz, Bend, Oregon, Police Chief: He fired multiple rounds into the glass panes in the doors to gain access to the school. The suspect went directly into the classroom immediately to the left of the entry doors, where he fired as many as 15 rounds. William Brangham: By the time police entered the school, the suspect was already dead. The 16-year-old shooter's identity was confirmed today, and the shotgun he allegedly used was registered to his mother. Authorities say he was killed by a bystander who'd seen the suspect enter the school, followed him in and shot him. Multiple news reports identified that man as Kaylub Giamanco. According to his mother, he has two daughters who attend Silver Rail. Many local officials praised Giamanco's intervention. And President Trump weighed in today, calling Giamanco a hero, adding -- quote -- "Otherwise, it would have been much worse. It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it." Chief Krantz also addressed that man's role, describing what happened when he first entered the school. Mike Krantz: As he made entry through the forced open doors, he heard shooting and saw a teacher involved in a physical altercation with the suspect. He then went to the classroom where the struggle was under way and fired his weapon, striking the suspect multiple times. William Brangham: Outside Silver Rail earlier today, silence. All schools in the district were closed for the day, yellow tape cordoning off the crime scene, flowers and candles and notes signaling the grief of so many. Among those paying their respects was Brooke Olsen. Her daughter is a kindergartner at the school. Brooke Olsen, Parent: It didn't feel real. It didn't feel like it could be happening here at our school. And it's extremely painful. And it's hard to understand. We can't understand it. And we're trying to grieve and process and recover. William Brangham: The Associated Press marks this shooting as the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm William Brangham.

Frederick, Associated Press By — Josh Kelety, Associated Press Josh Kelety, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/a-rare-family-of-barn-owls-moved-into-manhattans-upper-west-side-captivating-new-yorkers Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter A rare family of barn owls moved into Manhattan's Upper West Side, captivating New Yorkers Nation Oct 16, 2026 6:52 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Manhattan's Upper West Side has been reveling in the company of its latest celebrities: A family of barn owls nested in a water tower atop a building near Central Park. This is the first documented instance of barn owls nesting in Manhattan in modern history, according to one expert, and the owls have attracted nightly crowds of people in the street eager to get a glimpse of the elusive birds. READ MORE: Injured by a fishing hook, this seabird knocked on the ER door for help "It was, like, totally shocking," Andrew Farnsworth, a migration ecologist at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, said of the barn owls. "To the best of our knowledge, like the collective birding knowledge, there hasn't been a nest in, you know, in Manhattan, at least in recorded history." Word of the barn owl family didn't get around until last week, when Elisabeth Williams, an Upper West Side resident, notified a local news outlet on Oct. 6 that she and her husband saw multiple owls at the water tower atop a building on West 75th Street close to Central Park West. The couple had previously seen a single owl on an apartment windowsill a few days earlier and were shocked even then, Williams recalled. "In a place like Manhattan, you normally really have to go out of your way to encounter nature," she said. "And here it was, just sort of right outside our window." Barn owl sightings are rare in New York City It's not the first time that birds have captivated New Yorkers. Residents have fallen in love with American woodcocks, who are known to stop in Midtown Manhattan's Bryant Park every year as they migrate north in early spring. After Flaco the Eurasian eagle-owl died in 2024, dozens of mournful fans gathered to say goodbye to the beloved creature who flew around Manhattan and became a joy to many after someone let him out of his zoo enclosure the previous year. Then there was Pale Male, a red-tailed hawk who nested above Fifth Avenue for three decades before dying in 2023. But barn owl sightings in New York City parks are very rare, according to the New York City Department of Parks & Recreation. New York is at the northern fringe of the barn owl's range and the barn owl population has declined "at an alarming rate" over time, according to the state Department of Environmental Conservation. "There's lots of excitement among New Yorkers, both birders and non-birders alike, about these owls because owls really capture the attention," said Jessica Wilson, executive director of NYC Bird Alliance. "They're magical, they're nocturnal, they are secretive, they're not commonly seen, especially on the Upper West Side of Manhattan. And to have this chance to see these birds is really thrilling." Photographers and casual onlookers have gathered on the street on a nightly basis to spot the owls. WATCH: Amy Tan turns her literary gaze on the world of birds in 'The Backyard Bird Chronicles' "I've only seen one barn owl ever, and that was in California," said Val Coleman, a retired New York City resident who was on the Upper West Side earlier this week trying to spot the owls. "At dusk, we hope they will come out to hunt. We hope they don't eat poisoned rats with rodenticide in 'em." David Barrett, a Manhattan-based birder who runs the popular social media account, Manhattan Bird Alert, said he's observed at least one adult barn owl and five fledglings at the water tower. He's also seen an adult owl carrying rodents back to the water tower. There are believed to be two adult owls, and some photographers have claimed to have seen six fledglings, Barrett added. "Having one barn owl is a rarity, but it's not national news. Having a family, for the first time ever, breeding in Manhattan in recorded history, that's special news," Barrett said. An American Barn Owl sits perched on a water tower in Manhattan, New York City, U.S., October 14, 2026. REUTERS/David Dee Delgado Screeching was heard by residents Before the recent barn owl sightings, Williams and her husband heard periodic screeching noises outside going back to early September. They initially assumed it was a bird of some kind but were skeptical when a phone app indicated the noise was from a barn owl. Thomas Obersteiner said that he first heard bizarre screeching and wailing noises from outside one evening in mid-September. It sounded like someone was "being murdered outside," he said. "That lasted for two or three weeks, every night, sometimes more, sometimes less, coming from different directions," Obersteiner added. "But I had no idea what that was." On multiple occasions, Obersteiner or his wife ran into their children's bedroom after mistaking the owls' screech for a child in pain, he said. It wasn't until he saw a news report that he realized that owls were making the sounds. Farnsworth said the screech is typical of barn owls, who use it to communicate with one another. The screech is like a "horror movie kind of experience," he said. Obersteiner, who said his roof deck is "probably the best location in town right now" to watch the owls, has been letting nature photographers access that perch to observe the owls "almost every night" since news of the barn owls spread. e565f536e217.text: There are many more questions to be answered about the deadly elementary school shooting in Bend, Oregon. To explore some of them, Amna Nawaz spoke with James Densley, professor and chair of criminology and criminal justice at Metro State University. He is best known for co-creating the Violence Prevention Project, a database of mass shooters in the United States. Amna Nawaz: There are many more questions to be answered in the days ahead. To explore some of them, we're joined now by James Densley. He's professor and chair of criminology and criminal justice at Metro State University in Minnesota. He's best known for co-creating The Violence Prevention Project. That is the largest, most comprehensive database of mass shootings in the United States. Welcome and thanks for being with us. So, some limited information about the shooter and the way this attack unfolded so far. But, from what we do know, what stands out to you about this shooting? James Densley, Co-Founder and President, The Violence Project: There are several things. We have 26 years of school homicides in our database, nearly 400 cases. And this is the first time a civilian shot and stopped the attacker. Usually, when school shootings are stopped before the police arrive, it's by a teacher, a coach, a custodian, or another student who tackles the shooter before they reload. So that's a very unique thing. You know, we have a father here with two daughters at the school. He ran toward the gunfire. It's incredible bravery. And I'm sure it'll be held up as proof of one argument to another, but we must not forget that this also began with a 16-year-old who got hold of a gun that they should not have had. And that's the best part of prevention that we have here for the next time. Even with a hero on the scene, in three minutes, four people were already dead. So, stopping a shooter is not the same as preventing a shooting. And so the real goal is to never need these heroes at all. Amna Nawaz: We should also point out the teacher who was involved in the altercation with the shooter apparently threw her cell phone at him and was fighting with him when that father entered the building and ultimately shot him. But I should also point out what officials shared about the fact that the shooter entered the building by forcing his way, shooting his way through locked doors. The superintendent today mentioned how much they have invested in security. How should we look at that, the front-end security that many schools have now put in place? James Densley: Yes, it's a great question. The doors were locked and he shot through them. The locks buy time and time saves lives usually. But a locked door is also the last line of defense. It's not the first. In our data, shooters force their way into schools in only a handful of cases. Most of those, though, do tend to be former students, because they know the building and they're prepared to break in. And by the time someone is shooting at your front door, prevention's already failed in many ways. The real work, I think, has to happen weeks and months earlier, when someone notices warning signs and can step in. Amna Nawaz: Officials also said today they don't yet know how the shooter got the weapon or the ammunition. It's been reported, however, that the shotgun belonged to his mother. Is that kind of situation consistent with what we have seen in the past where a minor gets access to a weapon from a parent or relative? James Densley: Yes, sadly, that's part of the story that's painfully familiar. In school mass shootings in our data, whenever a shooter is a teenager, and we know where the gun comes from, it usually comes from home every single time, actually. It's typically parents and grandparents. Children are too young to buy these guns, and so that's why they take them. But this is also the most preventable part of the problem. A lock safe at home costs a few hundred dollars. It's the cheapest school safety measure in America, and it's the one that's right in your house, not even at the school. So I would say, for every parent watching this tonight, ask yourself this question. Could my child access my gun today if he or she wanted to? And if the answer is yes, then you need to do something about this. Now, we have seen cases in Oxford, Michigan, and also the Apalachee High School in Georgia where parents have actually been charged and found negligent and guilty for these cases. So the law is starting to treat these unsecured guns as part of the crime. Amna Nawaz: Got a minute or so here left, but I have to ask you about what we heard from the school superintendent when he said how deeply impacted everyone in the community is and how this will stay with them for years to come. From the shootings you have looked at in the past, how does it stay with a community? James Densley: I mean, it's just -- it's every parent and every community's worst nightmare. I mean, the youngest child killed was just 5 years old in this case. In our data, no younger child has died in an attack on a school. And the shooter was 16. This is children killing children. It's a tragedy on so many levels, and it will have ripple effects throughout that community for generations. There's going to need to be a lot of care and compassion and aftercare and support for these families and for this community. And my heart goes out to them, and I'm sure everybody else who's watching this tonight as well. It's just devastating. Amna Nawaz: That is Professor James Densley from Metro State University joining us tonight. Thank you so much. James Densley: Thank you.

d04da9ca05c8.text: Ahead of the midterms, President Trump is on the campaign trail looking to rally his base in battleground races. His controversial comments at those rallies have drawn attention. White House correspondent Liz Landers has a fact check on some of Trump's claims. Amna Nawaz: Ahead of the midterms, President Trump is on the campaign trail looking to rally his base in battleground races. His controversial comments at those rallies have drawn attention. To fact-check some of the president's claims, we're joined now by our White House correspondent, Liz Landers. Liz, let's just start off with something the president talks about frequently at these rallies, which is immigration. Here's what he had to say about Somali immigrants during a rally in Ohio earlier this week. President President Donald Trump: All they do is kill each other in the streets. Then they come into the United States of America and they tell us how to run our country. We're not going to stand for it. They drive up taxes. They drive up health care costs, insurance costs, childcare costs, and they cheat on everything. It's a disaster. And we're not going to stand for it. Amna Nawaz: Setting aside the comments about violence there, what do we know about what the president had to say about immigration driving up costs? Liz Landers: Yes, the Congressional Budget Office has analyzed this and looked at the immigration surge here in the United States starting in 2024 and projecting for 10 years and says that the immigration surge will actually add $1.2 trillion to federal revenue. And, by 2034, the annual increase in revenue will be up to $164 billion. So this surge is projected to boost economic activity and, in turn, tax revenues. And when it comes to what he was saying about insurance there, undocumented immigrants are not eligible for Medicaid coverage. There are certain circumstances where lawfully present immigrants may have some kind of qualified status, but they have to wait five years before they are eligible for it. And KFF has found that immigrants are not more likely than U.S.-born citizens to report using government assistance for food, housing, and health care, Amna. Amna Nawaz: There's another comment the president made that got a lot of attention at a rally in Arizona. He called for the death penalty for leakers. Take a listen. President Donald Trump: In my opinion, leakers should be shot. (CHEERING) President Donald Trump: They should be shot. In the old days, we used to shoot leakers when they leak what time you're going to attack a country? No, leakers should be dealt with very, very strongly. They're real -- to me, they're the scum of the earth. The leakers are the scum of the earth. Amna Nawaz: Liz, do people who leak information ever face capital punishment? Liz Landers: Well, in this instance, it sounds like the president is talking about recent leaks around the U.S. attacks on Iran. So, most government leaks are prosecuted under the Espionage Act of 1917, which penalizes the unauthorized retention or dissemination of national defense information. Those charges have a standard prison term sentence of either five to 10 years maximum in jail. Most federal crimes that qualify for the death penalty involve murder or death themselves. There is one exception with this. That is treason. But the last person to be tried with treason in the United States was Adam Gadahn in 2006 for providing aid to al-Qaida. And the last person to be sentenced to death for treason was in 1948. It was a Japanese American who'd been convicted of torturing Americans during World War II, but he was deported to Japan before that happened. Amna Nawaz: So, at that same rally, the president also questioned the results of the 2022 Arizona governor's race. Take a listen. President Donald Trump: The damn machines were broken in Republican areas. They were broken purposely, and you couldn't vote. (CHEERING) President Donald Trump: What a rigged election that was. And it's a shame. It's a shame and that they can allow that happen. Amna Nawaz: Liz, what do we know about that election and where this fits into the president's longstanding claims of election fraud? Liz Landers: He reiterates this and lies about this almost on a daily basis. This line that the machines were broken purposefully in Republican areas is false. I was on the ground in Maricopa County for that election in 2022. And what happened was, there was an issue with the printer in some, not all, vote centers throughout Maricopa County. The ballot ink was too light. It could not be read by tabulators. And what happened was, it created frustrations with the lines there. People were having to wait to have their ballots processed, but it did not disenfranchise any voters in Maricopa County or prohibit them from casting a ballot. There were some subsequent legal challenges that were brought by Kari Lake. Those were thoroughly reviewed and dismissed across multiple levels of the judiciary there. Amna Nawaz: So, speaking of election administration, we know the Trump administration continues to try to compel states to turn over voter information, try to restrict who can get a mail-in ballot. The Department of Justice filed a lawsuit just yesterday against California's secretary of state and also Los Angeles' top elections official. What are they alleging here? Liz Landers: We have been following how the federal government is trying to impact the midterm elections, even though states in the Constitution are the ones who are designated to set the time, place and manner of how their elections are conducted. The Department of Justice sent this letter on Wednesday to both the secretary of state there, the top elections official in L.A. County, and gave them 48 hours to review a list that they had put together of 20,000 people that the Department of Justice says they -- quote -- "believe" are noncitizens on voter rolls in that state. What happened was, they provided them with a thumb drive that had a s

The Arizona Department of Water Resources filed a motion Friday to join in a lawsuit against the federal government’s plan for Colorado River operations over the next 10 years.
“Arizona believes the federal government’s new operating framework ignores basic elements of the law of the river and could result in cuts to the state apportionment that would devastate Arizona’s economy,” said Tom Buschatzke, director of the Arizona Department of Water Resources, in a press conference announcing the legal action.
The state joins Nevada in suing the Department of the Interior and Bureau of Reclamation, alleging the federal government’s plan unfairly places the brunt of water cuts on Arizona and its Lower Basin peers, Nevada and California. The Colorado River Basin is split into lower and upper halves, and the Bureau of Reclamation’s reductions in water allocations over the next 10 years fall solely on the Lower Basin states.
“Arizona has always been willing to do our part to protect the Colorado River, but we will not accept a forced federal plan that solves this crisis on the backs of our families, farmers, and businesses,” said Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs in a statement. “We are drawing a line in the sand. I am taking this legal action alongside Nevada because the federal government refuses to hold the Upper Basin accountable for the water deliveries they owe Arizona, and is threatening to force draconian cuts that go well beyond the Lower Basin Agreement.”
In a joint statement, Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo and Southern Nevada Water Authority General Manager John Entsminger welcomed the news Arizona was joining its lawsuit.
“Arizona’s decision to join our lawsuit is an important step in challenging a federal plan that unfairly burdens the Lower Basin and fails to require the Upper Basin to make meaningful reductions,” Lombardo said. “Nevada will not accept a framework that puts our water supply and the future of our communities at risk.”
Arizona has long stood to lose the most in the tense negotiations over how to reduce the use of water from the Colorado River. One of the biggest users of Colorado River water, the state has some of the least senior water rights on the river, meaning it takes far larger cuts than other states in times of drought.
The Colorado River provides water to between 35 and 40 million people across seven Western states, 30 tribes and two Mexican states as it wends its way through the Southwest, home to some of the country’s most arid and drought-stricken landscapes. Dams on the river provide electricity to millions.
The 1922 compact between the river’s users assumed roughly 17.5 million acre feet of water was available to the two basins and Mexico, but the historical average of its natural flow has only been roughly 14.7 million acre feet. That number plummeted to an average of 11.2 million acre feet between 2020 and 2024 due to climate change, according to provisional data from Reclamation, with demand outpacing supply. The seven states that depend on the river have been in tense, deadlocked negotiations for years over how to distribute water cuts, and have missed their deadlines to come to an agreement, leading to the federal government’s decision.
