34d95b424642.text: By — Giovanna Dell'Orto, Associated Press Giovanna Dell'Orto, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/americas-politically-divided-jewish-community-braces-for-israels-elections Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter America's politically divided Jewish community braces for Israel's elections Politics Oct 17, 2026 2:41 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Jewish Americans feel they have a lot at stake in this month's contentious elections in Israel as three years of Mideast conflicts rile up emotions across the United States, from street protests to the midterm races. But they are sharply divided along political, religious and often generational lines on the preferred outcome in a vote that's perceived as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and held against the backdrop of the enduring trauma of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack, which triggered the war in Gaza. Please check your inbox to confirm. Netanyahu's supporters, especially among Orthodox Jews, believe he's protecting a country they love as central to their identity. Many liberal and younger Jewish Americans believe his policies have harmed Israel's global standing, engendering widespread anger that threatens them in the U.S., too. The moment is particularly fraught as antisemitism and antisemitic violence grow. Even harsh critics of Netanyahu's actions, whether over Gaza or Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank, argue that blame for attacks against Jews can't solely be laid at his feet. "A lot of American Jews are really torn. They want to shout from the rooftops, 'Stop the pogroms in the West Bank,' but also yell at everybody, 'Stop with allegations of genocide and double standards against Israel,'" said Rabbi Dan Levin of Temple Beth El in Boca Raton, Florida. Israel is important to Jewish Americans' identity Levin's large Reform synagogue is one of many across the U.S. hosting educational programs this fall because congregants feel "deeply emotionally invested" in the Israeli elections, even if, as non-citizens, they can't vote. Under Israel's complex, multiparty political system, the Oct. 27 election outcome is impossible to forecast. Polls suggest a tight race between a Netanyahu-led bloc and an alliance of rivals for control of the government. Many Jewish Americans have Israeli friends and family. More broadly, support for Israel is a key component of the religious identity of many U.S. Jewish adults ages 45 and older, particularly those who identify as religiously Jewish, according to a recent AP-NORC poll. READ MORE: Arab-led parties could decide the Israeli election, if anyone would partner with them The largest Jewish denomination in the United States is Reform, which emphasizes progressive values. Many Reform Jews see no contradiction between their liberalism and their Zionism — understood as the Jewish people's aspiration "to live as a free people in our land," said Rabbi Josh Weinberg of the Union for Reform Judaism, an umbrella group for more than 800 Reform synagogues in North America. But they worry about the growing power of the ultra-Orthodox in Israel's political and religious life, as well as settlement policies and the treatment of Palestinians in the West Bank, that they perceive as contrary to their values, Weinberg added. "If Netanyahu wins, I worry very much about the young generation of American Jews who may continue to be, I'll put it nicely, disenchanted, and who might just say 'OK, that's it. I'm giving up on Israel,'" he said. Only about 4 in 10 religious Jewish adults under 45 in the United States say that supporting Israel is "extremely" or "very" important for their Jewish identity, prioritizing instead other forms of connection, like celebrating Jewish holidays, according to the AP-NORC poll. Antisemitism is a key concern In the same poll, a majority of Jewish adults said prejudice against Jewish people is an "extremely" or "very" serious problem in the United States today. As the Israeli elections approach, many communities are worrying about their effects on antisemitism. "Some American Jews believe a different style of prime minister, one more similar to earlier ones who constantly talked about the desire for peace, will change the way American Jews themselves are viewed," said Jonathan Sarna, professor emeritus of American Jewish History at Brandeis University. Even Netanyahu critics, however, don't believe antisemitic acts would stop if Israel changes its government, especially when outrage at his administration's actions toward Palestinians is used to incite violence against all Jews regardless of nationality or political leanings. "'There is only one solution, intifada revolution' — we hear that as a call to rise up and use violence against Jews," Weinberg said of a popular protest chant referring to the violent Palestinian uprising. "So when someone says that in Ramallah, that's one thing. When someone says that in Minneapolis, what exactly are they calling for? That seems pretty clearly to us antisemitic." READ MORE: Scars from Oct. 7 fuel deep divisions over Netanyahu ahead of Israeli election But some think different Israeli policies would help stem the tide. "Somebody who decides that they're going to drive a car into a synagogue or attack Jews on the street, that is their responsibility. You can't blame that on Israel's actions," said Rabbi Jill Jacobs, CEO of T'ruah, a rabbinic human rights organization. "But … I think that it's going to be a very scary time for Jews around the world if there's another Netanyahu government and if it continues on its policy of expanding occupation, ethnic cleansing, and forever war." bb564c5aa1b9.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/no-kings-rallies-across-u-s-urge-voters-to-cast-ballots-early-ahead-of-midterms Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter No Kings rallies across U.S. urge voters to cast ballots early ahead of midterms Nation Oct 17, 2026 2:26 PM EDT Rallies organized by the No Kings network opposed to President Donald Trump were being held Saturday in cities and communities across the U.S., with an aim of getting people out to vote early in the midterm elections. The hundreds of planned events were being billed as nonpartisan, though they sought to build on nearly two years' worth of No Kings marches and demonstrations by people upset with Trump's presidency. People gather near the Lincoln Memorial during a "No Kings" protest as part of a nationwide day of action aimed at encouraging early voting ahead of the midterm elections, in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 17, 2026. Photo by Daniel Heuer/Reuters A band entertained what appeared to be a few hundred people in caps and coats Saturday at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C. Despite the chilly weather, many in the crowd danced to the tunes. "VOTE EARLY" and "HANDS OFF MY VOTE!" were among the many signs held aloft. At an Atlanta rally, City Councilman Michael Julian Bond told the crowd to urge others to vote ahead of the Nov. 3 general election. "The constitution gives you one power, right? That is the power to vote. Are you gonna use that power?" he asked. "You don't see Superman giving up his power," Bond continued. "You don't see Black Panther giving up his power. You don't see Wonder Woman giving up her magic lasso. So why would you give up your right, your power, your obligation to vote? Be a super hero, use your power. Go to the polls and vote." Demonstrators gather during a "No Kings: Vote Early" protest as part of a coordinated nationwide day of action aimed at encouraging early voting in the upcoming midterm elections in Manhattan, New York City, on Oct. 17, 2026. Photo by Eduardo Munoz/Reuters Trump has long been suspicious of mail voting, and has claimed without evidence that voting fraud cost him the 2020 presidential election. His administration sued California election officials Thursday, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for the midterm elections from people whom the federal government has identified as "likely" noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed. On Friday, the Justice Department warned that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution. Earlier Friday, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., and Dick Durbin, D-Ill., wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding that the Justice Department commit to not seizing ballots or other election materials before the midterm elections are certified. ed2e16984998.text: By — Susie Blann, Associated Press Susie Blann, Associated Press By — Katie Marie Davies, Associated Press Katie Marie Davies, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/zelenskyy-urges-support-for-new-u-s-sanctions-on-russia-put-on-hold-by-trump Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Zelenskyy urges support for new U.S. sanctions on Russia put on hold by Trump World Oct 17, 2026 2:02 PM EDT KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged supporters Saturday to speak out in favor of new U.S. sanctions against Russia, hours after President Donald Trump signed an executive order putting the sweeping restrictions on hold. The White House decision has heightened fears that Ukraine could be left exposed to Moscow's escalating attacks as winter approaches. READ MORE: Trump's decision to waive Russian sanctions outrages Congress, but no quick counter seen Overnight Russian attacks killed at least four people, including an ambulance driver, and wounded dozens, officials said. Ukrainian drones killed a woman in a Russian border region and disrupted flights at Moscow's airports, according to Russian authorities. In a social media statement, Zelenskyy called Trump's decision unfortunate but avoided directly criticizing the U.S. leader despite deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington in recent days. "A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelenskyy wrote. "This Act could have helped enormously – and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters." He separately thanked Democrats and Republicans who supported the legislation, saying that blocking it would encourage Russia to continue killing and that limiting Ukraine's ability to retaliate would not bring peace. "Nevertheless, we very much hope — and I personally hope — that the president of the United States of America will do everything possible to make (Russian President Vladimir) Putin stop the killing, stop the attacks on our energy infrastructure, and end this war," he said. Asked about contacts with Washington, Zelenskyy said Ukraine's lead negotiator, Rustem Umerov, had met Friday with U.S. presidential envoy Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law. Zelenskyy said the U.S. was working to arrange a three-way meeting involving him, Trump and Putin, potentially in the Middle East, Europe or the United States. Critics say Trump's decision helps Putin Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling Russia's 4 1/2-year-old war against Ukraine. The bill had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving. Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation. Trump told Congress that the pause was in the national interest but gave no further details. WATCH: Ukraine resumes strikes on energy targets, saying Russia never stopped its attacks Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who co-drafted the bill, criticized Trump's move, saying the president was turning his back on "the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies." "These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," Blumenthal said. Trump's unexpected decision comes a week after he had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine. Republicans and Democrats alike say the purchase will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine — without making a difference to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump's war on Iran. Starlink restrictions were planned, Zelenskyy says Zelenskyy said that Kyiv was investigating sudden speed restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, which is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication. The restrictions, imposed without warning early Thursday, cut the internet data connection when a communication terminal moves faster than 160 kph (100 mph). The cap forced Ukrainian drones to fly slower than usual, making it easier for Russian weapons to target or evade them. Zelenskyy said that there were no similar restrictions in European Union countries and that they apply only to Ukraine. "In other words, this is a planned operation," he said. It was unclear who was responsible. SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said this week that the U.S. government owns and controls the system, with decisions about its use resting with the U.S. military and, ultimately, the president. The Pentagon has not answered questions from The Associated Press about the restrictions. Trump told reporters Friday that he did not order restrictions on the system. He also doubted that the disruption came from Musk. "Well, I don't know if it was anybody, but it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been." Kyiv reports a 'massive' energy strike Moscow carried out a massive strike on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, targeting more than 15 sites across the country, Zelenskyy said. "The sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia's strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences," he said. Ukraine's air force said it intercepted all four of Russia's cruise missiles and most of the 332 attack drones it fired overnight. 4ea9c8e5a061.text: By — Rob Gillies, Associated Press Rob Gillies, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/how-alberta-separatism-went-from-fringe-cause-to-referendum Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter How Alberta separatism went from fringe cause to referendum World Oct 17, 2026 1:35 PM EDT EDMONTON, Alberta (AP) — For decades, Alberta separatism was a fringe cause. On Monday, voters in Canada's oil heartland will decide whether to take the first step toward a referendum on leaving the country. Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, is not voting to leave Canada on Oct. 19. Instead, voters will decide whether the province should remain in Canada or begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who called the vote but supports remaining in Canada, has said that support for starting the separation process, which was around 23% in a recent poll, is "still too high for my liking." READ MORE: Prime Minister Mark Carney says U.S. is trying to break Canada as Alberta votes on separation path Alberta has long feuded with the federal government over oil and federal power. Liberal prime ministers Pierre Trudeau and, decades later, his son Justin became deeply unpopular in the province over energy policy. Justin Trudeau's government imposed a national carbon tax and other climate measures that Alberta leaders said hurt its oil industry. Yet separatist parties typically drew only 1% or 2% of the vote, former Alberta Premier Jason Kenney said. Then came the pandemic and the Freedom Convoy, which paralyzed parts of Ottawa, the Canadian capital, and blocked major Canada-U.S. border crossings. "They needed a new cause," Kenney told The Associated Press. "And it naturally morphed into separatism." Pandemic-era restrictions supercharged separatism Men wave Alberta's provincial flags before Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney attends a Forever Canadian Rally, ahead of a non-binding referendum on Alberta sovereignty, in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, on Oct. 16, 2026. Photo by Jennifer Gauthier/Reuters Jeff Rath, a leader of the independence movement, said federal vaccine rules preventing unvaccinated Canadians from flying were his breaking point. "If Trudeau won't let me leave Alberta, I'm just going to pick up my whole province and go," Rath recalled telling a friend. "COVID was really the straw that broke the camel's back." "A lot of people were radicalized by the convoy," he said. The 2022 Freedom Convoy began over vaccine requirements for cross-border truckers but grew into a broader revolt against pandemic restrictions. Kenney said people mobilized over anger at globalization, vaccines and pandemic restrictions, while social media allowed previously isolated activists to find one another and organize. READ MORE: Carney and Macron deepen ties as Canada turns toward Europe and away from U.S. dependence "They found each other and they found a cause," Kenney said. Kenney said the movement also became more professional, building organizations, raising money and drawing in political operatives with campaign and fundraising experience. He also sees substantial overlap between separatist activists and people who support Russian President Vladimir Putin or believe conspiracy theories about Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Kenney stressed he was describing activists, not typical separation voters, whom he characterized as frustrated Albertans sending Ottawa a message. Kenney said the MAGA movement has been "inspirational" for some separatist activists. He said they "tried to infiltrate with at least some success" the United Conservative Party he founded. Smith replaced Kenney in 2022 after appealing to United Conservative Party members angry over COVID-19 restrictions. "Literally, you can look at the players," Kenney said of the convoy and separatist movements. "It's the same people." Carney finds unusual support in Alberta Prime Minister Mark Carney has made getting Alberta oil to new markets a national priority and backs a proposed pipeline to the West Coast. His more business- and energy-friendly policies, along with his opposition to U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war and 51st-state rhetoric, have made the federal Liberal leader unusually popular in conservative Alberta. Kenney, one of the most prominent conservative critics of Trudeau's approach to Alberta, said Carney "speaks as an Albertan," understands the province's grievances and aspirations, and is moving in the right direction on energy. Rath called Carney a "formidable opponent," saying "every major politician" in Alberta and Canada is against the separatists and acknowledged an uphill battle. He said he would be "thrilled" with more than 30% of the vote — well short of a majority. "Canada is facing real threats to our economy, to our security, to our way of life," Carney said. "We have to be strong and we are stronger together." Activists go to Washington Alberta sends roughly 90% of its crude oil exports to the United States, and separatists have taken their campaign directly to Washington. Rath confirmed he and other independence advocates met with U.S. State Department officials three times and presented a document outlining what an independent Alberta could offer the United States. Rath claimed people involved in the meetings were going directly to the White House and that a possible oil pipeline through the U.S. to the Pacific was "literally a topic of our last meeting with the U.S. State Department." The vote is a decision for the people of Alberta." Americans head to the polls on 3 November to decide how the rest of Donald Trump's presidency will play out.
Thousands of races are taking place across the US, at different levels of government. But the main event for voters will be electing members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers that make up Congress.
Both of them are currently controlled by the Republicans, the president's party. The success or failure of Trump's final two years in office could rest on the outcome.
Here's our visual guide to where the battle for power will be won and lost - from approval ratings, to key races and issues and the huge amount of money being spent.
Midterms come at bad time for Trump
One of the reasons the opposition Democrats have a chance to take back Congress is the president's low approval rating, which is a good indicator for how well his party could perform.
He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but it quickly fell into the 40s.
It was hovering around 42% when Trump decided to launch air strikes with Israel against Iran at the end of February this year but it fell below 40% shortly afterwards. It is currently sitting at about 37%.
Eight years ago, Trump's approval rating was significantly higher at this point in his first term, at 43%. Joe Biden's at the same point in his term was at 40%. In both cases, the sitting president lost control of the House in the midterms but kept hold of the Senate.
But Trump's poor ratings help explain why Democrats are hopeful of winning both chambers of Congress and why they are setting their sights on states that Republicans have won consistently in recent years.
The battle for the House
The current Republican majority in the House of Representatives, the lower chamber, is as thin as it gets - they have 218 representatives, which is the exact number needed to have control, plus one independent who votes with them.
Members of the House serve a two-year term so all 435 seats are up for election in November.
But most districts are not considered competitive because the party that holds them has such solid support that there is only one likely winner.
The Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, suggests that just 21 districts are "toss-ups" that could be won by either party.
Of those 21 toss-ups, 16 are currently held by Republicans and five by Democrats. If the Democrats win four of those on top of 29 districts classed as likely or leaning Democratic, they will win the House.
Historically, the midterms see a high number of seats changing hands in the House, usually in a protest against the White House. The average number lost by the president's party is 27, according to data, external going back to 1934. Of those 23 elections, the president's party has only made gains in three.
The battle for the Senate
The Republicans have a slightly stronger hold on the Senate. They hold 53 of the 100 seats while the Democrats have 45 and two independents who also vote with them.
Members of the Senate serve six-year terms so roughly a third are up for election every two years.
Thirty-five seats are up for grabs in November but analysis by the Cook Political Report suggests that only seven of them are toss-ups that could go either way.
Of those toss-ups, six are currently held by Republicans and one by Democrats. The Democrats would need to win four of those seats, plus the four classed as likely or leaning Democratic, to hit 51 and take control of the Senate.
But winning a majority is no easy task for the Democrats.
They need to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, where polls suggest the race is tighter than Democrats would like between Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, and his Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent.
And they would also need to pick up seats in states that Trump won by double-digits in 2024, including Alaska, Iowa and Ohio.
But polls suggest they have a chance, even in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally.
What are the key issues for voters?
Trump pledged to "end inflation and make America affordable again" in his 2024 election campaign but the cost of living crisis is proving to be the key issue for voters.
The president proudly declared that gas was "now below $2.30 [Â£1.74] a gallon in most states" in his State of the Union address on 24 February. But the war with Iran began four days later, disrupting Middle Eastern energy supplies and causing gas to hit $4 (Â£3.03) in the US.
The war became increasingly unpopular as its consequences reverberated around the world and ultimately hit American consumers in the pocket. One poll carried out in August found 63% of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of the situation.
Other issues that voters say are important to them include healthcare and immigration.
Trump has recently touted his policies around immigration as a big success, citing significantly lower border-crossing figures than in recent years.
Many Democratic candidates are focusing on the high costs of US health insurance and the impact of Trump's legislation on access to the healthcare system.
Can Trump defy political gravity?
Most signs point towards a successful midterms for the Democrats, but it wouldn't be the first time that Trump and his party have outperformed polls if they do win more seats than expected.
One of the few things in their favour is their huge financial advantage.

An 80m (263ft) luxury vessel has been repeatedly spotted in satellite images off North Korea's Wonsan coast from July to mid-October this year.
What stands out is the 50m swimming pool along the deck, with a cluster of waterslides at one end.
After sitting idle for months at a maintenance facility, it relocated in early July to waters off a strip of coastline known as the Kalma Peninsula.
This is close to Wonsan, a seaside resort with a sprawling villa used by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and his family.
It was not the only large vessel on the move. A handful of others were also repeatedly seen near Kim's villa, in satellite images analysed by the BBC.
The vessels are widely believed to be used by Kim and his family. Former North Korean officials, defectors and experts say it would be difficult for anyone unconnected to the regime's leadership to own or freely use vessels of this size.
"In winter, they would keep them at the shipyard. When summer came, they would bring them out and move them to Kim Jong Un's villa or towards Kalma, and use them for swimming and recreation," says Ri Jong Ho.
Ri was once an official at the Workers' Party's Office 39, which is believed to be involved in raising and managing foreign currency for the leadership.
The wealth of those who sit at the top of the secretive North Korean dictatorship is just as hard to pin down as the country's economic figures.
The United Nations and others rely on estimates to classify North Korea as one of the world's poorest countries, with an especially large military budget that funds a sanctioned nuclear programme.
Most North Koreans, according to a 2025 UN report, live under "systematic, widespread and gross human rights violations" with total state control, widespread forced labour, and chronic food shortages that leave an estimated 40% of the population undernourished.
But the regime has long been known to live in luxury.
We don't know the cost of the vessels seen in the satellite imagery, but comparable luxury yachts run from tens of millions to over $100m (Â£75m). Kim's much smaller, 29-metre Princess yacht was previously estimated to be worth about $7m.
While vessel locations alone cannot definitively establish the family's whereabouts, their movements - which overlap with gaps in Kim's public appearances - point to activities that would otherwise remain out of public view.
Wonsan is where Kim Jong Un spent part of his childhood with his mother, according to biographers and intelligence reports, and one expert told the BBC the city has been associated with the family since his father Kim Jong Il's rule.
A defector who served for 13 years guarding residences used by then leader Kim Jong Il - through the 1990s to the early 2000s - told the BBC the villas around Wonsan were used as a retreat by the elite. He recalls seeing dozens of children and teens waterskiing during summer.
North Korean state media rarely publishes reports about Kim being on holiday, instead framing such visits as official inspections or guidance. But defectors interviewed by the BBC appeared to be aware that the family spent holidays in Wonsan, suggesting that at least some North Koreans knew about it.
North Korean state media also claims Wonsan is home to high-rise hotels, restaurants, shops, sports facilities and water parks, and can accommodate nearly 20,000 visitors.
State media and Russian outlets have published images of small groups of Russian tourists visiting the Wonsan Kalma resort, which opened in July 2025. Although developed to attract foreign visitors, the resort is also open to local tourists.
A South Korean news report, citing an unnamed source, says some locals were offered four-night tour packages for around $100, a substantial sum for most North Koreans. The country's per capita GDP - around $667 in 2024, according to the UN - is a small fraction of South Korea's $36,227.
For the majority of North Koreans, holidays are out of reach. And while a growing middle class does exist, they might not have much time for leisure.
Defectors told the BBC that workers, office employees and cooperative farmers are legally entitled to 14 days of annual leave, but this is rarely followed.
Taking consecutive days off to travel is unusual. People typically take weekend trips or travel during national holidays instead of designated "summer holidays".
Even if leave is granted, travel itself is restricted, with official permission required for people to travel outside their city or county. Moving freely is sometimes as much a luxury as the holiday itself.
The BBC tracked four large vessels around Wonsan, measuring approximately 50m, 55m, 60m and 80m. All four vessels repeatedly appeared around Kim's Wonsan villa this year.
The largest vessel showed the clearest activity, moving from the dock to the waters off the Kalma Peninsula, where it has been since July.
Two of the other vessels - 50m and 55m - were repeatedly seen until the end of August around Tae and Sin islands, close to Wonsan.
Satellite images also showed four smaller boats alongside the 50m vessel.
Satellite imagery expert Jeong Seong-hak said the smaller boats ferried people, fuel and supplies to the larger vessel, adding that small islands like Tae and Sin offered "secluded maritime retreats where privacy can be maintained away from public view".
The 60m vessel was repeatedly seen near Kim's Wonsan villa until as recently as last week.
Though North Korea has never publicly disclosed the vessels' official ownership, BBC's analysis of historical satellite imagery found a large vessel with the same distinctive characteristics in Wonsan in 2002, when Kim Jong Il ruled North Korea.
Former NBA star Dennis Rodman, who visited the North in 2013, told The Sun that he had spent much of his seven-day visit with Kim Jong Un around Wonsan, where they went jet-skiing and horse riding.
He also described a 60m vessel they used as a cross between a ferry and a Disney boat. It is not clear if t

2854e798b24c.text: By — Shefali Luthra, The 19th Shefali Luthra, The 19th Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/the-republican-governor-candidates-walking-back-some-of-their-abortion-stances Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter The Republican governor candidates walking back some of their abortion stances Politics Oct 17, 2026 5:23 PM EDT This story was originally published by The 19th. Republicans running for governor across the country are backing away from abortion bans they once endorsed. U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor in Wisconsin, calls his state's 20-week abortion limit "settled law." Just three years ago, he co-sponsored a bill that would have banned abortion six weeks into pregnancy. Stacy Garrity, the GOP's candidate in Pennsylvania, has said during her campaign that she would "respect" the state's current law, which allows abortion until 24 weeks of pregnancy. Four years ago, she called on abortion opponents "to engage and make a difference" in state laws after the fall of Roe v. Wade. In Kansas, where abortion is legal until 22 weeks, Republican Ty Masterson has demurred when asked if, as governor, he would support a statewide referendum to eliminate the Kansas constitution's abortion protections. Masterson had previously spoken at protests in opposition to reproductive rights and won the backing of state and national anti-abortion groups. The candidates' retreat suggests that, even as reproductive rights fade from the national spotlight and polls show voters are far more likely to prioritize cost-of-living concerns, the political ramifications of pushing for new abortion restrictions remain substantial. The rhetorical distancing also moves political conversations away from an issue that overwhelmingly energizes Democrats. "That might be their strategy there, to try to demotivate Democratic turnout in the state to take abortion off the table as a voting issue," said Ashley Kirzinger, a pollster at KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research, polling and journalism organization. That's especially true in tighter races such as those in Wisconsin and Kansas, she said. Tiffany's, Garrity's and Masterson's campaigns did not reply to requests for comment. The 19th contacted multiple Republican-aligned pollsters who also did not immediately respond. WATCH: How abortion politics is blocking progress in women's healthcare About 60 percent of Americans believe that abortion should be legal in most or all cases, including about two-thirds of independents, according to a poll from The 19th and YouGov. That said, pushing for abortion restrictions has never been broadly popular. Even before Roe v. Wade was overturned in 2022, Republicans seeking general election typically would not campaign overtly on abortion bans, said Molly Murphy, a pollster and president of Impact Research, a Democratically-aligned polling firm. "It would get discussed in donor meeting hot mics, endorsement questionnaires, etc, but candidates wouldn't run on the fact that they'd ban abortion," she wrote in an email. Voters largely don't consider abortion to be "settled law," said Celinda Lake, a longtime Democratic pollster, noting that the share of voters opposing abortion bans has increased since the fall of Roe. "They feel like, 'Wait a minute, it can be taken away again.'" In some races, Democrats and their allies are trying to push abortion rights back under the microscope — a strategy geared toward energizing liberal voters, Kirzinger said. Wisconsin's Democratic nominee for governor, David Crowley, has said that, if elected, he would work with the state legislature to enshrine abortion rights into the state constitution — though it's not clear how expansive that protection would be or whether it might supplant the state's 20-week cutoff. Pine Tree State Prosperity, a political action committee associated with the national Democratic Governors Association, is running advertising in Maine that highlights anti-abortion remarks made by Bobby Charles, the state's Republican pick for governor. The Democratic nominee, Hannah Pingree, has led by double digits in recent polls. Charles' campaign did not reply to a request for comment. John James, has said that abortion is "decided." Four years ago, James said he opposed abortion in all cases, and he has compared the practice to genocide. His campaign did not reply to a request for comment. James' running mate, Jay DeBoyer, recently suggested leveraging a state constitutional convention to enact a 12-week abortion ban in Michigan, according to recordings of the remarks reported by The Detroit News and Michigan Advance. DeBoyer has since said publicly that abortion is a "settled" issue in Michigan, where voters in 2022 amended the state constitution to protect abortion before fetal viability. Some gubernatorial candidates are still pushing for abortion restrictions, albeit far less ambitious ones. In New Mexico, where Democrats are expected to keep control of the governor's mansion and already control both legislative chambers, Republican candidate Gregg Hull said he was "fully committed" to working with Texas Gov. Greg Abbott to reduce the number of Texans coming to the neighboring state for abortions. Hull has repeatedly called himself "pro-life" but also said that he would not change the state's abortion law, which imposes no time limits on the procedure, without legislative support. 07ccf07d27b8.text: By — Joseph Krauss, Associated Press Joseph Krauss, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/houthi-strikes-on-saudi-arabia-show-the-yemeni-rebels-growing-strength Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia show the Yemeni rebels' growing strength World Oct 17, 2026 5:04 PM EDT Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have put their growing military capabilities on display in recent weeks, repeatedly striking Saudi Arabia's main international airport hundreds of miles (kilometers) away and seizing territory inside Yemen near a key shipping chokepoint. At various times over the last decade, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, the United States, Britain and Israel have carried out punishing air raids on the rebels — only to see them grow even stronger. READ MORE: Saudi diplomat says Iran is encouraging Houthi escalation of attacks on the kingdom The Saudis have struggled to counter the latest attacks, even with far superior U.S.-supplied arms. A senior Saudi diplomat told reporters this week that Iran was encouraging the escalation and that over the summer the Houthis had spurned an offer to negotiate. The Houthis operate in a large and mountainous territory where they can disperse fighters and military infrastructure while threatening major oil facilities and key trade routes. Iran and its allies in Lebanon and Iraq provide expertise, training and sophisticated weapons, according to U.N. and other experts. A recent report found that the Houthis have tried to source parts from Chinese suppliers that are used to make precision-guided ballistic missiles with a range of roughly 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers). The rebels are increasingly well-armed The Houthis already have a wide array of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones — many resembling Iranian models — that can reach all the Gulf states as well as Israel. They have also used sophisticated anti-ship missiles and naval drones to strike vessels in the Red Sea, threatening a critical trade route. Iran denies arming the Houthis, which would violate a U.N. embargo. China has not directly responded to the latest report but says it has a "prudent and responsible" approach to military exports. Smuggled Iranian weapons and parts have been seized from numerous Yemen-bound shipments, and a report by U.N. experts in 2024 documented extensive military ties between the Houthis, Iran and its other allies. READ MORE: Iran-backed Houthis strike Saudi oil company Aramco's headquarters, officials say That report estimated that the Houthis had recruited up to 350,000 fighters by 2024, up from just 30,000 in 2015, when Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war against the Houthis and imposed a naval blockade. The Houthis can use relatively inexpensive drones and missiles to target oil and other infrastructure just across the border in Saudi Arabia, as well as tankers off the coast. And while Iran is believed to supply cutting-edge components like guidance systems, the Houthis can manufacture much of their weaponry domestically, and at a much lower cost than the state-of-the-art interceptors used by the Saudis. There are suggestions they may even be using artificial intelligence to try to build better missiles. Saudi Arabia has struggled to respond Saudi Arabia boasts an array of U.S.-supplied weapons, including sophisticated aircraft as well as advanced missile defenses used against Iran at the height of the war last spring. But with supplies of high-end interceptors under pressure, it's unclear how long it can ward off attacks — not only from the Houthis, but from Iran-backed militias in Iraq blamed for an attack that briefly shut down an east-west pipeline crucial for oil exports. In recent days, the Houthis have repeatedly struck King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh, leading to a wave of flight cancellations. They have also hit the headquarters of the national oil company, Aramco. Both are several hundred miles (kilometers) from Yemen. At least 19 people have been killed, school classes have been canceled, and the disruption threatens the kingdom's ambitious plans to transform itself into a global hub for business, tourism and sports. Vulnerable assets are scattered across Saudi Arabia's sparsely populated territory, which is roughly three times the size of Texas. Its border with Yemen stretches more than 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) through rugged desert areas. Airstrikes have had limited effect The Houthis, a Shiite religious and political movement rooted in northern Yemen, are attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports Yemen's internationally recognized government in the civil war. The Sunni kingdom, which has long feared the emergence of a well-armed ally of Shiite Iran on its border, joined the war in 2015 after the rebels seized much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa. Over the next seven years, Saudi Arabia carried out waves of airstrikes against the Houthis, often killing civilians. An array of Yemeni government forces and southern separatists struggled to push the Houthis back, and the battle lines moved little before a 2022 ceasefire. READ MORE: Why Saudi Arabia's military has struggled to defend the country against Houthi attacks The following year, after the outbreak of the war in Gaza, the Houthis began attacking Red Sea shipping in what they said was a blockade of Israel. The U.S. and the U.K. launched waves of strikes against the Houthis beginning in January 2024. U.S. President Donald Trump ordered an intensified air campaign early last year, with some 2,000 munitions dropped on over 1,000 targets, a U.S. military official told The Associated Press at the time. After weeks of U.S. strikes, the Houthis agreed to stop attacking American ships. Demonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row.
Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests.
The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time.
Protests which began in the summer have grown into a wider anti-government movement, with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration.
Many of the protesters in central Tirana wore gas masks or face masks, while volunteers handed out syringes of saline eyewash to reduce the pain from the tear gas which billows down the street.
The constant boom of petrol bombs could be heard exploding on Saturday.
During the afternoon, the focus of the protests shifted to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama on the city's main boulevard.
Here the crowds swelled to far larger numbers than on previous days.
Riot police faced a steady hail of cobble stones and fireworks, and responded with barrage after barrage of tear gas, some of the canisters landing far back in the crowds, causing panic.
Incensed by the gas, the crowds waited for it to clear, then renewed their attacks.
Black smoke from a burning vehicle and the sirens of police cars and ambulances split the afternoon.
As dusk fell, police special forces arrived to reinforce the riot police.
Many people have been injured on both sides, 80 people have been charged with disorder so far, and hundreds more have been arrested, or are under investigation.
The centre of the Tirana looks increasingly like a war zone, scattered with broken glass and burnt debris.
George, a 19-year-old medical student who works as an electrician to fund his studies, stood near the burnt-out education ministry building, a scarf wrapped round his face and goggles covering his eyes.
He is one of the thousands who have taken part in the increasingly intense protests which began in early June.
In his gloved hands he clutched two rocks intended for the police.
Asked if he was concerned about injuring them, he said: "We have mothers too. We have family too.
"We were peaceful for 135 days. Now we are trying to do like in Franceâ¦ we are trying to make a revolution.
"Our government doesn't want peace, so we are using violence."
Many of the protesters were even younger. Klea, 17, is in her first year of university in Tirana.
She said: "All the students are boycotting their university classes and left school to fight for our rights."
She alleged there were provocateurs among the protesters, smashing up stores and banks, to discredit the demonstrations.
Socialist Party Prime Minister Edi Rama has been in power for 13 years and has dominated Albanian politics, much like his main rival Sali Berisha, of the opposition Democratic Party, did for decades.
The students say they are against "the whole corrupt political class". So what is the alternative?
Osman Stafa, a prominent journalist for the News24 channel, who also describes himself as an activist for change, called for a "neutral, caretaker government for one year, to organise new elections".
The irony for the wider European community during this latest wave of unrest is that Rama has long been viewed favourably by the EU, which Albania aspires to join.
In a social media post on Saturday morning, he urged Albanian to "not forget that we have achieved extraordinary things".
He blamed the protests on the opposition Democratic Party, and on what he called "the sinister agenda of foreign actors, intent on halting our progress" towards EU membership, which he has promised by 2030.
He did not name which "foreign actors" he had in mind.
The latest protests have seriously tarnished Rama's carefully cultivated image as a charming leader, steering his country towards prosperity.
Parallel to the protests, a series of investigations by the special prosecution service also threaten his rule.
Set up under EU and US pressure in 2019, the prosecutors recently arrested the powerful secret service chief Vlora Hyseni.
She stands accused of helping a prominent businessman, former government official, and personal friend of Rama, Ergys Agasi, evade justice. The 39-year-old is under arrest.
Agasi, speaking through his lawyer, denied the allegations against him and said he had nothing to do with corruption. Hyseni told prosecutors that she contacted Agasi to try to recruit him to the intelligence services.
Several Albanian media outlets claim he acted as an intermediary between the prime minister and organised criminal groups.
Rama has admitted that he knows Agasi but denies any knowledge of illegal transactions.
"Edi Rama is caught between a rock and a hard place," Lutfi Dervishi, a political analyst and university lecturer, told the BBC.
"He's the victim of his own success. By concentrating so much power in his own hands, he has made himself the only person the people blame for their grievances."
Rama's Socialist Party has a comfortable majority, with 83 out of 140 seats in the Albanian Parliament. The next parliamentary elections are not due till 2029.

Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against education standards and the cost of living.
At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence" alongside an estimated 550,000 taking to the streets.
In Paris, there were significant clashes into the evening with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon on crowds.
Buildings were set alight in the capital and other areas, including in Limoges where a large fire in the town hall caused the roof to partly collapse.
Looting broke out in several cities, with widespread vandalism targeted against city halls and businesses also reported.
Sixty law enforcement officers were injured, including two who were taken to hospital unconscious, France's Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said.
In Paris, the main march appeared to be largely peaceful during the afternoon. A group of young people told the BBC they were "pacifists" who are "just trying to make things change, but nothing is moving".
However, as the day wore on some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles, including in iconic locations in the city centre like the Place de la RÃ©publique.
Shops were ransacked, at least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups.
Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons.
In Lyon, Mayor GrÃ©gory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy" for the city, telling BFMTV "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building".
Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze.
Fire crews also battled the fire at Limoges town hall, which the local prefecture said caused part of the building to collapse.
A young man "had his hand blown off by a grenade" in Saint-Ãtienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor RÃ©gis Juanico said on social media, adding: "Such a tragedy should never have happened."
The interior ministry said the protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers.
Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence.
Clothes and food shops were raided in Paris, while an Apple store in Lille was broken into and emptied.
Footage authenticated by BBC Verify showed a tourist train in Grenoble being driven by masked men along a narrow street in the city centre towards at least three riot police officers.
Hundreds of thousands of students have protested in recent weeks over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycÃ©es - secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.
On Saturday, their numbers were bolstered by trade union members and other protest groups.
These groups include the so-called gilets jaunes 'yellow vest' movement, who demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.
While France is no stranger to outbreaks of protest and disorder, this round comes as the country heads into a period of deep political uncertainty.
French President Emmanuel Macron will leave office next year and polls suggest April's presidential election could come down to a fight between the leader of the National Rally, Marine Le Pen, and Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon of the hard-left La France Insoumise party.
The latter took part in demonstrations in France and later accused police officers of "unleashing" on protesters, while condemning looting and arson.
France's Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu said his comments were "dangerous and cynical".
He earlier said police had faced "violence of extreme intensity" and some groups were using the protests as a "warm-up" for the presidential elections, adding: "No-one will impose their political agenda through violence."
Le Pen said "legitimate demands" voiced by protesters had been "held hostage by the far left", accusing MÃ©lenchon of fuelling the violence.
French President Emmanuel Macron said: "Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished."
The government has made apparent attempts at concessions, with Education Minister Ãdouard Geffray promising 3,000 extra supply teachers, during a television interview on 8 October.
However, the protests have continued and intensified.

At least 17 people have been killed and many more injured in a crush at an event in the Indian city of Kolkata to mark the Hindu festival of Durga Puja, officials say.
The incident occurred during sudden rainfall, which witnesses say prompted a surge of people to try to seek shelter.
West Bengal's Chief Minister Suvendhu Adhikari said a seven-year-old girl was among the dead, and that 25 people were being treated for injuries.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi described it as a "tragic" incident and said the regional government was providing help to affected families.
Six of the dead have been identified, Adhikari said.
A senior police official told the AFP news agency that an announcement caused "commotion" after it started raining and the crowd started "pushing, pulling and rushing forward and fell on the ground, leading to the stampede.".
Deadly crowd incidents, including during religious festivals, are not uncommon in India due to poor management and lack of adequate safety precautions.
Two years ago, 121 people were killed in Uttar Pradesh during a Hindu religious gathering.

A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys and called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating.
But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened and suggested it was part of a "coordinated campaign to smear Israel".
The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank.
The diplomats - from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church - had come to the largely Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah.
They were there to assess the situation on the ground after almost near daily attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to bring in their olive harvest.
Video footage from the scene showed masked settlers confronting the convoy. Reports suggest stones were thrown.
The Belgian authorities said a car from its consulate had a window smashed and a French mayor was assaulted. Video showed a man wearing a French tricolor sash slumped beside a vehicle.
Belgium's foreign minister Maxime Prevot condemned the attack and said Israel had a responsibility to bring those responsible to justice.
"Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," he said.
"As the occupying power, Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice.
"Impunity for violent settlers must end. Belgium will continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them."
Gideon Sa'ar, Israel's foreign minister, said he strongly condemned the violence by what he called "Israeli rioters". He said the foreign ministry was in contact with the ambassadors of the countries involved.
But he added: "Without detracting from the severity of the incident, it is unfortunate that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors' security."
The IDF said they "strongly condemn the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters."
"According to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack," they added.
But Netanyahu's office urged "caution before drawing conclusions" from reports about the attack.
It said the images on social media "do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility".
A statement continued: "Those circumstances remain under investigation. Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible."
It added that "these reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge".
Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux. The left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France told the AFP news agency the attack showed a tolerance by Israel's right-wing government for settler violence.
The mayor said the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground.
"It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged."
"The whole world needs to know what's happening there. For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here," he said.

Billionaire Tesla CEO Elon Musk is once again pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into a US election - this time with the aim of helping Republicans maintain their control of Congress.
Musk donated upwards of $200m (Â£150m) in the quarter that ended on 30 September, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings reviewed by the BBC.
The fillings were released with just over two weeks until the 2026 midterm election, where many races for the House of Representatives and Senate are close and Republicans risk losing their majorities in both the House of Representatives and Senate.
Musk also put significant money, $290m, and effort into helping elect President Donald Trump and other Republicans in 2024.
Here is where the richest person in the world has been donating this time around, and what it might mean for his businesses.
Most of the donations went to one group
The bulk of the money donated last quarter by the world's only trillionaire, $158m, went to the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) Pac, the filings showed.
It is one of the largest publicly known single political donations in US history, and some have suggested it is the biggest ever.
SLF is a super Pac backing Republican Senate candidates in tough races.
It quickly sent the money on to a group supporting Texas Republican Ken Paxton. The state attorney general, Paxton is at risk of losing to Democrat James Talarico in a race for a seat his party has held for decades. They have been polling neck and neck and the election's outcome is considered a bellwether for the future of Republican power.
Super Pacs are independent "political action committees" that can raise unlimited amounts of money and play a major role in funding US political campaigns.
Musk also donated more than $80m to the America Pac that he founded during the 2024 election.
Texas is a key focus for Musk
America Pac last quarter spent millions on digital communications, mailings and phone calls opposing Talarico, as well as thousands on political marketing to support Paxton.
At the same time, Musk donated another $10m to Lone Star Liberty Pac, a group primarily backing Paxton, records show.
The flow of money highlights a major theme for Musk: Texas.
In recent years, the tech CEO has been moving his business empire - including SpaceX, Tesla and X - to the southern US state after expressing frustration with operating in California.
Texas has offered Musk fewer government regulations and no state personal income tax and no corporate income tax.
Keeping politicians who favour looser government restrictions in charge, as Republicans typically have, could help maintain that environment for Musk.
And his big spending in Texas and in the Texas Senate race seems to point to Musk's understanding of that, political analyst Cayce Myers told the BBC.
"Republicans have a fundraising advantage this time, but fundraising by itself does not actually guarantee success," he said.
A broader trend for tech executives
For many voters this year, technology has become a top issue. People across the country are pushing for increased government oversight of artificial intelligence, data centres and social media.
That's something that has tech leaders like Musk developing closer ties to the Republican party, which historically has promoted lighter government regulation, Myers said.
"What [tech leaders] are looking at is a future where there is growing demand and call for regulation and I think they want to be in an advantageous position," he said. "We're seeing them shift, and fall behind Republicans."
Other tech leaders, such as OpenAI president and his wife Greg and Anna Brockman are also putting big money behind Republicans.
The couple donated $25m to the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc Pac last year.
Myer noted it's not just the tech sector, but industries like cryptocurrency and gambling where large sums of money are being donated in an attempt to exert influence.
"This is the idea of shaping the regulatory environment through contributions," he said.

How day of protests unfolded as disorder breaks out across France
An estimated 550,000 people took part in protests across France, demanding greater investment in education and action on the rising cost of living.
The demonstrations quickly descended into violence, with cars and buildings set alight and shops ransacked.
At least 1,200 people were arrested on Saturday as riot police deployed tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds.
The unrest follows weeks of student-led protests, with demonstrators joining forces to express growing anger over economic conditions and French President Emmanuel Macron handling of the crisis.
In a social media post, Macron denounced the violence and said that vandals and looters will be "prosecuted and punished".
BBC correspondent Adina Campbell reports from Paris.
Video editor: Zahra Fatima

- Published
Campaigners trying to examine the effects of the toxic waste scandal in Corby say they have found a presence of metals which could post a risk to human health.
Children in the Northamptonshire town have been born with birth defects, believed to have been caused when steelworks were demolished in the 1980s.
Charity Earthwatch Europe says trained citizen scientists have found potentially harmful levels of metal or metalloid at 52 freshwater sites across Corby.
The Environment Agency (EA) welcomed their work but said some metals occurred naturally and that its own evidence did not indicate "widespread or significant harm".
Earlier this year, Earthwatch Europe said its volunteers collected evidence that the presence of metals could harm aquatic life - findings that were disputed by the EA.
But this time, the group believes the samples show a potential effect on people.
Dr Sasha Woods, a scientific advisor for the group, said the results highlighted "where further investigation and remedial action may be needed".
"The findings indicate that some metals are present in freshwater at levels that could pose a risk to aquatic life, and in soil at levels that could impact human health, particularly in areas close to known historic waste sites," she added.
Earthwatch Europe said its trained citizen scientists were out collecting in July, which as well as the freshwater samples, included taking 28 soil samples.
It said at every freshwater site, at least one metal or metalloid was present, at concentrations exceeding the level where "no adverse ecological effects are expected".
Nickel was found in 28 freshwater samples and cadmium was detected in six, the charity said.
A spokesperson said the comparison between its summer and winter sampling indicated a "relatively constant source of pollution; likely groundwater and landfill leachate rather than urban run-off".
"Elevated concentrations of cadmium and nickel in freshwater, and cadmium and arsenic in soil, were largely confined to Deene Quarry and a former slag heap in Weldon," the group added.
Tracey Taylor, whose baby daughter Shelby-Anne died at four days old, has spent years campaigning for justice over the scandal.
In 2009, Justice Akenhead ruled in favour of 18 Corby families and that Corby Borough Council was negligent in managing the waste.
She hoped the new Earthwatch Europe report would mean "people are going to start to listen to us".
"It's got to stop," she said.
"I'm 30 years down the line, I don't need that apology, I don't need justice, but I will fight on for the children and the community of Corby, because the Corby community always come together and they support each other.
"They should not have to deal with this or be living with this on their land. It needs sorting."
Lee Barron, the Labour MP for Corby and East Northamptonshire, said "local authorities have a duty to inspect and identify sites where contamination is causing unacceptable risks".
He urged North Northamptonshire Council - which replaced Corby council in 2021 - to publish a plan "to make these sites safe".
An EA spokesperson said it was reviewing the Earthwatch Europe report alongside its own evidence.
"Our monitoring to date does not indicate widespread or significant harm to the freshwater environment across the Corby area," they said.
"We will continue to assess the evidence and take any further action needed."
A spokesperson for the council also welcomed the report and said it would "fully assess the data and supporting information".
"Residents can be assured that any credible evidence of a risk to human health or the environment will be thoroughly considered and investigated through the appropriate regulatory processes."

Two species of damselfly have been recorded for the first time in a woodland after the completion of a three-year project to restore habitat across seven nature reserves, a wildlife trust has revealed.
Work on the Ancient Astonbury and Wilder Woodlands project, in Hertfordshire, was made possible with a Â£162,698 grant from the National Lottery Heritage Fund.
An increase in flowers attracted more butterflies, with Silver-washed Fritillaries also recorded in much higher numbers during summer 2026 than in previous years, the Herts & Middlesex Wildlife Trust said.
The Beautiful Demoiselle and Willow Emerald damselflies were spotted at Astonbury Wood, close to Stevenage.
The seven sites that made up the project were Astonbury Wood, Balls Wood near Hertford, Fir & Pond Woods near Potters Bar, Gobions Wood near Brookmans Park, Old Park Wood in Harefield, Long Deans in Hemel Hempstead, and Hawkins Wood between Buntingford and Royston.
An ancient woodland, the size of a football pitch, was turned back into coppice management, to allow more light to reach the woodland floor and encourage flowers, insects and birds to thrive.
An area of hornbeam trees at Astonbury Wood was also coppiced in December 2025 and showed "strong regrowth following its first growing season, despite the dry summer," the trust added.
Further coppicing is planned to take place in the future. The practice is an ancient method of tree management, external which involves felling trees at their base to create a "stool" where new shoots will grow.
At Astonbury Wood, woodland glades were reverted to woodland after about 20 years without management.
"Clearing trees and dense bramble, followed by annual cutting and raking, is helping to restore these open habitats and the flowers and insects that depend on them", the trust added.
Iain Ward, wilder woodlands officer at the trust, said: "It has been fantastic to see these habitats responding so positively to careful management, and to see more wildlife making use of the restored glades and coppice areas."
He hopes more work can be carried out at Astonbury Wood to restore the ponds and prevent them drying out completely, as summers "become increasingly hot and dry".

- Published
Warning: This story contains descriptions of drug-taking from the start and discusses suicide
The few grains of fentanyl sit in the silver foil as a straw, held between Mike's lips, hovers above; a cigarette lighter below. The 48-year-old army veteran is crouched low in an alleyway in Columbus, Ohio's Linden neighbourhood.
"This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," he says.
The hit he's smoking cost three or four dollars.
"You can snort too much and you can't take it back. Kind of like a gunshot. Can't call the bullet back," he says.
He burns the foil and inhales. As the opioid takes hold, he grips the fence behind him. He sways as a low moan comes from deep in his throat; he could be humming a tune.
We've spent a few days with Mike - he's been our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets. Everyone seems to know him and he's regarded fondly. He helps out at a local pawn shop and gas station, and that's how he feeds his 20-year-old opioid addiction.
Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape.
Fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin, which is cultivated from poppies. It is now often cut with synthetic tranquillisers, which make reviving overdose victims more difficult. These are homemade threats, where cocktails of synthetics can be made in American basements and bathtubs.
We have Naloxone (brand name Narcan) in our pockets, in case anyone on our team comes into contact with fentanyl or anyone around us overdoses. It's a nasal spray that immediately reverses opioid overdoses and its widespread adoption has transformed the number of fatal overdoses in the United States.
At its peak in 2022, 110,000 Americans were dying from overdoses, mostly from opioids. The number has been dropping since, down to around 70,000 last year. But that doesn't mean the opioid crisis is over.
It's likely that the reversal drug in my pocket, which has saved tens of thousands of drug users' lives, would not have worked on Mike. Because he wasn't just smoking fentanyl.
The pupils in his milky blue eyes shrink to pin pricks. "Opioids make your pupils go smaller, but not that small," he says in a singsong voice. Even the fentanyl, dangerous enough on its own, has other synthetics added.
When we ask what he thinks his drugs have been cut with, he replies: "Xylazine, and the one we can't pronounce."
Medetomidine, is what he means. Like Xyalzine, it is also referred to as tranq and both are synthetic animal tranquilisers. "Large animal tranquilisers," as one recovery expert told me.
They help prolong the high from the fentanyl but are a sedative that slows breathing and, importantly, naloxone doesn't work against them. Xylazine also causes necrotic skin ulcers, wounds so deep they can make it down to the bone and are difficult to treat.
Recovery group offering hope
At the Glenwood Church on the other side of town, members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting. For many, their struggles are written in their care-worn faces, and their eyes are those of survivors of a great trauma.
They take to the stage at the front of the church and share their stories with a brutal and courageous honesty.
One man tells the story of his overdose in July 2022. Two paramedics worked on him, trying to save his life. He had naloxone drips in both arms. They hit him with the opioid reversal three times to no avail. "That's it, I'm gonna call it," said one of the medics. But the other insisted on one more try, and it was that which saved his life.
As the crowd shouts encouragement, Tonya takes to the lectern. She recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time from crack cocaine, a stimulant spiked with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid.
"It's not luck. I'm supposed to be here," she says with tears in her eyes. The audience yells its agreement.
Both in Columbus, and later in Chicago, we would hear of crack cocaine users who had died of overdoses after their drugs contained fentanyl. On the street, it's called a "hot dose".
"In the last 12 months in Franklin County [Columbus], 78% of fatal overdoses are from stimulants," explains Scott Sanders, 65, who runs Hope Dealers.
Scott is almost 10 years sober, a powerfully built man in his early 60s with an electric energy. When he asks the room to raise their hands if anyone has overdosed, most of the gathering does so.
"The crisis has just shifted," Scott tells me afterwards. "The tragedy is stimulant users who are purchasing crack think that's what they're getting, and they're not. They're getting crack mixed with fentanyl or other opioid cocktails and overdosing without being aware of it."
Overdose deaths among black men in Ohio are actually increasing, he adds.
His organisation works with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on a drug sampling programme. Participants bring their needles or pipes for swabbing and the samples are sent to the CDC's laboratory in North Carolina.
That's how we learned that Mike's instincts were right, he likely wasn't just smoking fentanyl. One of the drug kits he brought in tested positive for medetomidine.
"The drug supply in 2026 is this: we think we are buying crack but we're not, we're buying a number of different things," says Scott. "Today it is mixed, not just cut, but mixed with other drugs such as fentanyl or meth, and then other adulterants chemicals that are made in basements."
And it was basement-made synthetic drugs that would cause a dramatic increase in overdose deaths one state over, in Illinois.
I meet a dealer in Chicago who works for the Mexican cartels selling fentanyl. He would only speak to us if we agreed to mask his identity.
Challenged on his role in the 50,000 people dying each year because of the opioid crisis, he says he knows it is wrong. But when asked why he keeps doing it, he said the end justifies the means
