- Published
A large fire near a Canadian military base in Alberta has killed and injured some people, the defence minister said, without confirming the number of casualties.
The Canadian Armed Forces were working with local authorities to manage the fire and were looking into what caused it, David McGuinty said, describing the situation as "very, very active and delicate".
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said on X that a "serious incident creating a major fire" had occurred, adding his "thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected".
Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, where the fire broke out, is one of the country's busiest military training bases.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation describes it as "the principal base for live fire training exercises". About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a regular day, according to the CBC.
Saturday's blaze "spread rapidly due to high winds" and had torn through the fences of the base, the Municipal District of Wainwright said.
McGuinty told reporters he "cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory".
Alberta's premier Danielle Smith says the "significant and tragic fire" is "affecting many of [the province's] brave military personnel". Provincial authorities are in touch with the central government in managing and investigating the situation, she added.
It is unclear when the fire broke out, but the district first posted about the incident at about 17:30 local time (23:30 GMT).
Local authorities have urged residents to avoid the area and give all emergency vehicles right of way.
Neighbouring provinces have offered their support.
Saskatchewan premier Scott Moe says he has deployed resources to Alberta and is "ready to provide more if required", while British Columbia premier David Eby says his government has "reached out to Alberta to offer all possible assistance".

372b842aebd8.text: Some people don't like to make small talk . Others — especially younger Americans — say they simply don't know how to do it. Why it matters: A communication-skills app is betting that a baptism by fire in small talk can help rebuild social confidence — and it's hiring people to approach strangers to put that theory to the test. Driving the news: RiseGuide is hiring Chief Small Talk Officers — recently rebranded from Head of Hanging Out to stress the seriousness of the assignment. The monthlong gig pays each of up to three hires $2,000, plus a budget for outings to parks, bookstores and fitness classes, where they'll strike up conversations with strangers. Officers will rate their small talk skills before and after the assignment, with regular check-ins to assess their interactions. They'll also track conversation lengths and strangers' receptiveness, Anastasia Sliusarenko, RiseGuide's brand and reputation manager, tells Axios. "I'm personally rooting for applicants who kind of feel socially awkward," she says, because their improvement could be more noticeable. She acknowledges the irony of using an app to combat screen time, but says the ultimate goal is for users to "get off the app" and practice their skills in real life. What they're saying: "We actually know from research that something like social confidence can actually be trained... it's not a personality trait," Laura Berssenbrugge, a therapist who specializes in working with Gen Z and Gen Alpha, tells Axios. Social confidence doesn't have to look like the loudest extrovert in the room, Berssenbrugge adds. "That can be social confidence for them. Ours might look a little bit different, and that is absolutely okay." The big picture: Smartphones and personalized digital feeds may be changing how Americans find common ground and navigate conversations with strangers. Earlier generations often shared cultural reference points, from limited TV channels to major sporting events, that offered easy conversation starters. Today's algorithms instead feed people niche interests, reducing opportunities for common ground. Phones also offer an easy escape from awkward interactions, potentially reducing opportunities to practice face-to-face conversation. Zoom in: Even bars, once natural gathering places for spontaneous conversations, aren't immune to the shift, D.C.-area bartender Matty Pivec tells Axios. "If you're sitting at a bar, you kind of naturally fall into place of talking to the person next to you... If you have your phone while you're waiting for the bartender, it's much easier to avoid that." "It's become more of a chore than kind of a pleasant surprise to be able to hold a conversation with a stranger," he says, adding, "I think it's kind of a dying thing to go out and meet strangers." John Lemay, a 14-year veteran bartender at D.C.-area bar Spider Kelly's, partly blames dating apps: "Why would you engage in conversation with somebody [at a bar] if you can just check those boxes and wham, your perfect date pops up," he says. Between the lines: Avoiding strangers might spare people the anxiety of appearing awkward or "cringe," but it also cuts them off from the psychological benefits of casual interactions. Psychologist Ellen Hendriksen points to a study of Chicago rush hour commuters that found those who interacted with strangers reported more positive experiences than those who kept to themselves. Many "underestimated how much they were going to enjoy that," she says. The bottom line: The goal isn't to become an extrovert. It's to get comfortable with the discomfort of striking up conversations with strangers. Go deeper: Birding, silent book club, Mahjong and more: America's meetup explosion

A resident of Launceston, Cornwall, goes above and beyond battling weeds and overgrown pathways free of charge to keep fit and help the community.
Jeremy Vernon, 51, said despite having his kidney removed due to cancer he could not resist clearing neglected paths in his free time and it had made him a hit on social media.
In one area he cut back the brambles and scraped off all the weeds before spending several hours pressure washing the steps.
He said he did it due to "the satisfaction after walking down the path after it has been cleaned and the reaction you get from members of the public and people on social media that seem to appreciate what's being done".
Vernon is a self-employed steel erector who has worked on rollercoasters and movie sets, such as Death on the Nile and Ready Player One.
He had been living in Wiltshire until he discovered he had kidney cancer, had a kidney removed and moved back to Cornwall for what he called a "better, nicer pace of life".
"But work is still up London way, but when I get back down here I go for a walk see a mess get my shovel and wheelbarrow and start clearing places up.
"It keeps you fit and I think it is better than going to the gym.
"I rang Launceston Town Council, they explained the pathways are not theirs and gave me a number for Cornwall Council.
"I have rang them two or three times explaining that I have the public liability insurance but I don't have permission to be where I am so it kind of invalidates my insurance."
In a statement Cornwall Council said: "We support residents volunteering and our contractor Cormac oversees a range of community-led projects on council land, from working on woodland to re-wilding parks to weeding open spaces.
"Last year 60,000 hours of volunteering were undertaken on council land.
"To ensure volunteers can carry out their work safely on council land and indemnity insurance is provided we request that volunteers register with Cormac at volunteers@cormacltd.co.uk so we can give ongoing advice and support."
Resident Elz Ravenscroft asked Vernon if he would cut back the overgrown bushes on the pavement which her daughter used to walk to and from school.
"Jeremy has worked so hard for all of town and gone above and beyond for us all out of his own free time," she said.
"We're all so massively grateful for all his hard work and dedication to the town and town's people.
"From making the zigzag a safe space to walk through, to tidying up graffitied benches down the Ridgegrove to cut through a path."
She said: "The man honestly deserves so much recognition by the town council and beyond for all he's done."

9c3d99adf488.text:
Parisians wake up to protest damage and looted shops
Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against conditions in schools and the cost of living.
At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence", as shopfronts were smashed and stores looted.
For shop owners, this morning marks the start of clean-up efforts, with some reporting damages and stolen goods amount to â¬100,000 (Â£85,000).
The BBC's James Waterhouse reports from the streets of Paris outside damaged buildings.

e72299f124a8.text:
- Published
France awoke to scenes of widespread damage on Sunday after a day of riots and demonstrations, with shopfronts shattered, burnt out cars, charred bikes, and piles of glass and debris on the pavements of Paris.
Police arrested about 1,800 people on Saturday as some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for protests that were largely peaceful.
They were demonstrating against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings.
Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas.
In Paris, protesters clashed with riot police, who turned tear gas and water cannon on the crowds. During the day, some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles. At least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups.
Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons.
Further south in Marseille, protesters broke into the city hall by using a metal fence as a battering ram. In Lille, a McDonalds was set on fire, police said, and an Apple store in the city was broken into and looted.
More than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured in the unrest on Saturday, France's interior ministry said.
Around 1,500 shops and retailers were also damaged in the disturbances, the Retail and Trade Federation said.
On Sunday morning in Paris, residents surveyed the aftermath, which included the smashed glass frontages of designer stores including Ralph Lauren, Gucci and Versace.
Shopkeepers were out early with brooms, picking up large shards of glass as they began the clean-up. Rubbish trucks worked their way down some of the larger streets to clear some of the debris.
Many shops were daubed with graffiti, some reading "tax the rich" and "eat the rich."
The BBC visited a clothes shop close to the Place de la RÃ©publique which had been ransacked, with piles of clothes and furniture scattered across the shop floor.
The shop's distraught owner told the BBC he saw looters on the CCTV who were in the shop for just over an hour and a half, and that during that time he saw no police in the process.
The owner - who asked not to be identified - told the BBC he did not believe any of those who robbed the shop were genuine protesters against school conditions or the cost of living. He said the looters were taking advantage of the demonstrations.
Close to the Place de la RÃ©publique, a BBC reporter visited the Good Vibes bakery, whose glass front was completely shattered, and the Nicolas wine store, where every bottle was either stolen or smashed, leaving smell of alcohol lingering in the street.
CCTV footage shown on France's Channel 2 shows groups of teenagers, mostly wearing masks, in a shop selling mobile phones helping themselves to items from the shelves.
Student protests in France have seen hundreds of thousands take to the streets since they began late last month. Protesters have been demanding additional investment in their schools, criticising the lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.
France's Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said that while demonstrating was a fundamental right, there were "outrages" committed by "several thousand far-left individuals" who were determined to target public buildings and confront the police.
Later, they were joined by "delinquents who looted and ransacked numerous businesses in several cities in France", he said.
In the city of Lyon, Mayor GrÃ©gory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy", telling French outlet BFMTV that "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building".
Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze.
Fire crews also battled a fire at Limoges town hall, which caused part of the building to collapse. Local officials said the town hall was "largely lost."
"A wild horde" had "deliberately" set fire to the 143-year-old building, said Maurice Barate, the prefect for the Haute-Vienne department.
Elsewhere, a young man "had his hand blown off" by a small explosive in Saint-Ãtienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor RÃ©gis Juanico said on social media.
"Such a tragedy should never have happened," he said.
France's interior ministry said Saturday's protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also in Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse, and the western city of Angers.
Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence.

c4505593421b.text:
- Published
A herd of ponies on Exmoor is being gathered as part of an annual inspection.
Tippbarlake Exmoor Pony Herd has about 100 ponies, which are being gathered in Brendon Barton on Sunday.
Kristina Auckland, who looks after the herd with her family, said gathering ponies on Exmoor was a tradition that had been going on for generations.
She said members of the public were able to watch at Scobhill Gate from 10:00 for free but would be asked to donate to the Devon Air Ambulance.
Auckland said the ponies lived freely on Brendan Common and "we try and manage them from afar all year round".
"Once a year we will gather them in to have a bit of a closer inspection and make sure that they're all healthy and their welfare needs are met," she added.
The numbers of people watching the gathering had "steadily increased" over the last few years, which Auckland attributed to the rise of social media.
She added there were also many local families who came to watch yearly.
Auckland said they had chosen to collect donations for Devon Air Ambulance this year because it was "absolutely crucial" for people in rural communities.
"We're completely reliant on the air ambulance being able to help us, whether you're a farmer, a local resident, or someone visiting," she said.
She added: "Whatever anyone's able to donate, as as little or as much as possible is amazing."
Auckland said she wanted to "raise awareness of the breed and the role the ponies play in managing the common itself and what they can contribute to conservation projects around the country," she said.
"They are born to eat ... and they're really good at eating certain types of grasses and sort of managing habitats."
She added: "They're a really important part of Exmoor's heritage and we're so lucky to have many herds still living freely on the moor.
"We want people to understand their value and the role they play, and we want them to be here for generations to come."

724b31874806.text:
SAN ANTONIO, Texas—In Texas, suburbs have sprung up where oil pump jacks once bobbed.
At the Preserve at Medina, a subdivision of brick-and-siding starter homes in southwest San Antonio, students filed off a school bus on a hot afternoon. One child turned down Vesper Branch, a street with a plugged oil well ringed by a heavy black metal fence:
“CAUTION flammable gas,” a sign on the fence warned.
A faint smell of rotten eggs hung in the air, from low levels of hydrogen sulfide leaking from the well. Only the fence separated the child from the leaking well.
Oil hasn’t flowed from the Thompson Callaway Spears #1 well since it was plugged in 2006. But in recent years, the well has vexed Texas regulators and nearby residents. The state has replugged it five times, yet gas continues to leak. Since a housing subdivision rose around the well in the early 2020s, residents have filed repeated complaints.
Soil and air monitoring near the well has detected leaking methane and hydrogen sulfide. In June, contractors told the Railroad Commission, the state’s oil and gas industry overseer, that plumes of methane gas were moving through the soil toward homes in the subdivision, which could trigger an explosion.
“We had no idea when we moved here,” said Krystal Solis, who lives across the street with her husband and three children. “No one told us anything.”
Plugged wells are usually safe, but several in Texas have failed catastrophically in recent years, including at a Baptist church in the Permian Basin town of Grandfalls. From Canada to Southern California, legacy oil and gas wells have been linked to leaks, fires and explosions in residential areas.
Prospective homebuyers rarely know about old oil and gas wells before they buy property. Texas has no statewide laws regulating construction around plugged oil and gas wells. Real estate developers are not required to disclose legacy wells to potential buyers. This means that many people unknowingly end up living near plugged or orphan wells that could present future liabilities.
Laura Lopez, a spokesperson for the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, which regulates air pollution, said the hydrogen sulfide levels detected at the well could cause odors and trigger adverse health effects including headaches and nausea.
Developers of the Preserve at Medina and home builders D.R. Horton and LGI Homes did not respond to requests for comment.
“The well will be re-plugged using a different strategy and materials,” said Bryce Dubee, spokesman for the Railroad Commission, which has plugged the well five times. “This proposed operation is currently under review.”
Dubee said the RRC has conducted joint inspections with the TCEQ and county emergency personnel, which confirmed gas was emanating from the well.
“Both the RRC and TCEQ are now conducting regular monitoring of the area,” he said.
Old Oilfields Cause Fresh Problems
The Austin Chalk formation, from which the limestone walls of the Alamo were quarried, also produces oil and gas. A company called J.D. Collins drilled the Thompson Callaway Spears #1 well in 1955 on what was then the rural edge of San Antonio.
As the decades passed, the well changed hands many times. By the turn of the century, it was producing little oil. Rainer Energy sold the lease to Arben Oil, which sold it to Black Jack Services. February 2004 was the last month the company reported oil flowing at the well.
Black Jack Services plugged the well in 2006.
That same year, Toyota opened a manufacturing plant on San Antonio’s South Side, and development slowly encroached on the rural area along the Medina River. The well was forgotten until 2019, as construction began on the Preserve at Medina.
Developers discovered gas leaking at the site in 2019, according to a Railroad Commission document. In April 2019, commission inspectors confirmed hydrogen sulfide and methane were coming out of the ground near the well. The agency replugged the well later that year. By then the former operator, Black Jack Services, was in delinquent status with the Railroad Commission, so the state assumed the costs.
A staffer wrote in a subsequent report that the fix “seemed to have worked this time around.”
But the problems were only beginning.
The subdivision’s location among plugged oil wells—there are at least three more in the Preserve at Medina —is not unique. From Pittsburgh to Midland to Los Angeles, many residential developments are dotted with old wells.
“Unfortunately, people are buying property, including homes, and have no idea that it could have been built on top of a plugged well,” said Blake Scott, who through his Texas-based company Waste Analytics provides information about legacy oil and gas activities to people buying property.
Both plugged and unplugged wells have caused problems. On Aug. 26, 2021, an explosion ripped through downtown Wheatley, Ontario, Canada, injuring 20 people. Hydrogen sulfide had migrated from a nearby legacy gas well into a downtown basement, triggering the explosion.
In 2007, in Trinidad, Colo., a house under construction blew up, sending a worker into cardiac arrest. Regulators said methane from an abandoned gas well under the house caused the explosion.
In Newport Beach, Calif., several homes were evacuated in October 2025 following a methane leak from a 1920s-era oil well.
Earlier this year, a plugged well failed in the parking lot of the Baptist church in Grandfalls. The property was flooded with toxic wastewater.
“Plugged well failures seem to be rare,” said Adam Peltz, senior director and lead counsel at the Environmental Defense Fund. “But we also don’t know how often it happens.”
“If I had a message for homebuyers, it would be to do your own due diligence,” he said. “This is happening all over the country.”
Julie Range, policy manager for the Texas-based nonprofit Commission Shift, a watchdog that tracks the Railroad Commission, said disclosure of prior oil and gas activities should be required to protect home b

Picture a buoyant triangular steel or concrete platform roughly the dimensions of a baseball field. Now place a wind turbine taller than the London Eye on top, connect mooring lines to the seabed and power cables to the grid, and you’ve got a floating wind turbine.
This fantastical-sounding technology is real. At demonstration and small-scale projects in Europe, Asia and a single U.S. site in Maine, floating turbines are producing power. Multiple different platform designs have been field tested, from the aforementioned triangle to a single massive cylinder. But plans to build larger projects of 10 or more turbines, each capable of powering a neighborhood, have lagged behind early projections.
The business case for floating turbines, as opposed to their fixed-bottom counterparts, boils down to two points: they can do their thing making power farther from shore, where the high winds are and the people generally aren’t. In some places like California, the coastal shelf slopes so steeply that floating wind has been seen as the only option. But the engineering challenges of keeping buoyant, vibrating skyscrapers stable—and the high costs of solving them—serve as a potent counterweight.
An army of researchers, engineers and policymakers across the globe have thrown themselves at the problem. In the U.S., the Biden Administration declared a national goal of installing 15 GW—up from zero—of floating wind turbines by 2035, comparing it to efforts to put a man on the moon.
While such announcements often have a nationalistic, competitive edge, a robust network of collaboration has driven the development of this technology. From study trips to open-source designs, researchers, financiers, and developers across the globe have worked together to get the technology to the cusp of commercial viability.
Now, with project delays and policy reversals, the industry is facing a bit of a crisis. A wind trade association recently warned that “the commercialisation window cannot be assumed to remain open indefinitely.” Reports blame causes both independent of and connected to the sustained attacks on the U.S. offshore wind industry by the Trump administration.
To get through the rough patch, the industry is leaning into what got it here: collaboration.
Maine’s Floating “Goldilocks”
Habib Dagher traces the efforts to develop a floating offshore wind industry in Maine to the global energy crisis of 2008, when heating fuel prices spiked above $4 a gallon (The state is once again facing the same crisis, with fuel over $6 a gallon today).
“Maine was in a really tough spot,” Dagher, who heads the Advanced Structures and Composites Center at the University of Maine, said. “That’s when the governor came to our lab, and said, ‘What do we do?’”
Dagher had heard of floating turbines, which he thought well suited to the deep waters of the Gulf of Maine. He traveled to Norway to visit one of the earliest demonstration turbines, and created a program within the center to develop platforms suitable to Maine’s environment and supply chains.
When nearly 60 percent of Maine voters passed a 2010 bond measure to fund this research, Dagher said he felt that the center “had a mandate from voters in the state of Maine.”
The fruits of that investment are visible today in a concrete, plus-sign-shaped platform bobbing in the waters off Castine. The structure is a quarter-scale model of the center’s latest platform design and supports a 108-foot tall turbine. It was towed there by the cadets of the Maine Maritime Academy in May 2025.
During a recent tour on a calm day, the platform seemed not to move at all, though the turbine blades kept up a steady motion.
“We jokingly call [Maine] a Goldilocks of floating wind because the water depths aren’t that deep, the wind resource is really good…[and] the waves aren’t that bad,” said Anthony Viselli, chief engineer at the center.
Students from a class on the social and political dimensions of offshore energy at nearby Colby College, among the tour participants, peppered Viselli with questions about everything from the effect of soil structure on mooring (significant) to the maximum wave height a full-scale model could withstand (60 feet, give or take).
The turbine is also answering questions another way: Dublin Offshore, an Irish maker of mooring line technologies, is currently testing a shock-absorbing device on the model. The company won a competition for U.K. firms, co-sponsored by the center.
“For us, transatlantic collaboration has a very practical value,” Darren Hayes, technical director at Dublin Offshore, said in a statement. “This demonstration is the critical final step to deliver the evidence developers and investors need to move towards commercial deployment.”
In the same spirit, the center has made the technical specifications and software parameters for its alternative steel platform widely available, which Emma Edwards, a researcher at Oxford University who specializes in floating wind, called “incredibly instrumental” to further research on the technology.
The quarter-scale platform and turbine was only meant to be one more step in a long collaborative effort between the center, state government and private sector partners. The next included building 10-12 full-sized platforms and turbines at a proposed “research array,” for which the state signed a lease with the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management in 2024.
Last March, however, the developer suspended contract negotiations for a power offtake agreement, citing “recent shifts in the energy landscape.” The project is in limbo.
Reaching a Shared Understanding
In 2021, Maine launched the Offshore Wind Research Consortium, with representatives from state and tribal governments, fisheries, environmental groups and energy developers.

One of the best-known meteor showers is now active until 7 November.
The Orionids are particularly fast and can leave trails in the sky that last a few seconds after the meteor itself has gone.
The display occurs at around the same time each year when the Earth passes through a trail of dust and debris left behind by Halley's Comet.
The showers peak overnight from 21 to 22 October.
What are the Orionids?
The Orionids are particularly fast, entering the atmosphere at around 41 miles per second.
As tiny particles from Halley's comet enter the Earth's atmosphere they heat up and produce streaks of light across the night sky that we see as meteors.
Halley's Comet is one of the most famous comets in our Solar System and has been observed from Earth for centuries. It takes around 76 years to complete one orbit of the Sun and was last seen from Earth in 1986.
Halley's Comet is not expected to be visible from Earth again until 2061, but its debris will continue to produce meteor showers each year.
In fact, the Earth encounters material left behind by it twice a year, resulting in the Eta Aquariid meteor shower in May and the Orionids in October.
How can I see the Orionids?
The meteors appear to radiate from the constellation of Orion, which is where the shower gets its name, but they can appear anywhere across the night sky.
Under ideal conditions, around 10 to 20 meteors can be seen each hour at the shower's peak.
For the best chance of seeing them, find a dark location away from street lights and with as wide a view of the sky as possible.
Allow around 15 to 20 minutes for your eyes to adjust. You won't need binoculars or a telescope; the shower is best viewed with the naked eye.
Later in October, the Moon could affect how many meteors are visible at the peak of the Orionids, as as it builds to its full phase on 26 October.
This means its light could make some of the fainter meteors more difficult to see.
Brighter meteors, however, should still be visible, particularly from darker locations away from artificial light.
What is the forecast for the Orionid peak?
You will have noticed over the weekend that temperatures across the UK have dropped and it feels much more like autumn now.
The cooler feel will continue through this week, so if you do plan to spend time outside gazing at the sky, make sure you are wrapped up.
As the meteor shower peaks on Wednesday night, it currently looks as though rain will move away early in the night, leaving most areas with a clear view of the sky at times.
If you are not planning on viewing the shower until later this week, there is a chance that we could see much wetter and windier conditions sweep across parts of the country.
Keep an eye on the BBC Weather app to judge the best opportunities for clear spells in your area.

In a secret location in the Highlands of Scotland, there's a fast-flowing river that's the key to understanding the massive power of water.
It's where engineer David Mummery found himself more than a decade ago.
With a length of cord tied tightly across the river, he swam out, gripped firmly, and let the unstoppable current rush over as he sunk his head below the surface.
"As an engineer we do the maths and stuff," he says, "but sometimes you can get a lot more from actually touching the water and feeling it".
As he lay down in the powerful rapids, he visualised a new type of small-scale tidal energy generator.
It's an innovation he says could change lives for people in coastal communities.
"I'd be under the river, feeling the turbulence of the water rushing over me.
"Trying to envisage how this turbine needed to interact with that environment - to understand the way the water was working."
Mummery's idea became the Swimmer Turbine - a 50kw tidal generator named after his experience in the river.
Anchored to the sea floor, the fiberglass and steel device lies invisible below the water's surface. It can generate enough electricity to power about 30 homes.
He began tests in the river in early 2010s. On a patent lawyer's advice he found a secret location, far from curious Highland tourists and their cameras.
"You're trying to be quite discreet because you're working with new technology," he says.
It was in the first years of his company, Flex Marine Power, long before Britain was gripped by the soaring costs of an energy crisis.
The size of the Swimmer Turbine is what sets it apart from large tidal projects dotted around Scottish waters.
Scotland is a world leader in the sector at sites including:
- Nova Innovation - The world's first tidal stream array, deployed in 2016 in Bluemull Sound in Shetland
- MeyGen - The world's largest tidal array, with four large 1.5MW turbines on the seabed of the Pentland Firth
- Orbital O2 - The world's most powerful floating turbine, generating 2MW, anchored at Fall of Warness in the Orkney Islands
Mummery's turbine is ultra compact and low cost compared to these giant machines. Fishermen and local workers can build and install it themselves from their own village harbour.
"Can you imagine like an Ikea furniture kit? You get a shipping container and you'll open it up and it will be about 20 components.
"You'll bolt them all together and then you've got your turbine ready.
"There'll be a launch plan, you follow these instructions, then you'll be in the water."
Mummery's work did not always focus on small-scale power. Originally from Guildford, he studied mechanical engineering at Surrey University.
Before founding Flex Marine Power, he was a sought-after consultant in the UK energy sector. For a time he specialised in nuclear work and decommissioning, designing robots for pulling material out of contaminated tanks.
He moved north after falling in love with a girl studying at Glasgow University. Jo became his wife and they now live in the city suburbs with three young children.
Conveniently, Mummery's relocation came at a time when Scotland was establishing its reputation as a centre for marine power expertise.
In 2010 he took a secondment at Scottish Power Renewables on the ground-breaking Pelamis project in Orkney.
The 180m-long (591ft) Pelamis P2 - nicknamed the sea snake - was the first deep-water, floating wave energy machine to generate power for the national grid.
Ultimately, Pelamis went into administration in 2014, but the ill-fated device remains celebrated as a milestone in marine power innovation.
"The industry is littered with these examples of fantastic technologies and teams that do brave things that take decades," Mummery says.
"But at some point the market doesn't step up and they falter. Some really good ones have lasted the course, but others have not and it's sad."
Mummery says the UK has "phenomenal waters for tidal power" and he loved being a part of major projects - but couldn't shake a discomfort.
His work felt incongruous to the many small coastal communities he found himself in.
"I'd be going out on boats around Scotland doing sonar surveys with all these really expensive pieces of kit.
"But the equipment was all really big, utility-scale stuff that would weigh hundreds of tonnes, shipped by people from the mainland.
"All the people I was meeting in harbours or in the pub were fishermen. And they were knowledgeable and they were interested.
"I thought 'we've got to do this in a way that they can take the lead'."
That, he says, is what motivated his Swimmer Turbine idea.
In 2011 he left big projects behind to found Flex Marine Power and focus on his turbine concept.
He spent hours at his desk sketching, working out how to make the technology smaller and lighter.
He hired a student employee and found a sleek, glass office space outside Glasgow - which he quickly discovered wasn't entirely suited to an engineer and his tools.
"It was a lovely place, but I wasn't allowed to take a hammer drill into the office.
"We were trying to make prototype turbines under the desk so the landlord wouldn't see them when he came in."
Mummery turned to Clydeside's shipbuilding past in search of a more suitable workspace.
He presented a plan to convert former shipyards for marine technology research, and was invited to Greenock by Inverclyde's redevelopment authority.
"There were lots of empty sheds that hadn't been used for years," he says.
"They basically said 'we'll walk you around, you can pick a shed'. So I got the pick of the bunch right on the quayside."
Mummery now had direct access to the River Clyde for sea trials to test his models.
He developed a prototype which he successfully trialled in 2015 on the island of Luing, in the Firth of Lorn, near Oban.
It secured Flex Marine's first major investment and expansion the following year.
The next major step was in Northern Ireland in 2020, at Strangford Narrows in County Down.

Seal pups have been recorded at a nature reserve for the 12th year running.
Cumbria Wildlife Trust confirmed two pups had been spotted at South Walney Nature Reserve near Barrow, Cumbria.
The reserve is home to the county's only breeding grey seal colony and major haul-out site, a spot where seals come to shore for rest.
A record number of 14 seal pups were counted at the nature reserve last year, with the trust saying it hoped there would be "many more to come".
The pups were the first two healthy ones spotted at the nature reserve this season during a routine seal count.
Two were seen earlier in the summer but did not survive, the trust said.
Marine conservation officer Beth Churn said: "This is always an exciting time of year for us, and we hope that there'll be many more to come.
"We regularly reach double figures of pups, a trend that's been improving each year, so let's hope this season is a successful one for the colony."
The highest number of grey seals recorded to date at South Walney Nature Reserve was 563 in December 2024.
The previous highest seal counts were 518 in 2021, 483 in 2019 and 360 in 2018, showing an upward trend year on year.
Grey seals started breeding at South Walney in 2015 and pups have been recorded every year since.
"It's the result of concerted and ongoing efforts to keep disturbance of the seal colony to a minimum," Churn said.
"We work hard to make the beach safe and secure for the seals, so that they feel able to return here to breed."
There is no public access to the haul-out site at South Walney but three hides around the site let people see the seals from a safe distance.
A new hide at Groyne is currently being built and will include a telescope.
The trust is asking people to take care not to disturb the seal colony and maintain at least 100m (328ft) distance at all times.
"You can get good views of the seals with binoculars from a safe distance, so there's no need to get too close," Churn said.
"You'll know if you're too close because the seals will start to look at you and move nervously.
"If this happens, you should immediately start backing away quietly to avoid further disturbance."

People have been advised to keep their windows and doors shut due to a widespread fuel leak in the River Taff.
Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said it had received multiple reports about pollution affecting the Taff in places such as Nantgarw, Treforest and Taffs Well.
NRW said it found the source of the pollution at 19:30 BST on Friday but will not be naming it at this stage, and its officers are working to identify how it entered the drainage system.
Kerosene has now spread down almost 2.5 miles (4km) of the river, it added.
The environmental body also received reports of pollution affecting the Taff in Glan Y Llyn, Gwaelod-y-garth and Tongwynlais.
It said South Wales Fire and Rescue Service workers helped with specialist equipment to reduce the amount of kerosene entering the river.
"Our officers are again on site where action has been taken to significantly reduce the amount of pollution entering the tributary, whilst investigate work is ongoing to try and stop the pollution entirely," NRW said in a statement.
It is also taking samples to understand "the actual environmental impact of the spill".
Reports of a leak affecting one mile (1.6km) of the river were first received on Saturday morning from residents.
NRW later said it had spread as it continued "to investigate the source of the incident to understand how it is happening, stop the pollution completely and collect evidence".
Eurig Thomas, a resident in Taff's Well, Rhondda Cyon Taff, said: "It smelt like a petrol station, it hit you as soon as you came out."
Absorbent materials have been deployed to try and contain the leak.
Thomas added: "The river had a shiny sheen on it, the stream flows behind my house, it comes down from the GE factory and into the Taff.
"The smell has dissipated â but you can still smell it this morning."
Another resident, Sarah Llewelyn, added: "I haven't slept in three days. Friday afternoon lunchtime I opened the door and could smell fumes, it was burning my eyes."
She dubbed it "a national disaster".
"NRW have told us that up to 25,000 litres of kerosene has entered the river."
Gareth Llewelyn, a former hazardous materials environmental protection officer with South Wales Fire and Rescue service, said there was "no quick fix" and it needed "years not months" to restore.
He added: "I have visited the culvert across the road from the GE site yesterday and it was full of kerosene. It doesn't mix with water and will continue to pollute."
Llewellyn said the spill has "torn the heart out of our community", adding: "The village is Taff's Well â it's named after the river."
He said "now there's no animals, no birds" and all the fish have died.
NRW said the pollution was discharging from an underground surface water drainage system, but the amount of fuel had reduced significantly.
It added that its staff had been working with the fire service to install equipment to collect the fuel and that the smell had died down.
Water samples have been collected to check the damage the pollution has had.
Public Health Wales advised people living nearby to keep windows and doors closed, avoid any contact with the water and to call NHS 111 if they felt unwell.
GE has been asked to comment.

Russia has moved past ‘hybrid war.’ Why hasn’t Washington?
Europe is adapting to Moscow’s increasingly brazen and kinetic operations. The US should catch up.
On a recent September afternoon, David Petraeus, the former CIA director, was heading home by train from a security conference in Kyiv. What should have been a routine trip into Poland was upended when the state railway, Ukrzaliznytsia, ordered passengers off the train. Fifteen minutes later, Russian drones were heard overhead, and the train was struck shortly after the last passengers had been evacuated.
The attack is just one of the indications that Russia’s decades-long campaign against the West has outgrown the label of “hybrid war.” While Moscow’s efforts remain below the threshold of open war, they have grown more brazen and kinetic. And while European allies are moving quickly to counter Russia’s escalation, the United States lags behind.
The past few months have seen a striking number of Russian operations against Europe and a sharp change in tactics towards the United States. In August, a Russian drone carrying explosives struck the wing of a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport, a hub for NATO airlift to the eastern flank; the attack only failed due to a faulty detonator. That was just the most recent incursion into alliance airspace by Russian drones and even jets; IISS has tracked more than 100 confirmed or suspected incursions, including an explosive-laden drone shot down over Lithuania to a drone that struck an apartment building in Romania.
Of the train incident, Ukrzaliznytsia officials have said it was “entirely possible” that the drone had missed its intended target: a diplomatic train carrying two former prime ministers, Sweden’s Carl Bildt and the UK’s Boris Johnson, which had departed from Kyiv earlier than planned. Whether Petraeus was the intended target is irrelevant. The strike was a close call; injuring or killing a former U.S. official would have marked a sharp and reckless escalation in U.S.-Russian relations. This incident nevertheless reflects the Kremlin’s growing comfort with operations that put senior U.S. figures at risk.
Just days after that, the U.S. Justice Department announced a striking indictment that underscored how far the Kremlin’s escalation against the United States has gone. It charged five people connected to Russian intelligence with conspiracy to finance terrorism, and three of them with conspiracy to commit murder for hire. The network allegedly recruited people inside the United States to surveil and ultimately “eliminate” or “disappear” critics of Russia’s war in Ukraine. In one alleged plot, the network sought to have a Russian dissident killed on U.S. soil. Dozens of such plots have been uncovered in Europe but they have remained rare in the United States. This one places Russia alongside Iran, which has repeatedly plotted to kidnap or kill dissidents and former officials on American soil
Analysts have long believed that the Kremlin has sought to maintain deniability, plausible or implausible, when it moves against the West. Plausible deniability refers to a state’s ability to disclaim responsibility because the evidence is too ambiguous to act upon; implausible deniability refers to a state’s denial when attribution is obvious, often a way to signal with only a veneer of “escalation control” or aimed at its domestic audiences such as Russian-speaking communities rather than the targeted government. Yet the bold, sometimes sloppy character of the past year’s operations suggests the Kremlin is increasingly willing to forgo even that to continue to intimidate foreign governments and their citizens and to gather military intelligence. As the war in Ukraine has dragged on, economic pressure on the Kremlin has mounted, and Moscow appears to have entered a new phase in its conflict with the West. Raising the costs of Western support outweighs the value of deniability. At that point, these are no longer hybrid operations, but overt external operations.
European allies, for their part, have begun to escalate their own responses, even as diplomats and officials continue to describe the Russian threat as hybrid. Rather than simply announcing when a Russian drone or ship enters NATO territory, or summoning Russian diplomats, governments across Europe have begun shooting down drones and responding militarily. In late September, Poland’s Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk announced that Polish fighter jets would no longer need visual confirmation from a pilot before downing a Russian drone; radar-based “positive identification” would now suffice.
The United States, by contrast, continues to treat the Russian threat as largely latent. To be fair, Russia’s tactics on the European continent remain more brazen and kinetic than those it employs against the United States. But Washington’s NATO commitments alone make Russia’s campaign against Europe an American concern, and Moscow is now escalating against the United States directly as well. If the pattern observed in Europe holds, its operations against the U.S. will grow only more brazen and openly hostile. While some U.S. agencies may recognize the rising threat, as the DOJ’s unsealing of charges against the Russian network and CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s August visit to Moscow could demonstrate, Washington still remains divided on how to classify it, and much of that division stems from the White House itself.
Messaging from the White House over the past month alone is mixed. On Sept. 15, Attorney General Todd Blanche stood in the White House Rose Garden to announce charges against a Russian intelligence network accused of plotting to murder a dissident in the Washington area. Eight days later, the administration invited Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit in Miami. The same month, President Trump signed the most significant Russia sanctions legislation since 2017, only for his administration to reportedly weigh sanctions relief

0ecf26f9a553.text: Democrats are running surprisingly competitive races in traditionally Republican territory across the country this midterm election cycle , and it's putting GOP winning streaks at risk that stretch as far back as the 1930s. Why it matters: Democrats hope ending political droughts in states such as Kansas, Texas and South Carolina will help make inroads in what has long been off-limits territory. Kansas - 1932 Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas) is facing a surprisingly tough challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor who has significantly outraised the incumbent GOP senator. The two are neck-and-neck in the polls , and Cook Political Report rates the race a tossup. A Democrat hasn't won a U.S. Senate seat in Kansas since George McGill was reelected in 1932. Texas - 1988 Democratic state Rep. James Talarico is giving Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) a real run for his money in the Senate race. Talarico generally leads in polls by low single digits. Cook rates it a tossup. Texas has been a consistent heartbreaker for Democrats in recent cycles. They last won a Senate seat in the state with Lloyd Bentsen in 1988. South Carolina - 1998 Polls have routinely shown Republican Sen. Darline Graham , who was appointed to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham following his death in July, leading Democrat Annie Andrews by just a few percentage points. Andrews, like other Democratic Senate candidates, has raised colossal sums , while Graham has struggled as a political neophyte. Still, Cook rates the race as "likely Republican." The state has gone Republican in every U.S. Senate election since longtime Democrat Fritz Hollings was last reelected in 1998. Between the lines: Democrat Troy Jackson , if he defeats Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine next month, would be the first registered Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in Maine since 1988. That's a bit of a technicality: Independent Sen. Angus King has caucused with Democrats since he was first elected in 2012. Gubernatorial races Texas hasn't elected a Democratic governor since Ann Richards in 1990, but Democrat Gina Hinojosa is in a tight race with Republican incumbent Greg Abbott that Cook rates as "leans Republican." Democrat David Jolly is also hoping for an upset against GOP Rep. Byron Donalds in a race Cook also rates as "leans Republican." Democrats narrowly won the Florida governorship in 1994 and have lost ever since. Georgia's Keisha Lance Bottoms and Alaska's Jonathan Kreiss-Tompkins are both vying to be the first Democrats elected governor in their states since 1998. Cook rates Georgia as a tossup and Alaska as "leans Democratic." House races Democrats have never won Nevada's 2nd District, which was created in 1983. It has changed shape over time but has always been anchored in the rural north half of the state. Democrats feel they have a strong candidate in former state Assembly Majority Leader Teresa Benitez-Thompson and a weak opponent in former Air Force lieutenant colonel Dave Flippo . The party is also bullish about Montana's 1st District, where they hope the populist appeal of former smokejumper Sam Forstag will help him prevail over the GOP nominee Aaron Flint, a veteran and radio host. Democrats haven't won a U.S. House seat in Montana since 1994. Cook rates Nevada's 2nd Distric as "likely Republican" and Montana's 1st District as a tossup. The other side: Republicans are also competitive in a handful of races where they haven't won in quite a while. Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers is locked in a tight U.S. Senate race in Michigan with Democrat Abdul El-Sayed . He would be the first Republican elected to the Senate from the state since the 1994 GOP wave. Democratic Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek faces a close race with Republican Christine Drazan , who would be the first Republican elected governor of the state since 1982. Oregon is essentially the GOP's version of Texas: Republicans have lost by single digits in gubernatorial elections since 2002.

At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities.
The region's Governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being extinguished at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot following the attack, which also injured at least five.
A logistics centre belonging to Ozon - known as Russia's Amazon - and a data centre belonging to Facebook equivalent VKontakte were also hit.
Kyiv has not yet commented on the strikes. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday morning that Russia had targeted his country's energy sector 76 times since Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" last week.
Ukraine had paused its strikes on Russian oil facilities - which it says are to limit the main revenue stream for Moscow's war effort - for three days after the announcement, while accusing Russia of continuing.
It then resumed strikes earlier this week, drawing the ire of Trump, who called for a truce to facilitate a deal he struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to supply diesel.
Ukraine has struck St Petersburg before, though regions closer to Ukraine are threatened more often. The city's oil terminal was last hit in July.
Russia's defence ministry said it had shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory overnight into Sunday.
St Petersburg's governor said 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged in the attacks on the city, while Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed.
He also said mobile internet service disruption was possible.
Social network VK confirmed a drone had targeted its regional data centre, but stressed its services were available "as usual" after users reported outages in the early hours of the morning.
Ozon also confirmed its local logistics centre had been targeted by a drone, sparking a fire.
It said staff were evacuated and no one was injured, and that it was not accepting shipments from sellers at the location "as it is currently serving other operational purposes".
As well as numerous oil facilities across Russia, Ukraine has also mounted strikes aimed at disrupting the Russian economy more broadly. Earlier this month, it launched a series of attacks on Yandex, Russia's largest search engine, that led to service disruptions.
Relations between Washington and Kyiv have frayed since the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war, ahead of the midterm elections.
Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.
Trump's decision to temporarily suspend a raft of sanctions against Russia has brought fresh criticism, including from some US Republicans.
Both Russia and Ukraine have been striking one another's energy infrastructure with increasing intensity ahead of the winter, as Moscow's full-scale invasion drags on in its fifth year.
Russia says it hits targets used by Ukraine's military, though the UN noted on Friday that the first two weeks of October had been the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians in years.
Russian strikes on energy facilities have left hundreds of thousands without power, raising concerns about civilians enduring another freezing winter.
Zelensky said on Saturday that tens of thousands of people were still without power. Russia launched nearly 2,700 drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles in the past week, most of which were aimed at energy facilities, he said.

ba080683b709.text: In red states and blue, unconventional candidates are downplaying — or even disowning — party labels to tap into voters' deep disdain for Washington. Why it matters: They might not all win, but the sheer number of political outsiders connecting with voters tells us something about the electorate: It's angry and willing to take risks. The candidates — whether they come from the pulpit or the NFL sidelines — are making the same bet: Voters are tired of career politicians. Zoom in: Consider three unorthodox Democrats leading in Senate contests in three red states: a Presbyterian seminarian in Texas (state Rep. James Talarico), a megachurch pastor in Kansas (Adam Hamilton), and an Alaska Native in that state (former Rep. Mary Peltola, who once skipped a week of House votes to go fishing when Chinook salmon were running). Deep-blue Minnesota's Senate race features Michele Tafoya — a former NFL sideline reporter who's endorsed by President Trump but calls herself an independent Republican. She's mounting a serious challenge to Democrat Peggy Flanagan , the lieutenant governor. In House races, on the Democratic side there's a smokejumper in Montana (Sam Forstag), a 29-year-old barista in Colorado (Melat Kiros) and a Tejano singer in Texas (Bobby Pulido). Four independent Senate candidates are courting Democratic voters without running with a (D) next to their names — and sometimes without a Democrat officially in the race. In Nebraska, Dan Osborn, a union steamfitter and former factory mechanic, is mounting a serious independent challenge to Sen. Pete Ricketts, a former two-term governor whose family owns the Chicago Cubs. In Montana, Seth Bodnar , a former Army Green Beret and University of Montana president, is running as an independent for an open Senate seat. Democrats tried to persuade their nominee to drop out, but she stayed in the race. In South Dakota, Brian Bengs, a onetime park ranger, is challenging Republican Sen. Mike Rounds as an independent. Four years ago, Bengs ran against Sen. John Thune as a Democrat. In Idaho, former Army tank commander and tech executive Todd Achilles is running as an independent against Republican Sen. Jim Risch. (Achilles previously served in the Idaho House as a Democrat. The official Democratic Senate nominee dropped out of the race in July.) For many Republicans , quasi-Democrats running as independents amount to foul play — an attempt to deceive voters by discarding an unpopular brand. Between the lines: Even candidates with more conventional backgrounds are shading their biographies to meet the populist moment. In the Maine Senate race, Democrat Troy Jackson — who spent two decades in the state House and Senate before being term-limited out in 2024 — introduces himself as a fifth-generation Maine logger. Zoom out: The populist path to Washington is at least as old as President Andrew Jackson, who first took office in 1829. It's as fresh as President Trump. In recent years, there have been unorthodox candidates on both sides. Some succeeded; others didn't. Al Franken, famous for being a writer and actor on "Saturday Night Live," won a U.S. Senate seat in Minnesota in 2008 and served more than eight years before resigning. Herschel Walker, a celebrated college and NFL running back, couldn't find the end zone in his 2022 Senate race in Georgia. Say what you want about the 45th and 47th president: The New York developer with a penchant for gold leaf has connected with disaffected working-class voters. Democrats have struggled to match Trump's appeal to non-college-educated voters, but Trump has made their task easier this cycle with an unpopular war and tariffs that voters blame for high prices. The bottom line: A version of the insurgent-vs.-establishment battle played out in Democratic primaries earlier this year, when seven House incumbents went down — tying a 21st-century high . That included Kiros, the 29-year-old Colorado barista and democratic socialist who defeated a 15-term incumbent in the primary and is on a glide path to victory next month.

134b104b418b.text: Data: U.S. Census ; Map: Erin Davis/Axios California and Louisiana have something surprising in common: Both have among the nation's highest poverty rates when the cost of living is factored in, according to Census Bureau data. Why it matters: Southern states dominate America's traditional poverty rankings. But that familiar geographic divide starts to disappear when more of a family's financial realities are taken into account. Axios analyzed 2023-2025 state poverty estimates from the Census Bureau to see what happens when housing, taxes, medical expenses and government benefits enter the picture. What we found: Under the Census' traditional-style official measure, Louisiana had a 19.6% poverty rate and California was at 10.7%. New Hampshire was the lowest at 5.4%. The South is home to 10 of the 11 states where the traditional poverty rate significantly outpaced the national average. California's poverty rate jumped by nearly two-thirds to 17.8% under the broader Supplemental Poverty Measure , or SPM. Louisiana remained near the top at 19%. Maine posted the nation's lowest SPM rate at 6.4%, followed by Nebraska at 7.5% and Minnesota at 7.9%. How it works: The traditional measure compares pretax cash income with a family-size threshold that doesn't change by geography. The SPM adds benefits such as SNAP and housing assistance, factors in taxes and tax credits, subtracts work and medical expenses, and adjusts for geographic differences in housing costs. Zoom out: The official poverty rate fell for a third straight year to 10.2%, while child poverty reached a record-low 13.4%. Yet the SPM remained statistically unchanged at 13.1% — nearly three percentage points above the official rate . Real median household income hit a record $87,460 in 2025. Yes, but: The SPM doesn't replace the official poverty rate. Census designed it as another lens — one that captures resources and unavoidable expenses the traditional measure misses. The state figures also aren't single-year 2025 estimates. Census recommends three-year averages because state samples in the Current Population Survey are smaller. The bottom line: Income alone doesn't tell you whether a family can make ends meet.

Pope Leo XIV thanks wellwishers in first event after cancer surgery
Pope Leo XIV held his first public engagement since his lung cancer surgery on Sunday, as he recited the Angelus prayer from the window of Vatican's Apostolic Palace.
The surgery had taken place just a few days before, after Pope Leo had been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
After the prayer, he thanked the people who have prayed for him in recent days and said he appreciated the support. He added he will now gradually return to his commitments as he recovers.

7978fd2bc8f0.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky spoke Sunday with President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about the crisis between the countries and U.S. efforts to resume peace talks with Russia. Why it matters: It was the first call between Zelensky and senior U.S. officials since tensions spiked between their countries after Trump cut a diesel deal with Russia 10 days ago. Driving the news: The call took place amid assertions by Zelensky that the Trump administration was behind restrictions imposed on the Starlink and Starshield satellite systems used by the Ukrainian military. "Who made this decision? I don't know. I think that this is really both [White House and SpaceX] decision. If President Trump will decide tomorrow, or better today, if he will personally decide to lift this decision, it will immediately work as it was before," Zelensky said on NBC's "Meet the Press" Sunday. He added, "The message came from [the U.S.] government. I don't know from whom. It's the opinion of our generals, of our government, and of course also my opinion, that it was a message from the American government to limit the speed. And technically, SpaceX did it." Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that the U.S. government was not involved in the Starlink restrictions and said it has been restored. Ukrainian officials dispute that.

a7c7535e8169.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/jackson-doesnt-regret-telling-collins-to-shut-up-after-protester-interrupted-maine-senate-debate Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Jackson doesn't regret telling Collins to 'shut up' after protester interrupted Maine Senate debate Politics Oct 18, 2026 2:01 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Maine Democrat Troy Jackson says he does not regret telling Sen. Susan Collins that she should "shut up" after the Republican suggested a protester who interrupted their recent debate was one of his campaign's backers. READ MORE: What happened in the first Maine Senate debate between Collins and Jackson "She said that it was a Troy supporter. She accused me of setting that up. I had no idea who it was," said Jackson, a former president of the state Senate who is trying to deny Collins, the longest-serving Republican woman in Senate history, a sixth-term. He spoke in an interview with CNN's "State of the Union" that aired Sunday. During their final debate Thursday night in the closely contested race, as the Nov. 3 election nears a protester opposing data centers began yelling as Collins spoke. While moderators asked for that person to be removed, the senator said the demonstrator was "obviously one of Troy's supporters." Jackson responded: "Oh, shut up. I don't even know that kid." Watch the moment from the debate in the video player above. The Sunrise Movement group posted on its Instagram page that the outburst came from one of its members. In a caption of an Instagram post, the group's page said: "We're proud of this Sunrise volunteer who took action yesterday." The New York Times said the protester, Henry Elgie, a 19-year-old student at Bowdoin College in Maine, told the newspaper in an interview Saturday that he had "zero coordination" with Jackson's campaign. "I do not know Troy Jackson personally or at all," he was quoted as saying. The Sunrise Movement is a left-wing political advocacy organization that champions the Green New Deal, aimed at transitioning the U.S. economy to 100% renewable energy. The group, which has local arms around the country, regularly organizes protests, sit-ins and climate strikes. Jackson told CNN that he shook hands with Collins after each of their debates. "But what I'm not going to be is talked down to by Sen. Collins," he said. He added: "I'm fighting for Mainers and I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me and I'm not going to apologize for that." WATCH: Collins, Jackson face off in testy Maine U.S. Senate debate Collins told Fox News' Sean Hannity on Friday that she was "struck by how reflective the response, 'Oh, shut up,' was." Collins said "the fact that it seemed like such an automatic, quick reply was very telling." She cited what she said was "the reputation" that Jackson had in the Legislature "particularly when he's dealing with women with whom he disagrees. So in some ways it didn't surprise me." Some state lawmakers who worked with Jackson have criticized him as having a temper, including once throwing a plastic water bottle on the ground in frustration while disagreeing with a female lawmaker. Asked by reporters during the campaign about the confrontations, Jackson said, "I wear my heart on my sleeve." He took responsibility for his outburst and apologized to those he had confrontations with at the time. Jackson was asked on CNN about some Republicans who are saying there were stories that he was aggressive in his tone to women from his time in the Legislature and that his remark Thursday night was another example of that. Jackson said some Republicans have been spending millions "attacking me and my family, making untrue claims. … So it doesn't surprise me." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 2ab5965496b3.text: President Trump's top aides offered sharply different explanations this weekend of his Russian diesel deal amid a barrage of bipartisan criticism calling the move a gift to Russia. Why it matters: Oil, gas and petroleum products help finance Russia's war on Ukraine, and Trump's moves are bringing rifts within the GOP just ahead of midterm elections. Catch up quick: Late Friday, Trump waived new sanctions against Russia and tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy that would have taken effect under the bipartisan Graham Act he signed last month. That came just days after the administration waived certain sanctions as part of a deal aimed at enabling higher exports of Russian diesel after high prices have become a political millstone for Republicans. Driving the news: Energy Secretary Chris Wright argued Sunday on CNN's "State of the Union" that Russia could only benefit from the diesel deal if it scales back its war on Ukraine enough to increase exports. "This is a carrot to try to end a war. It's not an economic lifeline for Russia," he said. Yet Secretary of State Marco Rubio offered a different explanation Saturday, saying Russia would have sold the diesel regardless of Trump's intervention. "That diesel was going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, per a State Department transcript. The diesel deal "is an incentive to Russia, that if they can reduce the conflict with Ukraine, they can get an energy ceasefire or reduce the conflict such that they have diesel to export, we'll allow it to flow to world markets," Wright told ABC's "This Week." Context: Ukranian drone strikes against Russian refineries have dramatically hindered Russia's diesel exports. Ukraine resumed those strikes after Russia continued to hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure, despite Trump's claim that the two sides had agreed to an energy ceasefire. The combination of the Iran war — which has throttled supply and damaged Middle East refineries — and Russia's export decline have pushed up diesel costs. Zoom out: The Sunday shows and Rubio's remarks provided the Trump team's most detailed comments on Friday night's executive order , which declines to use new powers under the law named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). The move avoids putting fresh pressure on China and India, both major buyers of Russian oil. Rubio said Trump wants time to "analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the U.S. economy." Wright pointed to ongoing negotiations with China on trade and the war in Ukraine, stressing to CNN that Trump retains the power to impose the penalties later. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, on NBC's "Meet the Press," defended the recent decisions by pointing to sanctions the administration imposed on Russian oil and gas giants Rosneft and Lukoil in 2025. "No one has been tougher on Russian sanctions than President Trump," he said. The other side: A number of Republicans have criticized the White House. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) called the sanctions waiver "beyond irresponsible," while Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said the late Lindsey Graham "would be appalled." Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) called the waiver a "mistake," and Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.) said the U.S. should be increasing pressure on Russia and requested a classified briefing on the decision. What we're watching: As the midterms hit their final frenzied weeks, Republicans have shown an increasing willingness to put distance between themselves and Trump.

e5e7d8c7c805.text: President Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday, just nine days before Israel's Oct. 27 elections. Why it matters: Trump's decision to weigh in nine days ahead of the election could give Netanyahu a boost at a critical moment in the Israeli leader's fight for political survival, with most polls showing his coalition falling short of the 61 seats needed to form a government. What he is saying: In a Sunday post on Truth Social , Trump called Netanyahu "a Great Warrior Prime Minister" and a "great partner" in the war against Iran. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work [in Iran] ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Trump wrote. Trump called Netanyahu "the kind of Partner that the United States of America is demanding of Israel" and gave him his "Complete and Total Endorsement." Behind the scenes: Trump began planning his endorsement earlier this week. "I was always going to do that. I just didn't want to do it too soon," Trump told Axios in a short phone interview on Sunday. Trump said he endorsed Netanyahu because they have a "good relationship" and would "continue to do well" together if Netanyahu is reelected. "It is important that Israel has a person they can count on," Trump said. Asked if he could work with another Israeli leader, Trump said: "Maybe I will, maybe I won't. Who wants to take the chance?" The other side: Netanyahu thanked Trump for his endorsement in an X post. "Together we will complete the mission," Netanyahu wrote . Netanyahu's main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, told Israel's Channel 12 that he respects the U.S. president and appreciates what he has done for Israel. "But the elections are a domestic Israeli issue. The only ones who will decide are the citizens of Israel, and I will stand firm on this," Eisenkot said. The big picture: Trump had repeatedly declined to endorse Netanyahu in recent months amid growing tensions between the two leaders over Iran and Gaza. ⁠Some of Netanyahu's rivals urged Trump to remain neutral, Axios previously reported . Some of Trump's closest advisers believed his Middle East agenda would fare better if Netanyahu lost and a different government formed. Trump himself has been very frustrated with Netanyahu, including in recent weeks. In private conversations, Trump blamed Netanyahu for Israel's failures to prevent the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks. Trump called the prime minister "his own worst enemy" and questioned whether Netanyahu was damaging Israel's international reputation, according to two people who have discussed the matter directly with the president. However, Trump decided to stick with Netanyahu. Driving the news: Netanyahu and Trump discussed two weeks ago the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections, Axios reported . Trump initially seemed to be leaning toward accepting Netanyahu's proposal and resuming attacks, but he grew more hesitant and decided to wait until after the elections. In his endorsement, Trump seemed to suggest he would let Netanyahu strike Iran after the midterm elections, saying "we will soon finish the job." This is a breaking news story. Please check back for updates

a35b4cb33faf.text: By — Cara Anna, Associated Press Cara Anna, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/photographer-attacked-by-settlers-in-the-west-bank-feels-insulted-by-netanyahu Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Photographer attacked by settlers in the West Bank feels insulted by Netanyahu World Oct 18, 2026 1:13 PM EDT JERUSALEM (AP) — The photographer with The Washington Post who was attacked by Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank so badly that several vertebrae were broken said Sunday she was increasingly angry that Israel's military seems to protect settlers more than the Palestinians they threaten. The attack on Heidi Levine and Palestinians during the sensitive olive harvest — followed a day later by an attack on European diplomats in a Christian village — again highlights the rampant settler violence that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has blamed on a small number of troublemakers. WATCH: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians during olive harvest Levine, from her hospital bed, has told The Associated Press she was "shocked and insulted" that Netanyahu referred to the attack on her and others as alleged, adding that the prime minister "had all the evidence on the table." But she described the sharp condemnation of settler violence expressed to her in a call from Israel's president, and in a letter signed by several of the country's top former security and intelligence officials. All expressed shame over the attack. Netanyahu, two weeks out from close elections that could end his time in power, is again confronted with an issue that has drawn growing international condemnation. Much of the world considers the settlements in the West Bank illegal, and yet construction and expansion continue. Hundreds of Palestinians have been attacked and a few have been killed this olive harvest alone, which started in late September, rights groups have said. Olive trees, a central part of history and heritage for Palestinians, have been destroyed. Levine blamed "Jewish terrorists" for Thursday's attack and added: "I've been covering this region for over 40 years, and I have never seen this country in such a state as it is today." Levine praises a call from Israel's president Levine was recovering Sunday from injuries that included what appeared to be stab wounds in her buttocks, which required stitches. There was nothing new from police on the case, she said. U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee, whose recent comments have condemned settler attacks on U.S. citizens but not on Palestinians overall, called the attack on Levine a "despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards" and said they should spend years in prison. Separately, Israeli President Isaac Herzog called Levine, and Yair Golan, a former general and leader of the opposition Democrats party, visited. Netanyahu's main rival in the elections, Gadi Eisenkot, said on X that "a handful of criminals is burning up the last shreds of legitimacy left to the state of Israel." READ MORE: Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection Herzog was "actually very sweet," Levine said Sunday. "Down to earth, calling them thugs, inviting me for a personal hug. He's ashamed for what happened: 'These people are a stain on Israeli society.'" She said she has not heard from Netanyahu. She did receive, however, a letter signed by over a dozen former Israeli security, intelligence and other officials, including former Defense Minister Moshe Yaalon, former Mossad director Tamir Pardo and former Shin Bet director Ami Ayalon. "We are deeply ashamed that Jewish terrorists in the West Bank continue to inflict suffering on innocent Palestinians, assault those who come to their defense, and target those who document and expose their despicable conduct," said the letter, shared with the AP. "Their brutality brings disgrace upon Israel and the Jewish people. Such acts undermine Israel's security, its regional and international standing, and the moral fabric of our society. They represent a betrayal of everything we have devoted our lives to defending." The letter noted that "alas, with encouragement from the highest echelons of government," only a fundamental change in policy can end the "disgraceful phenomenon." Levine says she plans to return to work Levin told the AP that "I never wanted the story to be about me but about the people I've tried to document" over decades. She said she has sought to show how the violence is "increasing, becoming more and more dangerous." She has said the attackers — armed with bottles and slingshots — "were kicking me for like 10 minutes and I was trying to hold on to my cameras and my bag." Her helmet and protective vest, which was marked "PRESS," likely saved her from more serious injuries. READ MORE: Masked settlers attack European diplomats in the occupied West Bank But she and others have openly wondered who will protect Palestinians. Rights groups have said few settlers are ever punished for the attacks that have surged in recent years. "It's about time you do something, Mr. Prime Minister," Levine said. As for herself, she plans to return to work. "I've invested decades of blood, sweat and tears into this," she said. "They cracked my bones, they haven't cracked my spirit." Associated Press writer Sam Mednick in Tel Aviv, Israel, contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.
