Spain's Supreme Court has ruled the former president of Catalonia, Carles Puigdemont, can return without fear of arrest nearly a decade after going into self-imposed exile having led a failed independence bid.
The court upheld a decision to lift an arrest warrant for him linked to the referendum his regional government organised in 2017, in defiance of Madrid.
Direct rule was imposed on the region soon after the vote and Puigdemont fled to Belgium, where he has been based ever since - with a surprise appearance in Barcelona in 2024 prompting a police manhunt.
But the Spain to which he may return is much different from a decade ago, with Catalan independence now a marginal political issue.
Monday's ruling brings to an end a lengthy legal wrangle between the Spanish judiciary and the former Catalan president.
In 2024, Spain's socialist government introduced a controversial amnesty for dozens of Catalan politicians and activists who were involved in the secession drive, but the Supreme Court said Puigdemont and several of his colleagues should be excluded.
It argued this was because of the charges against them of alleged financial crimes around staging the referendum.
The Constitutional Court overruled that interpretation earlier this month, and on Monday the Supreme Court rejected an appeal by the far-right Vox party against lifting national arrest warrants for Puigdemont, as well as his former ministers LluÃs Puig and Toni ComÃn, paving the way for their return to Spain.
Puigdemont was elected as a member of the European Parliament (MEP) in 2019 and to the Catalan parliament in 2024 as leader of the region's centre-right Together for Catalonia (JxCat) party.
He had campaigned in the south of France, where he held rallies attended by supporters who travelled across the border to see him.
Puigdemont is known to have made at least one brief return to Spain since leaving the country, addressing a crowd of supporters in Barcelona prior to disappearing and escaping back over the border to France before he could be detained.
While he was living in Waterloo, Belgium, nine of his former colleagues were jailed for their role in the events of 2017. They were released when the Spanish government pardoned them in 2021.
Puigdemont has remained an active political presence, travelling across Europe to espouse the Catalan independence cause and fiercely criticising Spain's democratic institutions.
In a video posted on social media just as the Supreme Court ruling was announced, Puigdemont spoke of his reasons for staying abroad.
"My role was to stir public opinion, internationalise the conflict and work from the heart of Europe to explain the reality of Spain," he said.
It is still not known when he might return to Spain.
ComÃn, his former regional minister for health, plans to travel this week to Madrid, where he is due to carry out administrative procedures linked to his status as an MEP.
The referendum sparked the country's biggest political crisis since democracy was restored following the death of Francisco Franco.
The banned vote was met with a heavy police crackdown. The region's separatist majority declared independence after the vote - Madrid then dissolved parliament, sacked its leaders and called a snap election.
But Catalan independence is now a relatively marginal issue in Spain, with housing and immigration dominating the political agenda.
The parliamentary support of Puigdemont's JxCat party was instrumental in allowing current Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez to form a new left-wing Spanish government after the 2023 election.
But within Catalonia, JxCat has been struggling, with a far-right, pro-independence party, Catalan Alliance, taking many of its voters.
And next month, Spain's general election could see the far right enter government for the first time.

e4947a7b76cc.text: By — Michelle Chapman, Associated Press Michelle Chapman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/musk-pledges-to-give-a-share-of-his-spacex-company-to-every-kid-in-america-next-year Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Musk pledges to give a share of his SpaceX company to 'every kid in America' next year Nation Oct 19, 2026 9:55 AM EDT Elon Musk on Monday pledged to give one share of his company SpaceX to "every kid in America" next year. The offer arrived a day after artificial intelligence company Anthropic announced in a social media post that it will commit 5% of its shares to a new "public benefit" fund. READ MORE: Lawsuit says Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google made illegal agreement on AI slowdown In a response to that Sunday post, Musk wrote, "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public." Shares of SpaceX, which will report its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, closed at $146.03 on Friday. With approximately 73 million children under the age of 18 in the United States, that would put the value of Musk's pledge at about $10.66 billion. Anthropic said Sunday that the shares it is committing will go to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity within the company. The fund's worth will potentially increase as the shares grow in value. Musk did not provide further details on how his share pledge will be carried out, but did add in his post that "This will be the first of many." The announcements by Musk and Anthropic arrive as Americans grow increasingly wary of AI. A new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that most Americans, 64%, think AI is developing "too fast," while 27% say its development has been "about right" and only 8% say it's moving "too slow." Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Sam Altman, SpaceXAI's Musk and other prominent industry leaders said last month that AI's development needs to slow down. The consensus came after an Anthropic researcher resigned with a dire warning about the threats the technology poses to humanity. But obstacles including domestic and global competition, profit motivations and pushback from President Donald Trump all stand in the way of a coordinated effort to pace AI's development. Musk has quietly become the biggest known donor in this year's midterm elections, doling out more than $276 million since July to try to save Republican majorities in Congress. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and the company's five other cofounders established Anthropic as a public benefit corporation, a designation that for-profit companies select to balance financial goals and social impact. Anthropic is planning a massive initial public offering as soon as November. In June the company said that it had submitted a confidential filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for its proposed IPO. That same month, Musk's SpaceX made its Wall Street debut as a publicly traded company and made Musk the world's first trillionaire. Shares of SpaceX are down 35.3% since peaking days after that initial public offering, however, meaning Musk is a billionaire. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. People in the province of Alberta head to the polls on Monday to decide whether to hold a binding referendum at a later date on separating from Canada.
The vote was called earlier this year by the leader of the province, Danielle Smith, after a grassroots group gathered about 300,000 signatures on a petition that asked for a binding referendum on separation.
Many of those who support separation say the oil-rich province's economic growth has been stifled by the environmental policies of Canada's central government in Ottawa.
But those who want Alberta to remain part of Canada - who include Prime Minister Mark Carney - have called for the country to show unity in the face of external pressures.
Polls have suggested that the majority of Albertans would vote to remain in Canada, though the pre-vote debate alone has proven divisive.
Another group collected signatures for its own petition that opposed separation, which was signed by more than 400,000 people. The province's population is about five million people.
If Albertans do vote on Monday to move ahead with a binding referendum, that could happen as soon as 2027, Smith has said.
Smith's decision to allow Monday's vote came in spite of the fact that a court blocked the pro-separation petition, saying it failed to consult indigenous First Nations whose land would be affected if the province separated from Canada.
Following the judge's ruling, First Nations groups have branded Smith's decision to allow the voting process to play out as "undemocratic" and "authoritarian".
Smith, the leader of the United Conservative Party of Alberta (UCP), has defended her decision to put the issue to voters. She opposes separation herself, but says the process gives the province's residents a chance to have their say on the issue.
The key question on the voting paper will ask: "Should Alberta remain a province of Canada or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?"
The separatist movement is led by Mitch Sylvestre, a gun shop owner from the town of Bonnyville, and Jeffrey Rath, a lawyer based in Calgary. They are both members of a group called the Alberta Prosperity Project, which argues that the province's economic growth has been hindered by years of Liberal party rule in Ottawa.
Successive Liberal governments of the last 10 years have put environmental policies above helping Alberta develop its oil and gas sector, they argue. They say Alberta would get to keep more of its wealth if it splits from Canada.
Chris Scott, founder of pro-separatist group Let's Talk Alberta, told BBC News on the eve of the poll that the campaign had already achieved some of its goals, regardless of what happened on Monday. "The key is the conversation has started and it needs to continue," he said. "What's started can't be stopped now," he added.
Those who oppose separation say a newly independent Alberta would be left responsible for billions of dollars in debt. They warn that the uncertainty - which they liken to the UK's Brexit vote to leave the European Union in 2016 - would drive thousands of jobs and investment out of the province.
Pro-independence voters told the BBC in Edmonton over the weekend that they feel their voice is not heard in Ottawa, the national capital.
"We really need to send a message to Ottawa, " said Jennifer Trudeau, who calls herself a sovereigntist. She said she did not want a full divorce from Canada, but believes the province needs to "assert its rights".
At a separate unity rally in Edmonton, people told the BBC that they were proud Albertans but felt it was better to keep the country together.
"Alberta is a strong province, but it is important that it stays within a united Canada," said Michele Jackson.
"That is critical to me. I am Canadian 100%."
Micah Sellers called the question about whether the province should pursue independence "ridiculous".
"It's a waste of money," he said. "It's a distraction from real issues in Alberta and in Canada. I think if we're going to be asked, everyone should vote to remain."
Carney has called on voters to deliver a decisive vote against separation. Speaking at a rally on Thursday, he warned that the stakes were high.
"The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us," Carney said, echoing warnings he has made in the past about his country's ongoing trade war with the United States.
Alongside the separation question, Albertans will vote on nine other issues - a number of which focus on whether the province should have more control over its immigration system.
Hundreds of thousands of people had voted early by post ahead of Monday, and early figures suggested a strong voter turnout.
The province's election officials will count the ballots by hand, and have 48 hours to complete the task - starting from no earlier than 20:00 local time on Monday (02:00 GMT on Tuesday).
The key question, on separation, will be counted in its entirety first. Officials have said results should be available in the early hours of Tuesday.

- Published
A former Rwandan army sergeant major, who became an outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded in neighbouring Uganda.
Robert Kabera, 50, fled Rwanda after being accused of sexual assault, which he denied. He sought asylum in neighbouring Uganda, citing political persecution.
Ugandan police spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke on Monday said that Kabera's head had still not been recovered. His body was discovered by local residents on the outskirts of Kampala over the weekend.
The Rwandan government has not publicly commented on the killing. Several critics of Kagame have been killed, both in Rwanda and abroad.
His widow, Jeanne d'Arc Rwigema Uwizeye, told BBC Great Lakes in a written message that she now feared for her family's safety.
"It is scary. I feel crazy, the children and I don't have security," she said.
According to his family, Kabera had travelled to inspect a construction site about 45 km (30 miles) outside Kampala before his death.
Kabera built a public profile as a musician and YouTuber, attracting more than 144,000 subscribers to his channel, which featured over 800 videos, many criticising Kagame and his administration.
Reacting to news of his murder, exiled opposition group Rwanda National Congress (RNC) called for a thorough investigation and for those responsible to be brought to justice.
In a statement on X, the RNC said: "Today, his family is grieving, his voice is gone, and Rwandans in exile are confronting a terrifying question: where can we be safe?"
His death adds to concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living in exile.
In 2014, Patrick Karegeya, a former Rwandan intelligence chief who helped set up the RNC, was found dead in his hotel room in Johannesburg, South Africa.
Karegeya fell out with President Paul Kagame and was arrested twice, serving an 18-month prison sentence for insubordination and desertion before fleeing to South Africa in 2007, where he became a vocal critic of the government.
Following his death, Kagame made remarks widely seen as a warning to other critics.
"Any person alive who may be plotting against Rwanda, whoever they are, will pay the price. Whoever it is, it is a matter of time," he said.
In 2019, South African authorities issued arrest warrants for two Rwandans accused of murdering Karegeya.

Zambiaâs state miner and Abu Dhabi-based International Resources Holding (IRH) say they have patched up their financing dispute over Mopani Copper Mines, the development of which is a cornerstone of the southern African countryâs economic growth plan.
In a letter in September, Zambiaâs ZCCM-IH accused the Emirati company of failing to provide equity funding and taking on unapproved debt. The latest statement skirted the issue, describing new joint-exploration projects and saying they âremain aligned on the long-term developmentâ of the mine, but left funding questions open.
The truce followed a meeting in Abu Dhabi between Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema and IRHâs CEO on the day the letter became public. IRH paid $620 million in 2024 for a 51% stake in Mopani as part of a deal worth more than $1 billion. Neither side can afford a fight: Zambia, Africaâs second-largest copper producer, needs Gulf capital for its bid to more than triple its output to 3 million tons a year, and IRH aims to lift Mopaniâs production from 66,369 tons in 2025 to 300,000 tons by 2029.

- Published
More than 1,000 tower mustard plants have been successfully grown and planted out by volunteers in London.
It marks a successful first year for a major community-led effort to restore one of the capital's rarest native wildflowers, vital for bees, butterflies and rare moths.
Led by Citizen Zoo and Habitats & Heritage, the tower mustard project brings together a network of land managers, community groups, conservation partners and volunteers.
The plants, grown by volunteers, are being reestablished at sites across London, in regions where tower mustard was previously known to occur.
At the core of the project are the Mighty Mustard volunteers.
In March, they attended a workshop, learned how to sow the tiny seeds, and were given their own growing equipment, including pots, seed trays and soil.
Seeds were sourced from London's last remaining tower mustard populations in Lesnes Abbey Woods in Bexley and Stain Hill Reservoir in Richmond-upon-Thames.
Charlotte Harris, nature conservation manager at Habitats & Heritage, said: "[We] are passionate about engaging people in conservation initiatives. Through this tower mustard project, we have enjoyed giving local residents the unique opportunity to get hands-on in conserving one of London's rarest plants.
"We've found the volunteers have become really attached to [them]."
Seeds have now been planted at Wimbledon Common, Hounslow Heath, Lesnes Abbey Woods and Barnes Common.
Harris added: "We are hoping that this model can be used as a blueprint for helping other rare plants with volunteer input in the same way."
The final planting day is at Hampton Court Palace's Home Park on Tuesday, where plants raised separately by the Historic Royal Palaces Gardens Team and volunteers will be used.
Botanist Dr Mark Spencer has also provided expert support throughout the project.
Tower mustard, or Turritis glabra, is a native UK herb that has suffered steep decline due to habitat destruction and changes in land management.
It is thought to survive at around 30 sites across England.
The species is assessed as near threatened on the Great Britain Red List and endangered in England.
Growing to around one metre tall and producing delicate white flowers, tower mustard is associated with open and disturbed habitats and supports pollinators.
This community-led model builds on Citizen Zoo's successful Hop of Hope project which saw volunteers rear large marsh grasshoppers from eggs at home, going on to release the species in wetlands across Norfolk.
'We've lost 185 species'
Elliot Newton, director of rewilding at Citizen Zoo, said the company hopes to roll out more projects to preserve plants in the face of climate change.
"In London alone, we've lost 185 species of plant. They have gone extinct in recent history."
He said Citizen Zoo have many other plants on their radar, including copse bindweed, a native British climbing plant.
Tower mustard is the first plant species Citizen Zoo has worked with in London, joining a growing portfolio of rewilding projects that also includes beavers, water voles, German hairy snails and white storks.
The tower mustard project is funded by the Greater London Authority's Green Roots Fund and Thames Water.
The project brings together Habitats & Heritage, Barnes Common, Lesnes Abbey Woods, Wimbledon Common, London Borough of Hounslow, London Borough of Richmond upon Thames and Historic Royal Palaces.
Newton said: "These projects may sound small, but they're helping safeguard the future of the city."

GSMA, the global telecoms industry body, has urged African governments to cut the cost of radio frequency spectrum, arguing the expense is holding back investment in faster mobile networks. Reforms could add more than $120 billion to the African economy by 2035, expand 4G and 5G coverage, and raise productivity, it estimated.
The GSMA said spectrum charges as a portion of annual revenue are significantly higher than the global average for African operators â Botswana, Eswatini, Mozambique, and Zambia were named among the pricier countries. The push for cheaper deals, contained in a report from GSMAâs research wing, comes as more than $10 billion worth of licenses will need to be renewed within the next decade, just as many African governments are struggling to raise revenue and contain debt. In several markets, spectrum auctions have become significant sources of state revenue, creating tensions between governmentsâ fiscal goals and operatorsâ calls to use them as a connectivity tool.

The continentâs inventors are in the spotlight as Johannesburg prepares to host the final of the Royal Academy of Engineeringâs Africa prize. Previous participants have been given a boost in their quest to create life-changing tools. Atish Shah, who took part five years ago, told Semafor his Dar es Salaam-based company Roverlabs is now developing a bionic hand which uses electromyography technology to transform electrical impulses in muscle tissue into movement for amputees.
The firm uses 3D printing to manufacture customized assistive devices for people living with disabilities, including insoles, helmets, dentures, and braces. Next month, it is set to begin a home imaging service to ensure people living in Tanzaniaâs rural areas have access to X-ray and ultrasound technology.

Burundi signed a $1.4 billion electricity deal with US-backed Anzana Electric Group, which Washington says will strengthen American supply chains and support mining in the East African country.
The country has deposits of nickel, gold, and rare earths. But Burundi, like many resource-rich African nations, has struggled to develop large-scale mining due to power shortages, poor roads and the lack of a direct rail link to export markets. Only one in five Burundians had access to electricity in 2024, according to the World Bank.
The 25-year agreement, signed through Anzanaâs local subsidiary Weza Power, aims to connect more than 1.2 million households and businesses. It follows a US-backed agreement in March giving New York-listed mining company Lifezone Metals 14 months of exclusive access to assess Burundiâs Musongati nickel deposit, a metal used in stainless steel and some electric vehicle batteries. Washington is pursuing mineral partnerships across Africa to challenge Chinaâs dominance of global supply chains. Last month, US officials also pledged to help Kenya to develop its own mineral processing industry.

1bfc319bd564.text:
For decades, scientists have dreamed of getting Martian rocks into Earth’s laboratories — a Herculean feat that would revolutionize our knowledge of the Red Planet. An audacious mission from the Japanese space agency might offer the next best thing: rocks from Mars’ larger moon, Phobos.
That’s the task confronting the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft, due to launch October 19 at 3:41 p.m. EDT. The mission aims to crack the long-standing mystery of how Mars got its two odd moons by delivering a sample of Phobos to Earth in 2031. These rocks are no substitute for true Martian material — but given that NASA’s plans to fetch the Perseverance rover’s prized samples are in limbo, scientists are eager for even an indirect glimpse of Mars.
“It’s a chance to get a totally different sample and view of Martian materials,” says planetary scientist Briony Horgan of Purdue University in West Lafayette, Ind., who is not involved in the MMX mission. “It’ll be a great contribution to our sample collection back here on Earth.”
Focus on Phobos
If it’s successful, MMX will be the first mission to reach Phobos. Three previous spacecraft from Russia failed.
The MMX itinerary is action-packed: After launch, the spacecraft will spend about one year cruising out to Mars, then slip into orbit around Mars alongside Phobos for about three years. During its stay, the spacecraft will deploy a small rover named Idefix to scout the moon for good sampling sites. The main spacecraft will then make two landings to grab 10 grams of sample, about the weight of four U.S. pennies. It will use two different devices to snag the sample: One will drill two centimeters down into the rock, while the other will blow pressurized gas at the surface to collect loose material.
Once loaded up, MMX will zip past the smaller moon Deimos before making the one-year trek home to drop its cargo in Australia’s outback, just as Japan’s two previous asteroid sample-return missions have done. After the Japanese space agency JAXA sorts and catalogs the samples, it will share portions of them with other institutions.
Such a small handful of rock may not sound impressive, but it’s enough to thrill researchers. “A few grams of sample are going to be a real bonanza for scientists,” says planetary scientist Michael Zolensky of NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, where 15 percent of the sample will eventually end up.
MMX is designed to reveal the enigmatic origins of Phobos and Deimos — the only moons in the inner solar system besides our own. “The Martian moons are so different from [the] terrestrial moon: They are two, very small [and] very dark,” says planetary scientist Tomoki Nakamura of Tohoku University in Sendai, Japan.
The strange objects look like rocks that wandered in from the outer asteroid belt and got trapped around Mars. But their tidy circular orbits suggest they coalesced after a massive collision tore material off the Red Planet. Or perhaps they came about some other way that scientists simply haven’t imagined, says planetary scientist Kiyoshi Kuramoto of Hokkaido University in Sapporo, Japan. “The natural world often reveals aspects that exceed our expectations,” he says.
Studying the features and composition of Phobos’ surface could solve the mystery. But although MMX carries sophisticated instruments to explore Phobos, those observations may not suffice. Hence bringing rock back to Earth’s labs, where scientists can enlist equipment far too large or delicate to ever send to space.
Martian mysteries under the microscope
Although sample analysis will focus on understanding Phobos, researchers will also be able to use the rocks to fine-tune our understanding of Mars. For example, pinpointing the material’s age will allow scientists to calibrate the chronology of cosmic collisions in the neighborhood of Mars. Currently, scientists estimate ages on Mars based on a timeline based on our moon, which may not apply at the Red Planet.
Scientists even have reason to hope that stray grains from Mars will be hidden amid the MMX treasure. This material could be ancient relics of the two bodies mixing during a moon-forming process, potentially including grains that hail from deeper in the Martian crust than scientists have seen so far in rare meteorites the cosmos has delivered us. No matter how Phobos formed, the material could also include fresher debris flung off the Red Planet by cosmic collisions.
The biggest challenge may be positively identifying which grains came from Mars. Such lucky samples would lack valuable geologic context and be far from pristine. “They’re material that’s been blasted off Mars from some unknown location, micron-sized things, sitting on the airless body Phobos, getting irradiated by space,” says planetary scientist Nancy Chabot of the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory in Laurel, Md. Nonetheless, scientists are prepared to get creative and use the latest technology to tease out every secret they can manage in any sample they can snag.
MMX offers a very different type of sample return than what NASA has initiated with the Perseverance rover, which has spent years squirreling away fresh material drilled from the most interesting outcrops it can find. That’s all in hopes of a future mission ferrying the rock to Earth for scientists to hunt for signs of ancient microbes. But the U.S. Congress has axed funding for that successor due to spiraling costs and concerns about feasibility — particularly of accomplishing the first ever launch from Mars.
Even if MMX can’t give scientists the satisfaction of an ultimate Mars sample return, there’s still plenty to learn, says planetary scientist Vicky Hamilton of the Southwest Research Institute in Boulder, Colo., who is not involved in the mission. “It’s always a happy day when we’re getting a sample from another object in space and bringing it back to Earth to study,” she says.

000c9158113d.text: President Trump's moves to avoid new penalties on Russian energy sent shockwaves through Washington, sparking diplomatic tensions and political turmoil. Why it matters: Trump's push to lower energy prices ahead of the midterms could provide Russia an economic lifeline and is exposing divisions within his own party. Oil, gas and petroleum product exports help finance Russia's war on Ukraine. Catch up quick: Late Friday, Trump waived new sanctions against Russia and tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy that would have taken effect under the bipartisan Graham Act he signed last month. That came just days after the administration waived certain sanctions as part of a deal aimed at enabling higher exports of Russian diesel after high prices have become a political millstone for Republicans. Here's what's on our radar: A new rationale. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, in CNN and ABC appearances yesterday, called the diesel deal a "carrot" to get Russia to ease its assault on Ukraine. It's an "incentive to Russia, that if they can reduce the conflict with Ukraine, they can get an energy ceasefire or reduce the conflict such that they have diesel to export, we'll allow it to flow to world markets," Wright told ABC's "This Week." Ukrainian drone strikes have lowered Russia's refining capacity. Trump, in a Truth Social post yesterday, also cast his recent decisions as a way to get a peace deal with Russia. A new clock. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Saturday that Trump wants to take 60 days to review implementing the Graham Act in order to gauge its impact on the global and U.S. economies. A deteriorating relationship. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has sharply and publicly criticized both the diesel deal and Trump's decision to waive, for now, the Graham Act penalties. Trump's post, meanwhile, bashed Zelensky for hitting Russian refineries, "knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States." Republican rifts. Many GOP lawmakers and candidates, to varying degrees, have joined Democrats in criticizing Trump's Friday night sanctions waivers and the diesel deal days earlier. Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) told the AP that she disagrees with Trump's decision not to implement, for now, the bipartisan law named after her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). She's running for a full term after being appointed to replace her brother. Former Rep. Mike Rogers — the GOP candidate in Michigan's tight Senate race — also expressed concern with the decision but avoided directly criticizing Trump on CNN yesterday. Other Republicans were far harsher, including retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who called Friday night's move "beyond irresponsible." Lame duck rumblings. "A growing chorus of House Republicans is warning President Trump that they're ready to block additional Pentagon funding unless the administration gets tougher on Russia," The Hill reports. What we're watching: With the midterms just weeks away, more Republicans are openly breaking with Trump.

The News
Former Sen. Joe Manchin, I-W.Va., is traveling to Maine this week to campaign with Republican Sen. Susan Collins, according to details shared first with Semafor.
The moderate West Virginian said his visit is motivated by the attacks on Collins for voting too often in support of President Donald Trump.
Manchin will hit Maine on Wednesday with Collins and visit Androscoggin County, a fairly evenly divided part of the state. Collins is looking to emphasize her bipartisan credentials down the stretch as her opponent, Democrat Troy Jackson, leans on his progressive allies and campaigns as a blunt check on Trump.
In an interview on Sunday, Manchin said he âcanât rememberâ a bipartisan effort Collins wasnât involved in and that he wants to make sure the people of Maine understand how her style of legislating benefits the state.
Know More
From Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer on down, Democrats are attacking Collins for voting for Trumpâs nominees and his legislation, though she opposed the tax cuts law and Defense Secretary Pete Hegsethâs confirmation. Collins also helped tank Obamacare repeal in 2017, but Jackson has argued her opposition to Trump is often not decisive.
Democrats cite statistics showing Collins votes with Trump 90% or more of the time, but Manchin called those numbers âbullsh*tâ because they include mostly nominee votes. He said his trip is dedicated to âdebunkingâ the idea that sheâs been an enabler for Trump. âShe is not a Trump senator,â he said.
Manchin specifically mentioned the Electoral Count Act, a law intended to prevent another Jan. 6-style attempt to block an election result, which Collins sponsored. He also worked closely with Collins on the bipartisan infrastructure law.
âIn the Senate, Joe and I worked across the aisle to tackle some of our nationâs toughest challenges. Together, we built bipartisan coalitions to end government shutdowns, secure critical COVID-19 relief, and pass the bipartisan infrastructure law,â Collins said. âWe need more people in the Senate, not fewer, who are willing to put partisanship aside, listen to one another, and deliver results.â
Now that their debates are over, Maineâs Senate race is entering its final stage. And Manchinâs visit will contrast sharply with some of Jacksonâs high-profile progressive surrogates like Sens. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Bernie Sanders of Vermont; Jackson will hold a town hall with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., on Thursday.

688a9fe05734.text:
The News
The leading contenders in Nigeriaâs presidential election face a defining question: should the fuel subsidy be restored to ease the burden of rising energy costs?
President Bola Tinubu, who is seeking a second term in January, has repeatedly defended his decision to scrap a years-long subsidy program in 2023 to avoid wasteful spending and invest in infrastructure development. But his governmentâs introduction of a short-term petrol price discount this month to counter rising costs driven by the Iran war has reignited the debate as to whether a subsidy would make a more lasting return.
Tinubuâs main rivals say they plan to restore some form of consumer support if elected and have accused the president of panicking in the face of pressure to account for his decision, with polls opening in less than 100 days. SBM Intelligence, a Lagos-based advisory firm, found in a survey published in September that more than two-thirds of voters want the government to reinstate a fuel subsidy of some kind. Insecurity, which has worsened around the country, is also set to figure as a major point of contention.
The revived subsidy debate is shaping just about every conversation concerning the coming vote in Africaâs biggest democracy. Tinubu and his 17 challengers are hitting the campaign trail to sway voters whose collective purchasing power has weakened sharply in the last three years, in large part due to the five-fold rise in fuel prices in that period which has driven inflation and spawned a cost-of-living crisis. Its resurgence reflects Nigeriaâs history as the continentâs top oil producer and exporter that has consistently failed to convert its energy riches into broad-based prosperity.
For years, the vast majority of the crude oil produced in the country was exported because none of the governmentâs domestic refineries were fully functional. Imported refined products were then subsidized by payments from the state-oil company NNPC, enabling a multibillion-dollar largesse that grew into an increasingly opaque and corrupt scheme, according to government fact-finders and international observers. It was also costly: The programâs $10 billion in 2022 exceeded the combined budget for healthcare and education.
Tinubu has largely not faced widespread protests or strong political opposition since ending the subsidy. He has told Nigerians that his policy approach is shifting from offering âemergency treatmentâ â ostensibly to fix the faulty foundations of the economy he inherited â to enabling shared prosperity.
But in Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, he faces familiar challengers who are eager to make the coming election a referendum on the impact of energy costs. âBola made life expensive. I will work to make life affordable again,â Atiku said in a campaign video last week. Obi, the other heavyweight in the race, pledged to judge his leadership by metrics that would show Nigerians âeating better, living better, and escaping poverty.â
Know More
The sharp rise in energy costs that followed Tinubuâs subsidy removal led several businesses to shutter or reconsider operations in Nigeria. But while many questioned the absence of safety net measures to cushion the impact of Tinubuâs so-called shock therapy, the International Monetary Fund praised the subsidy removal, as did several economists. An IMF official last week cautioned Nigeria to avoid the temptation of reinstating a subsidy for political reasons.
The Dangote refinery in Lagos, which started supplying fuel in Nigeria two years ago, provides about 70% of Nigeriaâs domestic fuel needs. But the country still imports refined fuels. Both Dangote â which buys more than a third of its crude from international suppliers â and fuel importers are vulnerable to global oil price shocks.
The potential for further escalation in the Iran war, underscored by recent Iran-backed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, raises the question of how long Nigeria is prepared to extend the price cap that is initially planned to be in place for 30-days. âI think itâs highly likely that this gets extended, at least through the elections into Q1,â said Ikemesit Effiong, a partner at SBM.
BMI, a subsidiary of Fitch Group, expects the price cap to amount to up to 0.4% of Nigeriaâs gross domestic product by the second quarter of next year.
Alexanderâs view
Nigeriaâs subsidy debates are divisive because the program â once seen by many Nigerians as the only benefit they got from the state â has swallowed historically mammoth sums and is inextricably associated with corruption and state capture by a cabal of favored oil traders.
Many analysts say Nigeriaâs fuel subsidy burdened public finances and encouraged adverse behaviors like fuel smuggling. Together with changes that allowed the naira currency to float freely by market forces, Tinubuâs subsidy removal helped to improve Nigeriaâs fiscal stability and strengthen reserves.
But trialling a short-term fuel price cap points to a government reckoning with the pain it has inflicted. âThe removal of the fuel subsidy has been economically necessary, but socially painful,â Jervin Nadioo, an analyst at Oxford Economics Africa, told me. He believes Tinubu is âwell positioned to secure re-electionâ but growing public frustration over living costs suggests that an improved economic picture has not translated into sufficient relief for households.
Stop-gaps and sweeteners may sway some voters towards Tinubu in January. But it is more likely that the difficulties of the last three years have already hardened views about the candidates.
Room for Disagreement
The battle for political advantage ahead of elections should not obscure a reasonable expectation that governments can intervene to soften the pain of citizens, said Vahyala Kwaga, country head for Nigeria at policy research group BudgIT.

The Scene
A capital crunch is coming to the AI buildout thatâs already plagued by shortages of chips, power and materials.
âSoon, there will be shortages of capitalâ and lenders are starting to demand real returns, Tan Su Shan, who runs Southeast Asiaâs largest bank said at a Semafor World Economy Global Leaders Dinner in Bangkok.
âWhen the party will end, I donât know,â the CEO of DBS Group said at the event, held on the sidelines of the World Bank and IMF annual meetings. But âthere will come a point where people need to question the returns.â
Her bet: If youâre anywhere on the AI supply chain, you might be okay for, say, the next two years, but probably not longer than that.
Global investors are already showing âjittery nerves,â Tan said, following a chip selloff across global markets sparked by the Broadcom CEO Hock Tanâs comparison of AI investors to casino gamblers. A lot of investors have âno clue what they are investing in,â he said at DBSâs tech conference last week.
But the market reaction isnât necessarily bad, Tan argued. Unlike during the global financial crisis in 2008, she said, investors can see the weakness coming and thatâs starting to play out with more discerning buyers demanding risk-adjusted returns.
âTheyâre bringing up this ROI question, the capex question. The market is speaking, and I donât think itâs a bad thing,â she said.
Q&A
This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Shelly Banjo: The CEOs of Broadcom and Intel sounded the financial alarm on AI, likening investors to casino gamblers. Do you share that concern?
Tan Su Shan: Thereâs shortages in memory. Thereâs shortages in chips. Thereâs shortages in power. And soon there will be shortages in capital. So if youâre anywhere around that supply chain, the next two years youâre going to be okay. But what will then happen is that the users of AI will start demanding returns. Now those returns, the ROI, may or may not materialize.

They donât really know what the returns are, but theyâre just punting away.â I canât remember his exact words, but, sort of, itâs a casino. People donât know what theyâre doing. Itâs like mom gave you some money to go play video games, and youâre playing video games and wasting the money, and I think Elon Musk, latched on to that, he said, âNo crying in the casino.â

There was quite a lot of reaction. It does speak to the jittery nerves in the market. But the fact that weâre all talking about it is actually not a bad thing. Unlike previous crises where they just came upon us quite suddenly in one fell swoop, people are now bringing up this ROI question, the capex question. The bond market has spoken, right? Iâm demanding more returns for the kind of risk that weâre taking, both on the AI front and the US fiscal deficit. So I think the marketâs speaking and itâs not a bad thing.
Itâs not like there isnât a lot of money in the world, though. So where do these capital fears come from?
The US capital markets have convinced the whole world to invest in their growth companies. No matter how much money youâre losing, itâs okay. In the bond market, no matter how much youâre spending, itâs okay. The incredible genius of the US is its ability to hoover up investments from everyone â from sovereign wealth funds, to private individuals, to retail, down to the youngest investor. The kids are now in Robinhood buying SpaceX.
But with this massive hoovering of dollars into this concentrated bucket, there will come a point where people need to question the returns. When the party will end, I donât know.
The private credit market is also adjusting, which is not a bad thing. So Iâm hopeful that we could see an equilibrium.
How are you thinking about the projects that are locking in this long-term debt at higher rates, and how do you think about that risk for your bank and the customers that youâre serving?
The market is adjusting and a lot of the hyperscalers are tapping the market before their credit ratings get downgraded. But theyâre moving from being massive cash generators to becoming massive cash guzzlers, and that in itself will be a massive pivot.
Youâre sitting right in the center of all these geopolitical fault lines, with business in Taiwan, mainland China, and across Asia. How do you strike a balance?
This is a great time for middle powers. Thereâs two big powers, and then thereâs everybody else. And all these middle powers, everyone has this ability to stay open, stay world-based, and continue to transact with each other. And frankly, the better connected we are, the safer it will be for everyone. Why? Because AI unleashed with no guardrails and no sharing of best practices and no sharing of cyber know-how means no oneâs going to win. This is something that the world needs to take seriously.

bbbb41333f88.text: By — Rod McGuirk, Associated Press Rod McGuirk, Associated Press By — Charlotte Graham-McLay, Associated Press Charlotte Graham-McLay, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/australian-lawmaker-critically-injured-by-car-is-no-accident-prime-minister-says Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Australian lawmaker critically injured by car is 'no accident,' prime minister says World Oct 19, 2026 7:45 AM EDT MELBOURNE, Australia (AP) — A car hit an Australian federal independent lawmaker on Monday, critically injuring her in an apparent deliberate attack, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. The driver was arrested. Helen Haines, 65, was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her electoral district office mid afternoon in the city of Wangaratta in Victoria state, a police said. Albanese said the national counterterrorism team, incorporating police and intelligence agencies, was investigating. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear. We don't know what the motivation is," Albanese told Australian Broadcasting Corp. The 43-year-old driver was arrested at the scene by a passerby. He will be interviewed in relation to the incident, police said. "A knife was located by police and seized from inside the Toyota," police said. "At this stage, police are investigating as to whether this was an intentional act," police added. Haines, who was first elected to the Parliament in 2019, was taken to a hospital with critical injuries, police said. The episode has renewed safety concerns for Australian lawmakers, in a country where politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security officers present. But public incitement against officials is growing. Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett said in 2025 that threats against parliamentarians had doubled over the past three years. Police data showed more than 1,000 such threats against politicians in the 2025-2026 financial year, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Monday. Albanese told the ABC it was "unfortunate" that an increasingly polarized political climate had already led to security changes for Australia's lawmakers. "I think there has been a rise in temperature and there has been too much shouting, not enough discourse, not enough polite conversation and disagreement," he said Monday. There was "no question" that social media played a part, Albanese added. In Britain, murders of politicians have prompted bolstered security. Labour lawmaker Jo Cox was shot and stabbed in 2016 by a far-right extremist, and Conservative David Amess was stabbed in 2021 by an attacker inspired by the Islamic State group. In July, the former politician and reality TV contestant Ann Widdecombe was found slain with a hammer at her home. A man has been charged with murder and terrorism-related offenses. Graham-McLay contributed from Wellington, New Zealand. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Brazil's left-wing President, Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva, and his right-wing rival, Senator FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, have clashed in a debate held one week before the run-off presidential election.
Polls suggest the two candidates are neck and neck and the televised debate was hailed as a chance for both to sway undecided voters.
But the showdown was marked by personal attacks and analysts have warned that its aggressive tone may increase the abstention rate further.
In the first round of voting, held on 4 October, Bolsonaro defied opinion polls by securing a narrow lead over Lula.
Sunday's debate was the first of two before the vote. The second is planned for Friday, just two days before polls open.
FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro is standing for the Liberal Party after his father, Jair Bolsonaro - who governed from 2018 to 2022 - was sentenced to more than 20 years in prison for plotting to overthrow Lula after the latter beat him in the 2022 election.
The younger Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote in the first round, compared with Lula's 45.2%, with both falling short of the 50% of the valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round.
Since the return to democracy in 1988, there has been no instance in which the candidate who lost in the first round went on to win in the second but Lula has told his supporters that he will "win in extra time".
Analysts consulted by BBC News Brasil were struck by how much the debate was dominated not by issues but personal attacks.
Yuri Sanches from pollsters AtlasIntel said it was a debate in which no policies were discussed and there were no rational arguments.
"The independent voter, who is sometimes against Bolsonaro and sometimes against the Workers' Party [of Lula], came out of it with a very negative impression."
Lucas AragÃ£o from political analysis firm Arko Advice said Bolsonaro had appeared calmer during the debate and seemed to have managed to "get under Lula's skin".
Rafael Cortez from consulting firm da TendÃªncias Consultoria, however, argued that Lula had managed to score a goal when he said he would open up his financial and phone records and those of his family to judicial scrutiny, and challenged his rival to do the same before Sunday's run-off.
Many observers criticised the format of the debate, which was described as chaotic at times, with each of the candidates pacing around the TV studio as the other was speaking.
One heated exchange saw Bolsonaro telling Lula he should come stand next to him so that the two could talk.
Referring to alleged links between the senator and paramilitary vigilante groups, Lula said "I don't want to be close to you", and that he wanted to maintain "distance from the Bolsonaro family" and "the militia".
Bolsonaro, who has dismissed the allegations as fake news, in turn tried to bait Lula by saying, "On second thoughts, maybe it's better to keep my distance so that my wallet isn't stolen."
He also accused the Workers' Party of being corrupt, holding up the palm of his hand on which he had scribbled "CORRUPTO" (Portuguese for "corrupt).
"Take a piece of paper and a pen and jot down 'corrupt' and you'll see that it has two letters in the middle here together," he said, pointing to PT, the initials of the Workers' Party in Portuguese.
Bolsonaro, who is campaigning on a iron-fist approach to crime, challenged Lula to explain why crime rates had gone up during his four years in power.
He also alleged, without providing any evidence, that "the majority of convicts vote for Lula".
Lula shot back with a thinly veiled reference to FlÃ¡vio's convicted father, Jair, saying; "I wish it was 100%, even your father".

Medicine is moving toward a future in which a personâs DNA can help to predict disease risk, guide personalized treatment and inform therapies for genetic disorders. But as precision medicine and genetic therapies become more mainstream, the science behind these advances has a major gap: they do not work equally well for everyone.
Despite Africaâs central place in human origins and its extraordinary genetic diversity, people of African ancestry remain underrepresented in the genomic datasets used to understand disease, estimate health risks, and develop treatments.
Closing that gap is going to require more than just collecting more samples. It will take sustained investment in African scientists, research institutions, biobanks, and bioinformatics capacity. We propose an initial $100 million investment over 10 years to build a coordinated, African-led genomics initiative, with African governments, international funders and life sciences companies sharing responsibility for its success.
It will be worth the investment. We already know that studying genetic variation in African ancestry populations has helped reveal a biological mechanism that has benefited patients worldwide.
Recent studies of a protein called PCSK9 shows what researchers can gain by studying this diversity. In 2005, researchers identified naturally occurring variants in PCSK9, which is produced in the liver, among African American participants. These variants were associated with lower cholesterol. Follow-up studies linked these genetic variants to reduced coronary heart disease risk. These findings helped establish PCSK9 as a drug target and contributed to the development of PCSK9 inhibitors, a new class of cholesterol-lowering medicines now used around the world.
This story matters because the discovery began with human genetic variation that might otherwise have received less attention. A genetic difference can point to a biological pathway, and that pathway can become the basis for a treatment. There may be many more such discoveries waiting in populations that genomic research has overlooked.
The effects of underrepresentation are already visible in genetic risk prediction. Tools developed mainly with European-ancestry data can be less accurate when applied to people whose genetic backgrounds differ from the original study populations. As genomic medicine enters routine care, these gaps could influence how reliably we estimate disease risk or interpret a personâs genetic results
Closing the gap will need sustained investment into the continentâs ecosystem as weâve already suggested. Samples and data should not simply leave the continent while expertise and benefits accumulate elsewhere. African-led programs will need long-term support while communities must also have a meaningful say in how their data are used and share in the benefits.
Our $100 million proposal is a starting ambition, not a full estimate of what the continent will need. African governments and the African Union can help coordinate national commitments and regional collaboration. International research funders and philanthropies should provide sustained support. Pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies should contribute through equitable partnerships that recognize the value of African-led discovery.
This work should strengthen African health systems, too. Research can support local expertise and diagnostic capacity while helping identify treatments relevant to the continentâs health priorities. The scientific gains, however, could reach far beyond Africa. Ultimately, when research reflects more of humanity, we have a better chance of understanding disease and developing medicines that work for more people beyond Africa.
The world may be overlooking its next important medical discovery. Investing in African genomics is a practical way to look for it.
Segun Fatumo is Professor and Chair of Genomic Diversity at Queen Mary University of London and co-editor of the book Genomics in Africa published by CRC Press.

The Scoop
Saudi Arabiaâs sovereign wealth fund is tapping its portfolio companies to pay off 800 million riyals ($213 million) of debt held by the soccer club Al Nassr â where star Portuguese striker Cristiano Ronaldo plays â according to people familiar with the matter.
Public Investment Fund (PIF) is orchestrating corporate sponsorship deals to strengthen the Saudi Pro League clubâs balance sheet, which would help facilitate a sale to investors led by AC Milan owner RedBird Capital, these people said.
One person close to the fund described RedBirdâs interest as âearlyâ and cautioned that a deal might not be reached. RedBird has held at least two meetings with PIF about taking a 70% stake in the team, the people said.
RedBird and its partners would pay about 1 billion riyals ($267 million) for the stake, with Ronaldo himself expected to hold a 20% share. Other investors could include the privately held, Riyadh-based media, sports, and entertainment firm Saudi Media Company (SMC). Final terms have not been agreed upon and could still change, they said.
RedBird and PIF declined to comment. Al Nassr and Ronaldoâs representatives didnât immediately respond to a request for comment. Asharq Bloomberg previously reported that RedBird was leading a consortium in talks to buy a stake in the club.
Know More
Acquiring Al Nassr would help Gerry Cardinaleâs RedBird strengthen ties with Ronaldo, one of the worldâs most marketable athletes, whose investment firm, CR7, holds a 25% stake in UD Almeria, a club in Spainâs second division backed by SMC.
RedBird, which bought AC Milan in 2022 and manages roughly $21 billion, has built a reputation as a major media and sports broker, most recently financing high-profile media mergers involving Skydance, Paramount, and Warner Bros. Discovery.
Buying Al Nassr would put RedBird at the center of Saudi Arabiaâs multi-billion-dollar sports expansion, which had been on a tear before the government began cutting back on spending. The kingdom has used sports deals and hosted competitions to promote itself and encourage more active lifestyles at home. But after pouring billions of dollars into the effort, it now needs foreign investors to help turn around loss-making soccer clubs and the breakaway LIV Golf tournament.
Saudi Arabia spent around $900 million in 2023 buying up soccerâs biggest players like Ronaldo, Neymar Jr., and Karim Benzema in order to raise the profile of the kingdomâs league internationally. The government transferred ownership of several soccer clubs to PIF and other state-controlled companies to prepare the teams for privatization. The first fruit of that effort came this year when PIF sold a 70% stake in Riyadh-based club Al Hilal in August to Kingdom Holding, the investment company of billionaire Prince Alwaleed bin Talal â a deal that valued the club at about 1.4 billion riyals.
If finalized, people close to Al Nassrâs new owners say being part of a wider consortium would allow the team to cut costs and tap media and marketing partnerships with other RedBird and SMC portfolio companies. They also want to boost the clubâs profile in the US.
Notable
- Despite lofty expectations, Saudi league insiders say success means standards comparable to Dutch clubs rather than Europeâs elite. They hope stronger domestic competition will help develop Saudi talent ahead of the 2034 World Cup, Camilla Wright writes in a column for Semafor.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is set to hold an emergency security meeting on Monday after protests over the rising cost of living broke out into violent clashes in Milan.
More than 5,000 people gathered over the weekend. Police deployed tear gas and water cannons after protesters - many in masks - threw paving stones, bins and chairs at officers.
"To demonstrate is a right. To lay our cities to waste is not," Meloni said on Saturday, adding that "hooligans" had exploited the protests to "sow chaos".
Rioting and violence have broken out on the sidelines of mostly peaceful youth-led protests in other European countries including France, Spain and Albania.
Milanese Mayor Giuseppe Sala said he was worried it was a "new phenomenon" that "originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself".
Speaking to Italian news agency Ansa, he said he witnessed "smashed shop windows, looted stores, and frightened citizens", adding that "what happened here is what we are seeing in many cities around the world".
Clashes began on Saturday and continued into Sunday in Milan. More than 200 people were detained, 80% of whom were minors, Ansa reported.
The city's prosecutor's office has requested prison sentences for five adults arrested for looting, vandalism and resisting arrest, according to Italian news agency AGI.
Italian media reported that people - including police officers - were injured.
Violence between protesters and police also rippled into other cities in the north.
Meloni said people in Turin were detained while "carrying cobblestones and window-breaking hammers", while a train station in Bologna was closed as a precaution after similar disorder.
The prime minister - who is facing an election next year - also called on her political opponents to condemn the rioting.
"Do not be ambiguous about this," she said on X, explaining that condemnation must be "unanimous" because "any hesitation becomes justification".
Democratic Party leader Elly Schlein said her party had always condemned violence and that the rioting should not be used to stifle the voices of peaceful protesters across the country who are struggling to make a living, Ansa reported.
The violent disorder followed anti-government protests held by students in various Italian cities on Friday, and echoed similar unrest in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands took to the streets.

80f191318c4f.text: Bob Woodward — in an eye-opening excerpt from his forthcoming memoir, "Secrets," that's previewed in the new issue of The New Yorker — reveals that one of his best friends, the late Richard Darman, was also one of his best sources during the Ronald Reagan and George H.W. Bush administrations. "Darman was willing, even eager at times, to talk about the most sensitive intelligence matters, including N.S.A. intercepts and covert C.I.A. operations," Woodward writes in his book , out Nov. 15. "He was always careful not to talk about matters that would harm national security, I believed, but he would go right up to the edge — a reporter's dream source." Why it matters: Woodward, 83 — who followed the blockbuster Watergate reporting of his youth with a shelf of revelatory books about American presidents — gives a searingly honest account of the collapse of his friendship with Darman after a Post series that was damaging to Bush. Woodward details a disappointment in his Washington Post career and, in the case of a story where he was the responsible editor, a "moral failing." The New Yorker calls the Darman excerpt "A Dangerous Friendship," revealing the danger of "getting too close to a source." Woodward and Darman never reconciled, although "Secrets" describes their deathbed encounter. Woodward writes in his New Yorker debut that he and Darman, who controlled the paper flow to Reagan as staff secretary and was budget director for Bush 41, "had countless long lunches together — Saturday or Sunday — at the Madison Hotel, across the street from the Post , discussing government, journalism, and ourselves": "I felt like I was getting a master class in how government really operated. Plus, many scoops. In later years, Darman would drive out on weekends to our country house near Annapolis, Maryland, to spend large parts of the day with me and my wife, the journalist Elsa Walsh, who was particularly fond of him. Some people found him arrogant, but I loved his comfortable confidence as a friend and a source. It was part of what made him so extraordinary and valuable. He knew how to turn on the charm, and he did for both Elsa and me." Behind the scenes: "From critical national-security information to the colorful office tales he shared, Darman provided me with a gold mine of information," Woodward recalls. "I interviewed him in at least fifty-eight meetings or phone conversations. I have boxes filled with hundreds of pages of notes on our discussions. After our most important conversations, as is my practice, I typed a memo of one to six pages, laying out in detail what he'd said." Detailing Darman's " hatchet man " role, Woodward reveals that the "hardest of Darman's targets to dislodge was the First Lady, Nancy Reagan. While Darman poured scorn on her in private, describing her to me as a 'mean bitch,' he could not find a way to drive a stake into her heart." After a hard-won legislative victory, Darman told Woodward, Reagan said: "Whew! Ever feel like you shit a pineapple?" Keep reading ... Get "Secrets."

873fce935f6e.text: Elon Musk said Monday he'd give one of his shares in SpaceX to every "kid" in America next year. Why it matters: It'd be a roughly $11 billion giveaway at current stock prices, nearly double Michael Dell's record-breaking Trump accounts gift. What they're saying: " Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post to X just before 4 a.m. ET Monday. He did not specify if "kid" meant all minors under 18 or some other status, nor did he elaborate on what "first of many" meant. He also did not reply to X accounts asking if he meant all kids present in the U.S., or just citizens. By the numbers: Per the Census Bureau, there are just over 72 million people under 18 in the U.S. If each got one SpaceX share, at Friday's closing price of $146.03, that'd be a market value of a little over $10.5 billion. Musk owns billions of SpaceX shares, so the giveaway would make only a small dent in his holdings. Zoom out: Musk's announcement comes one day after Anthropic said it was setting up a new public benefit fund with 5% of the company's equity, an entity potentially worth $100 billion or more. Musk responded to Anthropic's news by saying "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," later adding "This is what I will be doing." This is a developing story.

The fire that killed four members of the Canadian military and injured dozens of others on Saturday spread with alarming speed, accounts suggest.
It broke out in a grassy training area at a base in the province of Alberta and spread rapidly due to strong winds.
"The fire was 1km (0.6 miles) away when the wind shifted," said Maj-Gen Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division of the Canadian Armed Forces. "It is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 30 to 60 seconds."
Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime". Officials have ruled out the possibility of "any terrorist activity".
The blaze began at about 16:00 (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases.
The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died.
Of the 39 injured people receiving care in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition.
Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told Canadian broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright.
Tributes are being paid to the servicemen who died.
Patricia Farrell, the mother of Shaun Farrell, wrote on Facebook that it was "with heavy hearts that we share the news that our son, Shaun Farrell, has passed away to be with our Heavenly Father".
Wong received a tribute from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, of which he was part. The regiment was "deeply saddened", it wrote in a Facebook post of its own. It sent "heartfelt condolences to [the group's] families, friends, and fellow soldiers".
The mother of Goulding, Sonia Monk, said her late son was an exceptional athlete and a natural leader. "He was always the guy who kept everybody's spirits up," she told CBC. "He really was the light of my life."
In account of Saturday's events, Rutland told reporters that members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range.
He told reporters that officials knew about the fire on the base for several hours, but it was decided that training "could carry on for a certain amount of time".
"I spoke to my commander last night, and he said within 30 seconds to a minute they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them," Rutland said.
Rutland said it was not yet known what exactly caused the fire.
Some witnesses had said they had heard explosions, fuelling speculation that oil and gas infrastructure may have been hit and sparked the fire. But Rutland said authorities "do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure".
The Canadian Armed Forces has said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity".
Forecasters had issued a wind warning on Saturday for large parts of Alberta, predicting wind gusts of up to 90km/h (66mph), Canadian broadcaster CBS said.
According to Rutland, the investigation may take at least a month.
Wainwright, about 130 miles east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries.
About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day.

d1ee7b6c7a51.text: The AI boom is about to rewrite the rules of global philanthropy, shifting its center of gravity to Silicon Valley, where the IPOs of AI giants Anthropic and OpenAI will create the world's largest charitable organizations. Why it matters: Rather than massive donations earmarked for renaming hospital wings or university graduate programs, expect the new wave of giving to mirror startup culture: flexible capital, ambitious bets and a search for measurable impact. Driving the news: Anthropic announced Sunday that it plans to launch a massive benefit fund with 5% of its shares. Zoom in : The company's pledge — which would amount to $100 billion if it reaches a value of $2 trillion in its IPO — will go to a public benefit fund and is set to grow as its valuation rises. Anthropic says the fund will be a wholly owned LLC, giving it flexibility to make large donations to nonprofits or distribute money directly to specific populations. The commitment builds on the pledges of co-founders to give away 80% of their equity. A program available to early Anthropic hires and used by a large number of company staffers matched donations at a 3:1 ratio. The company says roughly half its employees participate in donation-matching. The company says the fund's shares will not be used for lobbying or political giving in the U.S. or abroad. The big picture: Anthropic is joining OpenAI, which is controlled by a nonprofit foundation that holds a 26% equity stake in the company, worth about $130 billion based on the company's current valuation. The foundation has the power to appoint OpenAI's board. What they're saying: Anthropic says much of its public-benefit work — including AI safety and interpretability research, applied biomedical research and discounts for nonprofits and scientific institutions — will continue inside the company. The new fund is intended to make other kinds of giving possible at greater scale, the company says. Anthropic cited AI's effects on the labor market as one potential use and said it has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing that issue, but that "bolder approaches may be needed." Anthropic has not specified what those approaches would be, or whether the fund would make direct payments to workers affected by AI. Between the lines: Anthropic's founders and some employees have close ties to effective altruism, a movement ostensibly dedicated to directing resources toward causes where they may do the most good. Effective altruism has come under sharp criticism from the Trump White House, which has emphasized aspects of the movement that are far from the philanthropic mainstream. Those include an acute interest in animal welfare, as well as seemingly abstract ponderings about the value of life, including comparing that of an infant to an adult, or future people to present people. In an X post , Taylor Budowich, a former White House official, highlighted one such comment from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in 2010, when he said in a blog post that an adult death is "perhaps 2 or 3 times worse than an infant's death." Budowich also shared a few other "insane beliefs of those who make up Anthropic and how they think about prioritizing charitable giving." The bottom line : Anthropic's fund — and the charitable giving of a massive new cadre of millionaires and deca-millionaires — could become one of the largest vehicles for new giving. The bigger change may come with a new generation of Silicon Valley donors aiming to reset the agenda of modern philanthropy.

c6a9872690d0.text: AI is producing reality-bending midterm ads about defaced Bibles, upscale dinners and a board game with a "Death to America" playing card. Why it matters: The warnings about deepfakes are coming true. Election laws haven't kept pace with a world where campaigns can put words in opponents' mouths and create realistic-looking scenes that didn't happen. The Wesleyan Media Project found $137 million had been spent on 220 AI-generated ads through Oct. 11, mostly from Republicans. Four states have laws prohibiting certain uses of AI-generated deepfakes in political ads, while 27 more require some form of disclosure about their use. No federal law specifically regulates AI-generated political ads. The big picture: An Axios analysis found numerous political ads partly or fully made by generative AI, sometimes undisclosed. Georgia Senate: Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Senate Republicans, has run a series of AI-generated deepfake ads depicting Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff getting beauty treatments. The ads mock Ossoff's reported campaign spending on hair and makeup , saying he "talks pretty" but has "an ugly record" and "a lot to cover up." Ossoff said in a C-SPAN interview : "It is deeply troubling to see ... deepfake videos used to fabricate political advertising. And it's a s lippery slope toward the destruction of truth in political debate, and the ad should come down immediately." The ads don't disclose AI use, which Georgia law doesn't require. Michigan Senate: A super PAC called Front Line Action used AI in an ad depicting Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed in a fabricated family photo with podcaster Hasan Piker and four women wearing niqabs. Another AI-generated scene has El-Sayed playing a Risk-style board game with his half-sister , Eman Abdelhadi, and Piker. It depicts cards bearing statements that include "Death to America," "Do not Celebrate Thanksgiving" and "Celebrate 9/11." The group has defended the ad, telling CNN it is "grounded in El-Sayed's own public statements and documented reporting and records concerning him and individuals associated with or supportive of his campaign." The ad features both a written and spoken disclosure that it was "created in whole or in part with the use of artificial intelligence." New York governor: Republican Bruce Blakeman's campaign and allied super PACs have repeatedly used generative AI in ads attacking Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul, with varying degrees of disclosure. One AI-generated ad released by the Blakeman campaign depicts the Tooth Fairy struggling to come up with cash to give to children, saying she "just can't afford to be the Tooth Fairy in Kathy Hochul's New York." Another Blakesman spot says onscreen: "We asked AI what a truthful Kathy Hochul ad would look like." The ad features AI-generated scenes of Hochul attending an upscale dinner and standing outside a police precinct while a man asks her: "Want some crack?" Pennsylvania governor: A new ad from Republican candidate Stacy Garrity features an AI-generated version of Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro talking about taxes, abortion and data centers. The spot puts this quote in his mouth: "This ad was created with AI, thanks to big, beautiful data centers. Fact is, I was the one who fast-tracked data centers right here in PA, right after they handed me $5 million in political contributions." Shapiro spokesperson Manuel Bonder, in a statement to Axios, dismissed the ad as "cheap, dishonest AI bullshit." Texas Senate: Democratic candidate James Talarico has been a consistent target of AI-generated ads from both Republican Ken Paxton's campaign and outside super PACs. A Paxton campaign ad uses AI to depict Talarico defacing a Bible with crayon and saying, "In the beginning God was non-binary, and he wasn't a Christian. And God said, 'let there be six genders,' and there were." Talarico told NBC he "tried in the legislature to ban AI deepfake videos in political campaigns because they are misleading. They are lying about a candidate in this race." Kentucky's 6th District: No Going Back PAC, backed by President Trump's MAGA Inc., has run several ads using AI to boost Republican congressional candidate Ralph Alvarado. One ad features multiple AI-generated deepfakes of Democrat Zach Dembo, including one scene in which he stares into the camera. "I expected them to lie about my record, but I did not expect them to lie about my appearance," Dembo said in a statement to Axios, adding that "using AI to create fake or misleading images is the beginning of a very dangerous path for our democracy."

Researchers inspecting an object that some thought could have been the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane on a remote Pacific island say it is likely to be washed up trees.
The team travelled to a lagoon in the Taraia Peninsula on Nikumaroro, Kiribati, to confirm whether a shiny object first spotted on satellite imagery in 2020 solved the decades-long mystery of the pioneering pilot's disappearance.
But Purdue University, which has a leading role in the study, said the so-called Taraia Object "was likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula's sandspit".
By the time the team arrived at the site a good portion of the debris had fragmented and washed away, leaving only a single Y-shaped segment, the university said.
Images of the Taraia Object - which Purdue University said was visible in photography dating back to 1938 - led researchers to wonder if it was the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters.
"This mystery has been ongoing for 90 years and the mystery continues," said project director Rick Pettigrew, speaking from near the site of the object.
"The island has been holding on to its secrets and it continues to do so. I think eventually someone will find conclusive evidence here," he added.
Earhart's plane vanished without a trace in 1937 on the third-to-last leg of her attempt to fly around the world.
She had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her twin-engine Lockheed Electra when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea.
Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to then travel towards Hawaii before returning to California.
But their plane vanished while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote uninhabited coral island about 400 miles (644km) from Nikumaroro, to refuel.
One theory is Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway.
The research team had travelled for five days by sea to reach Nikumaroro and was forced to spend several days on their ship following rough seas and strong winds, delaying their search on the island.
They spent four days onshore investigating the site.
