Four Red Flags and One Truth Amid the Peptide Hype
Experimental peptides have become darlings among influencers, chiropractors, and doctors focused on longevity, antiaging, or “body optimization,” even though the FDA hasn’t approved them for safety or effectiveness. Health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and other leaders of the Make America Healthy Again movement have pushed to make unproven peptides more accessible — and they’ve gained traction.
On Oct. 14, a temporary “access policy” appeared on a White House docket, proposing to allow licensed pharmacies to make and sell certain unapproved peptides to people. Scientists at the FDA had advised against the measure at a meeting in July, warning that the drugs hadn’t been adequately vetted in clinical trials.
A panel that advises the FDA disagreed, however, voting to loosen restrictions. Many of the panel members are new appointees with financial stakes in the peptide industry. In an email, Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson Emily Hilliard said that every committee member satisfies the FDA’s ethics requirements.
“I voted ‘yes’ for patient safety, the greater good, and medical freedom,” Haleem Mohammed, one of the new committee members, said at the FDA meeting. He’s the chief medical officer of a men’s clinic that sells peptides, Gameday Men’s Health.
To make good decisions, consumers need to rely on accurate information, but much of the hype around peptides is misleading. KFF Health News flags four misleading phrases commonly used by those promoting peptides — and one truth.
Red Flag: Peptides aren’t drugs.
Gary Brecka, a co-chair of the MAHA Action committee, says peptides aren’t drugs in this episode of his podcast. He talks about using them to “help regulate cortisol, improve circulation, all kinds of things.” When peptides are used to treat, prevent, or cure conditions, or to affect the body’s function, they are, by definition, drugs.
“Peptide” is a general term for substances that are smaller than proteins but made of the same building blocks. Humans make many peptides, including insulin. Insulin is a drug when people inject it to regulate blood sugar.
“Most of the drugs we have had some antecedent in nature,” said Jacob Sherkow, a professor of law specializing in biotechnology at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. “Heroin is natural. No one in their right mind would call it not a drug.”
Brecka did not respond to requests for comment, but Chris Woodward, a public relations representative for him, said in an email that the health issues discussed on Brecka’s podcast do not constitute medical advice.
Red Flag: Peptides are safe because they’re natural.
Peptide promoters have suggested that peptides are safe because they’re natural. This clip of Brecka’s discussion with Brigham Buhler, a co-author of The Peptide Revolution and owner of a compounding pharmacy that sells peptides, is an example. Some influencers go further, saying that peptides are safe because they’re made by the human body. Buhler did not respond to requests for comment.
It’s murky territory. One of the most popular experimental peptides, BPC-157, was developed by Croatian scientists who isolated what they called “body protective compound” from gastric juices in the stomach lining. However, researchers have been unable to find a trace of BPC in the human genome, meaning it’s not made by humans, said Katrin Svensson, a peptide scientist at Stanford University. Researchers in Taiwan suggest the peptide is produced by stomach microbes, according to Undark magazine.
Even if BPC-157 and other peptides exist in nature, Svensson said, “natural things can be toxic.” People have died from taking too much insulin, for example. And drugs considered safe can still make people feel ill. To learn about safety, and whether the benefits of a drug offset the side effects, researchers conduct placebo-controlled trials. These reveal problems that might not be obvious in the short term, such as liver damage, as well as underlying conditions that could turn minor issues into something serious.
The FDA is considering lowering restrictions on BPC-157 and five other experimental peptides that have not undergone high-quality clinical trials and are not FDA-approved. “I am excited about peptides too,” said Svensson, whose lab studies several peptides that she hopes to develop into drugs. “But,” she added, “you need to show they’re not harmful.”
Red Flag: These peptides treat illnesses and heal injuries.
Kris Wusterhausen, one of the new appointees to the FDA advisory panel, has said that the experimental peptide BPC-157 “can reduce [acid] reflux disease” and treat “neurologic disorders.” He’s the founder of an antiaging company that sells the peptide and advertises “clinically guided peptide treatments.” He did not respond to requests for comment.
Such claims are common among peptide promoters who say that various experimental peptides treat muscle injuries, covid, inflammatory bowel disease, and more. But vanishingly few clinical trials have been conducted.
A summary of a small clinical trial testing BPC-157 as a treatment for inflammatory bowel disease was published in 2005, but it lacked critical details about how the study was conducted. FDA scientists who reviewed the summary called it “inadequate.”
Another small study concluded that BPC-157 relieved knee pain for 14 of the 16 patients involved, but it lacked a control group, meaning the participants might have felt better because of other factors, or their pain simply resolved over time.
In a 2025 review of research on BPC-157 as a treatment for musculoskeletal injuries, researchers warned that it should be “approached with caution” because of a lack of evidence. Flynn McGuire, a physical rehabilitation doctor at the University of Utah and an author of the review, said anecdotes about people having miraculous recoveries are even less reliable.

GOP Focuses on Fraud, Seeking To Redirect Voters’ Ire Over Healthcare Costs
Heading into the midterm elections, high healthcare costs rank among voters’ biggest concerns. But lately, there’s a twist giving the issue new momentum on campaign agendas: a focus on fraud in government health programs.
The administration of President Donald Trump has used claims of widespread wrongdoing to justify investigations, suspensions of billions of dollars in payments to states, and the cancellation of Affordable Care Act health coverage for hundreds of thousands of people.
The effort has opened a broader political fight over the extent of fraud and the administration’s response to it. Republicans say they’re safeguarding taxpayer dollars by going after bad actors. Democrats contend the administration has relied on insufficient evidence to target blue states and cut programs Republicans have long tried to shrink. Meanwhile, Trump’s pardons of executives convicted of healthcare fraud, administration moves to weaken some protections against abuses, and a high-profile error by Trump regulators stand in contrast with the administration’s proclaimed fraud-fighting goals.
The dispute is becoming a talking point for both parties leading up to the November election.
Republican candidates are trying to win voters’ confidence by emphasizing their efforts to halt what they say is the misuse of taxpayer dollars in federal health programs.
“Going after fraud gives Republicans a healthcare message when they would otherwise just be defending cuts to Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act,” said Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. The approach, he said, helps “blunt” those attacks.
Democrats, however, traditionally have an advantage on healthcare in general, with polls showing voters are more likely to trust them with such issues. Now Democrats are portraying Republicans’ fraud crackdown as a cover for the GOP’s weakening of safety net programs. But the GOP messaging could resonate at the ballot box.
About 44% of voters — and 54% of Republican voters — say say fraud in government programs is “extremely important” for candidates to talk about, according to a KFF poll conducted in mid-September, suggesting the fraud focus might be connecting with the GOP base. Such fraud is also the top issue rural Republican voters want candidates to talk about, based on a separate survey by KFF and the Associated Press.
It’s an issue that is hardly new, and government watchdogs have repeatedly documented fraud by health providers and brokers, as well as improper enrollment in government health programs. A report by the Government Accountability Office in March warned that the “sheer amount of payments in the Medicare program creates significant fraud risks.” And in a separate probe, GAO investigators were able to get subsidized insurance for fake ACA enrollees.
What has changed is the prominence the issue now occupies in national politics.
Administration’s Fraud Targets
Trump administration authorities have this year charged hundreds of people, including doctors, in alleged billing schemes. It has announced audits of state Medicaid fraud units and increased scrutiny of enrollment in federal programs, withholding billions of dollars in federal Medicaid payments over claims of lax oversight — with what Democrats say is a laser focus on blue states despite a lack of evidence.
The administration’s more expansive claims about fraud — and the actions it has taken in response — have generated fierce political clashes.
Most recently, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services canceled ACA enrollments covering 760,000 people. While Democrats have questioned the methods that found them to be fraudulent, federal officials said they included nonexistent consumers whose applications were submitted by brokers or agents who can earn commissions from insurers.
CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz said at a press event that the cancellations included people who had coverage through the ACA but hadn’t used it. He also said some had no Social Security numbers, calling that evidence of problems.
“About 35% of current people on the Obamacare system — 35%, more than a third — had never used the program. They haven’t bought a prescription medication. They haven’t seen a doctor. That just is not possible,” Oz said. “So we know there is fraud.”
Democrats and some health policy analysts challenge that conclusion. They say that younger and healthier people are much less likely to use their insurance and that not using their coverage doesn’t mean they were improperly enrolled. Critics also say the absence of Social Security numbers doesn’t necessarily establish fraud; for example, newborns can be added to their parents’ plans before receiving a number.
“This is yet another attempt by the Trump administration to kick hundreds of thousands of vulnerable Americans off their healthcare,” Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) posted on the social media site X. “Millions are already struggling to access healthcare—and this is their plan?”
There are political risks for the GOP as well. The disenrollment of alleged phantom accounts is likely to ensnare legitimate consumers, say health analysts and ACA advocates, leading to a potential backlash against Republicans if scores of people lose coverage just before the midterm elections.
States that tend to deliver for GOP candidates will be hit especially hard, they say, because ACA enrollees are concentrated in those states. The 4.5 million people in Florida and 4.1 million in Texas who have marketplace coverage account for nearly 40% of the country’s ACA enrollment, according to a KFF analysis.
Conservative health policy advisers say the administration took multiple steps to avoid canceling legitimate coverage, including attempts to contact consumers and requirements that additional criteria be met before coverage was terminated.

Letters to the Editor is a periodic feature. We welcome all comments and will publish a selection. We edit for length and clarity and require full names.
Not-So-Great Healthcare
Why doesn’t world-class medicine produce world-class health?
Hayat Norimine’s reporting gets at something that has bothered me for a long time about American healthcare (Priced Out: “As Health Insurance Costs Soar, Healthcare Workers Also Feel the Pinch,” Sept. 22).
We are very proud of U.S. medicine, and we should be. We are at the forefront of new treatments, our clinician workforce is unmatched, and we deploy technologies that seemed impossible just a few years ago. Yet we are in the middle of the pack compared with other countries, in terms of healthy lifespan and many markers of quality care.
At the same time, the cost of accessing care has become outrageously high. When clinicians stop getting health insurance for themselves and their families, you know something is deeply broken.
What good is our health system if most people cannot afford to use it?
One family in Norimine’s story went without insurance when their premiums climbed. Another person kept her coverage but waited weeks to see a doctor because of a $10,000 deductible. These are different problems, but both expose the distance between the care we can provide and the care people can actually access.
Insurance is supposed to help people get the care they need to stay healthy, not just when they are at death’s door. Yet the way insurance is designed can discourage someone from seeing a clinician early, filling a prescription, or following up before a problem gets worse. A clinician may say, “This is what you should do next,” while a person’s coverage gives them a reason to wait or decline.
That tension is not an accident. It is how the system was built. Doctors design care. Insurers design coverage. The two are put together in separate rooms by different teams, measured on different things, then handed to the same person as if they were one plan. No physician would design a $10,000 deductible; it just blocks people from investing in prevention and getting care early. But no physician was in the room when that threshold was set.
Making coverage affordable is essential. So is asking what that coverage enables people to do. If better health is the goal, the people responsible for a person’s health need a hand in shaping what their coverage pays for and when. Design coverage and care together, and it gets easier for people to get the care we know works while avoiding waste.
— Clay Johnston; Austin, Texas
On Dementia, Violence, and Sedation
Reading “Drugs Are Widely Used To Sedate Dementia Patients. Her Sons Wanted To Keep Her Off Them” (Sept. 30) inspired me to share my own experience.
My husband died of dementia about two years ago at age 86. It was not an easy journey. Dementia made him agitated for the same reason it does to others: People with dementia cannot tolerate being told “no.”
So when I had to tell him to stop driving, he became violent. I was told by an eldercare specialist that if my husband remained at home, he might kill me. So it was off to a memory care center, a really good and really expensive one. And he became violent and agitated there because he couldn’t come home, which was what he wanted, and which I could not safely handle. I was also aware that if he couldn’t make it at the memory care center, there was virtually no other place that would take him.
So did I say yes to medication? I did indeed. Even with the antipsychotic, my husband would become out of control. He often tried to “abscond,” as they say in memory-care speak. I also paid through the nose for one-on-one care, which kept him sort of safe. But one night, he fell in the bathroom and broke his hip. A hip replacement was suggested. He was suffering, he had absolutely no quality of life, and I turned the offer down. He was transferred to palliative care and died peacefully about five days later.
There is no solution to this problem that I can see other than medical aid in dying, which he probably would have refused. Me — I will not refuse. My current terror is that I might do this to my remaining family.
— Nora Staffanell; Monroe, New York
The issue is appropriate treatment, not simply drug avoidance.
Jordan Rau’s report rightly highlights the danger of using sedating medications simply to make people with dementia easier to manage. But inappropriate chemical restraint should not be confused with medically appropriate treatment of serious neuropsychiatric symptoms.
Psychosis, agitation, and aggression are distinct. Before prescribing medication, clinicians should identify the target symptom and look for reversible contributors such as pain, infection, medication effects, constipation, sleep disruption, sensory impairment, fear, environmental overstimulation, or the way personal care is being delivered.
Nonpharmacological, person-centered interventions should generally come first. The American Psychiatric Association recommends antipsychotics, outside of emergencies, only when agitation or psychosis is severe, dangerous, or causes substantial distress and after nonpharmacologic approaches have been assessed. When used, treatment should begin at a low dose and aim for the minimum effective dose.
However, nonpharmacological measures do not always suffice. In 2026, the APA reaffirmed that antipsychotics can benefit some older adults with behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia when used judiciously within a comprehensive treatment plan. Brexpiprazole, for example, received FDA approval in 2023 for agitation associated with Alzheimer’s dementia.
These drugs carry real risks, including increased mortality, sedation, orthostasis, extrapyramidal symptoms, cerebrovascular events, and falls. But untreated severe agitation or aggression also carries risks: distress, injury, emergency transfers, hospitalization, caregiver breakdown, and loss of placement.

SUNBURY, Ohio—A proposal for a large data center has upended politics in this Republican-leaning suburb of Columbus.
That could spell trouble for U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, a longtime fixture in state Republican politics who was appointed to his seat in 2025 after former Sen. J.D. Vance became vice president. Husted is running against Sherrod Brown, a Democrat who served three terms in the Senate before losing his seat two years ago.
In Sunbury, the Senate race is on the same ballot as a referendum that would ban large data centers. Supporters of the measure say they don’t trust either party to stand up to the influence of technology companies, but they have less faith in Republicans.
That sentiment extends across much of the state and could prove consequential in an election that may determine whether Democrats take control of the chamber.
“I’m very disappointed in both parties’ approach to my problem,” said Larry Thode, a Sunbury-area resident who voted Republican most of his life and whose property is next to a planned Amazon Web Services data center.
Thode blames Republicans more than Democrats because they’re the ones in power, he said. The party has controlled Ohio’s government for more than a decade, with Husted serving as lieutenant governor from 2019 to 2025. Republicans also control the federal government, with President Donald Trump supporting development of AI data centers.
Alicia Doty, Thode’s neighbor, shares this frustration. She has mainly voted for Democrats in the past, but feels like the party needs to be clearer in opposing large data centers.
That said, her concerns about Democrats are small compared to her disappointment that Republicans welcomed development. Husted’s campaign has said he supports thoughtful data center planning, with protections for consumers and respect for local communities, but Doty remains unconvinced.
“I don’t believe Jon Husted for a second,” she said.
Sunbury, a city of about 9,000, sits near the northeast edge of Columbus’ suburbs, where housing subdivisions fade into farmland and woods. The city is in Delaware County, which has Ohio’s highest median household income and a history of supporting Republicans.
Amazon Web Services is proposing to build a data center with electricity demand of several hundred megawatts in a farm field between Thode and Doty’s properties. Under the plan, Sunbury would annex the AWS land and allow it to be developed.
Opponents gathered enough signatures to put a measure on the local ballot that would bar data centers with electricity demand of at least 25 megawatts.
The backlash has been intense partially because Sunbury residents have watched how data centers transformed the farmland of New Albany, a city about 15 miles away. New Albany now has some of the densest concentration of data centers in the country.
“Decimated” is how Doty describes the nearby city, and she wants to avoid the same fate.
She noted the Sunbury proposal begins with one data center but planners have discussed building an industrial park south of her property that may attract additional data centers.
“Tin Ear”
Many communities across Ohio are pushing back on data centers and that opposition often overlaps with a distrust of politicians.
“There’s this kind of pitchfork populism about data centers that has really emerged,” said Kyle Kondik, managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball from the University of Virginia Center for Politics.
Brown has seized on the issue, while Husted is running in a party led by Trump, who supports data center companies and criticizes opponents of development.
Trump has misread public opinion on data centers, responding to voter anger with what Kondik called “a tin ear.” The response marks a departure from Trump’s past knack for tapping into political undercurrents, Kondik said.
Opposition to data centers is stronger in Ohio than other places. For example, 3 percent of Ohio voters in a recent New York Times/Siena poll said artificial intelligence and data centers were their top issue in the election, the most of any state with a competitive U.S. Senate race. In the same poll, Ohio voters said they trusted Democrats on the issue by 11 points, again the most of any state with a competitive Senate race.
Husted has said he welcomes development if a community wants it and rules are in place to avoid harm to residents. But he has struggled to advance legislation, including a bill he co-sponsored to curb data centers’ impact on consumer electricity prices that failed to pass the Senate.
“Let’s rise above the politics that often drag this place down and deliver for the American people and do our jobs,” Husted said on the Senate floor on Sept. 30, about the bill.
The measure fell short of the 60 votes it needed to overcome a filibuster. Most Democrats opposed the plan, saying its requirements were not strong enough to do much good.
A few days later, Brown announced his campaign was behind billboards declaring Husted is “The Face of Data Centers,” for the state government’s use of tax breaks to attract the projects.
“Ohioans shouldn’t be forced to subsidize these costs and Ohioans—not Jon Husted and his billionaire friends—should get to decide if data centers are built in their community,” Brown said in a statement.
Husted’s campaign did not respond to requests for comment.
Opponents of data centers in Sunbury, including Thode and Doty, said they feel like Brown’s focus on the issue feels more like a political calculation than a deeply held belief. Still, they credit Brown with responding to public concerns more effectively than Husted.

A pending regulation under White House review could expand access to peptides, largely unregulated substances that are popular with wellness influencers and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
In July, a panel of outside advisers to the Food and Drug Administration â which included individuals with connections to the peptide industry â narrowly recommended adding several peptides to the agencyâs list of products that can be compounded, or mixed at pharmacies, despite concerns from FDA scientists.
The American Academy of Peptide Medicine is slated to meet with the Office of Management and Budget on Wednesday to discuss the pending regulation.
Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding CEO Scott Brunner said Friday that the notice could be âpotentially significant, but we donât yet know what the policy says, which peptides it covers, or what conditions FDA may attach to their compounding.â

FREDERICKSBURG, Va. â In a matter of weeks, when the midterm results are tallied and the next campaign begins, Democrats with presidential dreams know the question will be coming.
Do Israelâs actions in Gaza constitute genocide?
The question flew at Democrats all year. Progressives generally said âyes.â Pro-Israel Democrats said âno.â Many rejected the idea that they had to use that word or were otherwise endorsing every action taken by the Jewish state.
As potential Democratic 2028 contenders fan out across the country this month, campaigning with battleground Democrats and building their win/loss scorecards, just two have said âyesâ to the question: Reps. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.
Khanna has been particularly direct, using interviews and public appearances not only to insist that Israel committed genocide, but also that Democrats who wonât say so are too weak to lead the party.
âIsrael has committed a genocide in Gaza, and we should have the courage to say so,â Khanna said at the Democratic National Committeeâs summer meeting in Texas â a historically red state where this yearâs top statewide Democratic nominees, Senate candidate James Talarico and gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, have not gone as far.
The question hasnât dominated the last few weeks of campaigning, with primaries long over and stark differences on Israel between most Democrats and Republicans. Last week, when Ocasio-Cortez made three campaign stops for Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, neither Democrat â and no audience members â brought up the topic of Gaza.
But the question still looms over the partyâs first wide-open primaries in eight years. Theyâll be the first since small armies of activists pressed Democrats to take more progressive positions on immigration, the environment, and criminal justice reform. In retrospect, many Democrats now think that the candidates in 2020 were too willing to bow to pressure with cameras rolling. There is no sign that anyone but Khanna or Ocasio-Cortez is moving towards a new Gaza answer that activists might prefer.
âI think we have to acknowledge the seriousness of the issue, the seriousness of whatâs happening in Gaza, the seriousness of whatâs happening in the West Bank,â Maryland Gov. Wes Moore told Semafor earlier this month at a campaign stop, when asked why he thought the word âgenocideâ was so important to many Democrats. Moore has accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of committing war crimes, but hasnât called the violence in Gaza a genocide.
âI think itâll be up to the voters to decide whether or not they feel that people are meeting the moment,â Moore continued.
Know More
When the Gaza questions do pick up again, most Democrats are likely to punt to the International Criminal Court â already a popular way to dodge them. The ICC has issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu for war crimes and crimes against humanity, but hasnât accused Israel of committing genocide.Â
âThe question of genocide is a question of whether a government has the specific intent to destroy a national or ethnic group,â Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., said in his first debate against challenger Mike Collins this month. âAnd that is a question for the International Criminal Court.â
That answer is unlikely to satisfy many Democratic primary voters, according to a poll of six early primary states conducted by YouGov on behalf of the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project.
In South Carolina, where Democrats opted to hold their first primary, 57% of likely primary voters said that Israel was âcommitting genocide against Palestinians.â In the other five early-voting states, the number was much higher: 78% in New Hampshire and Nevada, 76% in New Mexico, and 72% in Virginia. And in Michigan, where El-Sayed has said he will play an active role in the primaries if he wins his Senate race, eight in 10 likely primary voters agreed with the âgenocideâ term.
These are more lopsided numbers than other pollsters have found, but according to an Associated Press survey this summer, half of all Democrats now agree that âgenocideâ was the appropriate word to describe what they saw happen in Gaza.
âItâs certainly been a question that keeps coming up in debates,â said the IMEU Policy Projectâs spokesman, Hamid Bendaas. âAnd Iâd expect there will be a key 2028 moment where the candidates are asked to raise their hands with a yes or no.â
Some Democrats have tried to cancel the test before they can take it. In March, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear told Politico that âgenocideâ was âbecoming one of those new litmus tests that we said we would never do as a party again.â He wouldnât answer the question, but assumed heâd be asked again.
Democrats uncomfortable with the term have watched how even using it does not stop questions about their commitment to cutting off arms to Israel â the policy fight they expect, with a little less dread, next year.
In August, two months after he defeated Rep. Dan Goldman in New Yorkâs Democratic primary, Brad Lander joined a protest of a Hindu nationalist politician in Manhattan and was filmed being heckled as a âzionistâ â even though he said that the war âmeets the definition of genocide.â Last month, after Drop Site and New York magazine reported that consultants were urging Maine Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson not to say âgenocideâ so much, supporters began asking him about the war again, worried that heâd gone wobbly.
Davidâs view
If Israel elects another government led by Netanyahu, just days before the US midterms, the nuanced answers that many Democrats give to the âgenocideâ question will grow even trickier to land. The party has already shifted leftward. Rahm Emanuelâs endorsement of conditions on aid was an early signal that the field engaged in the âinvisible primaryâ would be less pro-Israel than Joe Biden.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has received mostly positive marks so far in Washington as chair of the Trump administrationâs AI task force, which is focusing on using current law to get AI companies to behave responsibly.
A number of people familiar with Claytonâs work tell Semafor his experience at the Securities and Exchange Commission and Office of the Director of National Intelligence aligns well with the two areas threatened the most by advanced AI: finance and national security.
âHe is hyper-competent and a problem-solver with good instincts, and thatâs why heâs so valued,â one former White House official told Semafor.
âHeâs just a guy who doesnât f*ck up and delivers results that they need and want, and so they just keep promoting him, because there arenât a lot of those.â
Paul Lekas, executive vice president for policy at the Software & Information Industry Association, said Claytonâs role atop the task force âsignals that the White House is focused on the national security dimension of super intelligence.â
Three industry sources told Semafor that the task force is now focused on staffing up to carry out its work.
As far as Claytonâs future goes, one tech lobbyist told Semafor to watch what happens on day 121 (the task forceâs work is supposed to be completed in 120 days).
âIf [Clayton] can get agencies approaching AI from very different directions to keep sharing information, coordinating decisions and agreeing on responsibilities â¦ his influence will last well beyond any one appointment,â the lobbyist said.
Others are skeptical the task force can accomplish much in such a short time period, arguing that eventually sweeping new legislation will be needed to regulate AI.

Trump administration officials and allies are starting to debate who will shoulder the blame if Republicans perform poorly in November.
The White House has witnessed an uptick in drama driven by the midterms, from maneuvering to replace chief of staff Susie Wiles to finger-pointing at James Blair, President Donald Trumpâs outside adviser whose recent work trip to Republika Srpska frustrated the president because of its proximity to the November elections.
Wiles seems safe; Trump has issued multiple emphatic endorsements of his chief of staff. Some suggest Blair will get blamed, though his tension with Trump has subsided for now.
Others predict Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could draw ire due to the unpopular Iran war.
It all depends on how Republicans measure up to the dire predictions â sources close to the White House say Republicans holding onto the Senate is likely to satisfy Trump at this point.
The White House dismissed the talk as âarmchairâ speculation.
âThese armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation to Semafor have no idea what theyâre talking about and are focused on themselves, not helping the President,â White House spokesman Davis Ingle said. âPresident Trump is laser-focused on maintaining Republican majorities in Congress this November, which is why he is traveling across the country highlighting the historic victories his Administration has delivered for the American people.â

Bangladeshi authorities say they were not informed of the recent execution of two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca until after it had taken place, local media reports.
A Bangladeshi man and woman were executed last Wednesday after being convicted of committing an "indecent act" inside a mosque, according to the Saudi interior ministry. The ministry did not specify the nature of the offending act.
Bangladesh says it has reached out to the Saudi Arabian government to ask for more details about the case.
The two Muslim countries share a close relationship due to their religious affinity and strong economic ties.
More than three million Bangladeshis work and live in Saudi Arabia, mostly in low-paying jobs, and news of the double execution has raised public concern in Bangladesh.
According to the Saudi interior ministry, the two Bangladeshi nationals were convicted and sentenced to death under "tazir", which in Islamic law refers to punishments left to the discretion of the judge.
The ministry statement said they were handed the sentences because of the severity of the offence, and the fact that they violated the "sanctity" of the mosque.
Bangladesh has reached out to the Saudi government about the offences involved and legal proceedings in the case, said state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam.
The government would consider next steps, such as the repatriation of the bodies, after getting information from Saudi authorities, Islam said.
She added that the government was committed to safeguarding the welfare and interests of Bangladeshis abroad.
The two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh, upon a request from the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah - but that list did not indicate that the pair had been sentenced to death, the Daily Star reported.
This is not the first time that foreign nationals have been executed by Saudi authorities.
According to Amnesty International, the country has executed around 100 people this year, many of whom are foreigners convicted of drug offences.
In 2011, eight Bangladeshi men were publicly executed in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh after they were found guilty of killing an Egyptian.
Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia overturned a death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan man over a comment he had made on Facebook, which had led to him being convicted of blasphemy. That decision came after the case sparked public outcry in Sri Lanka and spurred diplomatic efforts to seek clemency for the man.

196617a7e9c5.text: By — Marcia Dunn, Associated Press Marcia Dunn, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/japan-launches-spacecraft-to-mars-moon-in-mission-to-bring-back-soil-samples Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Japan launches spacecraft to Mars' moon in mission to bring back soil samples Science Oct 19, 2026 4:54 PM EDT A Japanese spacecraft rocketed toward Mars on Tuesday on an unprecedented quest to explore its mysterious moons and bring back samples. Five of the world's space agencies joined forces for the five-year mission that will attempt to land a robotic prospector plus a rover on Phobos, the larger and closer of Mars' two pint-sized moons. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, which is leading the bold sampling effort, launched the spacecraft before dawn from the country's main spaceport on Tanegashima Island. While NASA has successfully landed nine spacecraft on Mars over the past 50 years and China scored a 2021 touchdown, no one has ever ventured onto Phobos or its sidekick Deimos. And no one has managed to fetch samples from Mars, let alone its moons. If successful, bits of dust, soil and rocks from Phobos will arrive on Earth in 2031. "There's a lot of adrenaline and a lot of excitement and a lot of wow," said NASA astrophysicist Tom Statler, who's involved with the project. Japan has an edge going in, with two asteroid sample returns already under its cosmic belt. This photo provided by NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona, taken with NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, shows Phobos, one of Mars' moons, on March 23, 2008. Image courtesy of NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona via AP Phobos is a lumpy, potato-shaped rock just 14 miles (22 kilometers) or so across. Examining pieces of it can explain how Mars' moons — and possibly moons elsewhere — came to be. Dubbed MMX for Martian Moons Exploration, the $578 million mission features a hefty 5-ton spacecraft that should reach Mars by late next summer. It will sync up with Phobos' tight orbit around the red planet, before ejecting the French-German rover that's named Idefix after the white terrier in the Asterix comics. No bigger than a microwave oven, Idefix will plop onto Phobos by itself, bouncing for several minutes before coming to a halt in the moon's extraordinarily low gravity. The four-wheeled rover is designed to right itself if it lands upside down. All bets are off, though, if it sinks into soft soil or gets wedged between rocks, said the French Space Agency's Julien Baroukh. Once the rover's solar panels are deployed, the vehicle can no longer right itself, he added, which is why it will move at a glacial 1 millimeter per second (0.04 inches per second). Idefix will serve as a "scout for safety," according to Baroukh, as it prowls around Phobos for 100 days. Japanese flight controllers want to avoid powdery soil and rough terrain when the mothership — a four-legged stationary lander — descends to the surface to gather samples in late 2028 or 2029. The lander will spend just two hours on Phobos, drilling and vacuuming up at least one-third of an ounce (10 grams) of material, before launching back into space. It will study Deimos during a series of flybys before leaving the Martian neighborhood in 2030 and hustling back to Earth for a 2031 sample delivery in the Australian desert. It's a treacherous undertaking, with wreckage littering the path. The moons' names aren't exactly comforting: Phobos is Greek for fear and Deimos means dread. They're the twin sons of the god of war Ares — Mars in Roman mythology. Russia stumbled in all three of its Phobos attempts as well as many other Mars endeavors. In its only other Mars mission, Japan failed to get a spacecraft into orbit around the red planet. Even NASA has had its share of flops in a bid to answer the burning question: Did life ever exist on Mars? By studying Mars' moons, scientists hope to learn whether Phobos and Deimos formed in the aftermath of an ancient collision between Mars and a battering space rock. It's also possible that the moons might be stray asteroids that became ensnared in Mars' gravity. Either way, scientists anticipate finding traces of Mars on Phobos, making the samples an irresistible two-for-one that should help demystify planetary and moon formation, and perhaps even the recipe for life. The findings will help shape future Mars missions, including those by astronauts, said NASA's acting planetary science director Lindsay Hays. "It is a once-in-a-lifetime chance. We are part of the first sample return mission from the Martian system," said the Germany Space Agency's rover chief Markus Grebenstein. Japan isn't the only one looking to claim the scientific riches packed into the Martian system's rocks and dirt. China plans to launch a sample return mission to Mars in 2028, while NASA is still debating how to retrieve the more than 30 sample tubes collected by the Perseverance Mars rover, the new champion for off-Earth driving. Japan and China could be neck-and-neck in getting samples back from the Martian system. Both are targeting 2031. Japan is investing $350 million in this mission. NASA is contributing $87 million, the French Space Agency about $68 million, the German Space Agency about $56 million and the European Space Agency some $17 million. Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC that lives had been lost because there had not been time to warn citizens about ballistic missile strikes, saying: "It's dangerous... I think it's really very bad... People [have] already died."
The adviser also said restrictions to Ukraine's use of the Starlink internet network were ongoing.
The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing last week, as a row with the Trump administrations over its controversial deal to import Russian oil sent relations to new lows.
Despite the denials from Washington, many in Kyiv suspect the issues are not a coincidence.
On Monday morning, Zelensky wrote on social media: "Overnight two ballistic missile attacks were reported on the capital, one without warning, the second with only minimal time to take shelter."
Hours earlier, an interview the president did with NBC was published, in which he said intelligence sharing had been restored after a three-day pause.
"We are very thankful for this," he said. "Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles."
But Beskrestnov told the BBC that American intelligence continued to be incomplete and inconsistent, and that the US had failed to provide a clear explanation for the issue.
"This looks very strange," he said. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."
He continued: "And for example, last night we received it, but... one minute before the attack."
However, he said other collaboration with US continues, adding: "Intelligence data keeps flowing, and the issue is solely with the air raid alert component."
Beskrestnov also said the US had given no clarity about who was responsible for the ongoing restrictions to the Starlink internet network and its military service Starshield, which Kyiv uses to provide connectivity for drones, helicopters and military communications.
Last week, Starshield restricted the speed at which mobile units could move while staying connected to the network to 100mph (160km/h).
This has limited Ukraine's ability to shoot down incoming drones or to launch mid-range drone attacks into Russian-occupied areas.
Starlink owner Elon Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, which was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. Trump has denied involvement.
Beskrestnov said he thought both issues occurring at the same time was "probably" a deliberate move to put pressure on Ukraine.
He told BBC News: "It's probably the United States trying to say [to] us, 'let's have the conversation, negotiation with Russia, you should find the compromise'."
Beskrestnov also said Ukraine had its own radar data to provide some limited warning of incoming attacks, but was urgently looking into using alternative communication systems.
He added: "Now we understand that something begins to happen with Starlink, and we're not sure what will be the next step.
"We understand that we should be prepared for some problems in future. And now we're thinking about an alternative for Starlink, not only for air defence, for communication between our forces, between our staff, for civilians also, because we don't know what we should expect in future regarding Starlink."
On Monday, when asked about intelligence sharing, Trump said: "We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing."
Earlier, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had said there had not been a "pause" to intelligence sharing.
"I don't know where [Zelensky is] getting these things or why he's saying these things to the press," he told reporters on Monday.
Rubio said he could not comment on the incident, adding: "I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system."
The BBC has contacted Starlink for a response.
A White House official said there were no changes to intelligence sharing operations between the US and Ukraine.
The official spoke on background to discuss intelligence matters. Trump is focused on ending the war, the official said, and added that the US has provided more aid to Ukraine than any other country.
Russian attacks continued late on Monday, with Ukrainian officials saying at least six people were killed - including a toddler in her pram and an 11-year-old girl - in a drone strike near a park cafÃ© in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
Zelensky described the attack in which another 14 people were injured as "absolute atrocity".

CODY, Wyo.—On a warm October evening at a bar in downtown Cody, Wyomingites gathered to ponder the future of what some hope will be the Cowboy State’s next booming industry: data centers.
This summer, outgoing Gov. Mark Gordon signed an executive order titled “Data Centers the Wyoming Way” that he said would “guide responsible development in Wyoming,” while keeping the state an attractive landing spot for the enormous server warehouses that power the AI industry.
Data centers’ potential impacts on Wyoming’s precious water supply, already-rising electricity prices and prized public lands have rankled many corners of the state. Gordon acknowledged those concerns in a statement accompanying the release of the order, which is not binding.
Environmental groups in Wyoming agree that there need to be more guardrails on data center development, but they are not fully aligned on how to achieve that goal.
Wyoming’s chapter of The Sierra Club believes a moratorium on data centers could be useful in certain circumstances, but the group has not taken a position on the utility of halting development across the state. The Wyoming Outdoor Council sees a tangible opportunity to advance new data center policies with the incoming crop of legislators and a new director of the Department of Environmental Quality. But a moratorium, in their view, would not guarantee those guardrails and is therefore a risky way to spend environmental groups’ limited political capital.
“By its very nature, a moratorium is temporary, and a call for a moratorium on data centers would really be a stopgap,” Jocelyn Wulf, the Wyoming Outdoor Council’s data center campaign manager, told a few dozen Cody residents this month at the data center town hall the organization hosted.
Representatives from both organizations told Inside Climate News they believe the incoming crop of legislators has an appetite for changing how Wyoming manages data center construction.
Not everyone in Cody sounded convinced that data centers would be a net positive for Wyoming.
“What’s the benefit?” asked Anne Trosper, a lifelong Wyomingite who has worked in the oil and gas, and conservation industries. “Where does Wyoming get money out of this thing?”
Data centers pay property taxes and electricity sales taxes in Wyoming, in addition to hosting construction jobs in the building phase of the facilities, and employing a small number of permanent workers once they are up and running.
But data centers could provide tax revenue to Wyoming in another familiar if indirect way.
With data centers demanding enormous amounts of power—Google’s Project Tembo, formerly known as Project Jade, could use up 10 gigawatts of electricity, more than five times Wyoming’s statewide electricity consumption—many companies are choosing to meet that demand in Wyoming with fossil fuels.
Much of Wyoming’s tax base comes from royalties paid by the coal, oil and gas industries, and the state has championed the Trump administration’s support for fossil fuels.
To fuel the industry’s growth, some Wyoming counties are zoning parcels of land as industrial parks, exempting data center companies from obtaining permits under Wyoming’s Industrial Siting Act. The Wyoming Outdoor Council describes this arrangement as a “loophole” companies use to build quicker and skirt some public oversight.
“That means no comprehensive review process by state agencies,” Wulf told the Cody gathering, so communities wouldn’t receive the impact assistance payments associated with some projects that go through that process. “This is not to say that they are still not subject to state and federal laws, but we are losing out on that review process as a whole [because] local governments must then review these projects to the best of their abilities. Despite their best intentions, local governments do have more limited capacity for thorough review.”

Cheyenne, Wyoming’s capital, has spent years courting data center development with mixed success. While the new construction has created many temporary and some permanent jobs, the scale, size and impacts of the new projects have not been without controversy.
In 2025, WyoFile reported that Microsoft applied for an air permit to run 128 backup diesel generators for a data center complex south of the city.
This July, the Cheyenne Board of Public Utilities found that a contractor working on a data center project for Meta, the parent company of Facebook, accidentally introduced a rare bacteria into the city’s wastewater treatment system. That incident occurred after Cheyenne city council members voted against a proposed 12-month moratorium on data center development this May.
“Guardrails are the direction that we should be going in,” Emma Jones, an associate organizer at the Wyoming chapter of the Sierra Club, told Inside Climate News. “A lot of community members want to see groups advocating for moratoriums because [data center development] is moving too fast.”
But calling for a moratorium would be unwise without a plan for what to accomplish during the pause, she said. As a result, the Wyoming chapter of the Sierra Club hasn’t publicly supported or opposed a moratorium. “We don’t want to just push for a moratorium for the sake of having a moratorium,” she said.
Some at the Cody meeting agreed with the Wyoming Outdoor Council that the new lawmakers could be open to taking a firmer approach to regulating AI growth. “It’s just a huge responsibility,” Trosper said.
When asked whether a moratorium would be helpful given the compressed nature of Wyoming’s upcoming legislative session, which starts in January and lasts only a few weeks, Trosper said she was unsure.
“I’m undecided at this point,” she said.

f52a1283fb60.text: By — Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press By — Philip Marcelo, Associated Press Philip Marcelo, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/ex-openai-worker-accused-of-bugging-conference-room-planned-to-fly-to-saudi-arabia-prosecutors-say Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Ex-OpenAI worker accused of bugging conference room planned to fly to Saudi Arabia, prosecutors say World Oct 19, 2026 4:35 PM EDT SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — A former OpenAI engineer charged with secretly installing a recording device in a conference room to glean company details had been "mere days" away from absconding to Saudi Arabia before his arrest, federal prosecutors said in new court filings. Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, was also fired from his job at the ChatGPT maker, according to a government memo filed Sunday. His wife and young son left the country the day after his arrest on a one-way ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official, prosecutors said in the filing. "Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," federal prosecutors wrote. "He has ample resources —including his significant compensation from a decade of high-tech employment in the Bay Area and at least two bank accounts in Saudi Arabia — and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government." Prosecutors also noted Saudi Arabia has no extradition treaty with the U.S. as they seek to detain Alfozan until trial. A judge will consider the request Monday in federal court in San Francisco. Alfozan's lawyers didn't immediately respond to an email seeking comment ahead of Monday's hearing. But in their own court filings, they argued that Alfozan, who had worked at OpenAI since July 2025, had purchased one-way tickets for his family to Saudi Arabia more than two weeks before prosecutors allege the recording devices were installed. The defense said the couple planned to spend Alfozan's roughly two-month paternity leave in Saudi Arabia following the birth of their U.S.-citizen son. Prosecutors say after his arrest, Saudi officials purchased new plane tickets for the wife and son to leave the U.S. sooner than the Oct. 12 flight Alfozan initially booked. Alfozan's lawyers also argued that he was on track to become a naturalized U.S. citizen with an interview with federal officials scheduled next month. They said he has been a legal permanent resident since 2020, has lived in the U.S. for 15 years and attended MIT and the University of California, Berkeley. "This was a long-held dream for the Alfozan family, as it is for so many immigrants," his lawyers wrote. "His plan was always to return to the Bay Area, where his home, his career, and his community are." Rather than remain in federal custody, Alfozan's lawyers argue he should be confined to his family's home in the San Francisco suburbs, with GPS monitoring, travel restrictions and a requirement to surrender his passport. Prosecutors have not said what Alfozan might have wanted to do with the recordings, but say he was in "frequent communication" with a member of the Saudi royal family. They said the royal family member repeatedly tried to recruit Alfozan to an artificial intelligence venture being launched in Saudi Arabia. Alfozan told the unnamed person in WhatsApp messages that he wouldn't leave OpenAI until his stock was vested, even as he explored other career opportunities in the Middle Eastern kingdom, prosecutors wrote. Prosecutors say Alfozan concealed an audio recording device in toilet paper and plugged it into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room he wasn't authorized to access. They say security cameras captured him entering the room and checking behind the television after installing the device. It remained there for several days before being found Sept. 30. Prosecutors say the conference room was typically used for meetings involving company leaders, government officials and other executives and "discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information." OpenAI has said the recording device Alfozan used was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio-monitoring capabilities. They also said they had evidence Alfozan planned to place other listening devices elsewhere in the office. Alfozan has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, he faces a five-year prison sentence. aae21033c27f.text: By — Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/a-bitter-michigan-senate-race-rattles-jewish-and-muslim-voters-already-on-edge-over-the-war-in-gaza Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter A bitter Michigan Senate race rattles Jewish and Muslim voters already on edge over the war in Gaza Politics Oct 19, 2026 4:26 PM EDT WEST BLOOMFIELD, Mich. (AP) — For many voters in Michigan, the U.S. Senate race has become about far more than which party controls Washington. In the Detroit suburbs, some Jewish Democrats are confronting deeply personal questions about faith and identity as they weigh whether they can support their party's nominee. Just miles away in Dearborn, Arab American leaders who backed President Donald Trump two years ago are growing increasingly alarmed by Republican rhetoric. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The concerns are rippling through communities already shaken by Israel's war in Gaza that followed the attack on Israel by Hamas on Oct. 7, 2023. Now they are central players in the bitter open-seat race between Republican Mike Rogers, a onetime congressman, and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official who would be the country's first Muslim senator if elected on Nov. 3. Rogers has increasingly portrayed El-Sayed as an extremist and a threat to Jewish voters as the Republican tries to win over a traditionally Democratic constituency. Rogers laughed when a visiting Republican senator said El-Sayed slept in an Osama bin Laden jersey, and he agreed with a social media post calling El-Sayed a terrorist. Emotions were already raw before the latest escalation. In West Bloomfield, a synagogue recovering from an attack this year is only a half-hour drive from the "Wall of Tears" in downtown Dearborn memorializing children killed in Gaza. 3196d3576b03.text: President Trump wants to hold a trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi and Russian President Putin in China next month to discuss "denuclearization" — but not necessarily Ukraine. Why it matters: Such a summit between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia would be unprecedented. Trump has been talking for two years about his aspiration to reach a deal with Russia and China to reduce the number of nuclear weapons. But so far Putin and Xi haven't shown much openness to the idea. Driving the news: Trump is expected to travel to China in mid-November to participate in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' meeting in the city of Shenzhen. The Kremlin has been floating the idea of holding such a meeting since July. Putin raised the issue in two phone calls with Trump, including one last week. The Chinese government hasn't expressed willingness to hold such a summit. What he's saying: When asked on Monday whether such a summit could discuss ending the war in Ukraine, Trump said he wants to hold such a trilateral meeting, but in order to discuss other issues. "I would do it, not so much for Ukraine, we would have it to talk about denuclearization," he said.

e1dd86d307c1.text: By — Gisela Salomon, Associated Press Gisela Salomon, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/homeland-security-grants-temporary-deportation-reprieve-for-more-than-100000-ukrainians-and-sudanese Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Homeland Security grants temporary deportation reprieve for more than 100,000 Ukrainians and Sudanese World Oct 19, 2026 3:56 PM EDT MIAMI (AP) — More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire Monday. Temporary Protected Status was set to end Oct. 19 for about 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese. But DHS said an announcement "will be made at the appropriate time." Until then, the department said in a written statement, Ukrainians and Sudanese in the U.S. covered by those temporary measures "retain protection." The Department did not indicate how long they could stay or when a final announcement would be made on their status. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. DHS did not respond to a question about whether they can keep their work permits, but TPS generally allows people to work while their protections remain in effect. The decision Monday marks another incident where the Trump administration, which has previously sought to end these temporary protections from deportation and send people back to their home countries, has allowed people covered by the temporary status to stay in the country but without giving any guidance as to how long. Yuriy Boyechko, CEO of Hope For Ukraine, a nonprofit that provides humanitarian aid in Ukraine and helps resettle newcomers in the U.S., described the government's announcement as "last-minute patches." It is a "bandage that has been placed on a wound that does not solve the real issue," he said. "It's time for U.S. to come up with some normal path to permanent residency for all these people," Boyechko noted. He emphasized that they cannot safely return to Ukraine. The context of the decisions to keep the protections Watch the segment in the player above. The Trump administration has already terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria. But in a change in practice roughly a month ago, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans whose TPS was set to expire Sept. 9. In that case they also said that they were going to make a decision at the appropriate time and that in the meantime, people from El Salvador could continue to work and live in the U.S. Activists and a bipartisan group of lawmakers have been raising the alarm over the upcoming deadline for TPS to expire for Ukrainians, arguing that conditions remain unsafe for them to return home amid the war with Russia. Ukraine was first designated for TPS in April 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion two months earlier. The Biden administration subsequently extended the designation, most recently in January 2025, when DHS authorized an additional 18 months of protection through October 2026. The TPS program for Sudan was established in 1997, and since then, successive U.S. administrations have extended it due to the armed conflict and political instability that have plagued the African nation. The decision Monday comes two weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Trump's hard line immigration policies will face a test at the ballot box. The TPS program has offered protections for decades but is controversial The U.S. Congress created TPS in 1990 to prevent deportations to countries suffering from natural disasters or civil strife. It allows people already in the country to remain and work, for renewable periods if the homeland security secretary determines conditions are unsafe for their return. But it doesn't give them a pathway to permanent residency. Supporters say that using this tool protects people from being returned to dangerous situations and that uprooting people covered by TPS after years of living in the U.S. is cruel. Critics, especially in the Trump administration, say successive administrations have extended these protections for years regardless of what has happened in the home countries. Federal rules say TPS is automatically extended for six months if the secretary doesn't make a determination at least 60 days before the designation expires. Advocates are grateful for DHS decision, warn about the war "We're grateful for an extension, however temporary, for TPS holders from Ukraine and Sudan," said Myal Greene, president and CEO of World Relief, an organization that has provided humanitarian assistance in both countries. "We encourage the administration and Congress to consider longer term relief for women, men and children trying to carve out stability while their countries of origin remain in upheaval." Krish O'Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of Global Refuge, noted Ukraine and Sudan are not safe and meet the legal conditions for TPS to be extended. "Russia's war on Ukraine is nearing its fifth year, and Ukrainians are bracing for another winter under drone and missile strikes, driving civilian casualties and devastating critical infrastructure. Sudan remains locked in a brutal civil war marked by famine, widespread human rights abuses and the hallmarks of genocide," Vignarajah said. "It is not safe for these families to go home." Associated Press reporter Rebecca Santana contributed from Washington. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. b6eaabada8c6.text: By — Dan Gelston, Associated Press Dan Gelston, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/ap-source-eagles-qb-jalen-hurts-expected-to-miss-rest-of-season-after-blood-clots-found-in-lungs-and-leg Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter AP source: Eagles QB Jalen Hurts expected to miss rest of season after blood clots found in lungs and leg Nation Oct 19, 2026 3:42 PM EDT PHILADELPHIA (AP) — Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is expected to miss the rest of the season because of blood clots in his lungs, a person familiar with the situation told The Associated Press on Monday. The person spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of a health matter. Hurts was placed on injured reserve Saturday, two days after the Eagles revealed he has a blood clot in his calf. He missed the first of at least four games in Philadelphia's loss to the Carolina Panthers on Sunday. The Eagles and Hurts' agent, Nicole Lynn, released more information on his condition Monday. They said Hurts has deep vein thrombosis and a bilateral pulmonary emboli, meaning a blood clot has traveled from the legs to the lungs. His treatment involves blood thinners, and he will not be allowed to participate in any football activities until he is off them. The Eagles and Lynn said Hurts was expected to make a full recovery. "He is clinically stable and has no significant functional limitations," their statement said. The Eagles previously said Hurts was injured when he took a cleat to his calf area on Oct. 4 in a game against the Los Angeles Rams. Hurts informed the medical staff of the injury after practice on Oct. 8. The Super Bowl 59 MVP was back at practice the next day before the team left for London to play Jacksonville. Hurts was initially diagnosed by specialists in London with a left calf superficial vein thrombosis. Hurts hadn't missed more than two games in a season since becoming the full-time starter in 2021. He has led the Eagles to five straight playoff appearances, three NFC East titles and two Super Bowl appearances, beating the Chiefs 40-22 two years ago. Tanner McKee started for Hurts against the Panthers. McKee finished 26 of 45 for 215 yards and a touchdown in the Eagles' 25-14 loss to Carolina. The Eagles (2-4) have lost four consecutive games for the first time since 2020. Hurts has eight touchdown passes and three interceptions with 933 yards passing this season. He is in the middle of a five-year, $255 million extension, including $179.3 million guaranteed, that takes him through the 2028 season. The Eagles stunned fans when they drafted Hurts out of Oklahoma in the second round in 2020. They seemingly had Carson Wentz entrenched at QB and had more pressing needs. But Hurts supplanted Wentz and became one of the top quarterbacks in the NFL. AP Pro Football Writer Rob Maaddi in Tampa, Florida, contributed to this report. 5c6300d5d58b.text: By — Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/longtime-cnn-anchor-christiane-amanpour-leaving-network-after-a-storied-career-of-43-years Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Longtime CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour leaving network after a storied career of 43 years Nation Oct 19, 2026 3:35 PM EDT Longtime CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour, who began as an entry-level assistant and rose to become one of the most visible correspondents and anchors on TV, reporting from war zones and hot spots for decades, will be leaving the network after 43 years. Amanpour, the network's chief international anchor, will scale back her daily show, "Amanpour," on CNN International to once a week at the beginning of 2027, and end it in May, leaving the network the following month. She said in a statement Monday that she looks forward to "interesting new projects down the line." Amanpour, 68, also will end her PBS show, "Amanpour & Co," at the end of the year, she said in her statement, shared by CNN. She will continue her podcast, "The Ex Files," with her ex-husband, Jamie Rubin, a former U.S. diplomat. "After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!" Amanpour said. She added she would "always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: Always be truthful, not neutral." No reason given for her departure Amanpour did not give a reason for her departure, nor did she specifically mention changes at her network. But her exit coincides with a new era at CNN as it comes under a new owner, Skydance. After a yearlong process, Skydance-owned Paramount closed its $81 billion buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6. The merger unites under one roof two giants in TV news — CBS and CNN. On a personal front. Amanpour has spoken openly about her 2021 diagnosis of ovarian cancer and two later recurrences, calling it "the invisible killer." She has urged others to "get all the scans that you can." Amanpour joined CNN as an assistant in Atlanta in 1983. In his own message Monday, CNN's chief executive, Mark Thompson, wrote that at the time, her promise was not universally appreciated. "Famously, one of her bosses told her back then that she didn't have what it took to become a foreign correspondent — or to hold any on-air role at all," Thompson wrote. "Boy, did she prove him wrong!" Fame came during the first Gulf War Amanpour became a reporter, and an international correspondent seven years later. She earned fame in the early 1990s, covering the Gulf War, conflict in the Middle East and many other hot spots. War reporting is "a sense of mission, it's a sense of purpose, it's a sense of being able to tell a story," she said. She aimed to bring international news — including complicated stories — to American viewers. "I've never believed that things are too complicated to put on American television," she told The Associated Press in 2023. I've never talked down to an audience. I've never believed that they just want to know what's happening in their backyard." Amanpour also noted that her upbringing gave her a unique perspective. "Because of my upbringing — I'm half-Iranian and half-British — I've had the great privilege of being able to see the world from two very distinct perspectives," she said. "I've always spoken out about the need to bridge gaps. I know we can live in a world that's not 100% tribalized." In her remarks Monday, Amanpour thanked her field crews and show teams. "From my very first big exciting assignment covering the first Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between, it's the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much," she wrote, "as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favor." Across hundreds of miles of the northern Gulf of Mexico, a deep-water ecosystem collapsed after the massive 2011 Deepwater Horizon oil and gas spill, and recovery is uncertain, new research concludes.
The study, published Monday in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, found that animal populations, including octopus, krill, squid and shrimp declined by 60 to 85 percent in the three-and-a-half years after the spill, with few signs of recovery since. Krill and lanternfish, both foundational species in the Gulf’s food web, were among the hardest hit. The findings also suggest that the die-off is causing genetic bottlenecks that could further hinder ecosystem recovery.
The researchers identified it as the “fastest and most severe faunal decline reported for Earth’s largest ecosystem type” ever documented. The widespread die-off of marine organisms may also reduce the ocean’s ability to transport carbon dioxide from the atmosphere to the deep sea. After ruling out other factors, such as water temperature and oxygen levels, the researchers identified the Deepwater Horizon blowout as “the most parsimonious explanation” for the ecosystem’s collapse.
Comprehensive natural resource damage assessments and restoration efforts involving federal, state and tribal trustees are still underway. In 2016, BP agreed to a $20.8 billion settlement, including up to $8.8 billion for environmental restoration.
Remote ocean depths and habitats miles below the surface may seem buffered from the impacts of human activity, the authors wrote, but their findings suggest an industrial disaster pushed part of it into a diminished state with “limited resilience to facilitate recovery.” They said their findings also show that proposed industrial deep-sea mining could damage the ecosystem before baseline conditions are assessed.
A Transoceanic drilling rig, operating for BP about 50 miles southeast of the Mississippi Delta, exploded on April 20, 2010. The explosion and fire killed 11 people and triggered the largest accidental marine oil spill in history.
Oil and gas spewed uncontrollably from the broken well nearly a mile deep for 87 days, ejecting 4.9 million barrels of oil at a rate of about 400 tanker trucks per day, enough to fill up 1.2 million cars. The spill also released about 7.7 billion cubic feet of fossil gas into the deep sea at a rate of 88 million cubic feet per day, enough to supply about 820,000 U.S. homes. State and federal agencies, including the EPA, also authorized BP to apply 1.84 million gallons of chemical dispersants to try to reduce the impacts.
Some of the oil and gas dissipated and was transported out of the deep Gulf of Mexico region. Some coated barrier islands and devastated coastal wetlands and shellfish habitat and some settled onto the ocean floor, where currents can stir it back into the water. But enough hydrocarbon and chemical-dispersant remnants stayed suspended long enough to do almost immeasurable harm.
A series of studies since the spill have shown a wide range of toxic effects on marine organisms, from impaired development and reproduction to increased mortality and lasting health problems in dolphins and whales. The new paper suggests that lingering pollutants may interfere with some species’ ability to find mates in the dark by disrupting their highly developed sense of smell.
Scientists on Slippery Decks
The impacts continue to ripple through the ecosystem, said lead author Tracey Sutton, a professor of marine and environmental sciences at Nova Southeastern University in Florida. A 2024 study found an 80 percent decline in deep-diving toothed whales, he said.
“We used to have a big resident population of sperm whales right off the Mississippi River, but we haven’t seen a sperm whale in 10 years,” he said. Large predators need big, occasional dense patches of prey, and those have disappeared, he added.
Scientists have developed accurate ways to count fish. For this study, they started with a baseline from nine months of sampling in 2011 and compared it with nine subsequent surveys between 2015 and 2023. The researchers sampled deep-pelagic habitat along a large grid around the spill site from about 650 feet below the surface to about a mile down. The deep-pelagic zone accounts for about 90 percent of the Gulf’s total volume.
Across a grid of stations, scientists on slippery decks lowered and hoisted nets that open and close at different depths, with experts from different species groups to identify the catch. They sampled around noon and midnight to account for species that migrate vertically each day. Ship-mounted scientific echosounders provided an independent check, measuring sound reflected by marine life in the water column.
The research is “comprehensive and carefully composed,” marine biologist Bruce Robison, a senior scientist at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute, said via email. “There is no other study that I know of with such an incredible number of net samples,” added Robison, who did not participate in the new study.
The research focuses on species that are not commercially fished and shows for the first time that human impacts can deplete marine life even in very deep ocean water, he said.
“It is important for the public to understand just how disastrous this oil spill was,” Robison said. “The Gulf has not recovered and it’s been over 15 years.”
Robison said other activities, such as deep-sea mining, could also have severe negative consequences for deep-water pelagic ecosystems by discharging wastewater containing metals or lubricants.
Three lines of evidence—net hauls, acoustic surveys and genetic sampling—corroborate each other, which is “unusually strong evidence to support his conclusions,” said Jeffrey Drazen, a marine ecologist at the University of Hawai’i at Manoa, who did not participate in the new study.
The study examines all possible causes of the decline and shows only one aligns with the scientific evidence, he said.
