He voted for the costly Iran war and spiking gas prices." In Nebraska, Democratic candidate Chris Backemeyer says families are drowning. "And Mike Flood opened the gates. Flood voted six times for Trump's tariffs and the Iran war, flooding us with higher prices on groceries, gas, cars and medicine, costing us a thousand dollars more a year." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. And in Iowa, a group called Vote Vets Action Fund said Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson voted five times for the Iran war, "giving us record prices for gas and fertilizer." Those ads are but a few examples of how Democrats and aligned advocacy groups are using an unpopular war as they challenge Republicans, aiming to win back power in the House and Senate. It's the culmination of a strategy Democrats launched in the spring, when they began to repeatedly bring up war powers resolutions aimed at ending the conflict. The votes had little practical effect, but forced lawmakers to go on record and take a stand. READ MORE: 13 races that will determine control of the Senate Now those votes are being highlighted in campaign ads across the country, according to an Associated Press analysis of data from AdImpact, which charts media spending. In some cases, the Republicans targeted have never served in Congress before, so they couldn't possibly have voted on the various war powers resolutions. Even then, Democrats are portraying them as destined to be rubber stamps for President Donald Trump when it comes to the war. Tying the war to the cost of living The Associated Press analyzed data on broadcast and cable ads aired from Sept. 1 through Oct. 14 in the most competitive midterm races. The analysis focused on House and Senate races rated as either tossups or leaning Democratic or Republican by the Cook Political Report. A smaller number of streaming ads were also examined. At least half of the 50 races featured Iran-related ads, most of which included household cost-of-living messages. All told, the ads aired on TV more than 43,000 times since Sept. 1, costing an estimated $42 million. The AP used both AdImpact's own issue designations along with additional analysis of the ads' language to identify them. Of the 65 unique Iran-themed ads identified by the AP, 61 of them stressed household cost-of-living messages such as rising prices for fuel and other items. The Republican playbook Republicans are largely ignoring the Iran war in their ads. Their best strategy is to go after Democratic weaknesses so voters say "this guy is worse," said Ron Bonjean, a Republican strategist. "In the end, you're trying to get as many Republicans out to vote for you as possible and bring over some independents," Bonjean said. "And talking about the Iran war is really not a winning message because you're playing on the Democratic turf." The major themes addressed in the Republican advertising since Sept. 1 are taxes and crime, followed by issues tied to character, healthcare and immigration. Watch the segment in the player above. Some Republicans have sought to distance themselves from the Iran conflict outside the airwaves. In Michigan, Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers has said the "war with Iran needs to end — and end quickly." His opponent, Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, has run ads saying that a billion dollars a day is going to a war "we have no business fighting" and he was running to "invest our tax dollars here in Michigan." In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins emphasized in a recent debate that she voted nine times to end the conflict, prompting Democratic challenger Troy Jackson to say she voted five times to "make it happen." In all, the Senate has voted 14 times on resolutions seeking to halt or restrict Trump's military action against Iran. The House has held six such votes since the conflict began in late February. In the latest House vote, seven Republicans ended up siding with Democrats in voting to end the war. That includes four Republicans seeking reelection in highly competitive districts: Tom Barrett of Michigan, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn in Iowa. Barrett and Fitzpatrick had voted previously to remove U.S. troops from hostilities, but the yes votes were the first for Miller-Meeks and Nunn, reflecting the growing weariness with the war. Where Iran ads are most prevalent While the Iran war ads made up about 5% of the total TV spots aired across the competitive races, some contests leaned into the topic heavily. The highest concentration was in California's 48th Congressional District in the San Diego area. Roughly a third of the 12,000 aired ads touch on Iran. Democrats are seizing on a remark that Republican Jim Desmond made in the early days of the war, in which he said "no pain, no gain" as part of an interview on Real America's Voice. He also said in that interview he believed the higher prices were just "a spike" and would come down once the U.S. eliminated Iran's nuclear capability. e8c07bb6cef2.text: By — Bill Barrow, Associated Press Bill Barrow, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-trump-and-first-lady-unveil-new-task-force-on-womens-health-research Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Trump and first lady unveil new task force on women's health research Politics Oct 19, 2026 3:16 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Monday directed the federal government to bolster federal research into women's health, a move pushed by his wife, first lady Melania Trump. Watch the event in the video player above. The Republican president signed an executive order that creates a new women's health division at the National Institutes of Health and a White House task force to focus on the issue. That panel was set to hold its first meeting Monday after the Trumps held a Rose Garden signing ceremony. WATCH: How abortion politics is blocking progress in women's healthcare "Beginning today we will change the reality of women's health," Melania Trump said. "Previous generations fought for women's rights. Our generation will fight to discover the cures that will ensure a woman can live her life in health and to the fullest." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The president, who spoke after his wife, said the order will "promote new research and really go after the understudied diseases affecting women." The order is also intended to promote diagnostic technology and improve treatment. White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who recently completed treatment for breast cancer, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. will lead the White House task force. Donald Trump said the task force will coordinate with various federal agencies and programs. The order does not include specific funding goals. WATCH: Documentary explores why U.S. mothers lack support systems found in other countries The initiative comes after a series of meetings the first lady had with federal health officials. The president called it a "historic action" and praised the first lady's work. "She's accomplished so much," he said before pivoting into unscripted commentary on White House renovations, including the patio stone that now covers what was once the Rose Garden lawn. Shifting back to women's health, the president expressed surprise that some of the order's requirements had not already been imposed. "Who the hell wouldn't have a women's health division?" he said, after recalling that he'd asked Melania Trump, "Are you sure they don't have that?" The executive order calls for targeting maternal health, mental health and endometriosis. It also mentions other health concerns and diseases, including Alzheimer's, osteoporosis, heart disease and stroke. Melania Trump helped shape the order and the task force in consultation with physicians, White House officials, Kennedy and the Republican president. The initiative adds a new dimension to her policy portfolio as first lady. In Donald Trump's second term, the first lady has focused on improving foster care systems and expanding technology and artificial-intelligence access in education. In Trump's first presidency, the first lady's signature initiative, Be Best, focused on child well-being, safe social media use and reducing drug abuse. The White House ceremony comes weeks before Nov. 3 elections and as Donald Trump's job approval ratings have declined, including among women. About 4 in 10 independent women supported Trump during the 2024 election against Democrat Kamala Harris and in the pre-presidency period, according to AP-NORC polls. That dropped to around a quarter in the opening months of this midterm election year, the period marked by Trump's hard-line immigration crackdown in U.S. cities and the opening weeks of the Iran war. Cooper, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/democrat-marie-gluesenkamp-perez-fights-to-keep-a-foothold-in-conservative-pacific-northwest-district Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez fights to keep a foothold in conservative Pacific Northwest district Politics Oct 19, 2026 2:48 PM EDT CHEHALIS, Wash. (AP) — Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez carried a dull kitchen knife and two pairs of rusty scissors through a county fairgrounds south of Seattle. She handed them to Beverly Phoenix, who sat hunched over a table in the back of an exhibit hall, volunteering to help neighbors breathe new life into old tools. Now she offered advice to a member of Congress on using a Dremel, a handheld oscillating device, to sharpen the blades. It was an unassuming campaign stop that reinforced Gluesenkamp Perez's message of self sufficiency. The owner of an auto repair shop with her husband, Gluesenkamp Perez has positioned herself as someone who can help her party bridge the divide between urban and rural, blue collar and white collar, left and right. If Democrats are going to take back control of the U.S. House, they need to hold districts like this one in Southwest Washington, which twice elected Gluesenkamp Perez while also supporting President Donald Trump in all of his campaigns. Although the party has been fixated on whether to accommodate the burgeoning progressive movement, Democrats' willingness to make room for more moderate and unorthodox members could be even more important to winning and maintaining a durable majority. "We are a really independent community. What we want is respect for our priorities, for our values," Gluesenkamp Perez said. When that causes friction with party leaders, she said, her job is "explaining my community to D.C., not letting D.C. try to define my community's priorities." To prove herself, Gluesenkamp Perez, 38, will have to win a very different kind of campaign this year. In her last two elections, she faced Republican Joe Kent, who had connections to extremists. Now she's up against a more mainstream opponent in John Braun, a businessman and state legislator with a better shot at appealing to the district's moderate voters. Gluesenkamp Perez is a lightning rod for progressive criticism The Pacific Northwest has a reputation as a bastion of progressive politics, but Washington's 3rd Congressional District is more complex. It includes both the northern portion of the Portland, Oregon, metro area and expansive rural territory with economies centered around fishing, logging and manufacturing. By balancing those competing interests, Gluesenkamp Perez sometimes finds herself in a lonely group of Democrats siding with Republicans. She opposed President Joe Biden's student debt relief and voted for a Republican election proposal backed by Trump. She supported the Laken Riley immigration bill and defense legislation that included restrictions on abortion and climate change initiatives. She voted to censure fellow Democratic Reps. Al Green of Texas and Rashida Tlaib, and she introduced a resolution to reprimand Democratic Rep. Chuy Garcia for quietly maneuvering to essentially hand his seat to a trusted aide. Tensions flared again last month when Gluesenkamp Perez twice voted with Republicans on procedural issues, an apostasy in the traditions of Capitol Hill, where lawmakers are expected to stick with party leaders when it comes to such matters. As a consequence, Republicans were able to force a vote on a resolution condemning socialism, putting some Democrats in an awkward spot in an election year. "I get upset with her too at times, but you know, I also understand that she represents 800,000-plus people and that's 800,000-plus opinions for differing views," said Dale Benjamin, a 66-year-old retiree and self-described "Bernie progressive" who lives in Battle Ground. "I'm very thankful to her that she's willing to do that, especially in such a divisive place and time that we're in right now." Gluesenkamp Perez has prioritized legislation that bolsters her blue collar identity and the specific industries in her district. She's a strong proponent of "right to repair" legislation that would ensure consumers and independent businesses can repair things like tractors, cars and digital devices without going to the manufacturer. And she's gone to legislative war against the sea lions that congregate around Columbia River dams, feasting on salmon and steelhead before they can reach fishermen. She has pushed for legislation that would make it easier to kill animals that she calls "Corolla-sized vermin." "People sometimes treat my agenda like it's like quirky, and I'm like, this is actually very normal where I'm from," Gluesenkamp Perez said. More moderate Democrats are likely headed to Washington Democrats can't take control of the House without winning at least a dozen districts that voted for Trump. If they pull it off, many of the party's newest members of Congress — the ones who could deliver the majority — could resemble Gluesenkamp Perez more than the democratic socialists who won a string of primaries in blue districts this year. Democratic leaders will need an agenda that speaks to moderates if they want to stay in power, said Jim Kessler, executive vice president for policy at Third Way, a Democratic group that advocates for centrist policies. "What Democrats need to realize, when you win these seats, you're in rental property. You don't own them," Kessler said. "You can keep them as long as you tend to them, but it just takes one bad cycle and they're gone." Speaking of Gluesenkamp Perez, Kessler said "she's carved out her own brand and she is able to survive in a hostile environment." f615783b8ed4.text: By — Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press By — Anne D'Innocenzio, Associated Press Anne D'Innocenzio, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/consumer-concerns-grow-as-retailers-adopt-ai-assisted-pricing-tools Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Consumer concerns grow as retailers adopt AI-assisted pricing tools Economy Oct 19, 2026 2:35 PM EDT U.S. consumers aren't just frustrated with high prices. They're angry and confused about the increasingly high-tech ways that restaurant chains and major retailers are setting those prices. Digital price tags are rapidly replacing paper ones in grocery aisles. Artificial intelligence tools help businesses decide what to charge by predicting how customers might respond. Terms like "dynamic pricing" and "surveillance pricing" are stirring anxiety on social media, where users wonder if different people are getting different prices for the same product. Americans have grown accustomed to changing prices when booking flights, hotel rooms and rides, but the prospect of everyday spending shaped by algorithms they don't understand and personal data they may not realize they're sharing has touched a nerve. "There are major tensions happening right now between who's really going to have the power with some of these algorithms and usage of bots and AI: the companies or the shopper," said Katie Thomas, who leads an internal consumer behavior think tank at the management consulting firm Kearney. Companies using the technology say some concerns stem from misconceptions about how their pricing tools work. Walmart CEO John Furner said in a blog post last month that digital price tags save workers' time and keep prices up to date. He said the labels aren't used to raise prices based on the weather, time of day or individual shopper. "We price the product, not the person," Furner wrote. But companies aren't always transparent about the customer data they collect and how it's used, which has made consumers suspicious and led to speculation. For example, social media posts falsely imply that electronic shelf labels Walmart plans to put in all its U.S. stores scan shoppers' faces or cellphones to set individualized prices, Thomas said. Lawmakers and regulators are taking action. Legislators in at least 30 states have considered pricing bills this year, including measures addressing algorithmic and personalized pricing, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. The Federal Trade Commission has proposed an enforcement policy warning businesses that failing to disclose their use of personal data to set individualized prices could violate consumer protection law. Here are some of the pricing practices and technologies drawing scrutiny. Dynamic pricing can raise and lower prices What it is: Dynamic pricing means adjusting prices in response to changing market conditions, including supply and demand. An airline that adjusts ticket prices as departures approach is using dynamic pricing. Uber's practice of lifting fares when demand outstrips the supply of available drivers, such as during rush hour, is a type of dynamic pricing known as surge pricing. Why it matters: Frequent price changes extend well beyond food. Decodo, a web data company, tracked price changes in 2025 across products ranging from electronics to clothing and home improvement supplies. About half the U.S. changes it recorded were decreases, contrary to consumers' assumptions that dynamic pricing only raises prices, said Gabriele Vitke, a senior product marketing manager. Digital price labels are coming to more US stores What they are: Digital displays that let stores update shelf prices electronically instead of replacing paper tags. Why it matters: Digital price labels, long used in Europe and Asia, are drawing more attention as they spread to major U.S. retailers like Walmart and Whole Foods. Consumer advocates have argued that digital labels could eventually be used for surge pricing or personalized pricing. Labor unions also have opposed the technology. READ MORE: Inflation worsened last month to 3.7% as midterm elections near The electronic shelf labels make frequent changes easier but don't necessarily lead to higher prices during periods of strong demand. Retailers typically update electronic shelf prices on a regular schedule, often weekly, because shoppers value consistency, said Asa Farquhar of Relex Solutions, a retail technology company. Researchers who tracked prices at an unnamed grocery chain found "virtually no surge pricing" after the labels were introduced. "Changing prices throughout the day, the way airlines or rideshare apps do, is exceedingly rare in grocery and general merchandise today," Farquhar said. Personalized pricing, also called surveillance pricing, draws on customer data What it is: Personalized pricing means offering customers different prices and discounts based on their locations, incomes, web-browsing habits and other information about individuals or groups of shoppers. Some advocacy groups and regulators use the term "surveillance pricing" for the same practice. Why it matters: It's unclear how widely businesses use personal information to customize prices. An FTC staff report released in January 2025 found that intermediaries offering tools that can tailor prices and promotions worked with at least 250 clients, including grocery and clothing retailers. Lawmakers in Maryland, New Jersey and Connecticut recently enacted restrictions on using shoppers' personal data to determine what they pay. The Maryland and New Jersey laws focus on groceries, with exceptions for certain loyalty discounts and other promotional offers. Connecticut's legislation covers a broader range of retail purchases. The US has ordered all artificial intelligence (AI) technology from the Chinese firm DeepSeek to be removed from most government systems.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has banned all use of DeepSeek within civilian government agencies, and any technology built with the aid of its AI models.
As a powerful AI model that is open source - meaning it is free to access and less expensive to use - DeepSeek has been seen as a disruptive force in the ongoing AI technology race.
While the DHS notice did not detail the exact security concerns surrounding DeepSeek, the White House has this year criticised AI firms from China.
The DHS, DeepSeek, and the Chinese embassy in Washington DC have been contacted for comment.
The DHS made the order public on Monday, but the ban took effect from the end of July.
The order is specific to civilian agencies, including the Department of the Treasury, the Department of State and the Department of Justice. However, agencies within the Department of Defense are excluded.
The ban follows criticism of Chinese AI from the Trump administration, and from American firms.
White House tech lead Michael Kratsios wrote earlier this year in an internal memo that "malicious exploitation" of American AI firms had been occurring, mainly by rival firms in China.
Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which are poised to list on the public stock market in the coming months, have also claimed to have had their AI models essentially copied by some Chinese AI firms, including DeepSeek.
US president Donald Trump has made clear that he sees China as the key US rival when it comes to development of AI, something he sees as crucial to the future of the country.
DeepSeek has grown in popularity since its initial public release in 2025, with models being in such demand that the company's servers have gone down at times.
While DeepSeek's free chatbot app is one of the most downloaded apps in the Apple App Store rankings, its AI models are also used by US tech companies. Companies like Snowflake, Vercel and OpenRouter all incorporate DeepSeek in their offerings to customers.
Startups have flocked to open source models like DeepSeek.
For a technology or AI developer, using DeepSeek in their work costs a fraction of what a closed model like Google's Google's Gemini, Anthropic's Claude or OpenAI's Codex would.
Similarly, the expense borne by DeepSeek to develop its models has been astronomically less than what it has cost US AI firms to develop their own.
Last year, DeepSeek said it took about $6m (Â£4.5m) to train the debut version of its model, while the costs associated with OpenAI's GPT-4 were roughly $100m. Such revelations sent tech stocks tumbling.
The most recent version of DeepSeek was released last week. Users of the model have praised it online, saying it beats even the most advanced AI tools out of OpenAI on common tasks for AI tools like computer software coding.

88e595b18aee.text: By — Steven Sloan, Associated Press Steven Sloan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/iowa-is-testing-whether-democrats-can-win-rural-voters Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Iowa is testing whether Democrats can win rural voters Politics Oct 19, 2026 2:12 PM EDT NEW HAMPTON, Iowa (AP) — Standing in the doorway of his home near the corn and soybean fields that blanket this stretch of northeast Iowa, Dave Roethler doesn't know what happened to the Donald Trump he supported during his first presidency. Trump did a "heck of a good job" back then, the 70-year-old school custodian said. But now Roethler laments an economy in which "it's the middle-class families that are taking the big hit" while Trump is "going to come out way ahead." He scoffs at the Republican president's effort to win accolades such as the Nobel Peace Prize or a spot on Mount Rushmore. "I think he has delusions of grandeur," said Roethler, who plans to support Democrats next month in a state that has become a midterm battleground after Trump carried it by 13 percentage points two years ago. The president will return to Iowa twice before the election to rally supporters. Democrats face a steep challenge in winning rural communities like this one in Chickasaw County, a onetime party stronghold that swung sharply to the right in the Trump era as a broader realignment swept through much of the agricultural Midwest. But by simply narrowing their losses with appeals to voters such as Roethler, Democrats hope to become newly competitive from Iowa and Kansas to Nebraska and Ohio. Josh Turek, the Democrat running for a U.S. Senate seat in Iowa, said his party has "looked at this math problem incorrectly." "You've got to go out there in these rural counties and trim the margins," he said in an interview. Competitive races in states that usually aren't Republicans know they are on defense in these states. Trump recently held a rally in Nebraska to boost U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts and will do the same for U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas on Monday. Republicans are pumping money into both states before the Nov. 3 election. Few places represent the party's challenge like Iowa, where Democrats are mounting spirited campaigns for governor, U.S. Senate and several U.S. House seats, including the 2nd Congressional District, which encompasses much of the state's northeast and was considered reliably Republican until recently. With tariffs disrupting the agricultural economy and the war in Iran driving up gas prices — diesel surpasses $6 a gallon in Iowa — U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., swung through the district to ask voters to keep his fragile majority in place. WATCH: As cancer rates fall nationally, Iowa sees a troubling rise in diagnoses "This state is so important to us," Johnson said in Cedar Falls. The Republican erosion was evident about 45 miles north in New Hampton. A few houses away from Roethler, 69-year-old Bill Stonecypher voted for Trump in 2016, expecting him to apply his business acumen to governing. Now Stonecypher plans to vote for every Democrat on the ballot for the first time in his life. "I just know it's a mess and it's going to take years to fix," he said. Another neighbor, 70-year-old Deb Thorne backed Trump in 2024 but said he hasn't followed through on his pledge to lower costs. "He lied to us," she said. "I'm looking more at Democrats for everything." How a candidate for governor is reaching beyond the party base Democrats in Iowa are buoyed by Rob Sand, the state auditor whose campaign for governor is built on explicit overtures to independents and disaffected Republicans. A few dozen people gathered recently in an American Legion hall in St. Ansgar, a square-mile town near the Minnesota border. Sand opened by describing a "pretty standard upbringing" centered on hunting, fishing and church. He distanced himself from the fighting over cultural issues that has bogged down the national party. A few heads in the room nodded as he spoke of opposition to transgender girls playing on female sports teams. "All that stuff was stuff that nobody was talking about back when we were in high school," said Sand, whose opponent is Republican Zach Lahn, a political newcomer. The only reason he was a Democrat at all, Sand said, was that he had to pick a party to participate in primaries and he thought Democrats were stronger on issues like clean water and protecting public land. Jim Wherry, a Republican member of the Mitchell County Board of Supervisors, attended the event and said Sand "has a pretty good chance." "My big thing is sometimes things get focused on urban areas," he said. "So I like that he's actually incorporating rural Iowa." Sand, who has won two statewide elections as state auditor, said he's received support from voters who also backed Trump. "One of the things that people who vote for both of us find in common is that we say what we think and we're dissatisfied with the political system," he said. Democrats are boosting rural investments Democrats are stepping up their rural investments. The Democratic Governors Association has directed $10 million each to campaigns in Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Wisconsin and could spend elsewhere ahead of the election. "What I see is a map that has grown and grown and grown and that is good for Democrats," Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who leads the DGA, said in an interview. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which is focused on retaking the House, launched a rural engagement program for the first time this election cycle, including polling, paid media and staff. The group has made a six-figure investment in television advertising in Iowa's 2nd Congressional District alone. Democratic candidate Lindsay James, a chaplain who often speaks of her faith to connect with voters, could see a boost because the district includes Sand's hometown of Decorah. ad1512785fcf.text: By — Rob Gillies, Associated Press Rob Gillies, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/carney-fights-to-keep-canada-united-as-albertans-consider-path-to-independence Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Carney fights to keep Canada united as Albertans consider path to independence World Oct 19, 2026 2:01 PM EDT EDMONTON, Alberta (AP) — Voters in Canada's oil-rich Alberta province were deciding on Monday whether to begin a process that could lead to independence, testing national unity as Canadians rally against U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war and threats to claim Canada as the 51st U.S. state. Monday's vote is not a direct referendum on independence. Alberta, home to most of Canada's proven oil reserves — the fourth largest in the world — will decide whether to remain a province or begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation. More than 1.35 million Albertans, or 43% of eligible voters, cast advance or special ballots ahead of Monday's referendum, an unusually high level of early participation that underscores the intense interest in the province's future. Polls close at 8 p.m. local time, with results expected in the hours afterward. Alberta is Canada's oil heartland and cowboy country, a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment toward Ottawa runs deep, but has not traditionally translated into widespread support for independence. But even if Albertans reject the proposal, separatist leaders say the movement has transformed a fringe cause into a force in provincial politics and is not going away. Prime Minister Mark Carney urged Albertans to deliver a decisive vote for unity. "Vote like Canada's future depends on it because it does," he told a rally Friday in Edmonton, where he grew up. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who called the referendum despite opposing independence, cited a poll showing just 22% support for separation, a figure she said was still too high. The vote also comes as Alberta reels from a grass fire that suddenly shifted into a military training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, killing four service members and injuring 39, including 19 critically. Crowds erupt when Carney talks about the US The biggest cheers at Carney's rallies in Calgary and Edmonton came when he spoke about diversifying Canada's trade away from the United States. The applause showed how Trump's trade war and annexation threats have fueled Canadian nationalism even in traditionally conservative Alberta. Liberal prime ministers have long faced resentment from Albertans over federal energy policies, but Carney has emerged as an unusually popular figure by backing policies more friendly to fossil fuels, such as a proposed oil pipeline to the Pacific Coast. READ MORE: How Alberta separatism went from fringe cause to referendum Joining Smith in a show of unity against independence, Carney warned that the referendum comes at the "worst possible time" and urged Albertans not to use their votes merely to send Ottawa a message. Smith, who frequently clashed with Justin Trudeau, praised Carney for improving relations. "I think what we can agree on is that we have had some real change in the last 18 months," she said Friday. Smith opposes separation By calling a referendum she opposes, Smith acknowledged pressure from separatist activists within her governing United Conservative Party who helped bring her to power. Some of those activists helped oust former Premier Jason Kenney in 2022. Kenney said separatism had traditionally been a fringe cause, with independence parties typically attracting only 1% or 2% of the vote. He said the pandemic mobilized activists angry over public health restrictions and government authority. Separatist leader Jeff Rath said federal COVID-19 vaccine mandates drove him toward independence, while Tanya Clemens, co-chair of Let Alberta Decide, said pandemic restrictions spurred political organizing. Keith Wilson, the group's other co-chair, was a lead lawyer for the 2022 trucker convoy that paralyzed downtown Ottawa for weeks in a protest against vaccine mandates and other COVID-19 restrictions. Alberta's longstanding grievances with Ottawa Wilson argues that Alberta's grievances go deeper. With much of Canada's population concentrated in Ontario and Quebec, he said Liberal governments can win elections without significant support in Alberta, leaving the province vulnerable to federal policies opposed by its energy industry. Wilson argues that Carney's proposed Pacific Link pipeline illustrates the dysfunction, saying federal restrictions have discouraged private investment and could leave taxpayers financing the project. At the same time, Wilson rejects Alberta becoming an American state. "I have no interest in substituting a master that rules over my children's future, who's in Ottawa, with a new one who's in Washington," he said. Other separatist leaders have sought contact with the Trump administration. Rath and fellow independence advocates met three times with U.S. State Department officials in Washington to discuss Alberta's future. Chief Sheldon Sunshine of Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation condemned those meetings, calling them "absolutely treasonous to the people of Canada, people of Alberta." Sunshine said Alberta cannot leave Canada without First Nations' consent, citing treaties that predate the province — and said his nation would remain part of Canada even if Albertans vote for independence. Separatists see success even without victory No matter the outcome, the referendum campaign has generated unprecedented discussion about Alberta's place in Canada, Wilson said. "I think we've already hit success when you look at the voter turnout," he said. "People are engaged and people are talking about this topic at a level that's unprecedented historically." ff97606f4ef5.text: By — Dánica Coto, Associated Press Dánica Coto, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/haitian-gangs-target-foreign-troops-in-biggest-attack-since-force-began-operations Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Haitian gangs target foreign troops in biggest attack since force began operations World Oct 19, 2026 1:45 PM EDT SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico (AP) — Gangs in Haiti opened fire on an armored vehicle over the weekend, leaving four soldiers from El Salvador unaccounted for in the first major attack since an international gang suppression force began operations in the violence-wracked Caribbean country. The attack occurred Sunday in Croix-des-Bouquets, a once-peaceful community in Haiti's capital, Port-au-Prince, that is now controlled by violent gangs. The armed forces of El Salvador said in a statement Monday that the four aviation technicians were returning to camp when their armored vehicle was attacked with explosives and set on fire. The military noted that the four men managed to flee the burning vehicle and it is working with international forces to "establish contact and determine the location of our military personnel." Salvadoran authorities said that helicopters were dispatched to the area but they, too, came under fire as they dispersed armed men in the area. "Multiple attempts to approach by land and air have been made, but these have been hampered by the intensity of the fighting," the Salvadoran military said. The weapons and ammunition gangs are using are not made in Haiti and will continue to find ways to enter the country, Wien-Weibert Arthus, Haiti's deputy permanent representative to the U.N., told the U.N. Security Council Monday. "This latest episode is a reminder, as if we really needed one, of the fact that the security challenges in Haiti are complex and complicated," he said. "We hope that those who are missing will be able to go back to their families unscathed." Gang violence has displaced nearly 1.5 million people, a record, across Haiti in recent years, with more than 5,700 people killed or injured from January to mid-September, and more than 230 others kidnapped, according to the U.N. A warning from the U.S. Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the U.N., condemned the attack during the U.N. Security Council meeting on Haiti. "We believe the four men survived, but they do remain unaccounted for," he said. "We will bring you home." Waltz said that gangs attacked the armored vehicle with "hundreds of bullets and explosives." "To the gangs and gang leaders who carried out this cowardly attack, if you think you're going to intimidate this coalition into retreat, you have made a terrible mistake," he said. The gang suppression force said in a statement that it's assessing the situation and has advised residents where the attack occurred to remain indoors. READ MORE: Hundreds attend funeral in Haiti for 4 victims of brutal gang attack that killed 47 "Gangs are testing the gang suppression force," Jack Christofides, the force's special representative, said at the U.N. Monday as he noted that attacks against the force have recently increased. He warned that gangs have carried out reprisal killings in some areas following operations by Haitian and international forces, and that they have pushed deeper into places including the community of Kenscoff and the Artibonite region. "The reality is that we cannot be everywhere at once," Christofides said. Haiti prepares for an election despite violence The area where the armored vehicle was targeted is controlled by gangs including Chèn Méchan; Kraze Barye, led by Vitelhomme Innocent; and 400 Mawozo, led by Lanmo Sanjou. Both gang leaders have been sanctioned by the U.N. and the U.S. Romain Le Cour, head of the Haiti Observatory at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, said that while some gangs have been under pressure since the suppression force was deployed, "others want to show that they can strike back." "If these soldiers are indeed being held, the groups gain (an) edge to negotiate and to pressure the security forces," he said. In September 2025, the U.N. Security Council authorized the 5,550-member force to replace a former Kenya-led multinational force that struggled with a lack of funds and resources as it tried to help Haiti's National Police quell gang violence. The gang suppression force has more than 2,000 troops on the ground in Haiti, including soldiers from Chad, Jamaica and Guatemala. "The force is making a difference with what it has," Christofides said, adding that authorities have started to see early signs of reduced gang influence and control in certain areas. No one has claimed responsibility for the attack on the Salvadoran troops. It comes as Haiti prepares for its first general election in more than a decade and showcases the power of the gangs that control an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince. Carlos Ruiz Massieu, the U.N. special envoy to Haiti, said at Monday's meeting that electoral preparations "have reached an unprecedented level of progress." He said that more than 35 parties and political groups have registered, along with 3,500 candidates. Among them is former Haitian President Michel Martelly, who was sanctioned in November 2022 by Canada and in August 2024 by the U.S., which accused him of facilitating drug trafficking and sponsoring multiple gangs. 9c6f9f81e099.text: By — Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/on-campaign-trail-jeffries-says-republicans-are-divorced-from-reality Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter On campaign trail, Jeffries says Republicans are 'divorced from reality' Politics Oct 19, 2026 1:24 PM EDT TOLEDO, Ohio (AP) — House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said Sunday the election climate is holding firm for Democrats as he campaigned for Rep. Marcy Kaptur in a heavily contested Ohio congressional district that is crucial for majority control of the House. Jeffries also slapped back at President Donald Trump's abrupt decision to waive sanctions on Russia and said there will be a bipartisan effort in the House to pursue a new sanctions package that the president would not have the ability to waive. "It's shocking, but not surprising, that an American president would do so much to undermine the cause of democracy, freedom and dignity for the Ukrainian people," Jeffries told The Associated Press after visiting church services in Toledo. Jeffries, who is in line to become House speaker if Democrats win back the majority, has traveled to some 50 cities campaigning for Democratic candidates. He said the House Republicans are "divorced from reality" in thinking — as Speaker Mike Johnson recently suggested — that the Nov. 3 election will be a repeat of the 2024 sweep that put Trump in the White House and Republicans in Congress. "The climate continues to hold firm," Jeffries said, about the Democrats' chances. "We are working hard across the country, continuing to make the case that we need dramatic change as opposed to the status quo," he said, "and that Democrats are going to be the only ones to fight to make this country affordable." Ohio races are key to control of Congress The Buckeye State is being fiercely contested in these midterm elections that will determine control of Congress. While much attention has been on the Senate race between Republican Sen. Jon Husted and Democrat Sherrod Brown, the House races are a district-by-district slog key to unlocking control of that chamber. The Toldeo-area House seat has been a top priority. Kaptur, who has held office for decades, is the longest-serving woman in the House. But Trump has carried the district and Republicans are trying to flip it. Kaptur defeated GOP candidate Derek Merrin two years ago, but he is making a repeat play for the seat. READ MORE: Trump wants the midterms to be all about him. Based on Democrats' ads, they are happy to oblige "We work very hard," Kaptur told AP. "We don't just work at elections. We work to make a difference in the lives of people." In August, Kaptur, 80, was heading to church when the vehicle she was riding in as a passenger was struck. She was hospitalized with injuries suffered in the car accident, but said she has since recovered. Jeffries said Kaptur is a legendary figure in the Great Lakes Region. "Once again, she's going to defy all expectations," he said. Trump's waiver of Russia sanctions roils campaigns The area has been home to a large Ukrainian American population, and Kaptur is founder and co-chair of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, a bipartisan group of lawmakers with particular focus on the country. 8113b3ad5a88.text: By — Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/justice-department-charges-more-than-2-dozen-foreign-nationals-in-california-sweep-targeting-noncitizen-voters Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Justice Department charges more than 2 dozen foreign nationals in California sweep targeting noncitizen voters Politics Oct 19, 2026 12:53 PM EDT LOS ANGELES (AP) — Federal authorities have arrested more than two dozen foreign nationals Monday in California, who authorities said have illegally registered and voted in U.S. elections. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The statewide sweep is part of a Trump administration effort to root out noncitizen voting ahead of next month's midterm elections, even though data shows that the problem is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races. The arrests also reflect a further escalation in a simmering voter roll fight between the federal government and California that came into focus last week when the Justice Department sued the state and later warned that local election workers who knowingly process or tabulate ballots submitted by noncitizen voters are at risk of investigation and potential prosecution. The Justice Department said all of those arrested as part of a sweep dubbed Operation Protect the Vote are lawful permanent residents — but not U.S. citizens who are permitted to legally vote. They are charged with crimes including making false statements on a naturalization application and submitting fraudulent voter registrations. California emerges as a flashpoint for voting dispute The federal government has made noncitizen voting a priority this year, demanding detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states. Before Monday, the Justice Department had charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election. A flurry of activity has unfolded in heavily Democratic California, which is not typically regarded as a key battleground state but does have a handful of competitive congressional races that could help determine which party controls the U.S. House for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term. Over 23 million people are registered statewide. READ MORE: DOJ says California officials who process ballots from suspected noncitizens risk prosecution The administration last week sued California to prevent it from counting mail ballots from people the federal government has identified as "likely" noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed. The complaint was filed after California officials were given, and did not meet, a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contained a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters. A warning for poll workers On Friday, the Justice Department followed up with a letter warning that state election officials who knowingly process ballots cast by noncitizen voters are at risk of investigation. "The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring a federal crime are significant. Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful," warns the letter from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general at the Justice Department. It adds: "If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime." The letter is addressed to the Los Angeles County Counsel's office and also is copied to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan, effectively putting the entire state on notice. In response to the letter, Logan said his office is focused on conducting a fair and secure election while noting that Election Day is a mere 18 days away. "The U.S. Department of Justice has chosen to litigate their unverified assertions of voting eligibility. At this point, it is best for this to be addressed in court," he said. Associated Press writer Eric Tucker contributed to this report from Washington. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. CNN's chief international anchor, Christiane Amanpour, has announced she will leave the organisation next year after more than four decades.
"After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!" Amanpour said in a statement., external
The 68-year-old said she "looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral".
CNN chairman Mark Thompson described her as "one of the most trusted and beloved journalists anywhere" and said the network will take time to celebrate her "before she departs next year".
Amanpour began working for CNN in 1983 as an assistant on the international news desk, and went on to become one of the network's best-known correspondents, often reporting on conflicts and wars.
She has presented her own nightly interview program on CNN International since 2009.
In a memo to staff on Monday, Thompson wrote: "Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months.
"Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I'm very sorry to see her go, but I've come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.
"In the meantime, on behalf of the entire CNN leadership team, I want to thank Christiane for 43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship," he added.
In her own statement, Amanpour said she wanted to thank "all the amazingly talented people I've worked with throughout this incredible journey. Especially my beloved show teams and field crews."
Amanpour reflected on her "very first big exciting assignment covering the First Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between".
"It's the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much," she continued, "as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favour."

As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory feeling: that attacks like that could not happen here, and that it was only a matter of time until they did.
Australians will tell you this is a largely peaceful society with a comparatively civil public discourse. Violence targeting politicians has been rare, the bungled assassination of Labor leader Arthur Calwell in 1966 now a distant and fleeting memory.
But MPs and public figures â backed by experts â have been warning of a volcano of threats against them as social cohesion cracks, polarisation intensifies and the tone of debate grows hotter.
And on Monday, their worst fears appear to have been realised.
Independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car and severely injured outside her office in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta.
Police say a 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene, and a knife seized, but they have not said Haines was hit deliberately.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, however, swiftly described the incident as an apparent attack.
He was briefed by federal police â whose counter terror squad is helping state officers investigate â and told the national broadcaster: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."
Though he stressed no motive had been confirmed, Albanese earlier got emotional as he talked about the growing fear amongst MPs that they would end up targets.
Earlier this year Albanese himself was evacuated from his official residence over a bomb threat. As of August, about 20 cases in which people were accused of making violent threats against him were winding their way through courts around the country.
In recent years, politicians here have been mailed bullets. Female MPs â and in some cases their children â have been threatened with sexual violence. A Jewish MP's office has been firebombed, a Sydney mayor's car has been torched and countless other politicians have had their workplaces vandalised.
Just last week Small Business Minister Anne Aly said she had received a wave of death threats after a politician from the opposition said she should be "shamed and stoned in the square" over a tax policy.
According to government statistics, there were 1,067 reports of "harassing and threatening behaviour" against "high office holders" in the year to June: an increase on last year.
"We tend to bury our head in the sand and say, 'Not here', but this has been happening now for well over a decade," Josh Roose, a Deakin University Professor on violent extremism, tells the BBC.
Socioeconomic strain, growing mental health problems in the community, "grifters" who benefit politically or financially from whipping up further discontent, and a "carcinogenic" online environment are drivers of the trend, he says, which has dramatically escalated since the pandemic.
But the political class must also take responsibility for their role, he adds.
"We've seen a willingness to cross previously sacred terrain - you know, not targeting individuals, not targeting their families - but we now see that this is part and parcel of Australian political life.
"This is occurring at both ends of the political spectrum."
And experts like him warn it is not just politicians who are vulnerable: it is members of the media, academics, court officials and other public figures too.
Mike Burgess, the head of Australia's spy agency, has warned for years that the spectre of political violence is looming in Australia.
"Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack," he said in his annual threat assessment for 2026.
And the Federal Police have said it is not just ideology motivating cases in recent times. "Grievance" is radicalising people.
"They're feeling distanced, they're feeling alone, they're looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose," Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC earlier this month.
There have been frustrated rumblings in Canberra from some MPs who say security arrangements have not changed with the climate and â if a political motivation for this incident is confirmed â one of the greatest tenets of the nation's political culture could now be at risk.
It is not abnormal for you to run into your local member at the shops, or chat to them at the footy, and many open up their offices for constituents who want to raise concerns or share ideas.
Haines is particularly renowned and respected for that, Albanese said on Monday night.
"Here in Australia, it is a good thing that politicians are able to go about their community and engage with people," he said.
"I don't want to see a political system in which you can't have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the street, at street meetings, public forums â that's an important part of our democracy."

A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing, external in California.
US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the AI firm, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and say a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest.
It was argued the 35-year-old engineer therefore posed a flight risk and should be detained, pending trial.
The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.
Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder.
The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.
A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted.
He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated.
The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed.
It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son.
Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same.
On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official.
"Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued.
The FBI investigation is ongoing.
Alfozan is scheduled to âappear â in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (Â£188,000) fine.

More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local authorities say.
A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city, which was being used as a training centre for recruits to the security forces and police.
The head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, condemned what he called the "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response".
The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations".
Yemen's devastating civil war has flared up in recent months.
At the start of October, pro-government forces launched a major offensive that aims to retake territory in western Yemen that is controlled by the Houthis.
With air support from a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states, they managed to regain control of territory on the Red Sea coast that overlooks the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, which the Houthis captured in a surprise assault in September.
However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib and al-Jawf provinces.
The Houthis have also responded to the Saudi air strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
Monday's attack in Shabwa is one of the deadliest reported since the start of the escalation.
Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces. According to a preliminary assessment, 53 were killed and more than 200 injured, it added.
A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground.
Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based. Some of them were in a critical condition, he said.
Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target.
He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes".
The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.
In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children.
According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks.
The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August.
In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donald Trump.
"The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president," the former US president wrote on X, calling the probe "so appalling".
The White House defended the inquiry, saying the justice department was "focused on restoring law and order".
Last week, homeland security agents searched the Minnesota Democrat's Washington DC home as part of an investigation into her immigration status. Born in Somalia, Omar moved to the US with her family as a child.
US media outlets have reported that the probe is tied to her American citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995.
Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date.
Obama said in his X post on Sunday that her father became a naturalised citizen when she was 17, and not yet legally an adult, which then gave her citizenship.
"Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen," he wrote.
"If this becomes the new normal," he added, "there's no reason to believe it will stop with her - or that future presidents, in either party, won't do the same."
According to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services, a child born outside of the US automatically becomes a citizen when he or she has at least one parent who is a citizen by birth or naturalisation, or he or she is under the age of 18, and is a lawful permanent resident living in the custody of a citizen parent.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis denied the investigation was politically motivated.
"Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes," she said in an emailed statement to the BBC.
"The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe."
Trump has often argued that federal criminal investigations against him as he campaigned for re-election were politically motivated.
The investigation into Omar could lead to the justice department seeking to "denaturalise" her, or revoke her citizenship. It would have to prove there were material lies in the naturalisation process.
In 2023, Republicans removed Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee for comments and tweets she made about Israel, which drew bipartisan criticism.
Omar has said that Trump has targeted her for years with "baseless lies and smear campaigns" and called the investigation "the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation".
But Trump has said the investigation had "nothing to do" with him, while describing Omar as a "terrible person" and a "complainer".
Federal agents reportedly seized her phone, computers, notebooks and passport in the raid a week ago.
Her lawyers have demanded the government return her belongings, CBS News, the BBC's US partner, has reported, arguing in a letter sent on Friday that the seizure of property had violated restrictions put in place by a judge to protect her work as a federal lawmaker.
The lawyers also alleged agents did not duly notify Omar or the House of Representatives general counsel that a search would be taking place and kept her from contacting her attorney for more than an hour, according to CBS.
Democrats characterised the raid as the president attempting to interfere with the legislative branch of government. Republicans, meanwhile, have said Omar should be treated the same as anyone else under the law.
When Obama first ran for president, and throughout his two terms in the White House, Trump repeatedly raised questions about his citizenship, asserting he was not born on American soil and was disqualified from serving in office. Obama released two records proving he had been born in Hawaii.
Obama did not mention that history in his X post on Sunday.

Curraghs Wildlife Park has experienced its busiest October weekend ever after the birth of eight capybara pups, which staff say have "delighted" people and boosted conservation funding.
The pups were born to two females within days of each other, on 26 September and 1 October.
Their arrival has sparked huge public interest, with the park's manager Kathleen Graham saying the reaction to this "overload of cuteness" had been extraordinary.
"The car park was full, it was like a bank holiday. Everybody coming to see the capybara babies," she said.
The arrival marks a milestone for the park, which last welcomed a single capybara pup four years ago.
Graham said the scale of this year's births has been "a super overload of cuteness really."
The animals, native to South America, are the world's largest rodent, and thrive in wet marshland environments.
Graham said the pups' appearance on social media immediately drew far more attention than expected, and the surge translated directly into visitor numbers
"They have been delighting people. Even grown men were like cooing," she laughed.
Although capybaras are not endangered, Graham said they play a vital role in helping visitors understand threatened wetland habitats
The park is part of the European Association of Zoos and Aquaria's Eaza Wetlands for Life campaign and sits on a Ramsarâdesignated wetland.
Graham said the pups helped highlight how wetlands supported both wildlife and people.
"We rely on wetlands to soak up excess rainwater. And they're management systems, really. So they need looking after and protecting," she said.
'A lot of joy'
The pups' popularity also directly supported conservation work, she explained, as each visitor contributed Â£1 to the park's conservation fund unless they opted out.
"Although themselves [capybaras] may not be endangered, they've actually created a lot of extra money this weekend for the conservation fund and spread a lot of joy and oohs and aahs," she said.
The fund supports projects locally with Manx Wildlife Trust and internationally, including work in the Pantanal, where wild capybaras live.
She said the pups arrival had lifted spirits at a time when many people were seeking moments of joy.
"I think when there's so many just awful things that happen in the world, sometimes these little things just give us a bit of light relief, don't they?," she added.

"Look at this beautiful guy," Trump said at a Saturday rally in Kentucky, referring to U.S. House candidate Ed Gallrein, a former U.S. Navy SEAL with an angular face who stood nearby the stage. "Central casting." That's a common refrain from Trump, who owned the Miss Universe beauty pageant and grew his clout on the reality television show "The Apprentice" before entering politics. Aesthetics have long been part of the president's measuring stick, either as a source of praise or target for ridicule. Now, Trump is deploying his handsomeness appraisals as he boosts Republican candidates in a midterm election which already includes debates over which candidates are more masculine. The outcome will determine whether Republicans keep control of Congress or Trump faces emboldened Democratic opposition in Washington. WATCH: An accounting of Trump's promised payouts and questions they raise Soon after Trump touted Gallrein's beauty on Saturday, he mentioned Sen. Jon Husted, the Ohio Republican running for reelection, and described him as "a perfect person, good-looking guy." "I examined his ass," said Trump, eliciting laughter. "I never did that with a man before. I examined his ass. And then I looked at his shoulders. I looked at his feet. I looked at his hand. I looked at his jawline." It was a reprise of Trump's droll assessment from an earlier rally in Ohio, when he also touted Husted's past as a college football player. Not all Republicans are so lucky, as Ken Paxton has learned. "I don't really like the way he looks," Trump said about the Republican Senate candidate in Texas during the party's midterm convention as Paxton stood nearby grinning. Trump previously said that "it's so insulting to him, but I might as well say it." He added that Paxton's conservative record as attorney general "speaks a lot louder than the suit he's wearing that doesn't look so great." Democrats are far from safe from the president's visual judgments. Trump says Paxton's opponent, Democratic candidate James Talarico, reminds him of Alfred E. Neuman, the freckled, gap-toothed MAD magazine mascot. And he had a disparaging assessment of Sen. Jon Ossoff, a Democratic heartthrob with a jawline rivaling Husted's. Trump compared him to Pee-wee Herman, the comedy character with a waxy face and widow's peak, while rallying for Ossoff's opponent, Rep. Mike Collins, in Georgia on Friday. "Somebody said, 'He's a good-looking man,' I don't think he's a good-looking man," Trump said. "I actually think Mike Collins is a good-looking man, and he's all man." He then moved on to Republicans' nominee for Georgia governor. "And I actually think that Rick Jackson is a very handsome, distinguished, beautiful-looking guy," Trump said. "But anyway." 9f90235753e9.text: The Supreme Court on Monday agreed to hear a challenge to the Reconstruction-era ban on distilling alcohol in private homes. Why it matters: Americans can legally brew beer or make wine at home, but making whiskey, vodka or other spirits can land them in federal prison. The Supreme Court could change that. Driving the booze: SCOTUS will review Department of Justice v. McNutt, an April ruling by the conservative 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that found the nearly 160-year-old home-distilling ban unconstitutional and an overreach of Congress' taxing power. Distilling in your home carries a penalty of up to five years in prison, a $10,000 fine or both. The 6th Circuit reached the opposite conclusion in a separate April ruling for Ream v. Department of the Treasury, arguing Congress can restrict distilling at home to protect federal alcohol tax collections. What they're saying: Advocates argue that Congress overstepped their powers by banning distilling in the home through a measure meant to prohibit fraud from commercial distillers, per the Associated Press . The government says Congress acted within its authority as the restriction was intended to stop producers from evading federal excise taxes, per AP. Lifting the ban, the government argues, could undermine Congress' authority to enforce federal tax laws. Friction point: Both appeals courts agreed Congress' taxing power alone doesn't authorize the ban. They split over whether it is a permissible way to collect liquor taxes under the Constitution's Necessary and Proper Clause. Reality check: You didn't hear this from us, but the practice of distilling hooch and moonshine still happens in the U.S. despite the federal prohibition . Some states, like West Virginia, allow some home distilling. But, much like marijuana, those state laws don't override federal law. Advocates hope the Supreme Court will strike down the federal ban and its associated criminal penalty. Why distilling drinks at home is banned Flashback: Congress banned distilling spirits in homes and connected properties in 1868, during the Reconstruction, as part of a crackdown on widespread tax evasion. The restrictions also cover certain premises where beer or wine is made. Yes, but: Federal law allows Americans to brew beer and make wine at home, but not distill spirits. Distilling spirits requires a process that gives people a more concentrated drink and can involve fire hazards and dangerous contamination risks. What happens if SCOTUS overturns the ban? What's next: Even if SCOTUS strikes down the ban, this doesn't mean people can start distilling automatically. Federal alcohol-production rules could limit what people could do at home. The government currently requires permits, registration and tax compliance for the production of distilled spirits. States could also impose their own bans, which would limit what people can make in their homes. The bottom line: SCOTUS could make it easier for Americans to produce their own liquor, but overturning the ban wouldn't necessarily mean anyone could legally set up a still in their backyard … yet.

Local curfews may come into force in French towns following a weekend of disorder.
Most of the protesters were peaceful in expressing their opposition to rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
But others - dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas - set fire to cars, shops and buildings.
The scale of the destruction - including to some iconic landmarks - has shocked many in a country used to street protests.
The damage in the capital city is extensive. Shop fronts have been broken and stores looted.
The iconic Place de la Republique was vandalised, too.
A yellow vest - representative of the movement which helped co-ordinate the weekend protests - was draped around the body of the Statue of the Republic, erected in 1883.
Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, took over parts of the capital and wreaked havoc.
Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people but police struggled to contain smaller groups of people roving around the city attack businesses.
The full extent of the damage did not become clear until dawn broke on Sunday.
Further south in Marseille, protesters broke into the city hall by using a metal fence as a battering ram.
A bust of Marianne - symbol of the French Republic - was damaged and knocked to the floor in Marseille as people ransacked the building.
City Mayor BenoÃ®t Payan was furious with the "almost total lack of control" by the security forces.
"The world's sixth largest power does not deserve this. The world is watching us, this morning we are the shame of Europe," he said.
In the city of Lyon, Mayor GrÃ©gory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office, housed in a 19th Century building, was "a tragedy".
Fire crews also battled a fire at Limoges town hall, which caused part of the building to collapse. Local officials said the town hall was "largely lost".
"A wild horde" had "deliberately" set fire to the 143-year-old building, said Maurice Barate, the prefect for the Haute-Vienne department.
French authorities have admitted they lost control of cities to the protesters.
Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez offered his resignation - which has been rejected.
Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu has given local mayors the power to introduce partial curfews in some parts of the country, which he says is designed to protect people and businesses.
But the French are holding their breath - in anticipation of another chapter in this protest next Saturday.
